 Dodger Point Lookout was restored in 2017 with the assistance of volunteers and grant funding from Washington's National Park Fund and the REI Foundation.

name: Evergreen Mountain Lookout
loc:
Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest 
                    Snohomish County, Washington
desc: Built in 1935 by the U.S. Forest Service, Evergreen Mountain is one of only two intact historic lookouts remaining on the old Snoqualmie National Forest. The 14' x 14' L-4 ground house also saw year-round use in World War II as an Aircraft Warning Service site. It has been adopted and restored by the Seattle Area Explorer Scout Search and Rescue Group with support from the Mountaineers and Quest School. Due to road washouts, it is now accessible only by a seven-mile trail. Materials were airlifted to the site by the 141st Army Reserve Aviation Battalion.

name: Fire Lookout Museum Lookout
loc: Spokane County, Washington
desc: The Fire Lookout Museum Lookout located in Spokane, WA is actually a combination of parts salvaged from seven L-6 lookouts that had been torn down. At one time, more than 200 of these 8' x 8' wood USFS-design cabs stood in the Pacific Northwest, now only three remain at their original locations. Some were constructed on top of log towers up to 99' tall. This restored structure on a 6' wood tower also includes lookout memorabilia. It is open by appointment with Ray Kresek.

name: First Butte Lookout
loc:
Okanogan National Forest 
                    Okanogan County, Washington
desc: Built by the Forest Service in 1938 and staffed year around in 1942 as a World War II Aircraft Warning Station, First Butte Lookout remains an active detection site. The 14' x 14' L-4 with catwalk sits atop a 28' timber tower.

name: Flagstaff Lookout
loc: Stevens County, Washington
desc: Flagstaff Lookout in northeastern Washington is one of the last active DNR lookouts in the state. The site was first used by the U.S. Forest Service in 1935 (Colville National Forest) and transferred to the Washington Department of Natural Resources in the late 1940s. The present 40' wooden tower with DNR flattop 14' x 14' cab with catwalk was constructed in 1971.

name: Flattop Mountain Lookout
loc:
Gifford Pinchot National Forest 
                    Skamania County, Washington
desc: Twice featured in National Geographic Magazine, Flattop Mountain Lookout in Washington's Gifford Pinchot National Forest has a stunning view of Mt. Adams.  The two story ground house with 12' x 12' cab featuring slanted solid glass windows, was to have been a prototype replacement for the standard U.S. Forest Service lookout in the Pacific Northwest, but the relatively mundane R-6 flattop design won out.  No longer in active use, and found recently to be located 40' across the boundary on state land, the lookout was almost removed to make way for a microwave tower.  A fast-track restoration initiative is underway in an attempt to save the historic structure.

name: Fosback Lookout
loc: Stevens County, Washington
desc: Fosback Lookout is located on private land overlooking the Little Pend Oreille River in northwestern Washington. It was originally built by the Washington Dept. of Natural Resources on Monumental Mountain near Colville in 1965, replacing a state tower dating to 1945. Staffed until the mid 1980s, the lookout was declared surplus. The 14' x 14' flattop DNR cab with catwalk on a 10' wood tower was sold in 1996 to FFLA member Rod Fosback who carefully moved it to his own woodland. Fosback Lookout is again ready for staffing, should fire conditions warrant, as a volunteer service to the community by the Fosback family.

name: Funk Mountain Lookout
loc:
Okanogan National Forest 
                    Okanogan County, Washington
desc: First established as a tree platform in 1914, Funk Mountain Lookout is one of the oldest in the Northwest still in existence. A ground L-5 cab was added in 1935 and replaced in 1943 by the current L-4 cab with catwalk on a 40' treated timber tower. Used sporadically for the past decade, it was returned to service by the Okanogan National Forest in 2000.

name: Goat Peak Lookout
loc:
Okanogan National Forest 
                    Okanogan County, Washington
desc: Constructed in 1923 by the old Chelan National Forest and staffed every year since, Goat Peak Lookout offers spectacular views of the Methow River valley and the North Cascades, an area with frequent lightning strikes. Reach by trail from Early Winters campground, the original D-6 cupola cabin was replaced in 1950 with the current L-4 with catwalk on a 15' timber tower.

name: Gobblers Knob Lookout
loc:
Mount Rainier National Park 
                    Pierce County, Washington
desc: Gobblers Knob Lookout to the southwest of Mt. Rainier is the closest to the peak of the four lookouts in the National Park and a popular hiking destination. Built in 1933, the two story frame NPS design structure with 14’x14’ live-in cab with catwalk has been restored and is also used by backcountry rangers as a standby detection site.

name: Granite Mountain Lookout
loc:
Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest 
                    King County, Washington
desc: This lookout has provided views of the Cascades since 1955. It replaced a previous 1924 lookout on the same site. It is staffed by volunteers from June through September each year.

name: Graves Mountain Lookout
loc:
Stevens County Park and Museum 
                    Stevens County, Washington
desc: One of the last classic L-4 cabs built (in 1955), Graves Mountain Lookout stood for 30 years in the Colville National Forest in northeastern Washington State. It replaced a 72' pole tower with L-6 cab and log cabin built by the U.S. Forest Service and the CCC in 1934. In 1985 the Stevens County Historical Society moved the lookout piece-by-piece to the Stevens County Park and Museum overlooking the Town of Colville. The faithfully-restored lookout is open to the public daily.

name: Green Mountain Lookout
loc:
Snoqualmie National Forest 
                    Snohomish County, Washington
desc: Green Mountain Lookout, in the Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, has not been actively used for fire detection in many years, but one would not know it. The structure, a classic L-4, 14- by 14-ft ground house once common in the Pacific Northwest, has been lovingly restored by the Friends of Green Mountain. The organization is one of the original volunteer groups to come forward and help maintain a lookout.

name: Heybrook Lookout
loc: Snohomish County, Washington
desc:
This wooden tower, approximately 63 feet high, is standard but its cab is unique. It looks like an R-6 flattop design, but it is not. The cab was designed by the Forest Products Lab in 1963 at the request of the USFS Region 6 engineers. They were looking for lightweight materials, including new wood products recently available but not yet used for lookout cab construction. Besides being lighter weight, the cab was to be prefabricated off site, then packed in bundles that could be delivered on site by helicopter. This a procedure similar to how the L-4 cabs of the 1930s were packaged to be delivered by mule train. Being a trial design, they elected to construct it at a location accessible by road. 
 For whatever reason, cost or maintenance, this design has not been used again.

name: Hidden Lake Peak Lookout
loc:
Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest 
                    Skagit County, Washington
desc: The gable roof L-4 groundhouse lookout built by the U.S. Forest Service atop Hidden Lake Peak in 1931 was staffed until 1958 when many lookouts in the north Cascades were closed. In 1961 Dr. Fred Darvill and the Skagit Alpine Club obtained a special use permit to restore and maintain the scenic historic structure which is popular with hikers.

name: High Rock Lookout
loc:
Gifford Pinchot National Forest 
                    Lewis County, Washington
desc:
Undoubtedly one of the most spectacular lookouts in America, High Rock is on the Gifford Pinchot National Forest just south of Mt. Ranier National Park. The 14' x 14' gable roof L-4 ground house with catwalk was built in 1929 and staffed the same year. It is perched on the edge of a 1200' sheer cliff. The historic site is carefully maintained by the Forest Service and is reached by a 1.6 mile trail which is usually free of snow by July 1. The NHLR certificate was presented at the Circle of Stewards meeting in June 2001 to Harry Cody, District Ranger and Bud Panco, longtime High Rock observer. 
 As of 2024, the tower was undergoing a restoration involving transporting the cabin off-site for repair.

name: Indian Mountain Lookout
loc:
Idaho Panhandle National Forests 
                    Pend Oreille County, Washington
desc: Indian Mountain Lookout has been staffed every season since the first tower was constructed in 1933. The current 40’ wooden tower (the second on the site) was built in 1953 and supports a 14’ x 14’ L-4 live-in cab with catwalk. When the Kaniksu National Forest had over a dozen active lookouts, Indian Mountain was ranked first for initial detection reports. Administered by the Priest Lake Ranger District, the lookout is located just west of the state line in Washington.

name: Kelly Butte Lookout
loc:
Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest 
                    King County, Washington
desc: The first lookout at Kelly Butte on the Snoqualmie National Forest was D-6 12'x12' cupola cabin build in 1926. In 1950 it was replaced by this 1932 14'x14' ground house with catwalk and staffed until the 1980s. Completely restored in 2011 with a new access trail, it is currently active as a fire lookout and staffed by trained volunteers.

name: Kloshe Nanitch Lookout
loc:
Olympic National Forest 
                    Clallam County, Washington
desc: The first lookout at Kloshe Nanitch on the Olympic National Forest was a D-6 wooden cupola groundhouse built in 1917. With the later addition of North Point Lookout, it was gradually phased out as a detection site. However, in 1996 the Forest Service rebuilt the historic cupola design, upgraded to current construction codes, as an interpretive site and recreation rental. The lookout is accessed from the USFS Snider Work Camp. Due to improvements to the access road, it is wheelchair accessible. The lookout offers spectacular views of Mt. Olympus, Lake Crescent and the Sol Duc River. It is located at the transition zone between the lower western hemlock forest and the high elevation silver fir so it has a beautiful diverse display of wildflowers. As of October 15, 2012, the lookout has now been removed. See link to article below.

name: Knowlton Knob Lookout
loc: Okanogan County, Washington
desc: Overlooking some of the driest flash fuels in Washington, Knowlton Knob was developed by the State Div. of Forestry in 1934 with a ground L-4 cab. In 1966 the present 40' timber tower with 14' x 14' DNR flat-gable was built. It was in service until 1997 when it went to emergency status.

name: Kresek Fire Tower
loc: Spokane County, Washington
desc: The Kresek Fire Tower located east of Spokane is a 50' Aermotor tower with a 7' x 7' metal cab. It was originally erected on Spades Mountain on the Coeur d'Alene National Forest in 1941. In 1964 the tower was given to the Idaho Dept. of Lands and moved to Long Mountain near Sand Point. Declared surplus, it was moved again to its present location on 30 acres by Dave Kresek (Ray's son). It can be visited with prior appointment through the Fire Lookout Museum.

name: Leecher Mountain Lookout
loc:
Okanogan National Forest 
                    Okanogan County, Washington
desc: The first lookout on Leecher Mountain was a 1920 tree top crow's nest which is still there. In 1921 a Sears windmill tower with 6'x6' cab was constructed, and a ground house living quarters added in 1922. In 1941 a live-in L-4 on an 11' timber tower was built and the windmill tower moved to the Twisp Smokejumper Base for use as a training loft.  The present L-4 on a 41' tower was moved there from Chiliwist in 1954. The lookout has been recently renovated.

name: Lookout Mountain Lookout
loc:
Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest 
                    Skagit County, Washington
desc: The first lookout on the Mt. Baker National Forest was a cathedral style cupola erected on Lookout Mountain in the remote North Cascades in 1928.   The present 15’x15’ R-6 flat roof live-in cab was constructed by in 1967 and is a popular hiker destination with great views.

name: Lookout Mountain Lookout
loc:
Okanogan National Forest 
                    Okanogan County, Washington
desc:
Lookout Mountain has served as a fire detection site since at least 1911. 
 With the highest number of first fire reports in the Methow Valley, Lookout Mountain Lookout was placed in standby status by the Okanogan National Forest in 1998. 
 Established as a camp in 1916, a log cupola was built in 1931. The present classic 14' x 14' L-4 with catwalk on a 25' timber tower was constructed in 1937. Lookout Mountain served as an Aircraft Warning Service site during World War II. 
 The cabin was repainted as a volunteer project in June 2022.

name: Lookout Point Lookout
loc: Spokane County, Washington
desc: The Lookout Point Lookout is located just north of Spokane, WA overlooking a high fire-prone urban/wildland interface. The 40' wooden tower with DNR flattop 14' x 14' cab with catwalk was first constructed on Mica Peak near the Idaho border. In 1956 it was moved to its present site and staffed until 1995.

name: Miners Ridge Lookout
loc:
Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest 
                    Snohomish County, Washington
desc: One of Washington’s most remote and scenic lookouts, Miners Ridge is located within the Glacier Peak Wilderness on the Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest. Reached only by a 12 mile hiking trail, the 20’ wooden tower with a L-4 1 4x 14’ live-in cab with catwalk was constructed in 1953. It is the third on the site, the first being a cedar shake cabin, and the second a similar 20’ tower. The lookout has been active for 65 years.

name: Mount Adams Lookout
loc:
Gifford Pinchot National Forest 
                    Yakima County, Washington
desc: This 12'x12' wood frame D-6 cupola ground cabin with 1/4 size second story cupola was built by the U.S. Forest Service in 1918. One of the hardest to reach lookouts in the U.S., materials were packed up the mountain by mules to 4 miles below the summit, then hauled by four men to the summit using a deadman/rope technique. The structure was in service from 1921 to 1924 as a fire lookout. In 1932, miners began extracting pure sulfur from the volcano's summit vent, and lived in the cabin. Two lean-to additions were tacked onto the original cabin for their use during the next decade. The entire building has been entombed in the summit glacier since mid-20th century and only becomes visible for a few weeks in very dry summers.

name: Mount Bonaparte Lookout
loc:
Okanogan National Forest 
                    Okanogan County, Washington
desc: Mt. Bonaparte on the Okanogan National Forest in north central Washington may have been used as early as 1906 as a tent camp lookout. The first 12' x 12' flat-hewn tapered wall groundhouse with tower was constructed in 1914 and the house portion remains today as a storage building. The present 15' x 15' R-6 flattop cab and catwalk on a 20' timber tower was built in 1963 and remains in active service.

name: Mount Constitution Lookout
loc:
Moran State Park 
                    San Juan County, Washington
admin: Washington State Parks and Recreation Commission
desc: Mt. Constitution is the only lookout in the San Juan Islands of Puget Sound in Washington. The architectural inspiration for the five story stone tower came from the ancient watch towers of the Caucasus Mountains in Europe. Built by the CCC in 1937, it was staffed by the Division of Forestry (now DNR) until 1967, when the more than 10,000 annual visitors forced the construction of a second more isolated lookout tower used solely for detection. The replacement tower is now gone, and the stone tower is maintained by the State Parks Commission.

name: Mount Fremont Lookout
loc:
Mount Rainier National Park 
                    Pierce County, Washington
desc: Constructed by the National Park Service in 1934, Mount Fremont Lookout is located at the end of a high, treeless ridge with outstanding views of Mt. Rainier.  The two story frame building with 14’x14’ live-in cab with catwalk is reached by a scenic trail and used by backcountry park rangers and was recently restored.

name: Mount Pilchuck Lookout
loc:
Mount Pilchuck State Park 
                    Snohomish County, Washington
admin: Washington State Parks and Recreation Commission
desc: Mount Pilchuck Lookout has been a U.S. Forest Service lookout since 1921. The present wooden L4 14x14’ groundhouse was built in 1943 and staffed until 1957. The site was transferred to the Washington State Parks and Recreation Commission and in 1989 that agency cooperated in a reconstruction of the lookout by the Everett Branch of The Mountaineers. Reached only by trail, it is used as an interpretive site.

name: Mount Spokane Vista House Lookout
loc: Spokane County, Washington
admin: Washington State Parks and Recreation Commission
desc: The first of five lookout structures on Mt. Spokane, Washington was built in 1933 by contractor E.O. Fieldstad using native stone found on the summit. The two-story stone vista house has a second story dormer on the north to be used as a fire lookout. In 1948 a 85’ wooden live-in tower was constructed, but it collapsed the first winter with an overload of ice. A shorter 45’ tower was built in 1959, to be replaced 13 years later with a 40’ tower. In 1979 the present 40’ tower was built and is still in service. The stone lookout is owned by the State Parks Commission. The towers belong to the Department of Natural Resources.

name: North Mountain Lookout
loc:
Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest 
                    Skagit County, Washington

name: North Twentymile Peak Lookout
loc:
Okanogan National Forest 
                    Okanogan County, Washington
desc:
The first lookout, a log cabin, was established on North Twentymile Peak on the Okanogan National Forest in 1920. A D-6 cupola lookout was constructed in 1923. Now used for storage, it is one of only nine remaining of more than 200 that were built in the Northwest. 
 In 1947 a 30' timber tower with a 14' x 14' hip roof L-4 cab with catwalk was erected. Last staffed in 1988, it is now maintained as an emergency lookout.

name: Oregon Butte Lookout
loc:
Umatilla National Forest 
                    Columbia County, Washington
desc: At one time there were 200 gable-roof L-4 lookouts throughout the Northwest (pre-1933), and now fewer than 15 remain. Built in 1931, Oregon Butte Lookout on the Umatilla National Forest in southeastern Washington is one of them. Accessible only by trail, it is located within the Wenaha-Tucannon Wilderness and was in active status until 1972. In 1980 the structure was restored and has since been regularly staffed.

name: Park Butte Lookout
loc:
Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest 
                    Whatcom County, Washington
desc: Sitting on a ridge above timberline on the southern flank of Mt. Baker is Park Butte Lookout. The 14'x14' live-in L-4 with catwalk was constructed by the Forest Service in 1932 and was in service until 1961. Since then the Skagit Alpine Club has maintained it. When Mt. Baker threatened to erupt in the 1970s, the restored lookout served as an observatory for volcano monitors. It is also listed on the National Register of Historic Places.

name: Puyallup Ridge Lookout
loc: Pierce County, Washington
desc: If awesome views were the criteria for registration, the Puyallup Ridge Lookout would be a contender for the head of the list. The evening alpen glow from Mt. Rainier is spectacular. Built by the Washington Department of Natural Resources in 1964, it may be the last new detection site established in the state. Its service was short lived, having been phased out in the 1970s. The 30’ wooden tower supports a 14’ x 14’ live-in flattop cab with catwalk. Access to the structure, which is in need of restoration, is by special road permit through private timberlands (Plum Creek Timber Co. and Champion International).

name: Pyramid Mountain Lookout
loc:
Olympic National Park 
                    Challam County, Washington
desc: Pyramid Mountain Lookout features a custom-designed cabin with an attached storage shed. It was built specifically to be used to spot enemy aircraft during World War II in 1942. Once the war was over, it was abandoned and decommissioned. It is still standing as of July 2015.

name: Red Mountain Lookout
loc:
Gifford Pinchot National Forest 
                    Skamania County, Washington
desc: The R-6 wooden flattop 15' x 15' cab on a 10' timber tower located on nearby Red Mountain in the Gifford Pinchot National Forest is an example of the design that replaced the L-4 lookouts. Built in 1959, it is the fourth lookout on the site. During 1942-43 Red Mountain -- often subject to severe weather -- was staffed 24 hours a day as an Aircraft Warning Station before the days of radar. The CCC garage, which was renovated as a living quarters, is still there.

name: Red Top Lookout
loc:
Wenatchee National Forest 
                    Kittitas County, Washington
desc:
On August 26,1997, a group of lookout enthusiasts gathered at Red Top Lookout on the Wentachee National Forest in Washington to dedicate the lookout on the National Historic Lookout Register. The event capped a two-year restoration effort by the Friends of Red Top Mountain and the Cle Elum Ranger District. 
 The L-4 wooden cab with catwalk on a 10’ timber tower had been battered by 45 years of weather and was beginning to show it. It replaced a D-6 cupola ground house built in 1928. The lookout is now back in active service both for fire detection and a public information site for the 350 million year-old jasper geodes which are found nearby.

name: Salmo Mountain Lookout
loc:
Colville National Forest 
                    Pend Oreille County, Washington
desc: Salmo Mountain in the Colville National Forest is in the northeastern corner of Washington (three miles west of the Idaho line and two miles south of the Canadian border). It has been the site of four lookouts -- a pole tower with platform, a log cabin, a 30’ L-4 live-in, and the present 15’x 15’ R-6 flattop with catwalk on 10’ wooden tower built in 1964. The lookout was last staffed in 1976.

name: Shriner Peak Lookout
loc:
Mt. Rainier National Park 
                    Pierce County, Washington
desc: Located on one of the most picturesque sites, Shriner Peak Lookout has a stunning view of Mount Rainier. The two-story wooden frame structure with 14’x 14’ cab and catwalk is representative of a standard National Park Service design of the 1930s. The oldest of four lookouts remaining in the Park, it has been restored following the original plans. It is still used in critical fire weather.

name: Slate Peak Lookout
loc:
Okanogan National Forest 
                    Okanogan County, Washington
desc: Located at the end of the highest road in Washington, Slate Peak Lookout was first constructed as a gable roof cupola in 1924. In 1954 an L-4 ground cab was moved intact from Leecher Mountain, and two years later the Air Force removed 40' from the summit (including the lookout) for a radar station that was never built. The lookout was put on a 41' tower. With stunning views of the North Cascades, it is maintained for emergency use.

name: Sourdough Mountain Lookout
loc:
North Cascades National Park 
                    Whatcom County, Washington
desc: Sourdough Mountain lookout was built on the Mt. Baker National Forest in 1933 and transferred to the National Park Service when the North Cascades National Park was created by Congress in 1967. The L-4 groundhouse replaced a cupola lookout dating to 1917. A popular hiking destination, the lookout continues in active service.

name: South Baldy Lookout
loc:
Colville National Forest 
                    Pend Oreille County, Washington
desc: There are some places in the U.S. that receive more than their share of winter, and South Baldy Lookout is one of them. Located in the Colville National Forest in northeastern Washington, the 14’x14’ R-6 flatroof atop a 41’ wooden tower was constructed in 1960 and is the fourth lookout to occupy the site. The first was a one-room log cabin built in 1909, which was replaced by another log cabin in 1915 and a cupola lookout in 1929.

name: Steliko Lookout
loc:
Wenatchee National Forest 
                    Chelan County, Washington

name: Stranger Mountain Lookout
loc: Stevens County, Washington
desc:
No stranger to lookouts, Stensgar Mountain was first used for fire detection in 1930 when a platform tower and cabin were built by the Washington Division of Forestry. Somewhere over the years Stensgar morphed into Stranger Mountain Lookout, and no less than four structures have occupied the site. The original platform tower was replaced by a 50' pole tower with L-6 cab in 1936. That in turn was replaced by DNR flattop live-in cab with catwalk on a 40' wooden tower in 1959 which only 24 years later was replaced with the current updated DNR flattop cab on a 42' wooden tower in 1983.
 

 
Additional information courtesy of Ray Kresek:  "Stranger ("Stensgar" on most maps), a DNR live-in lookout tower near Chewelah, WA was successfully moved intact 30 miles from atop the mountain to the Colville fairgrounds last month without as much as a broken window, after two years of negotiations with the DNR.  It had to be removed from the mountain.  In a dream-come-true fashion, Stevens County Fair manager Lori Matlock was able to fit the use of nearly a dozen pieces of donated heavy machinery into a fine tuned clockwork that made it all happen.  A boom crane, on the mountaintop to install a new Homeland Security facility, was able to pluck the entire cab and catwalk off its 40' wooden tower.  A large DNR flatbed truck received it for the first leg of the trip.  A couple miles down the steep, narrow road off the summit, a larger truck and lowboy trailer, loaned by a local logging contractor, hauled the twenty foot wide load via all of the backroads into downtown Colville.  Waiting at the fairgrounds were 2 giant forklifts from a local sawmill, to gently set it on the ground.  The tower's original legs were re-set on concrete piers, cut off at 13';  and a few days later there just happened to be another construction crane available at 4pm.  It took but a few minutes, and the Stranger Lookout tower was up in the air again.  Total cost:  $25.  The rest was all donated."

name: Sugarloaf Mountain Lookout
loc:
Wenatchee National Forest 
                    Chelan County, Washington
desc:
One of the earliest established lookouts (1914) in what was then the Chelan National Forest, Sugarloaf Mountain Lookout has been staffed every summer since and oversees some of the fastest burning forest fuels in Washington. 
 The 1933-vintage L-4 cab was moved to the site in 1949, replacing a cupola cabin. The lookout was threatened by the 120,000 acre Entiat Fire in 1970, and again in 1994 by the 180,000 acre Tyee-Hatchery Fire. The structure was saved by a Ft. Lewis fire crew, but the outhouse and garage were burned.

name: Sullivan Mountain Lookout
loc:
Colville National Forest 
                    Pend Oreille County, Washington
desc: Three lookouts have graced Sullivan Mountain. The first was built in 1926 and featured a cupola cabin. It was replaced in 1935 by a 20-foot pole tower with an L-4 cab. The present 20-foot treated timber tower was built in 1959 and borders the Salmo-Priest Wilderness Area. Last used in the 1970s, it is presently abandoned with the upper stairs removed to limit access.

name: Suntop Lookout
loc:
Snoqualmie National Forest 
                    Pierce County, Washington
desc:
Suntop Lookout is located 15 miles northeast of Mt. Rainier, Washington within the Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest. Built in 1932, it is one of only two L-4 ground house structures remaining on the old Snoqualmie National Forest. It was used as an Aircraft Warning site in World War II and the road to it was not completed until 1956. Located in a high alpine meadow with excellent view of Winthrop Glacier, the lookout is a popular tourist destination and is staffed by volunteers. 
 As of 2025, the lookout has been renovated inside to reflect fire equipment from 1960s, including some old USFS artifacts such as a crank phone, old helmet, and wire insulators. Other recent efforts added a trail from the parking area, deck around the lookout and a ramp from the south side that enables lookout to be reached by disabled persons.

name: Table Rock Lookout
loc:
Walla Walla Ranger District, Umatilla National Forest 
                    Columbia County, Washington

name: Thorp Mountain Lookout
loc:
Wenatchee National Forest 
                    Kittitas County, Washington
desc: This original 71-year-old lookout on Thorp Mountain is one of the gems of the north central Cascades. Built in 1930 on the Wenatchee National Forest, the 14' x 14' L-4 gable groundhouse has been in service ever since. The lookout was completely refurbished in the summer of 2007 and is now being staffed seven days a week.

name: Three Fingers Lookout
loc:
Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest 
                    Snohomish County, Washington
desc: When Darrington District Ranger Harold J. Engles and trail foreman Harry Bedel decided to construct a lookout in 1931, they picked a high rock spire overlooking thousands acres of old-growth timber on the Snoqualmie National Forest to the east of Seattle, Washington. All the materials had to be lifted the last 1,000 feet via a windlass made from telephone wire. Although the Three Fingers Lookout was staffed for only ten years and abandoned in 1943, the daughter of the last observer led the project to restore the 14 x 14 L-4 groundhouse in 1986. Efforts to keep the building were encouraged by retired Ranger Engles who lived to see the project completed before his passing in August, 1993.

name: Timber Mountain Lookout
loc:
Colville National Forest 
                    Pend Oreille County, Washington
desc: The first lookout on Timber Mountain in the ColviIle National Forest in northeastern Washington was a 50’ pole tower with a L-4 cab atop. The existing 41’ treated timber tower, featuring an R-6 flattop live-in cab and a catwalk was built in 1959 and staffed until 1981. The lookout fell into disrepair until the Pend Oreille Anthropological Society and the U.S. Forest Service began restoration in 1995 as a "Passport in Time” project.

name: Tower Mountain Lookout
loc: Stevens County, Washington
desc: Located in the Spokane Indian Reservation, this is 53-foot steel live-in tower was built in 1975. It is staffed every summer. It is the first tower at this site. Signs in route indicate the location as Lookout Mountain but a sign on the tower says Tower Mountain. A nearby hillside is higher and the obvious high point.

name: Tunk Mountain Lookout
loc: Okanogan County, Washington
desc: Tunk Mountain Lookout was built by the U.S. Forest Service on the Okanogan National Forest is 1933. It was an L-4 cab on a 40’ pole tower. In the 1950’s the Washington Dept. of Natural Resources took over the tower and in 1966 replaced it was the current 40’ timber tower with a 14’x14’ WDNR cab with cat walk. Declared surplus in the 1990s, it was purchased by W.R. Morrison and kept on site with a special use permit. In 2004 the lookout was purchased by American Resources and was again staffed for a month in 2005 during reconstruction of nearby Bonaparte Lookout.

name: Tyee Mountain Lookout
loc:
Wenatchee National Forest 
                    Chelan County, Washington
desc:
The Tyee Mountain Lookout made national headlines in the summer of 1994 when it reported the devastating Tyee Fire as a small lightning strike. The fire burned for weeks (180,000 acres) and the damage included 22 homes and the Tyee outhouse. The hip-roof L-4 14’ x 14’ groundhouse with catwalk was built in 1952 by the Wenatchee Nat. Forest.
 

 
On Feb. 8, 2013, Ken Jones reported: "I have been advised by the Entiat RD Fire Mgmt Officer that Tyee LO can not be used, even by volunteers, because the lightning protection system is apparently not up to code. Cost to upgrade the system would be several thousand dollars, which isn’t in their budgets. Therefore, there are no plans to utilize Tyee in the foreseeable future. Considering all the repair and maintenance work that has been done so far, this is a real shame."

name: Watch Mountain Lookout
loc:
Gifford Pinchot National Forest 
                    Lewis County, Washington
desc: There have been a number of lookouts above the north side of the Cowlitz valley in the Gifford Pinchot National Forest, but only one remains. The first lookout at Watch Mountain built by the state to protect private land was an L-4 cab. In 1940 a cabin was added. The present 14’x14 DNR flattop cab with catwalk was built on the western end of the ridge in 1963. Used primarily as an electronic facility, the land has been acquired by the Forest Service.

name: Winchester Mountain Lookout
loc:
Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest 
                    Whatcom County, Washington
desc: Located in a subalpine setting within the Mt. Baker Wilderness and with views of Mt. Baker, Mt. Shuksan and the Picket Range, Winchester Mountain Lookout is a popular destination with hikers. The 14x14’ L-4 ground house was built in 1935 and staffed until 1966. It fell into disrepair but in 1982 the Mt. Baker Club obtained a special use permit to restore and maintain the structure which is open to the public.

name: Jumpoff Lookout
loc:
Wenachee National Forest 
                    Yakima County, Washington
admin: US Forest Service - Wenachee National Forest
desc:
Also known as 'Jumpoff Joe' Lookout. The first structure developed about 1923 with a D-6 cupola cabin. Between 1958 and 1961, the current R-6 flat top ground cabin replaced it. The lookout has been used sporadically since the 1960s on an emergency basis.   
  Mike Hiler and “Friends of Jumpoff” began that summer to stabilize the lookout. Since then, the roof covering was repaired and is now water tight, shutters were repaired and replaced and the cabin was cleaned and efforts are made to keep the structure tidy and hospitable.   
  Over the next several years, the shutters got back on with plexiglass openings so visitors won’t pull them off to see inside. The water damaged floor was repaired, cabinets were repaired.   
  Mike Hiler helped drive this and he was the lookout on Jumpoff during 1969 to 1973.

name: Armstrong Mountain Lookout
loc:
Colville Indian Reservation 
                    Okanogan County, Washington
desc:
The 100′ Aermotor steel tower is the original and only lookout on the summit, built in 1939. The site has been abandoned since 1952 and the ground cabin living quarters as well as the roof of the lookout have disappeared. 
 Aermotor steel towers were built by the Aermotor Company of Chicago, IL, founded in 1888. In the 1920s, a few steel towers started showing up in the Pacific Northwest and in the 1930s, several more were built predominantly east of the Cascades. -trailchick.com

name: Clearwater Lookout
loc:
Umatilla National Forest 
                    Garfield County, Washington
admin: US Forest Service - Umatilla National Forest
desc:
The current MC-39 steel tower was built in 1933 by a Civilian Conservation Corps camp who spent several months in the Asotin District. The tower is 90′ tall according to a Umatilla National Forest Inventory, 94′ tall according to Ray Kresek, and 82′ tall according to other sources. No matter the exact height, it’s a darn cool steel tower! 
 The single story cabin at the base of the lookout was built two years later in 1935, also by the Civilian Conservation Corps and the cabin is available for nighly rentals through the Umatilla National Forest. 
 In August of 2021, the Clearwater Lookout, thanks to its height, was used as a temporary repeater site on the Lick Creek (Dry Gulch) fire in southeast Washington. The tower remains available for emergencies. 
 Aermotor steel towers were built by the Aermotor Company of Chicago, IL, founded in 1888. In the 1920s, a few steel towers started showing up in the Pacific Northwest and in the 1930s, several more were built predominantly east of the Cascades.

name: Cody Butte Lookout
loc:
Colville Indian Reservation 
                    Ferry County, Washington
desc:
Built in 1931, this 45' steel Aermotor tower has been staffed most summers. 
 It is unknown if this is the original frame cabin living quarters from that time. 
 -firelookouts.com

name: Cornell Butte Lookout
loc:
Okanogan National Forest 
                    Okanogan County, Washington
admin: US Forest Service - Okanogan National Forest
desc:
This 42′ all steel lookout was built in 1958, then purchased by a private party in 1996 and slated for removal.   
  According to the Forest Service, Cornell hasn’t been used regularly since 1971, but no funding exists for removing the tower, which has been heavily damaged and vandalized.   
  The North Star Fire in September 2015 burned the surrounding area, sending embers into Cornell’s cab that caught some of the floor boards on fire. The bottom stairs were removed for visitor safety.

name: Franson Peak Lookout
loc:
Washington State Forest Land 
                    Ferry County, Washington
desc:
Franson Peak was developed in 1934 with an L-5 cab, then a 15′ treated timber tower with L-4 cab replaced it in the 1950s. That L-4 cab was moved to the Molson Museum when the current structure.  
  A 15′ tower with DNR live-in cab, was built in 1986. Franson was last staffed in 1995 and shares space with a few communications towers at the summit.  
 Franson Peak served as an Aircraft Warning Service site from March to October 1942.

name: Gold Mountain Lookout
loc:
Colville Indian Reservation 
                    Ferry County, Washington
admin: US Forest Service - Colville National Forest
desc:
Gold Mountain started as a lookout camp in 1914, then an L-4 cab was built in 1938. In 1963, a 20′ wooden tower with R-6 flat top cab was built and then the present 100′ steel tower was constructed in 1986. 
 Gold Mountain is the tallest live-in tower in Washington state and is staffed every summer. 
 In 1943 it was reported by the Colville Examiner that many teachers were employed as fire lookouts across the Colville National Forest, including Mr. and Mrs. Floyd Tolleson, from Colville on Gold mountain.

name: Goodman Hill Lookout
loc:
Joint Base Lewis-McChord 
                    Pierce County, Washington
admin: Department of Natural Resources - Washington State Division of Forestry
desc:
This 100' wooden tower with 8x8' cab, built in 1955, has been abandoned since 1970. Located on the Joint Base Lewis-McChord, the structure has been threatened with demolition in recent years. 
 Access is restricted but possible by contacting the base.

name: Johnny George Mountain Lookout
loc:
Colville Indian Reservation 
                    Ferry County, Washington
admin: US Forest Service - Colville National Forest
desc:
This 100′ steel Aermotor tower, built in 1938 by the Civilian Conservation Corps, is the only tower ever on the site, and is staffed sporadically during the summer. Aermotor steel towers were built by the Aermotor Company of Chicago, IL, founded in 1888. In the 1920s, a few steel towers started showing up in the Pacific Northwest and in the 1930s, several more were built predominantly east of the Cascades. 
 In 1943 the Colville Examiner reported that many teachers were staffing fire lookouts across the Colville National Forest, including Mr. and Mrs. Walter Peterson from Malott on Johnny George. 
 A plaque at nearby Keller Butte commemorates fire lookout Ramona Peone, who spent 40+ years manning both Johnny George and Keller Butte lookouts. Her    obituary from 2015 in the Grand Coulee Star    talks of the details of her fire lookout life.

name: Keller Butte Lookout
loc:
Colville Indian Reservation 
                    Ferry County, Washington
desc:
A camp lookout was established at Keller Butte in 1932. In 1933, the first Civilian Conservation Corp camp for the district was opened with 75 men who worked on building the Cache Creek Road, a new road from Cache Creek summit to Park City, and a road from the summit to the new lookout tour atop Keller Butte. In 1935, an 80′ 3-legged wooden tower with 7×7 cab and accompanying L-4 ground house for living quarters was constructed. 
 The Colville Examiner in 1943 reported that many teachers were staffing lookouts on the Colville National Forest and Miss Josephine Volger was stationed on Keller. The present 67′ steel live-in tower, built in 1964, is staffed every summer. 
 A plaque at Keller Butte commemorates fire lookout Ramona Peone, who spent 40+ years manning both Johnny George and Keller Butte lookouts. Her    obituary from 2015 in the Grand Coulee Star    talks of the details of her fire lookout life. 
 The Chuweah Creek fire, started July 12, 2021 by lightning, burned across the north shore of Buffalo Lake and across Keller Butte Road north of the lookout. The fire was eventually contained at 36,000+ acres.

name: Lorena Butte Lookout
loc:
Private Land 
                    Klickitat County, Washington
desc:
The first known structure on Lorena Butte was an L-4 cab in 1937. In 1953, the owner of Lorena Butte, Irving Bath, leased his land to Washington DNR and the following year, in 1954 a DNR cab was built atop an 8′ rock formation. The site replaced nearby Simcoe Butte. 
 In 1974, the current DNR live-in cab was built atop a 10′ concrete slab and last staffed in 1993. In 2006, the cab was moved from the summit southwest down the ridge due to local mining operations. The concrete slab base built in 1974 remained. The lookout has occasionally been staffed in the new location during high fire danger times, most notably in July 2013 when a lightning storm swept across the area. 
 Lorena is now available for nightly rentals through the private land owners,    Lefever Holbrook Ranch .

name: Meadow Butte Lookout
loc:
Washington State Lands 
                    Klickitat County, Washington
admin: Washington Department of Natural Resources - Division of Forestry
desc:
This tiny crows nest cab was constructed in the early 1940s primary to watch over railroad logging operations.   
  Built atop an 86′ pine tree, the site utilized a tent cabin for living quarters. The Division of Forestry took ownership of the lookout in 1944, outfitting it with a fire finder and radio.   
  The lookout was abandoned in 1958 but the structure still remains.

name: Mebee Pass Lookout
loc:
Okanogan National Forest 
                    Skagit County, Washington
admin: US Forest Service - Okanogan National Forest
desc:
The Mebee Pass fire lookout is believed to be the last remaining L-5 of its kind. These tiny 10′ x 10′ structures were prefabricated and typically hauled into a secondary lookout site by horse or mule by the US Forest Service and temporarily staffed during times of high fire danger. 
 Two members of the Forest Fire Lookout Association hiked up to Mebee in 2002 and found the structure severely neglected and barely standing. A helicopter was used to bring in materials to do emergency repairs. 
 John Scurlock, a well-known talented aerial photographer based in the North Cascades, photographed Mebee on flights in 2006 and 2008. During a flight in 2013 he became concerned that the frail lookout wouldn’t last much longer and spearheaded a restoration effort as well as the creation of the “Friends of Mebee Pass Fire Lookout” organization. 
 In 2013, Scurlock partnered with several volunteers and the Methow Valley District Ranger Mike Liu to clear the neglected trail to Mebee to begin restoration efforts. The crew sawed through hundreds of fallen trees and rigged a rather treacherous log crossing across Granite Creek, where a bridge has been out for years. It took them much of the summer of 2013 to clear the trail. With $3,000 of donations in the bank, the crew was able to repair the foundation, replace the roof, repair deteriorated walls, and install a lightning rod. Hi Line helicopters of Darrington assisted in flying in 1,100 pounds of equipment that included lumber, siding, posts, crew supplies, and specially ordered Alaskan yellow cedar shingles. 
 Scurlock and crew were attentive to historical detail to maintain the structure’s integrity. Their herculean efforts saved this wonderful historical structure for generations to come. Another round of work parties to install windows, shutters, and a proper door are in the early planning stages for possibly 2022.

name: Monument 83 Lookout
loc:
Okanogan National Forest 
                    Okanogan County, Washington
admin: US Forest Service - Okanogan National Forest
desc:
Monument 83, also known as Holdover Peak, is located on the US-Canadian border and was first established in the 1920s as a camp with tree platform. In 1930, a log cabin cupola was constructed and celebrated as the northernmost lookout in the United States until surveys later determined it to be on Canadian soil. The cupola is now British Columbia’s southernmost lookout. In 1953 the United States built a 30′ treated timber L-4 tower on the US side of the border, reinstating Monument 83 as the northernmost lookout in both Washington State and the US. The lookouts were last used in the 1970s and both structures remain intact. 
 The name “Monument 83” is important for positioning the site along its place on the border, which is 83 miles from mile zero at Peace Arch Park in Surrey B.C.. From the summit it’s possible to see the United States-Canada Border Slash, a 20-foot-wide clearcut running the length of the border. Check out    Atlas Obscura    for some interesting trivia and tidbits about the Border Slash. 
 Another bonus on Monument 83 is a carved wooden gravestone bearing the inscription: “Pasayten Pete, shot by L.E. Lael, 26-8-61”. It’s been said that Pasayten Pete was a beloved pack mule. 
 Monument 83 was an Aircraft Warning Service site from July to September 1942.

name: Moses Mountain Lookout
loc:
Colville Indian Reservation 
                    Okanogan County, Washington
desc:
Moses Mountain was established as a lookout in 1914 with a crows nest tree platform and cabin. In 1923, a 30′ pole tower and cab replaced the tree, then a 35′ steel tower was constructed in 1930. 
 The current 123′ Aermotor steel tower was built in 1938 and is the tallest lookout tower in the Pacific Northwest. Aermotor steel towers were built by the Aermotor Company of Chicago, IL, founded in 1888. In the 1920s, a few steel towers started showing up in the Pacific Northwest and in the 1930s, several more were built predominantly east of the Cascades. 
 Moses was abandoned in the mid-1980s and evidence suggests that the 1930 tower was moved to    Grizzly Mountain    in 1941.

name: North Point Lookout
loc:
Olympic National Forest 
                    Clallam County, Washington
admin: US Forest Service - Olympic National Forest
desc:
The North Point L-4 lookout cab was built in 1939, used for several years, then sporadically in the 50s before being abandoned in 1969. 
 The lookout has since been converted into a communication tower, but it’s still considered a standing structure in its original location. 
 It was believed that North Point was initial a patrol point for the nearby Kloshe Nanich site, but with its higher and more favorable location, likely replaced Kloshe Nanich all together.

name: Omak Mountain Lookout
loc:
Colville Indian Reservation 
                    Okanogan County, Washington
desc:
An L-4 cab lookout was first constructed on the summit of Omak Mountain in 1935 by the Civilian Conservation Corps. 
 In 1943 it was reported in the Colville Examiner that many teachers were employed as fire lookouts that summer across the Colville National Forest, including Miss Rachel Butte from Chewelah Junior High on Omak Mountain. 
 The L-4 was replaced in 1968 by a 20′ timber tower with R-6 flat cab, then again in 1986 with the present 53′ all-steel live in tower that is still staffed in summer. 
   Lookout added to NHLR as a National Lookout Register listing until it reaches 50 years of age.

name: Quartz Mountain Lookout
loc:
Mount Spokane State Park 
                    Spokane County, Washington
admin: Washington State Parks Dept - Mount Spokane State Park
desc:
The existing lookout structure on Quartz Mountain was originally built on the summit of Mount Spokane in 1979 by the Washington Department of Natural Resources. It sat 40′ high and was used for fire spotting until it was permanently decommissioned in 1994. 
 Eventually the DNR gave up on costly ongoing repairs and the lookout was destined for demolition until Park staff and the Advisory Committee requested that it be given to the Park. 
 In June of 2001, crews scrapped the tower and the 9,000 pound cabin was lifted with a crane and moved by truck to the Mount Spokane State Park ranger’s residence, where it would sit while paperwork and permits were processed. 
 Finally in late August of 2004, a state parks maintenance crew made the old road to Quartz passable for heavy trucks, poured 4 concrete pillars, and stretched the limits of a boom crane moving the existing cab atop its new 10′ tower on Quartz Mountain. 
 In 2005, the lookout joined a    rental program    and can be reserved from June-September each year for about $100/night.

name: Satus Peak Lookout
loc:
Yakima Indian Agency 
                    Yakima County, Washington
desc:
Satus Peak is known for severe wind and over a different structures have been blown away or severely damaged by wind. In fact, this area is known to the Yakama as The Place Where the Wind Lives. 
 Numerous structures have been on the summit, starting with a cabin in 1920, a 10’x10′ cab in 1933, another cab in 1957, a heavy timber and frame cab in 1960, then a steel and wooden cab on 4′ concrete pillars in 1967. A lookout staffing the structure in 1967 told a story of cowering behind the firefinder during a windstorm that blew out the windows and caved in a wall. 
 The present steel structure was built in 1976 on a 2-story concrete foundation. It is constructed of reinforced iron beams and walls with steel-framed triple strength Thermopane windows. The lookout at Satus is staffed every season though the Yakama National Fire Management team says that finding lookouts is very difficult.

name: Signal Peak Lookout
loc:
Yakima Indian Agency 
                    Yakima County
desc:
Signal’s first fire lookout in 1920 was a pole tower with tent camp, later replaced in 1935 by a 3-legged 55′ wooden tower with 8’x8′ cab and ground house with living quarters. 
 The current 68′ Aermotor tower was moved in 1964 from nearby Panther Creek. Aermotor steel towers were built by the Aermotor Company of Chicago, IL, founded in 1888. In the 1920s, a few steel towers started showing up in the Pacific Northwest and in the 1930s, several more were built predominantly east of the Cascades. 
 Curiously, the lookout has no guy wires and one of our Yakama tour guides joked that as a child, he and his friends would climb the lookout and rock it back and forth. He also told us a story of a lookout locking herself in the ground house because of a Bigfoot that had come up the road.

name: Strawberry Mountain Lookout
loc:
Colville Indian Reservation 
                    Okanogan County, Washington
desc: The existing 54′ steel International Derrick tower was built in 1936 and had an accompanying L-4 cab for living quarters. The cab was destroyed by a fallen tree years ago. Strawberry was staffed into 1938, then abandoned.

name: Tolmie Peak Lookout
loc:
Mount Rainier National Park 
                    Pierce County, Washington
admin: National Park Service - Mount Rainier National Park
desc:
The Tolmie Peak fire lookout was built in 1933 according to the typical National Park style two-story structure. The upper level houses a lookout station with storage at the ground level. The design was prepared under the supervision of Edwin A. Nickel of the NPS Branch of Plans and Designs.  
 Tolmie was named after William Fraser Tolmie, a member of Hudson’s Bay Company who spent several months living at Fort Nisqually in the early 1800s. Tolmie set out on a botany excursion up the Puyallup River Valley with Native American guides, subsequently becoming the first non-native to set foot inside the present day boundaries of Mount Rainier National Park. Tolmie was known for building strong relationships with indigenous peoples. 
 The Tolmie fire lookout was placed on the National Register of Historic Places in March 1991 and is sometimes volunteer staffed in the summer.

name: Wellpinit Mountain Lookout
loc:
Spokane Indian Reservation 
                    Stevens County, Washington
desc:
The 53′ steel tower on Wellpinit Mountain was built in 1964 and replaced the Spokane Mountain fire lookout just four miles to the north. The old historic D-6 at Spokane Mountain burned during the 64,000 acre Carpenter Road Fire in 2015, started by an arsonist. 
 The lookout at Wellpinit was originally planned for Spokane Butte but the Colville suggested that Wellpinit would have wider views of the Spokane Reservation as well as electrical service. 
 In 2010, the lookout at Wellpinit called in the Line Fire and in 2021, the Sherwood Fire, started on July 21st from a lightning storm, came within only a mile or two of the lookout.

name: Whitestone Ridge Lookout
loc:
Colville Indian Reservation 
                    Ferry County, Washington
desc:
Whitestone was first established as a fire lookout camp in 1922, then an L-4 ground house was built in 1935 by the CCC for an approximate cost of about $900.  
   By 1960, the cabin was in very poor shape due to age, weathering, and shifting of the rocks upon which the foundation was built. A new lookout was proposed and a 20′ tower with R-6 cab replaced the L-4 in 1964.   
  In 1985, a third structure was built on the summit, the existing 53′ steel tower with live-in cab. It remains staffed every summer.

name: Whitmore Mountain Lookout
loc:
Colville Indian Reservation 
                    Okanogan County, Washington
desc:
The Whitmore L-4 cab was built in 1934 1/4 mile northeast of the    current steel lookout . In 1935, it was accompanied by a 3-legged 60′ wood tower with 7’x7′ cab. Both structures were built by the Civilian Conservation Corps for a reported $1,046. The L-4 cab still remains on site, though in very poor condition.  
 It was reported in 1960 that 60° of the surrounding area was not visible from the lookout due to its location and elevation and that the 3-legged wood tower was deteriorating and unsafe. Sometime in the following years, permission was granted from a private land owner to build a    53′ all-steel live-in tower . The lookout still exists today and is staffed every summer. 
 The lookout is locked but you can climb the stairs to a viewing platform just below the cab. Enjoy big views of the Coulee area, Omak Lake, and North Cascades. This is a seldom visited area of Washington that is unique and beautiful! 
 On August 3, 2021, lightning started the Whitmore fire, which eventually burned over much of the Whitmore Mountain area. Firefighters dug a hand line around the historic L-4 lookout and also wrapped it for protection. Both Whitmore lookouts survived.

name: Ned Hill Lookout
loc:
Olympic National Forest 
                    Clallam County, Washington
desc: This primitive wooden lookout was constructed in 1933.

name: Rocky Butte Area Tower
loc: Douglas County, Washington
desc: Not much is known about the history of this 90-foot Aermotor MC-39 tower. It is believed to have previously been used on an Indian reservation for fire detection work, but at its current location, it hosts communications equipment. It is believed to have been at this current site since at least the mid-1980s.

name: Acker Rock Lookout
loc:
Umpqua National Forest 
                    Douglas County, Oregon
desc: At one time more than a dozen lookouts covered the Tiller Ranger District on the Umpqua National Forest. Today only Pickett and Acker Rock remain. Perched on a high rock formation 2000' above the valley floor, Acker Rock Lookout offers a stunning view of the mountains northwest of Crater Lake National Park. Originally the site of an L-4 constructed in 1934, it was replaced by a R-6 flattop groundhouse in 1964.

name: Aldrich Butte Lookout
loc:
Malheur National Forest 
                    Grant County, Oregon
desc: Although located within the Malheur National Forest, Aldrich Butte Lookout was built and is staffed by the Oregon Dept. of Forestry. It is a standard three story ODF flatroof design with 14’x14’ cab and catwalk. First used as a lookout site in 1934, the cabin was replaced in 1959 and burned by vandals the same year. The present lookout was constructed in 1960 to the same standard. In active service, its coverage includes state, BLM, and private land.

name: Antelope Mountain Lookout
loc:
Malheur National Forest 
                    Grant County, Oregon
desc: This 15'x15' R6 cab with catwalk atop a 31' tower at Antelope Mountain Lookout on the Malheur National Forest was moved here from Lake Butte in 1974. The first lookout at the site was an L-4 cab on a 30' tower built in 1930.

name: Applegate Butte Lookout
loc:
Winema National Forest 
                    Klamath County, Oregon
desc: Located on the Winema National Forest, Applegate Butte Lookout is a 80’ steel Aermotor tower with metal 7’x7’ cab built in 1936. Abandoned in the 1960’s, the tower is sound.

name: Bald Butte Lookout
loc:
Fremont National Forest 
                    Lake County, Oregon
desc: Bald Butte is the only remaining L-4 gable roof lookout on the Fremont National Forest in Oregon. Located on a bare, treeless mountain top at 7,536’ the 14’x14’ groundhouse was constructed in 1931 and restored as a Passport In Time (PIT) project in 1993-94. In 1945 the observer found a Japanese incendiary balloon near the summit with five unexploded bombs intact. Now used only on a emergency basis, the popular lookout was placed in the cabin rental program in 1995.

name: Bald Butte Lookout
loc:
Ochoco National Forest 
                    Harney County, Oregon
desc: The first lookout at Bald Butte on the Ochoco National Forest was a 45' pole tower with a 8x8' cab and ground residence constructed in 1931. Built in 1959, the current 41' timber tower with a 14' x 14' R-6 wooden flattop cab with catwalk is staffed as needed.

name: Bald Mountain Lookout
loc:
Fremont National Forest 
                    Klamath County, Oregon
desc: A telephone line was strung from the Oatman Ranger Station to Bald Mountain in 1917.  In 1918 fire-finding equipment was installed.  In 1928, a steel tower under 30' with an Aermotor 12'x12' live-in cab was constructed. This was a new design for Aermotor and only a few were ever erected.  In 1941 the Fremont National Forest constructed the present lookout, a classic L-4, hip-roof with catwalk on a 29' 6" treated timber tower.  Besides the Forest Service, this site has been operated by the Walker Range Patrol and in the early days by the Klamath Forest Protective Association.

name: Baughman Mountain Lookout
loc: Douglas County, Oregon
desc: Baughman Mountain Lookout was put into service by the Douglas Forest Protective Association (Oregon) in 1925. The first tower was a crow's nest atop a Douglas-fir tree. In 1934 a 10' round timber, trestle type, tower with an L-4 cab was constructed.  In 1953, a 50' treated timber tower with an Amort style cab was erected on a point about one and a half miles to the east. In 1979, the present 54' 6" steel tower with a 14'x14' flattop cab with catwalk was assembled from the recycled Shivigny Mountain lookout, which was dismantled in the fall 1978. The lookout is in active service.

name: Black Butte Lookout
loc:
Deschutes National Forest 
                    Jefferson County, Oregon
desc: There is an extraordinary amount of fire lookout history atop Black Butte within the Deschutes National Forest in Oregon. The original D-6 cupola lookout was built in 1922 and is still in use in 1994. In 1934 a 82’ wooden tower with 7x7’ cab was constructed for better visibility. The 1934 tower structure collapsed in the winter of 2002….due to heavy ice and snow loads during a winter storm. In 1980 a new ground quarters cabin was built and in 1994 work began on a new 65 tower with 10x 10’ cab. Black Butte is a scenic and popular hiking destination and is still staffed for fire detection.

name: Black Butte Lookout
loc:
Malheur National Forest 
                    Grant County, Oregon
desc: The first structure, built in 1936, was a 20' pole L-4 tower. A garage was added at one time. The original pole tower legs were replaced with treated timber legs in 1964. The concrete piers were redone in 1994.  It is staffed as needed.

name: Bland Mountain Lookout
loc: Douglas County, Oregon
desc: The lookout at Bland Mountain has an unusual history. Built in 1947 with a 25’ wood tower, it was lowered in 1996. The ODF 14’x14’ flattop cab with catwalk was remounted on a 20’ tapered metal tower that formerly held a water tank at the Oregon Dept. of Forestry Canyonville office. It is a “one of a kind” result! It is staffed by the Douglas Forest Protection Association.

name: Bly Ranger Station Lookout
loc:
Fremont National Forest 
                    Klamath County, Oregon
desc: The first lookout in Bly was established by the Klamath Forest Protective Association at their Ranger Station located a short distance to the east of the Forest Service Station.  This was an open platform atop the District warehouse. In 1958, a 20 foot wooden tower with a unique 7x7 flat roof cab, with catwalk, was constructed at the Bly, U.S. Forest Service, Ranger Station. This tower has been relocated to a local park.

name: Bolan Mountain Lookout
loc:
Siskiyou National Forest 
                    Josephine County, Oregon
desc: Bolan Mountain Lookout on the Siskiyou National Forest just north of the California line has a long history as a fire detection and aircraft-warning site. In 1917 a cupola cabin was constructed on a log crib base. This was replaced in 1953 with a L-4, hip roof 14’x14’ cab on a 15’ wood tower. The legs were later removed at the cab placed on a low stone base. The site was recently restored with an expanded catwalk including a deck to one side. Now on emergency status, it is in the lookout rental program.

name: Bull of the Woods Lookout
loc:
Mt. Hood National Forest 
                    Clackamas County, Oregon
desc:
Located on the crest of the Cascade Mountains in the heart of the Wilderness Area of the same name, Bull of the Woods Lookout is a special place. One of a handful of lockouts remaining of the many that once dotted the Mt. Hood National Forest, it is today used occasionally as a backcountry guard station. The first lookout on this site – in the 1920s -- was a small pole and shake cabin. The current classic L-4 cab with catwalk on a 10’ treated timber tower was built in 1942. The tower frame was prefabed at the Zibzag CCC camp. The cab itself was a precut kit provided by the Alladin Co. The structure is historically intact and is listed on the National Register of Historic Places. 
 The Lookout was last staffed in 1963/64. 
 Bull of the Woods Lookout was tragically lost in the Bull Complex Fire in September 2021.

name: Bunker Hill Lookout
loc: Coos County, Oregon
desc: Located at the headquarters of the Coos Forest Protection Association in Coos Bay, Oregon, Bunker Hill Lookout is unique for several reasons. Its very presence at the CFPA Headquarters alludes to the importance of fire lookouts as symbols of forestry and fire control. Constructed in 1996, the modified Oregon Department of Forestry flattop cab with catwalk is atop a 40' steel tower transferred from the Coast Guard. It replaced an observation platform on the water tower dating to 1939. Used for training lookout personnel and in emergencies, the structure will be listed on the National Lookout Register until 50 years old.

name: Calamity Butte Lookout
loc:
Malheur National Forest 
                    Harney County, Oregon
desc: Calamity Butte has been in continuous use for 65 years, and in that period has probably lived up to its name! The wooden, ground level 14’ x 14’ live-in structure is a “Supervisor Hall Special” built on a revised California design. A predecessor design of the popular L-4 model, it is one of only two such lookouts known to remain in Region 6 (Oregon & Washington). This U.S. Forest Service lookout is still in active use on the Malheur National Forest.

name: Calimus Butte Lookout
loc:
Winema National Forest 
                    Klamath County, Oregon
desc:
Calimus Butte has been active each summer since 1931, first by fire guards of the Klamath Tribe and then by the Winema National Forest after it was established in 1961. Constructed in 1930, it was a hub of reservation fire activity by 1932 with four crank-type phone lines converging on the lookout. 
 Prior to that, in 1922, a guard cabin was constructed a couple hundred feet north of the summit, this being the hub. The Klamath Indian Agency operated the lookout until about two years prior to the Termination act of 1961.The lookouts on the reservation were operated by the Klamath District of the Oregon Department of Forestry. A large portion of forest was retained by the tribes, this known as the Indian Forest. 
 Calimus was located on this forest and was until the mid-70;s was an Oregon Dept. of Forestry lookout. When the forest was sold to the US Government in the mid-70's it became part of the Winema National Forest. It is one of only eight cupola lookouts standing in Oregon and one of three still staffed.

name: Carpenter Mountain Lookout
loc:
Willamette National Forest 
                    Linn County, Oregon
desc: The first lookout at Carpenter Mountain on the Willamette National Forest was an open sided fire fighter shelter built in 1917. In 1935 the CCCs constructed the current 68 year old station. It is the only remaining example of a hip-roof L-4 with catwalk on the Forest. Recently restored it is reached by a one-mile trail and is again in active service. It is also listed on the National Register of Historic Places.

name: Chase Mountain Lookout
loc: Klamath County, Oregon
desc: The Oregon State Forest Department’s Chase Mountain Lookout is either one-of-a-kind, or at least unusual. The 21’ metal tower, with a 12’x12’ metal cab with catwalk was constructed in 1951 by Holland Sheet Metal Co., replacing a 10’x10’ ground house established on the site in 1928 and moved to Hambelton Butte in 1949. The stair entrance is inside the cab rather than on the catwalk. In active service, much of what this lookout sees is in California.

name: Cinnamon Butte Lookout
loc:
Umpqua National Forest 
                    Douglas County, Oregon
desc: Cinnamon Butte Lookout on the Umpqua National Forest went into service as an L-4 cab on a 30’ pole tower. The present R-6 flattop with catwalk on a 44’ treated timber tower was first erected on Buster Butte in 1955 and moved to Cinnamon in 1976. It remains active.

name: Clear Lake Butte Lookout
loc:
Mount Hood National Forest 
                    Wasco County, Oregon
desc: The original 110 foot tower on this site was built in 1932, and was replaced with the present 41 foot flattop tower in 1964.

name: Coffin Mountain Lookout
loc:
Willamette National Forest 
                    Linn County, Oregon
desc: The first lookout on Coffin Mountain on the Willamette National Forest was a platform built in 1906 and replaced in 1921 with a D-6 cupola cabin. Fifteen years later an L-4 ground house was constructed and replaced in 1984 with the present 15'x15' R-6 flattop with catwalk.

name: Cougar Pass Lookout
loc:
South Central Oregon 
                    Douglas County, Oregon
desc: The first structure on this site was a 30' L-4 wooden tower built in 1936. That was replaced with the present 50' treated timber tower with live-in Amort cab, which is presently occupied by packrats only.

name: Courtney Butte Lookout
loc: Wallowa County, Oregon
desc: This lookout is available for rental.

name: Devils Peak Lookout
loc:
Mt. Hood National Forest 
                    Clackamas County, Oregon
desc: Once there were more than 50 lookouts on the Mt. Hood National Forest, including one at the summit of the 11,245’ peak, but today only six remain. The first structure at Devil’s Peak Lookout was a 12’x12’ log cabin with cupola built in 1924. It was replaced with an L-4 ground cab in 1933. The current L-4 cab with catwalk on a 10’ treated timber tower was constructed in 1952. Now inactive.

name: Dixie Butte Lookout
loc:
Malheur National Forest 
                    Grant County, Oregon
desc: The first lookout on Dixie Butte on the Malheur National Forest was a cupola cabin in the early 1920s which was replaced with an L-4 ground house in 1935. The present 15’x15’ R-6 flattop ground house was built in 1968 and remains in active service.

name: Dog Mountain Lookout
loc:
Fremont National Forest 
                    Lake County, Oregon
desc: The first lookout was an Alidade in the teens. In 1918 the Lookout was Bertha Covert, one of many women that staffed lookouts during the manpower shortage of WW I. In 1926 a D-6 cupola lookout house was built. In 1947 a L-4 cabin was constructed at a cost of $2700.00. In 1997 an attractive new two-story 15'x15' lookout house was built for a mere $82,213.92. The cab is devoted to detection activities with living quarters on the first floor. It is in active service.

name: Drake Peak Lookout
loc:
Fremont National Forest 
                    Lake County, Oregon
desc: The biggest excitement at Drake Mountain Lookout on the Fremont National Forest comes when lightning strikes the adjacent propane tank. Drake's Peak was first used as a patrol lookout and had fire-finding instruments installed in 1915.  At some time later a small building was built. In the summer of 1927 a standard Forest Service road was constructed next to the summit. A D-6 cupola was built there in 1928.  The present L-4 ground house was constructed, brand new, next to the cupola in 1948 at a cost of $3451.47. Drake Peak (elev. 8352’) has the distinction of being the highest lookout with road access in Oregon.

name: Dry Mountain Lookout
loc:
Ochoco National Forest 
                    Crook County, Oregon
desc:
With the name Dry Mountain there is little wonder that the lookout is still staffed. The 70' Aermotor tower with 7' x 7' metal cab was constructed in 1932. The southernmost lookout on the Ochoco National Forest overlooks National Forest and BLM land.
 

 
To the north is Snow Mountain Lookout. Together Dry Mountain and Snow Mountain provided fire surveillance over the lower Ochaco sections (Burns Unit). To the south you can see clear to the Nevada-Oregon border. Northern flowing weather is easily seen from this vantage (up to 100 miles to the south). Lookouts stationed here can provide early warning when cumulus buildup is forming to the south. Dry Mountain is the first location northern-flowing dry air meets mountains and forest. The dry air is created by Oregon's and Nevada's high desert to the south. Moisture build-up then travels to the north, which is the typical summer flow for this region. Dry Mountain is an ideal location to observe lightening storms and would be considered a high fire activity location from August through October.
 

 
In 2000 and subsequent years that lookout has been staffed in extreme weather by BLM.

name: Dry Soda Lookout
loc:
Malheur National Forest 
                    Grant County, Oregon
desc: Dry Soda Lookout is a vintage USFS 60’ CT-2 wooden tower with a L-4 hip roof 14’x 14’ cab and a wooden catwalk. The structure is in good condition and a rappelling platform has been added at the 45’ level. The Malheur National Forest lookout is still staffed for fire detection each year.

name: Dutchman Butte Lookout
loc: Douglas County, Oregon
desc: With US designation #333, it is appropriate that Oregon's Dutchman Butte Lookout would be a three-legged tower! Located in the big timber country of Douglas County between the Pacific Ocean and the Cascade Mountains, the site first had a 12' wooden live-in tower in 1936. The 15' guyed three legged steel tower was obtained from the U.S. Air Force and erected in 1970. The tower was located on Fairview Peak as part of a Radar site. It was dismantled and moved by a DFPA crew and a portion of it was used in the construction of the lookout.  It has an Oregon Department of Forestry 14' x 14' flattop live-in cab with catwalk and is staffed by the Douglas FPA.

name: Dutchman Peak Lookout
loc:
Rogue River National Forest 
                    Jackson County, Oregon
desc: Dutchman Peak is the last of the original cupola lookouts still in use.  Located near the California—Oregon state line, on the Rogue River National Forest, the structure was built in 1927 and is one of the oldest lookouts remaining in service in the United States. It is a favorite stop on the Mt. Ashland Loop Road and for hikers on the nearby Pacific Crest National Scenic Trail.

name: Eagle Butte Lookout
loc:
Warm Springs Indian Reservation 
                    Wasco County, Oregon
desc: Built in 1935, the 107’ Aermotor tower with 7’x7’ metal cab at Eagle Butte continues in active service. Located on the Warm Springs Indian Reservation, it is closed to public access. It has ground house living quarters.

name: East Butte Lookout
loc:
Deschutes National Forest 
                    Deschutes County, Oregon
desc: The first lookout at East Butte on the Deschutes National Forest was a L-4 on a 30' wooden tower. When the Forest Service replaced the structure in 1995, they built a new vintage model L-4 gable roof cab on a 20' wooden tower. Although a faithful reproduction and still in active service, the structure will be listed on the National Lookout Register until it becomes 50 years old. There is a historic restored garage on the site.

name: Fairview Peak Lookout
loc:
Umpqua National Forest 
                    Lane County, Oregon
desc:
Fairview Peak is located in the Bohemia Mining District southeast of Eugene. An observer's cabin was built on the summit in 1912, followed by an open-air Alidade tower in 1914. A D-6 cupola was built in 1921 at a cost of $876.99, and it was augmented in 1936 by a 30-foot tower with an L-4 cab. The 1921 cupola was retained as a place to stay for visitors before becoming a storage building. 
 The site was used for an Air Force gap filler radar station from the late 1950s through 1964. 
 The present 53-foot tower with R-6 cab was built in 1972.

name: Fall Mountain Lookout
loc:
Malheur National Forest 
                    Grant County, Oregon
desc: Constructed in 1933 on the Malheur National Forest in eastern Oregon, Fall Mountain Lookout is a 18’ pole tower with a L-4, 14’x 14’ cab featuring a wooden catwalk. The cab remains well-preserved in near-original condition, but the tower had to be replaced in 1953.

name: Fivemile Butte Lookout
loc:
Mount Hood National Forest 
                    Wasco County, Oregon
desc: The first Five Mile Butte Lookout on the Mt. Hood National Forest was a pole tower in the 1920s. In 1932 an L-4 cab atop a 30' pole tower was erected, but it collapsed under snow ten years later, to be replaced again with another L-4 on a stronger tower. This R-6 cab on a 30' tower was built in 1957 and is in the rental program.

name: Flag Point Lookout
loc:
Mt. Hood National Forest 
                    Wasco County, Oregon
desc:
Located east of Mt. Hood with a great view of Oregon’s highest peak, Flag Point Lookout is both an active fire detection station and a very popular winter lookout rental site. The first structure was a 6’x6’ cab on a 40’ pole tower in 1924. It was replaced in 1932 with an L-4 on a 30’ pole tower. The present R-6 flattop on 41’ timber tower was constructed in 1973. 
 The lookout was destroyed by the Grasshopper Fire on July 31, 2026. 
   Grasshopper Fire Update   
 
  Mt. Hood National Forest- US Forest Service's Post -   Point Fire Lookout Fire officials have confirmed that the Flag Point Fire Lookout was destroyed by the Grasshopper Fire last night.

name: Flagtail Mountain Lookout
loc:
Malheur National Forest 
                    Grant County, Oregon
desc:
The first Flagtail Mountain Lookout was a tree crows nest in the early 1920s. A 20’ pole tower with L-4 cab was built in 1933 and in 1960 the present R-6 14’x14’ flattop cab with catwalk was constructed. 
 As of 2025, the lookout was being staffed by veteran observer David Sheffel.

name: Foley Butte Lookout
loc: Crook County, Oregon
desc: Foley Lookout first went into service as a crows nest in 1932 and two years later was replaced with a 60’ wooden tower and cab. In 1953 the Oregon Dept. of Forestry built the present 40’ laminated wood tower with a hip roof, permanent overhang 14’x14’ live in cab with catwalk. It is in active service.

name: Fox Butte Lookout
loc:
Deschutes National Forest 
                    Lake County, Oregon
desc: In 1919 a heliograph was set up on the west point of the butte.  In 1920 a telephone line was built to the western point from the Cabin Lake Ranger Station.  In 1924, a standard D-6 cupola was constructed on the western point.  In August 1926 a fire swept over the summit completely burning the cupola.  A pole tower and a ground cabin for living quarters was constructed. The current 80’ steel Aermotor tower with metal 7’ x 7’ cab was built in 1933 on Fox Butte and the cabin from the western point was moved to the tower site on the eastern point. In 1934 the garage was built. The present ground cabin, a gable-roof L-4, was moved from Sixteen Butte in 1948.

name: Frazier Point Lookout
loc:
Malheur National Forest 
                    Grant County, Oregon
desc:
One of the last and best of its kind, Frazier Point Lookout is a classic L-6 wooden cab with catwalk on a 100’ guyed treated timber tower. The Malheur National Forest station, including a ground house living quarters, was constructed in 1940. 
 As of July 2019, an inspection notice attached to the tower indicates it has been condemned due to major deficiencies. The access stairs are boarded over.

name: Gold Butte Lookout
loc:
Willamette National Forest 
                    Marion County, Oregon
desc: The L-4 14’x14’ house with catwalk on Gold Butte was constructed in the Willamette National Forest in 1934 by the CCC. Eight years later a cabin was built several hundred feet north of the lookout station and staffed year-around as part of the Aircraft Warning Service in World War II. The cabin and garage are gone, but the lookout -- which was last staffed in the late 1960s -- was saved by a hiking group. The Pacific Crest Trust Fund has raised money and provided volunteers to restore the structure which is still used in periods of high fire danger.

name: Green Peter Lookout
loc: Linn County, Oregon
desc:
