Built in 1929, the 12' x 14' shake and frame cabin was abandoned in 1948 but survived and was restored in 1983 as a Kootenai National Forest rental. A high elevation site and located a few miles south of the Canadian border, the lookout was difficult to reach and often fogged in.

name: Saddle Mountain Lookout
loc: Powell County, Montana
admin: Montana Department of Natural Resources and Conservation
desc: Built by the Blackfeet Fire Protection Association in 1936 and transferred to the Montana Dept. of Natural Resources in 1971, Saddle Mountain Lookout is the last of the original 1930s pole L-4 cabs taller than 10’ and still in use without significant alteration.

name: Scalplock Mountain Lookout
loc:
Glacier National Park 
                    Flathead County, Montana
desc: Scalplock Lookout is the southernmost lookout in the Park, overlooking Theodore Roosevelt Pass -- route of the Burlington Northern Railroad and U.S. Highway 2.  Built in 1931, it is a 14'x14' cab with 10' enclosed tower and roof extended over the catwalk.

name: Seven Point Lookout
loc:
Kootenai National Forest 
                    Sanders County, Montana
desc: Seven Point Lookout is the only remaining gable-roofed L-4 on a tower in the Northern Rockies Region, and has the distinction of being located on three national forests without being moved. It was built in 1930 by the U.S. Forest Service on what was then the Cabinet National Forest, later changed to the Kaniksu National Forest. In 1973 much of the Trout Creek Ranger District was transferred to the Cabinet Ranger District of Kootenai National Forest and the lookout was abandoned. Due to its remoteness, it was not heavily vandalized and restoration was undertaken in 1996 as a Passport in Time project.

name: Sex Peak Lookout
loc:
Kootenai National Forest 
                    Sanders County, Montana
desc: Sex Peak Lookout was named by two Forest Service foresters in the 1920s, reportedly after the topic of conversation that day. Whether or not the tale is accurate, there is no doubt the name has enhanced the popularity of the lookout in the cabin rental program. The L-4 groundhouse with catwalk was constructed in 1948 and staffed until the mid-1970s. It was refurbished and placed in the rental program in 1986.

name: Skookum Butte Lookout
loc:
Lolo National Forest 
                    Missoula County, Montana
desc: Constructed in 1928, Skookum Butte Lookout is one of only three remaining L-5 log/frame ground houses remaining in Montana and Northern Idaho. It is located on the Lolo National Forest on the state line southeast of famed Lolo Pass. The lookout has not been regularly staffed since sometime prior to 1965, but remains relatively intact. The Montana Chapter of FFLA plans to initiate restoration in 1996.

name: Star Peak Lookout
loc:
Kootenai National Forest 
                    Sanders County, Montana
desc: In 1907 the first forest lookout on the old Cabinet National Forest (and the State of Montana) camped in a tent just below the summit of Star Peak (formerly Squaw Peak). Three years later in 1910, the stone cabin was built just below the summit and still stands. The present L-4 on a stone base was built in 1952 and remains the only active lookout on the Cabinet Ranger District.

name: St. Mary Peak Lookout
loc:
Bitterroot National Forest 
                    Ravalli County, Montana
desc: St. Mary Lookout is the eighth tower to be listed in Montana and the first by the U.S. Forest Service. The Bitterroot National Forest structure was originally an L-4 on a 40' tower built in 1931, but it blew down in 1951. The current structure (1953 vintage) is a 14'x14' wooden cab with catwalk atop a 10' natural stone base.

name: Stark Mountain Lookout
loc:
Lolo National Forest 
                    Mineral County, Montana
desc: As the artwork and photo attest, Stark Mountain Lookout on the Lolo National Forest is in the heart of Montana lightning country. That has not deterred Virginia Vincent who has staffed the lookout for 30 years. The multiple fires in the picture were taken August 4, 2000 by FFLA member Vincent who saw many of them burst out at the time of the strike in the middle of the night. In all there were 32 fires ignited on the Ninemile Ranger District that day. The first lookout at Stark was a L-4 on a 30' pole tower. It was replaced by the present R6 flattop on a 20' treated timber tower in 1964 and remains very active.

name: Strawberry Lookout
loc:
Helena National Forest 
                    Jefferson County, Montana
desc: Erected in 1941, Strawberry Lookout is the last structure of its type on the Helena National Forests. The registration also includes a one story log ground house below the 65’ Aermotor tower with 7’x7’ metal cab.

name: Swiftcurrent Lookout
loc:
Glacier National Park 
                    Glacier County, Montana
desc: Constructed in 1936, Swiftcurrent Lookout is one of the newest and most unique lookouts. The 14'x14'cab sits atop a 10-ft stone base.  The gable roof is covered with a flagstone and mortar roof surface.  A popular hiking destination, it is the only lookout in the Park without a catwalk.

name: Thoma Lookout
loc:
Flathead National Forest 
                    Flathead County, Montana
desc: One of the early gable roof L-4 US Forest Service groundhouses, Thoma Lookout is located on the Flathead National Forest. Built 81 years ago, it has just been restored.

name: Tony Peak Lookout
loc:
Kootenai National Forest 
                    Lincoln County, Montana
desc: Smiling forlornly on a relatively low mountain point overlooking a fire-prone railroad, Tony Peak Lookout was approaching collapse until the Forest Fire Lookout Association arrived in Libby, Montana for its 1999 western summer meeting. A visit to the site led not only to an immediate restoration effort by the FFLA to prevent further deterioration, but also to the establishment of the Tony Peak Award by the National Forestry Association in recognition of sensitive and appropriate siting of the electronic facilities in the vicinity of historic structures. It is one of 8 hip roof L-4s on the Kootenai National Forest.

name: Union Peak Lookout
loc: Granite County, Montana
desc: The Blackfoot Forest Protective established Union Peak Lookout as a crow’s nest tree platform in 1930.  Five years later it was replaced by a 70’ steel tower.  In 1963 the present 15’x15’ groundhouse with slightly sloped gable-flattop roof., a unique BFP design, was constructed and remains in service.  In 1973 the Montana Dept. of Natural Resources and Conservation assumed responsibility for the lookout.

name: Up Up Lookout
loc:
Lolo National Forest 
                    Mineral County, Montana
desc: This 41' treated timber tower with R-6 flat cab, built in 1966 on a beautiful rock pinnacle in the Bitterroot Mountains of western Montana at an elevation of 5900', was preceded by a 20' pole tower and L-4 cab built in 1934, which was used as a lookout until at least 1965. The present lookout was finally staffed again in 1995 for the first time in several years. The lookout has been added to the Recreation Rental program. This 41' treated timber tower with R-6 flat cab, built in 1966 on a beautiful rock pinnacle in the Bitterroot Mountains of western Montana at an elevation of 5900', was preceded by a 20' pole tower and L-4 cab built in 1934, which was used as a lookout until at least 1965. The present lookout was finally staffed again in 1995 for the first time in several years. The lookout has been added to the Recreation Rental program.

name: Wam Mountain Lookout
loc:
Kootenai National Forest 
                    Lincoln County, Montana
desc: One of the last gable roof L-4s, Wam Mountain Lookout was constructed in 1931 by the Forest Service atop a 7,121' peak in the Whitefish Range in Montana. Last used for fire detection in the 1950s, the lookout escaped destruction probably because of its remote location.

name: West Fork Butte Lookout
loc:
Lolo National Forest 
                    Missoula County, Montana
desc: West Fork Butte is the only pre-1936 design hip-roof L-4 ground house lookout remaining in western Montana. It was generally staffed up to the late 1980s and has been extensively renovated by the Montana Chapter of the Forest Fire Lookout Association.

name: White Mountain Lookout
loc:
Lolo National Forest 
                    Mineral County, Montana
desc: The first White Mountain Lookout on the Lolo National Forest was an L-4 cab on a 40' wooden tower built in 1934. It was replaced in 1953 with this L-4 cab with catwalk on a 41' timber tower and is planned for restoration.

name: Williams Peak Lookout
loc:
Fish Creek State Park 
                    Mineral County, Montana
admin: Montana Department of Fish, Wildlife & Parks
desc: This lookout's cab was an exhibit at the 1967 World Scout Jamboree at Farragut State Park in Idaho.  In 1969, the lookout was erected at Little Joe, near St. Regis.  In 1977, it was moved to Williams Peak, replacing a 1934 30' L-4 tower.  The lookout is located on former industrial timber land that was acquired by Montana Fish, Wildlife and Parks.

name: Yaak Mountain Lookout
loc:
Kootenai National Forest 
                    Lincoln County, Montana

name: Yager Butte Lookout
loc:
Custer National Forest 
                    Powder River County, Montana
desc: This 53-foot treated timber flat cab lookout was built in 1958.

name: Ziegler Mountain Lookout
loc:
Kootenai National Forest 
                    Lincoln County, Montana
desc: When the 30' pole L-4 tower was built at Ziegler Mountain Lookout in 1928, the 50-mile long Lake Koocanusa and Libby Dam right below it did not exist. When the 32' new timber tower with 14' x 14' flattop cab and catwalk was constructed next to it in 1959, the two co-existed for awhile before the L-4 came down. The lookout remains active.

name: Porcupine Ridge Lookout
loc:
Glacier National Park 
                    Flathead County, Montana
desc: Porcupine Ridge lookout is a classic 2-story NPS frame cab, built between 1939 and 1940. It not used for fire detection purposes much after 1972, but is still there and used by backcountry rangers.

name: Mission Lookout
loc:
Swan Lake Ranger District 
                    Lake County, Montana
desc: Mission Lookout sits at 3.700 feet above Swan Lake and offers views of the Swan Valley and Mission Mountains. Many fire lookouts began their life as a simple structure: a firefinder on a mountain peak, a tall tree to climb, or even a slightly more comfortable crows' nest structure, such as Mission Mountain Lookout was, at least for part of its close to 100-year life. A 25' platform tower was built in 1921, with a cabin for living quarters built in the 1930's along with a newer, 35' wooden platform. The present tower, a 41' treated timber with R-6 flat cab, built in 1959, is still used for emergencies, and is also on the rental program. The caption on one photo reads: "Mrs Art Halverson being helped down from first Mission Lookout Swan District By R.H. Gatiss." The other picture of the same structure is a pen and ink drawing from a 1923 photo, from Early Days in the Forest Service, Vol. 4. The last three are photographs of the 1959 structure that sits on the peak today.

name: Helena Fire Tower
loc: Lewis and Clark County, Montana
desc: This tower was originally built in 1876 as the second tower at this site. Known as the Guardian of the Gulch, it was last used in 1931 but has been maintained as a historic site.

name: Cooney Lookout
loc:
Flathead National Forest - Swan Lake Ranger District 
                    Missoula County, Montana
desc: Located near Condon, Montana on a hillside roughly 700' above the Swan River, up the flank of the Swan Range, the first tower was a 20' L-4 built in 1933 while the present 30' treated timber tower with R-6 flat cab was built in 1968 and is primarily staffed by volunteers during the summer.

name: Little Napa Point Lookout
loc:
Swan State Forest 
                    Lake County, Montana
desc: The first permanent lookout consisted of a school bus with an attached cupola that was used from 1969 through 1976.  Finally, in 1977, the present 20' wooden live-in tower was constructed. It is available for emergencies but is not regularly staffed.

name: Holland Ridge Lookout
loc:
Flathead National Forest - Swan Lake Ranger District 
                    Missoula County, Montana
desc: Holland Ridge lookout has had a long career as a fire detection point. First established with a camp in 1921, a 14x14' stone & shake cabin, built in 1931, is still there and has had some maintenance in recent years. A gabled L-4 cab,  was built at some point in the early 1930s, but was then abandoned in 1953 and is no longer standing at the site.

name: Spotted Bear Mountain Lookout
loc:
Flathead National Forest  - Spotted Bear RD 
                    Flathead County, Montana
desc: Spotted Bear Mountain lookout was first established in 1916 with a 2-story 13x13' log cabin. The present 20' treated timber R-6 tower was built in 1963 and is regularly staffed in the summer. There is also a patrol point 2 miles northwest.

name: Mud Lake Lookout
loc:
Flathead National Forest - Spotted Bear RD 
                    Flathead County, Montana
desc: The Mud Lake Lookout was established in 1921 with the original gabled-roof design (instead of the later hipped roofs) L-4 built in 1932. The lookout is described as the only remaining “original” lookout left in the Bob Marshall.   Abandoned in 1972, the lookout was threatened by a a forest fire in 2000, but has had ongoing restoration work being conducted by the Northwest Montana Fire Lookout Association.

name: Jumbo Mountain Lookout
loc:
Flathead National Forest - Spotted Bear RD 
                    Powell County, Montana
desc: Located in the Bob Marshall Wilderness, this R-6 flat cab, built in 1957, replaced an L-4 cab from 1937. It was used for emergencies into the 1970's, and has been semi-regularly staffed since 2001.

name: Coal Ridge Lookout Cabin
loc:
Flathead National Forest - Glacier View RD 
                    Flathead County, Montana
desc: Coal Ridge actually consists of three lookout points along the ridgetop. The first was a cabin (still there, also called the Moran Patrol Cabin) at the northwest point (7285') in 1928. A 24' pole platform tower was added in the 1930's 1.5 miles southeast of the cabin at the 7100' level (ruins). Then in 1935 a 20' pole L-4 tower was constructed 1 mile southeast of the original cabin at the 7105' level. Used for emergencies in the 1960's, part of the ruins are still standing.

name: Cyclone Peak Lookout
loc:
Flathead NF - Glacier View RD 
                    Flathead County, Montana
desc: This 41' treated timber tower with R-6 cab, built in 1967, replaced a 40' pole L-4 tower from 1935. It is staffed in the summer.

name: Werner Peak Lookout
loc:
Northwestern Land Office 
                    Flathead County, Montana
desc: Developed in 1911 with a log cabin 1 mile east, a D-1 log cupola cabin was added on the summit in 1914. By 1941, a 10' pole L-4 tower was constructed, replaced by the present 2-story concrete & frame live-in tower in 1983. It is staffed during emergencies and is also available to rent in the summer through the Stillwater State Forest office. The L-4 cab was moved to a museum 1 mile south of Kalispell in 1987.

name: Stahl Peak Lookout
loc:
Kootenai NF 
                    Lincoln County, Montana
desc: This cupola lookout cabin was built in 1926, was used for emergencies into the 1960's.

name: Mount Marston Lookout
loc:
Kootenai NF 
                    Lincoln County, Montana
desc: Developed in 1932 with an L-4 cab, the present 10' concrete base topped by an R-6 flat cab, built in 1962, is staffed in the summer.

name: Black Butte Lookout
loc:
Kootenai NF 
                    Flathead County, Montana
desc: Initially used as a patrol point in the 1920's, the first tower built was a 35' pole L-4 in 1939. In 1973, an 8x8' cab was installed atop the radar installation, with no living quarters. The present 45' all-steel live-in tower was constructed in 1983 and is staffed every summer.

name: Elk Mountain Lookout
loc:
Kootenai NF 
                    Lincoln County, Montana
desc: Developed in 1923 with a 10x10' frame cab and roof platform, a 10' pole tower with L-4 cab was built in 1940 1/4 mile southwest of the summit. Suffering from vandalism and decay, the tower now lays in ruins. There is also an L-6 cab 1 mile northeast of the lookout.

name: Davis Mountain Lookout
loc:
Kootenai NF 
                    Lincoln County, Montana
desc: The present 60' steel tower with 7x7' cab and ladder access, along with the accompanying log cabin, were built about 1931, and have been abandoned for several years.

name: Warland Peak Lookout
loc:
Kootenai NF 
                    Lincoln County, Montana
desc: Developed in 1934 with the present 100' steel tower with 7x7' cab and an accompanying 10' pole tower with L-4 cab for living quarters, Warland has not been used since the late 1960's. The L-4 finally collapsed over the winter of 2012-2013.

name: Calx Mountain Lookout
loc:
Kootenai NF 
                    Lincoln County, Montana
desc: The first lookout structure here was a crow's nest tree platform, built in 1921, and still there 1/8 mile south of the present lookout. In 1934, a 40' pole L-4 tower was built on the middle of 3 summits. This was apparently destroyed in 1974. In 1984, the present steel tower was moved from Johnson Peak near Whitefish. The lookout has been staffed in recent years.

name: Swede Mountain Lookout
loc:
Kootenai NF 
                    Lincoln County, Montana
desc: Overlooking the town of Libby, the first lookout was a 50' pole tower with L-4 cab in 1934. This was replaced with the present 53' treated timber tower with R-6 flat cab in 1964. It is staffed every summer.

name: Quartz Peak Lookout
loc:
Kootenai NF 
                    Lincoln County, Montana
desc: Started in 1934 with a cabin, which burned down in 1954, the present 60' steel tower was built in 1935, and has been abandoned since the late 1960's.

name: Lost Horse Lookout
loc:
Kootenai NF 
                    Lincoln County, Montana
desc: First used in 1921 as a camp lookout, the present 10' pole tower with L-4 cab was built in 1934, but has remained unused for many years. It was threatened by a forest fire in 1994.

name: Webb Mountain Lookout
loc:
Kootenai NF 
                    Lincoln County, Montana
desc: Developed in 1930 with a 14x14' Columbia Falls "redi-cut" cab, this unique structure was replaced in 1959 with the present 10' concrete base topped with an R-6 flat cab. There was also a 35' tree platform 1/2 mile west of the lookout. The cabin is in the rental program, and was threatened by a forest fire in 1994.

name: Baldy Mountain Lookout
loc:
Kootenai NF 
                    Lincoln County, Montana
desc: Developed about 1910 with a 45' pole platform tower, and replaced in 1927 by a log cabin with L-6 cupola, the present 30' treated timber tower with L-4 cab was built in 1957. It is available in the rental program.

name: Tripoint Lookout
loc:
Custer-Gallatin National Forest 
                    Carter County, Montana
desc: This 60' steel tower, built in 1936, at one time had log cabin living quarters. Not used in several decades, it is the easternmost lookout in Montana.

name: Diamond Butte Lookout
loc:
Custer-Gallatin NF and Montana BLM 
                    Powder River County, Montana
desc: Established with a cabin moved from Yager Butte in 1958, this R-6 flat cab atop a 10' concrete base, built in 1970, is available as an off-season rental.

name: Badger Peak Lookout
loc:
Northern Cheyenne Tribe 
                    Rosebud County, Montana
admin: Northern Cheyenne Agency - Bureau of Indian Affairs
desc: Built in the 1930s, this steel tower was still standing as of 2016.

name: Black Spring Lookout
loc:
Northern Cheyenne Tribe 
                    Rosebud County, Montana
admin: Northern Cheyenne Agency - Bureau of Indian Affairs
desc: No information at this time.

name: Bull Creek Lookout
loc:
Northern Cheyenne Tribe 
                    Big Horn County, Montana
admin: Northern Cheyenne Agency - Bureau of Indian Affairs
desc: No information available at this time.

name: Wolf Mountain Lookout
loc:
Crow Tribe 
                    Big Horn County, Montana
admin: Crow Agency - Bureau of Indian Affairs
desc: No information at this time.

name: Pryor Lookout
loc:
Crow Tribe 
                    Big Horn County, Montana
admin: Crow Agency - Bureau of Indian Affairs
desc: No information known at this time.

name: Garnet Mountain Lookout
loc:
Custer-Gallatin National Forest 
                    Gallatin County, Montana
desc: Established with a camp lookout in 1930, the first permanent structure didn't arrive until 1950. The 2-story 9x9' frame cab was moved second-hand to the summit from a Fish & Wildlife observatory on Lincoln Mtn. In 1962, the present 10' concrete base with R-6 flat cab was built. The lookout is now on the rental program.

name: Porphyry Lookout
loc:
Helena-Lewis and Clark National Forest 
                    Cascade County, Montana
desc: First developed in 1937 with a 40' pole L-4 tower, the present 40' treated timber tower with R-6 flat cab replaced it in 1960. It is staffed every summer.

name: Hogback Mountain Lookout
loc:
Helena-Lewis and Clark National Forest 
                    Lewis and Clark County, Montana
desc: Established with an L-4 cab in 1936, the present R-6 flat cab atop a 10' concrete base, built in 1961, may be staffed in the summer.

name: Rogers Mountain Lookout
loc:
Central Land Office 
                    Lewis and Clark County, Montana
admin: Montana Department of Natural Resources and Conservation
desc: A latecomer to the lookout age, this 2-story hip-roofed live-in cab, built in 1978, is available for emergencies.

name: Willow Mountain Lookout
loc:
Bitterroot National Forest 
                    Ravalli County, Montana
desc: This 10' concrete base with R-6 flat cab, built in 1966, is staffed nearly every summer. It may have replaced Palisade Mtn. L.O. located 2 miles southeast.

name: Patrol Mountain Lookout
loc:
Helena-Lewis and Clark National Forest 
                    Lewis & Clark County, Montana
desc: A camp was established here in 1923, followed by a log cabin in 1925. The present R-6 flat cab, built in 1962, is staffed in the summer.

name: Prairie Reef Lookout
loc:
Helena-Lewis and Clark National Forest 
                    Lewis & Clark County, Montana
desc: First developed with a camp lookout in the 1920's, an L-4 cab was built in 1931. The present R-6 flat cab, built in 1968, is staffed every summer.

name: Beartop Lookout
loc:
Helena-Lewis and Clark National Forest 
                    Teton County, Montana
desc: This site started as a camp in 1928 and was followed, in 1933 at a cost of $650, by the current L-4. A throwback to the early days of lookouts and the Forest Service, this is the first and only lookout structure ever to occupy this space and is the only, usually staffed, original L-4 lookout in the Bob Marshall Wilderness Complex.

name: Jocko #2 Lookout
loc:
Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribe 
                    Missoula County, Montana
desc: A 40' treated timber tower with R-6 flat cab was built in 1969.

name: Pistol Creek Lookout
loc:
Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribe 
                    Lake County, Montana
desc: Originally constructed at another site, this 53' treated timber tower with R-6 flat cab, built here in 1970, is staffed during the summer.

name: Ferry Basin Lookout
loc:
Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribe 
                    Sanders County, Montana
desc: About 1935, a 14x14' cabin was built. This was replaced by the present 20' treated timber tower flat cab in the 1970's. It is staffed every summer.

name: Camel's Hump Lookout
loc:
Lolo National Forest 
                    Mineral County, Montana
desc: The first lookout here was a 20' pole tower with L-4 cab built in 1935. This was replaced by the present 41' treated timber tower with R-6 cab in 1960. It is staffed every summer.

name: Monture Hill Lookout
loc:
Private Property 
                    Powell County, Montana
desc: A 30' pole tower with open-air 5x5' cab was built about 1935, replaced by the present 30' pole L-4 tower in 1945 by the Blackfoot-Clearwater Timber Protective Association. It was unused for many years and is now abandoned. There is no public access to the site.

name: Monument Peak Lookout
loc:
Fort Belknap Tribe 
                    Blaine County, Montana
desc: Built sometime on the early 1930s, little else is know about this cupola based lookout.

name: Jackson Ranger Station Lookout
loc:
Private Property 
                    Beaverhead County, Montana
desc: Built sometime in the 1930s, this platform atop garage is still there but is now on private property.

name: Wisdom Ranger Station Lookout
loc:
Beaverhead-Deer Lodge National Forest 
                    Beaverhead County, Montana
desc: This platform atop the ranger station warehouse was built in the 1930's and is still there.

name: Alder Ridge Lookout
loc:
Eldorado National Forest 
                    El Dorado County, California
desc: Overlooking the South Fork American River Canyon on the Eldorado National Forest, Alder Ridge Lookout was constructed by the CCC in 1936. It is a 60’ Aermotor tower with a 7’x7’ metal cab. In 2004 a Passport In Time project restoring the tower and ground residence was completed.

name: Allen Lookout
loc: San Mateo County, California
admin: California Department of Forestry & Fire Protection
desc:
Allen Lookout was originally built as an air traffic control tower at Salinas Army Air Base. It was moved to this location in 1966 by inmate labor. The tower was closed in 1981. It replaced a 1941 wooden lookout, remnants of which remain as a utility building on the site. 
 The tower features an open steel X-braced tower. It is 22' 7" by 22' 7" at its base an 51" 6" high. The 225-square foot metal frame cab has a pyramidal hip roof. The tower is now surrounded by heavy foliage on all sides.

name: American Camp Lookout
loc:
Stanislaus National Forest 
                    Tuolumne County, California
desc: This 60' steel tower features a 7'x7' cab. It was built in 1930 by the California Department of Forestry and operated until 1969. It is abandoned and managed as a standing ruin today.

name: Angora Ridge Lookout
loc:
Lake Tahoe Basin Management Unit 
                    El Dorado County, California
desc: Angora Ridge Lookout is now closed but still stands although trees now block part of the view. The site, which first went into service in 1914, is managed by the Lake Tahoe Basin Management Unit (USFS). It is unique in that all three lookout ground houses built there over the years have been maintained and retain their original designs.

name: Annette Lookout
loc: Kern County, California
desc: Annette Lookout was constructed by the Kern County Fire Department in 1939. The design is unique to the county. The structure was generally intact during a visit in 2009. The roof has since blown off and the structure is in a serious state of decay.

name: Antelope Mountain Lookout
loc:
Lassen National Forest 
                    Lassen County, California
desc: Antelope Peak was first used as a lookout in the early 1900s and a two-story structure was constructed by the CCC in 1933. The current tower -- a unique design -- was built in 1975 as a joint project between NASA, the Department of Energy and the U.S. Forest Service. Still in active use, it has the distinction of being the first lookout in the U.S. to be fully equipped with solar power.

name: Anthony Peak Lookout
loc:
Mendocino National Forest 
                    Mendocino County, California
desc: Built in 1932, Anthony Peak Lookout is a L-4 pyramid roof design. The wooden 14’x14 live-in cab with catwalk sits atop a 10’ wood tower that was enclosed in 1941 for year-long staffing as an enemy aircraft warning station during World War II. The lookout, which remains active, was restored in 1993 through the cooperative efforts of the U.S. Forest Service and the Twin Rocks Landowners Association.

name: Argentine Rock Lookout
loc:
Plumas National Forest 
                    Plumas County, California
desc: Scenically perched on a rocky peak on the Mt. Hough Ranger District of the Plumas National Forest, Argentine Rock Lookout was in active service until 1980. Construction on the 11' enclosed tower with C-3 cab and catwalk was begun in 1934 and first staffed in 1936.

name: Armstrong Hill Lookout
loc:
Eldorado National Forest 
                    El Dorado County, California
desc: Armstrong Hill is an Aermotor 7x7 Observation only cabin atop an 80 foot X-Brace open steel tower. The site was furnished with a BC-201 Fireman-Lookout Cabin for the operator's residence.

name: Babbit Peak Lookout
loc:
Tahoe National Forest 
                    Sierra County, California
desc: One of the classic “Dunce Cap” lookout cabs, Babbit Peak Lookout on the Tahoe National Forest is a prime example of a California region design with a steep roof pitch developed in 1923 and copied by other Forest Service regions throughout the U.S. although very few examples remain.  In Oregon the design is known as the “Supervisor Hall Special.” Most of the D-5 cabs had a lower roof pitch. In good condition, the station is an active detection site.

name: Baker Point Lookout
loc:
Sequoia National Forest 
                    Tulare County, California
desc:
It is hard to find a more beautiful lookout location than Baker Point on the Sequoia National Forest in California's southern Sierras. Originally reached only by a difficult trail (two mules were killed during construction in 1950), The current hike from the trailhead is 2 miles and relatively easy. 
 Baker Point Lookout offers spectacular views. Currently used only in emergencies and still a key radio repeater site, the 14' x 14' BC-301 cab with catwalk is on a 20' wooden tower. 
 An adjacent ground house was built in 1943 for likely Aircraft Warning Service use during WWII.

name: Bald Mountain Lookout
loc:
Butte County, California 
                    Butte County, California
admin: California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection (Cal Fire)
desc: Original (1934) CCC era lookout built for USFS was transferred to CDF in the late 1950s. In 1973 the BC-3 cab was replaced by a 732-6A type cab design. The remodel is Plan Number 757-lA. Facility record's correspondence states that except for page one, cab plans were "the same as used on previous lookouts; for example, Fredonyer Lookout." Staffed as needed.

name: Bald Mountain Lookout
loc:
Eldorado National Forest 
                    El Dorado County, California
desc: There have been four stations at Bald Mountain Lookout on the Eldorado National Forest. The current lookout is a CL-100 14’x14’ metal live-in cab on a 30’ steel tower.

name: Bald Mountain Lookout
loc:
Inyo National Forest 
                    Mono County, California
desc: One of only two lookouts remaining in the southern eastern Sierra, the original Bald Mountain Lookout structure was built in 1943 by the Civilian Public Service, an agency following the CCC staffed by conscientious objectors of World War II. The current 16’ x 40’ concrete block lookout with 10’ x 10’ steel cab was built by the lnyo National Forest in 1963. Besides lookout quarters, the base includes two garages and a storage room.

name: Bald Mountain Lookout
loc:
Sequoia National Forest 
                    Tulare County, California
desc: The CL metal 14' x 14' cab with corrugated flat roof may not be the most attractive lookout in the woods, but the 1950s design has proven to be durable. When the Sequoia National Forest replaced the Bald Mountain Lookout in 1954, materials for the cab and the 40' Aermotor tower were hauled in by the mule train. The road did not reach the 9430' mountain for another decade. Historically, a "lightning rod," it is still in active service, and often used to relay fire traffic for the BLM and the Inyo National Forest.

name: Bald Mountain Lookout
loc:
Sierra National Forest 
                    Fresno County, California
desc: First there was a cabin at Bald Mountain Lookout on the Sierra National Forest dating to 1905 and one of the first in the state.  It was replaced in 1911 by a wooden tower, and the current 20' H-brace metal tower was built in 1934.

name: Baldy Mountain Lookout
loc:
Klamath National Forest 
                    Siskiyou County, California
admin: US Forest Service - Klamath National Forest
desc:
Baldy Mountain or Happy Camp Baldy Lookout is a California Region 5 Plan BC-301 on a 10 foot enclosed timber tower. 
 The lookout was constructed in 1938 and is not currently staffed.

name: Ball Mountain Lookout
loc:
Klamath National Forest 
                    Siskiyou County, California
admin: US Forest Service - Klamath National Forest
desc: A lookout existed on the Ball Mountain site from 1922 or earlier. An open platform tower with a BC-201 Fireman Lookout Cabin was replaced in 1940 by a California Region 5 Plan BC-301 cabin atop a 30 foot enclosed timber tower.

name: Baltic Peak Lookout
loc:
Eldorado National Forest 
                    El Dorado County, California
desc:
Constructed in 1931, Baltic Peak Lookout is a 80’ Pacific Coast Steel tower with 7’x7’ metal cab. Similar to a LS-40 Aermotor tower, it is made of a lighter steel and is a significant example of a pre-CCC fire tower design. The Baltic Peak Lookout has been disassembled at its original location and moved in sections (4) to Gold Bug Park in Placerville, CA. 
 As of 2017, the city has not reassembled the lookout and was considering selling it to any interested party.

name: Banner Mountain Lookout
loc: Nevada County, California
admin: California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection - Nevada-Yuba-Placer Unit (Cal Fire NEU)
desc:
The original platform tower was constructed in 1911. 
 CDF remodeled the original 1926 Aermotor cab to accommodate the addition of a catwalk in 1961. The original lookout residence burned in 1962. The replacement house and garage were constructed in 1963-4. Although newer than the tower both buildings conform closely to what could have been erected contemporaneously with the tower. There are nine, 601 Aermotor Company towers in the CDF system. (MVF 10/91)

name: Basalt Hill Lookout
loc:
Los Banos 
                    Merced County, California
admin: Department of Forestry and Fire Protection (Cal Fire)
desc: Overlooking the San Luis Reservoir State Recreation Area, Basalt Hill Lookout was built in the 1950s. It is a 16'x16' CalFire octagonal cab on a 20' enclosed tower.

name: Bear Mountain Lookout
loc: Shasta County, California
admin: California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection - Shasta-Trinity Unit (Cal Fire SHU)
desc:
Bear Mountain (Shasta-Bear) Lookout is a Plesha design, Plan No. 1548-lA. The steel tower was erected around the original 1933,  CCC era lookout (L-601 with BC-301 cab). After demolition of the older tower and cab, the new tower was then finished off with a second story room and 732-6A type cab. This "phased" construction explains why the subject building is 90 degrees off axis. (Lookouts are generally orientated to the cardinal points). The tower is composed of square ( 9"x9"x28') steel columns which were originally intended for use in the construction of above ground, atomic bomb testing towers. This was the first tower CDF constructed using these materials. The lookout is an excellent example of a low maintenance, high vandal proof building type. 
 Shasta-Bear Mountain Lookout is located upon a southwest tending ridge that has a pronounced escarpment along its southeastern face. The area is covered in pine, oak and brush. The Bear Fire overran this location in 1990, forcing the evacuation of the lookout station. The site has restricted access, being some 5 miles from paved road, behind locked gates.

name: Bear Mountain Lookout
loc: Siskiyou County, California
admin: California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection
desc:
The tower was constructed in 1975 and is based on Plan Number 998-lA. It features 12" (diameter) steel columns for the tower legs. Cross bracing is angle iron and steel rods, caps are steel I-beams. The tower's interior walls are unfinished, the corrugated aluminum siding is attached directly to the tower's framing with no insulation. A small partition does extend part way around the sink and shower. The cab is the standard 732-6A design. The lookout is slightly off the cardinal points. This lookout has solar panels installed, with no generator back-up power (previous equipment had been struck by lightning). 
 Bear Mountain ("Siskiyou" was added by CDF to distinguish it from the other "Bears") is a distinct prominence located in the mountainous region between Mount Shasta and the Modoc Lava Flat. This station is within Siskiyou County. Vegetation is fir, pine, cedar and sage brush. The location has been a favorite "hang out" for porcupines. The tenacious little creatures have eaten up automotive break linings, belts, hoses and even chewed on the tires. A number of the critters have been dispatched with traps and more "permanent" solutions in order to quell the vandalism. The battle continues. The station is some 6 miles from paved road. (MVT 10/91) 
 The lookout has been occasionally staffed by US Forest Service personnel.

name: Bear Mountain Lookout
loc: Fresno County, California
admin: California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection - Cal Fire Fresno-Kings Unit (FKU)
desc:
The 60 foot tower and 7x7 observation only cab is an Aermotor Company product, possibly erected as early as 1927. The house was built by the CCC's and is based on the Forest Service BC-201 plan. The garage is also a CCC era building. This detection site was initially a State-Federal cooperative lookout. The residence has the highest integrity of the five BC-201 buildings still left in CDF ownership. The interior has few alterations (chiefly the installation of bathroom facilities and newer kitchen counter tops). Siding, windows, flooring, paneling, cabinets and roofing are either original or like original. The associated garage is also near original. During the 1950s, CDF allowed the Weather Modification Company to install a flat roof on the tower's cab for the private firm's instruments. (This "sun deck" saw enthusiastic use by lookout operators, low flying aircraft dubbed the station "Bare Mountain"). 
 Bear Mountain is a distinctive prominence north of the State Highway 180/Squaw Valley area. Vegetation is oak woodland and brush. The lookout is not readily accessible to the public, being over 4 miles behind a locked gate. A paved road leads to the station. This is an intensively used communications site (with significant electromagnetic radiation). (MVT 10/91) 
 As of 2007, the garage and residence cabin had been removed.

name: Big Hill Lookout
loc:
Eldorado National Forest 
                    El Dorado County, California
desc: Located in the heart of the Eldorado National Forest, Big Hill Lookout is a center of fire control operations. The original 14’x14’ lookout of 1935 on a 23’ tower was burned by the disastrous Cleveland Fire of 1992. The current 14’x14’ cab with catwalk was built in 1993 along with an attractive groundhouse residence. There is also a seasonal helicopter air attack base on the site. The lookout and base are both active in fire season.

name: Big Hill Lookout
loc:
Hoopa Indian Reservation 
                    Humboldt County, California
desc:
Very little is known about Big Hill Lookout. Apparently built in the 1930's according to Thornton's 1986 survey. Big Hill was the only structure noted in the survey to have been built by the Bureau of Indian Affairs in California. 
 The design is similar to Green Mountain Lookout located in Mariposa County, a 1942 CDF built structure.

name: Black Fox Mountain Lookout
loc:
Shasta-Trinity National Forest 
                    Siskiyou County, California
admin: US Forest Service - Shasta-Trinity National Forest
desc:
The current Black Fox Mountain Lookout was constructed in 1939. The cabin is a California Region 4 Plan BC-301 on a 30 foot enclosed timber tower. 
 This structure replaced a California Region 5 Plan 4AR on an open K-brace steel tower.

name: Black Mountain Lookout
loc:
Fresno County 
                    Fresno County, California
admin: California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection - Fresno Kings Unit (Cal Fire FKU)
desc: The CCC built this lookout for the Sierra National Forest in 1934. CDF assumed sole operation of the lookout in 1952, adding the room beneath the cab soon thereafter. The stairway was recently replaced with a nearly free standing structure adjacent to the lookout tower. It radically alters the traditional appearance of this facility. This is the only L-SOl in the CDF&FP fire detection system with the original BC-301 cab. (MVT 10/91)

name: Black Mountain Lookout
loc:
Plumas National Forest 
                    Plumas County, California
desc: Constructed in 1934 by the CCC, Black Mountain Lookout is a classic C3 14’x14’ live-in cab with catwalk of an original Forest Service R-5 design (California Region). It is mounted on an 11’ enclosed timber tower and located on the Plumas National Forest. Black Mt. L.O. Grand opening on the Plumas National Forest is open as a recreational rental effective May 26, 2011. The fee is $60 per night stay.

name: Black Mountain Lookout
loc:
San Bernardino National Forest 
                    Riverside County, California
desc:
The newest lookout on the ldyllwild Ranger District of the San Bernardino National Forest in southern California was built on Black Mountain in 1962. It is 14’x 14’ CL-100 steel cab with flat corrugated metal roof and metal mesh catwalk, located on top of a solid rock outcrop. In active use through the 1980s, it was restored by the Forest Service and volunteers in the Lookout Host Program, and is now staffed by Lookout Hosts seven days a week. 
 The San Jacinto Ranger District was a part of the Cleveland National Forest until 1926. The original structure at Black Mountain was a California Region 5 Plan 4AR cabin on a 10 foot open timber tower built in the late 19-teens or early 1920's. The structure was moved to Barton Peak in 1934. This location was discontinued when the new lookout was completed at Black Mountain in 1962.

name: Black Rock Mountain Lookout
loc:
Shasta-Trinity National Forest 
                    Trinity County, California
admin: US Forest Service - Shasta-Trinity National Forest
desc:
Black Rock Mountain was constructed in 1935 for the Trinity National Forest. The structure is a California Region 5 Plan BC-301 cabin on a 20 foot open timber tower. 
 The structure is in poor condition but still stands as of 2017.

name: Blacks Ridge Lookout
loc:
Lassen National Forest 
                    Lassen County, California
admin: US Forest Service - Lassen National Forest
desc:
Blacks Ridge Lookout is an Aermotor 45 foot X-Brace open steel tower with a 7x7 foot observation only cab. The tower was constructed in 1934. 
 A California Region 5 Plan BC-201 Fireman Lookout cabin was constructed in 1938 as a residence for the lookout operator.

name: Bloomer Hill Lookout
loc:
Plumas National Forest 
                    Butte County, California
admin: California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection
desc: Financed and built cooperatively between the US Forest Service, The California Division of Forestry and Butte County. The tower, an Aermotor Company product, is believed to have been erected in 1925. The cab modification took place in 1959. The CCC era BC-201 residence was replaced by the CDF in 1973. The house's planning number is 660. There are nine, 60' Aermotor Company towers in the CDF&FP fire detection system. All of CDF&FP's Aermotor Company cabs have had catwalks added, windows replaced and catwalk access doors installed.

name: Blue Mountain Fire Lookout
loc:
Stanislaus National Forest 
                    Calaveras County, California
desc:
The subject building replaced a CCC era lookout. The site was originally a primary fire detection point for the Stanislaus National Forest. The existing structure is based on CDF Plan No. 809RA, a variation of the traditional 809R plans. This is the only single story 809R tower in California. The building is in excellent condition and has undergone few alterations since its erection. The cab's interior boast of two beautiful oil paintings. The two landscapes were painted on the walls by a former lookout operator. A 240 sq. ft., wood frame garage is located next to the parking area, below the lookout tower. This building has a concrete slab foundation, asbestos tile siding and wood shingles on a gable roof. A small pump house and redwood water storage tank are located on the west side of the summit. 
 Blue Mountain is a large, southwest tending ridge located north of the South Fork of the Mokelumne River. The lookout is perched upon a sharp peak, with steep topography on all sides. The area is heavily timbered in pine, fir, cedar and oak. A radio vault and tower are southeast of the lookout. The station is 16 miles from paved road, access is restricted. (MVT 10/91) 
 Calaveras Ranger District, 6,071' elevation - The Forest Service leased 1 acre of property on Blue Mountain in 1914 for the purpose of a fire lookout and supply station. Originally established prior to 1908, the first permanent lookout was built in 1911 from wood from the first Calaveras Ranger Station.he Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC) built the second lookout in 1934. Cal Fire now operates the current lookout, built in 1966. (Stanislaus National Forest)

name: Blue Mountain Lookout
loc:
Modoc National Forest 
                    Modoc County, California
admin: US Forest Service - Modoc National Forest
desc:
The original structure, a California Region 5 - 4AR design on a 20 foot steel tower was completed in October 1929. 
 The current lookout, a CL-100 design was constructed and completed in October 1962 at a cost of $20,314. 
 The lookout is currently staffed during the fire season.

name: Blue Ridge Lookout
loc:
Klamath National Forest 
                    Siskiyou County, California
desc: Located in the Klamath National Forest in northern California, Blue Ridge Lookout is unusual in that it is one of only three 80’ Aermotor towers with 7’x7’ cabs constructed in the state. The site was used during the Second World War as an Aircraft Warning Station and is still staffed each year for fire detection.

name: Bolivar Lookout
loc:
Klamath National Forest 
                    Siskiyou County, California
admin: US Forest Service - Klamath National Forest
desc:
Bolivar Lookout is located on Craggy Peak. The cabin is a CL-100 all steel design on a 9 foot block tower and replaced the previous structure in 1960. The roof had blown off the original structure, it was replaced by a temporary tent and construction commenced on the new structure in late 1960. 
 The previous cab was a California Region 5 Plan BC-302 that was in place prior to 1939. The Southern Pacific Railroad deeded the property to the Forest Service in 1939.

name: Bonanza King Lookout
loc:
Shasta-Trinity National Forest 
                    Trinity County, California
admin: US Forest Service - Shasta-Trinity National Forest
desc:
Bonanza King is a California Region 5 Plan 4AR built in 1934. A very late use of this design.  
 An Aircraft Warning Service residence cabin was added in WWII so the lookout could be staffed 24 hours a day.

name: Boucher Hill Lookout
loc:
Palomar Mountain State Park 
                    San Diego County, California
admin: California Department of Parks and Recreation - Palomar Mountain State Park
desc:
The California state lookout on Boucher Hill located in Palomar Mountain State Park (which is located adjacent to the Cleveland National Forest) was constructed in 1948 but has been inactive since 1983. The structure is an excellent example of the CDF 809R design on a 30 foot enclosed, K-brace tower with a 15x15 octagonal cab. The lookout is 1 of only 3 remaining examples of the pre-1950 unique, California only design. Boucher Hill has hosted a fire lookout since the early 1920’s. The original structure was a small, observation only cab on a 20-30 ft tower built by the Forest Service. This lookout was replaced in 1934 with an enclosed 30 ft wood tower and a 14x14 4AR cab. The lookout and site were transferred to the California Department of Forestry (CDF) in 1936. The current 1948 tower was updated in 1973 with aluminum siding and new windows in the lower tower living quarters. 
 A substantial structural stabilization/restoration project was completed by CAL FIRE and DGS during 2011-12 as mitigation for potential impacts to the lookout (an historic building) associated with a communication facility replacement project. The planning and design phase of the project included reviewing the original 809R model lookout tower plans as well as following the technical advice of the DPR historian assigned to the project who made key decisions during the project that ensured the historical integrity of the structure was retained. In this manner the repairs all conformed to applicable guidance included in the Secretary of Interior’s Standards for Treatment of Historic Properties. 
 Forest Fire Lookout Association volunteers staff the lookout to provide fire detection and an interpretive experience for park visitors. The lookout is staffed every day during fire season.

name: Branch Mountain Lookout
loc:
Los Padres National Forest  
                    San Luis Obispo County, California
admin: US Forest Service - Los Padres National Forest
desc:
Branch Mountain Lookout was built in 1935. The structure is a California Region 5 Plan BC-301 on a 30 foot K-Brace open steel tower. 
 Branch Mountain was last staffed in 1992 according to it's logbook entries. The small ground cabin is noted in Thornton's 1986 Survey as a WWII Aircraft Warning Service built structure.  
 The lookout site is completely surrounded by private property and is not accessible to the public. Be sure to read Bob Burd's interesting Trip Report on the 'Links' tab.

name: Breckenridge Lookout
loc:
Sequoia National Forest 
                    Kern County, California
desc: The original tower at Breckenridge Lookout on the Sequoia National Forest was built in 1912 as a tree stand with a small, partially-enclosed cab. It was replaced in 1938 with a wooden tower with an L-4 cab. The present L-4 with catwalk on a 40' steel tower was constructed in 1942. Used as an aircraft warning site in World War II, the lookout is in active service.

name: Brush Mountain Lookout
loc:
Six Rivers National Forest 
                    Humboldt County, California
desc: This lookout was built in 1979.

name: Buck Rock Lookout
loc:
Sequoia National Forest 
                    Tulare County, California
desc: The 4A style 14’x 14’ lookout was built from 1917 to 1923 when it was replaced by the 4AR model. Buck Rock Lookout, constructed on the Sequoia National Forest in 1923, is one of only three 4As remaining. It is reached via a suspended flight of stairs.

name: Buckhorn Bally Lookout
loc:
Klamath National Forest 
                    Siskiyou County, California
admin: US Forest Service - Klamath National Forest
desc:
Buckhorn Bally Lookout is a Region 1 revision of the Region 5 BC-301 on a 13 foot enclosed timber tower, built in 1933. 
  The Aircraft Warning Service used the Lookout for an observation post during the winter of 1942.

name: Bully Choop Lookout
loc: Shasta County, California
desc: Located on the western edge of the Whiskeytown National Recreation Area in northern California, Bully Choop Lookout takes its name from the Indian phrase “Bo-li Chu-ip,” which means “high sharp peak.” Built by the California Dept. of Forestry and Fire Control in 1978, it replaced an earlier lookout dating from the 1930s. It is the first on the Register of a unique and durable CDF design. The 14 x 14’ live-in cab has slanted windows. The slightly gable roof extends over the catwalk for a permanent overhang/shade. The tower is 10’ steel I-beams covered with corrugated steel. Still in active service, the lookout is open to the public via a 14-mile road.

name: Bunker Hill Lookout
loc:
Eldorado National Forest 
                    Placer County, California
desc: Bunker Hill Lookout is a one-of-a-kind structure built by Joe Bauman who was a long time Forest Service employee in 1942. The original station on the Eldorado National Forest was a 14’x14’ live-in R-5 cab. Later it was one of three sites selected to receive this special stone tower (the other two are on the Lassen and the Los Padres National Forests).

name: Burney Mountain Lookout
loc:
Lassen National Forest 
                    Shasta County, California
admin: US Forest Service - Lassen National Forest
desc:
Burney Mountain hosted a lookout structure prior to 1936. The original structure was a California Region 5 Plan BC-301 on a 10 foot enclosed timber tower. 
 A new lookout replaced the original structure, a Plan CL-100 13x13 cab on 10 foot block tower in 1966.

name: Butler Peak Lookout
loc:
San Bernardino National Forest 
                    San Bernardino County, California
desc:
One of the crown jewels of the Southern California lookouts, Butler Peak Lookout overlooks Big Bear Lake and the scenic Angeles-San Bernardino Crest high country just north of the Los Angeles basin. Built by the CCC in 1933, the the cab is a Region 5 Plan BC-301 14’ x 14’ wooden ground house with catwalk is perched on a rock outcrop. 
 A very popular tourist destination, the tower is staffed by volunteers, and is normally open from Memorial Day weekend to Labor Day weekend, sometimes past Labor Day weather permitting. The normal "open" tower hours are every day from 9:00 am to 5:00 pm. Most likely there will be volunteers there to welcome you and share the "tower" experience, but if the tower is closed due to no volunteers to fill the schedule, you can still go up to the tower. Just make the short trek to the tower, climb the stairs, and enjoy the spectacular view from the tower catwalk! 
 Bruce D. Risher served as the last paid lookout operator in 1981. The tower was taken out of service then reopened with volunteer staffing in 1986. 
 Butler Peak is again being staffed by Southern California Mountain Foundation volunteers as of August 2022 after a 3 year closure due to storm damage to the access road. 
 The Butler Peak Lookout will celebrate its 90th anniversary in 2026.

name: Cahto Peak Lookout
loc:
Mendocino National Forest 
                    Mendocino County, California
admin: California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection
desc: Cahto Peak Lookout was dedicated July 10, 1934, following construction of a road to the summit of Cahto (Signal) Peak by the U.S. Forest Service. The site is one of the highest points in Mendocino County and is easily visible from 35 miles away. The lookout has not been staffed since 1990 due to budget cuts.

name: Calandra Lookout
loc: Monterey County, California
desc: Once widespread across California, only four L-601 towers remain in the Dept. of Forestry inventory. Calandra Lookout with an BC-301 cab was constructed in 1942. The name of the mountain is actually Williams Hill. There is a stone and concrete monument at the site which has a bronze plaque that reads: "Calandra Lookout is named in memory of Assistant State Forest Ranger Joseph Calandra who saved a companion but lost his life in the Bixby Mountain Fire of 1939." In 1945 Assistant State Forest Ranger Nesgis and Edward Gates of U.S. Forest Service died in a fire within sight of this station.

name: Call Mountain Lookout
loc: San Benito County, California
admin: California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection San Benito-Monterey Unit (Cal Fire BEU)
desc:
This L-601 tower with BC-301 cab is a classic example of the 30 foot "Dutch Windmill" lookout constructed in 1935. The CCCs erected many of these structure types across California during the 1930s. There are a few alterations: aluminum sheeting, steel fire escape ladder, catwalk bracing and composition roofing added; catwalk railing and upper story staircase replaced; and some interior renovations. Metal bands along the length of the northeast tower leg were installed to arrest further checking. Restoration would enhance the original craftsmanship. In 1958, a 60 sq. ft., wood frame generator building was built next to the tower. It has a concrete slab foundation, "v" groove siding and a wood shingle covered gable roof. A 3/3 fixed window is centered on the west gable end, a replacement door is on the east end. 
 The lookout, located along the rolling summit of a northwest tending ridge, is about a mile north of the highest peak in the Call Mountains. Oak woodland predominates. A 10,000 gallon concrete water storage tank (constructed in 1967) is near the lookout. A metallic telephone line comes in from the northeast. The site is not readily accessible to the public, being about 5 miles from paved road, behind locked gates. (MVT 10/91)

name: Calpine Hill Lookout
loc:
Tahoe National Forest 
                    Sierra County, California
desc: A beautifully restored classic California design, Calpine Hill Lookout is an example of a Tahoe National Forest ranger district seeking partnerships to keep important lookouts.  Built in 1934 by the CCC, it is a C-3 14’x14’ wooden cab with catwalk on an enclosed 17’ tower.  Living quarters are on the first landing.

name: Camp Six Lookout at Bear Basin Butte
loc:
Six Rivers National Forest 
                    Del Norte County, California
desc: The original lookout on Bear Basin Butte was built in 1924 but was struck by lightning and burned in 1936. The Camp Six Lookout was constructed by the CCC in 1934 on Upper Coon Mountain. In the l950s the site was compromised with a number of electronic facilities and the lookout decommissioned. Restoration of the Camp Six began in 1991, but vandals soon damaged the lookout further, causing the Forest Service to remove, rebuild, and relocate it at the Bear Basin Butte site. Administered by the Smith River National Recreation Area, it is a popular site within the recreation cabin rental system.

name: Castro Peak Lookout
loc:
Henninger Flats Forestry Unit 
                    Los Angeles County, California
admin: County of Los Angeles Fire Department, Forestry Division
desc:
Built in 1925 on Castro Peak, the highest point in the Malibu Hills west of Los Angeles at coordinates N 34.085989 W 118.785362, Castro Peak Lookout was an 8'x8'-foot metal cab on a 22-foot tower. It was built and operated by the Los Angeles County Forestry Department until it went out of service in 1971. In approximately 1978, it was moved to L.A. County Fire Department’s Henninger Flats Forestry Unit, which occupies an island of county property in the Angeles National Forest on the south slope of Mt. Wilson, site of an historic observatory. At Henninger Flats, the tower was refurbished, stocked with 1925 period artifacts, and mounted on a 7-foot tower as a historic public education display, and part of the Forestry Unit’s visitor center/museum. 
 In 2025 the Los Angeles Country Fire Departrment dismantled the lookout at the Henninger site.  Their intention is to erect it on the Los Angeles County Fairgrounds (Fairplex) in Pomona, California.  There it will be part of the America’s Great Outdoors exhibit area, along with the former Johnstone Peak Lookout. 
 Additional information on the 1925 location can be found at the Former Fire Lookout Registry  website .
agency: County of Los Angeles Fire Dep

name: Chalone Peak Lookout
loc:
Pinnacles National Park 
                    Monterey County, California
desc:
Chalone Peak Lookout was built by the California Department of Forestry in what was then Pinnacles National Monument in 1952. Ownership was transferred to the National Park Service in 1990. The 16' x 16' octagonal wood cab sits atop a 20' steel tower enclosed with aluminum siding. Built in 1952, the cab is the oldest of the revised 809R design in CDF's collection. The revision features plate glass windows set on an angle to reduce glare. 
 As of 2018, the National Park Service has prepared a preliminary estimate of the cost to restore the tower. $200,000 is needed to stabilize the structure, but no funding has been identified.

name: Chews Ridge Lookout
loc:
Los Padres National Forest 
                    Monterey County, California
desc: Chews Ridge Lookout on the Los Padres National Forest was built in 1924 on a 12’ metal tower.  The cab was destroyed by fire in 1977 and rebuilt in 1978.  It was replaced in 1984 with an R-6 Flat design.  The tower was taken out of service approximately 1990.

name: Colby Mountain Lookout
loc:
Lassen National Forest 
                    Tehama County, California
desc: Twenty five miles south of Lassen National Park stands Colby Mountain Lookout in the Lassen National Forest. The first lookout on the site was built in 1912 and replaced by the CCC in 1934. The 14' x 14' L-4 cab with catwalk sits atop a 30' steel tower.  This lookout also has a commanding view of the south face of the Mt. Lassen National Volcanic Park to the north and the Ishi Wilderness to the west. Still in active service, it is open from June until late October.

name: Cold Spring Mountain Lookout
loc: Mendocino County, California
desc:
Cold Spring Lookout is a CDF 809R cab with an enclosed 29' steel tower. The 1965 station has been closed and is in good condition. 
 The lookout cabin is the post 1950 design with angled windows. It was last staffed in 1990.

name: Collins Creek Baldy Lookout
loc:
Klamath National Forest 
                    Siskiyou County, California
admin: US Forest Service - Klamath National Forest
desc: Collins Creek Baldy was constructed for the Klamath National Forest in 1934, a California Region 5 Plan BC-301 cabin on a 20 foot  enclosed timber tower.

name: Cone Peak Lookout
loc:
Los Padres National Forest 
                    Monterey County, California
desc:
The original 13 X 13 wooden cab ground house on a rock foundation had a hipped "dunce cap" roof, and was called a "California Lookout" design. It was hauled up the two-mile steep and narrow trail in pieces by mules. With its coastal location, it served the Aircraft Warning Service during World War II. The roof was replaced with a flat roof in 1959, which could accommodate landing a Bell-47 helicopter. The wooden sides were subsequently replaced with metal siding, which has well protected the structure from fires and vandalism. The last known lookout to staff the facility worked there until 1990. 
 As of 2018, the cab is being used to hold radio repeater equipment. Because of this, the tower cannot immediately be reactivated for fire tower usage.

name: Copernicus Peak Lookout
loc: Santa Clara County, California
admin: California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection - Santa Clara Unit (Cal Fire SCU)
desc: The original lookout was erected on top of the watter tank in 1931.

name: Cottonwood Pass Fire Station and Lookout
loc: Kings County, California
admin: California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection
desc:
This building is the only one of its kind. (Vina Helitack, similar in appearance, is a wood frame version of this building.) This combination fire station and lookout is CDF Plan 804, according to notes from a 1991 evaluation by Mark V. Thornton. A 10,000 gallon concrete water storage tank remains. The lookout is known to have been in operation in the early 1980's but is now abandoned and has been partially open to the elements and roosting birds. One former CDF Captain, once stationed there, said they put their bedposts in coffee cans to keep scorpions from climbing. Another former firefighter assigned there said that the on-duty personnel would take turns up in the tower while on (engine) shifts. 
 Three former CDF firefighters shared these anecdotes about their time at Cottonwood Pass: 
  David Hosler:  I use to sleep outside on the water tank. When the lights went out in the barracks, there were so many crickets it sounded like the cricket tub in a bait shop. 
  Mike Snyder:  I worked there in 1985. Cottonwood had been closed for a couple of years but CDF decided to reopen that summer. It was a busy season so we were gone a lot. When we were there we were on death patrol for removing, snakes, scorpions, rats , mice and crickets! 
  Marsha Colby:  I worked at Cottonwood Pass as a seasonal firefighter during the bicentennial year of 1976. Many years of drought left the grass out there very sparse to say the least. Therefore there were almost no veg fires in our response area. We did go to the propane loading dock fire in Avenal. We did not man the lookout that year and it was shuttered most of the time unless Sanger called us to get a cross on another lookout reading or to verify a report. Weather watching from on top of the water tank was awesome. You could watch the thunderheads form. Water came from Coalinga in a water tender once a week. So we conserved or we might go without. One day late in the season I was in the kitchen and heard a strange noise outside and went out the kitchen door and walked over to about 8 feet from the flag pole. About that time the flag pole got hit by lightning. I hustled back inside and changed shorts. It started raining and about 2 days later I was out of a job. Fond memories of the scorpions and the rest of the desert critters out there.

name: Crane Flat Lookout
loc:
Yosemite National Park 
                    Mariposa and Toulumne Counties, California
desc: The first permanent lookout in Yosemite National Park, Crane Flat was built by the NPS in 1931 before the CCC. It and Henness Ridge are fine examples of the Park Service Rustic Architecture. The first story with garage is of stone, topped with a 13’ x 13’ wooden cab with catwalk.

name: Cuyama Peak Lookout
loc:
Los Padres National Forest 
                    Ventura County, California
desc:
Built in 1934, Cuyama Peak Lookout is a modified L-4 atop a 20’ steel “H” braced tower. The Los Padres National forest site was also used by the Aircraft Warning Service in World War II. The AWS cabin is one of only four remaining in California. 
 Updated images show the lookout cab has collapsed on the tower platform. The AWS cabin has collapsed and is a debris pile now. Cuyama Peak Lookout will be added to the Former Fire Lookout Sites listings.

name: Deadwood Peak Lookout
loc:
Sierra National Forest 
                    Madera County, California
admin: California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection
desc:
The tower and cab were constructed by the Civilian Conservation Corps for the Sierra National Forest. CDF took over the site in 1950 and added the "Cook's Quarters" (utility room below the cab) in 1952. Building materials complimentary to the cab were used for this addition. Thus, the structure is still highly reflective of its CCC roots. Minor alterations include: aluminum siding, composition roofing, and guard rail additions; shutter replacement; and various interior revisions. A steel fire escape ladder is on the north side of the tower. The utility room houses a water pump system, refrigerator, bedding and storage cabinets. A 300 gallon concrete water storage tank is at the base of the tower. CDF has only two L-401 towers. 
 Deadwood Peak is situated upon the apex of Potter Ridge. The five mile long, southeasterly tending summit is located to the southwest of Oakhurst. The area around the lookout station is predominate in oak woodland, with brush and pine intermix on the lower mountain slopes. There are microwave dishes on the lookout and radio vaults and towers at this site. The area is not readily accessible to the public, being some 4.5 miles from paved road, behind locked gates.

name: Delilah Lookout
loc:
Sequoia National Forest 
                    Fresno County, California
desc: While operational only during high fire danger in recent years, Delilah Lookout on the Sequoia National Forest has been a detection site since 1916. In 1924 a tower with a ground residence went into service until 1959. The present 40' metal tower with live-in cab was moved to the site in 1967 from Lenore Naval Air Base.

name: Digger Butte Lookout
loc:
Lassen National Forest 
                    Tehama County, California
desc:
Digger Butte Lookout was built in 1936 and underwent few modifications. The 20' L-401 tower was one of only two remaining in the state system. It supported a BC-301 wood frame cab. The lookout was removed in 2009. Its cab was placed in storage. 
  2012 Update: The Digger Butte lookout tower and cab will be preserved through relocation of the lookout to the CAL FIRE Mobile Equipment Facility in Davis where it will be restored and opened to the public. The garage and out-buildings will not be preserved. Due to the ongoing State budget crisis, a schedule for completion of actions can not be made with certainty but the project has already begun with the intention of being completed by January 1, 2015. Specific actions CAL FIRE intends to undertake to complete the tasks of preserve and maintain the lookout tower and cab:  
   Disassemble the remaining steel tower structure and relocate it to Davis, California.  Prepare the new site location and pour a new tower footing.  Reconstruct the steel tower.  Rebuild the tower cab.  
  Once the lookout has been successfully relocated and reassembled, the CAL FIRE Tehama-Glenn Unit will place the historic fire-finder plotting device and a log book from the 1970’s to 1988 which contains many signatures from those who have visited the lookout when it was in operation. In addition, an old CAL FIRE historic weather station from another lookout (Eagle Peak Lookout also in Tehama County) has been saved so it too may be relocated and utilized there as another way of highlighting the history and usage of fire lookouts in California. The fire-finder, logbook, and old weather station are presently being stored at the Tehama-Glenn Unit Headquarters. (First Ten-Year Update to theCalifornia Department of Forestry and Fire Protection Management Plan for Historic Buildings and Archaeological Sites - 2012)

name: Dixie Mountain Lookout
loc:
Plumas National Forest 
                    Plumas County, California
admin: US Forest Service - Plumas National Forest
desc:
Dixie Mountain is a rare, surviving California Region 5 - Plan 4AR design. Built in 1928 on an enclosed 10 foot timber tower. 
 Dixie Mountain continues to be staffed during the fire season.

name: Don Landon Lookout
loc: Lassen County, California
admin: California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection - Lassen-Modoc Unit (Cal Fire LMU)
desc:
Don Landon Lookout was constructed in 1974, replaced an older structure, which had been erected in 1948. That building was dedicated to the memory of Donald A. Landon, a "State Forest Ranger and Soldier who died on a battlefield in Europe on October 6, 1944." The detection site covers territory once protected by the Shaffer Mountain Lookout Station, located east of Susanville. That lookout was closed in the early 1950s. The existing Don Landon Lookout is based on Plan Number 880-lA. The tower plan is the same as Fredonyer's. Landon's tower plans reference Plan Number 350 (Pattymocus) for cab details. The cab is essentially a 732-6A design. 
 An older garage stands next to this lookout. The 240 sq. ft., wood frame building has a concrete slab foundation, replacement plywood siding and asphalt composition roofing. The doors (located on the northwest end) appear to be original 
 The subject station is located upon Greens Peak, which is part of a southeast tending ridge situated to the south of Eagle Lake. There are large fire scars in the vicinity of this peak. Local vegetation is brush, sage, pine and fir. The site is not readily accessible to the public, being about 4 miles from paved road. (MVT 10/91) 
  The original structure was opened on September 4, 1949 and named in honor of Don Landon, a California State Forester who was killed in World War II. (Tim Purdy Presents)

name: Dow Butte Lookout
loc:
Lassen National Forest 
                    Lassen County, California
desc:
Dow Butte Lookout is the first to be listed in the NHLR that has been moved from its mountaintop and restored at a museum site. Originally constructed in 1939 by the CCC on the Lassen National Forest on the eastern side of the Sierras, it has a R5-C3 14’ x 14’ cab and was staffed until 1982. One of only five cabs of its kind in Region 5, it has been moved to the Eagle Lake interpretive site.
 

 
Additional Information submitted by Roger Neal, Engine Crew 1971-72:  "In 1971 the engine crew from Bogard Ranger Station rebuilt the concrete stairs from the parking lot to the base of the tower. I was one of the fire crew “mules” carrying two five gallon buckets of cement at a time, up and down over the boulders at the base.  The only good part was we started the pour from the top and it got to be a shorter carry as the day got hotter and hotter.
 

 
"The lookout was a woman retired school teacher.  She removed the door from the outhouse so that she could “enjoy the million dollar view.”  There was a single wire telephone line from the lookout to the Guard Station at Dow Wells. The station is also gone.  In 1972, the Dow Wells station was manned with an engine crew.  Since we were down in a hole, we could not receive radio communications from the dispatcher in Susanville.  The lookout  would crank the telephone which sometimes rang at the Guard station, and then relay information from dispatch.  If that didn’t work, which was a regular occurrence, she would call us on the radio.  Every spring, we had to walk the entire route of the cable, climb trees and splice repairs.  In typical USFS wisdom, we always started at the bottom of Dow Butte and hike up the butte to the lookout."

name: Duckwall Mountain Lookout
loc:
Stanislaus National Forest 
                    Tuolumne County, California
desc: This 100' steel tower with a 7'x7' cab was built by CCC workers in 1935. A BC-2 residence, still in use, is located next to the tower. The lookout is still used during emergencies.

name: Duncan Peak Lookout
loc:
Tahoe National Forest 
                    Placer County, California
desc: Located on Little Bald Mountain on the Tahoe National Forest, Duncan Peak Lookout is the third detection station on this site. The first was a 10’ tower built between 1910 and 1915. In 1917 a ground house was built just north of the current structure and dismantled in 1941. The present 14’x14’ BC-3 groundhouse with catwalk was constructed in 1943.

name: Duzel Rock Lookout
loc: Siskiyou County, California
admin: California Department of Forestry & Fire Protection
desc: Duzel Rock Lookout is part of CalFire's Siskiyou Ranger District.

name: Dyer Mountain Lookout
loc:
Lassen National Forest 
                    Lassen County, California
admin: US Forest Service - Lassen National Forest
desc:
Dyer Mountain Lookout is a California Region 5 Plan BC-301 Cabin on a 15 foot enclosed timber tower. This 1934 built structure is owned by Lassen National Forest (LNF) but used by CDF under a Special Use Permit. 
 First 10-Year Update to CAL FIRE’s Management Plan for Historic Buildings and Archaeological Sites - 2011-2012: Although the lookout is owned and used by Lassen National Forest (LNF), CAL FIRE uses the lookout and mountain top as a communication site under the terms of a Special Use Permit 
 The lower room of the lookout is currently used by CAL FIRE to house radio equipment and associated hardware. The tower has not been used as a lookout since 2007. While in use for lookout purposes, the lookout directly benefited the Almanor and Eagle Lake Ranger Districts along with the Plumas National Forests Mount Hough District when staffed. CAL FIRE does not currently staff the Dyer Lookout and has ceased any further use as a lookout due to the unsafe condition of the building and the fact that state funding to support lookouts was permanently cut approximately 15 years ago. 
 The high elevation of the site and difficulty of access during winter months has significantly impacted the condition of the tower. Guy wires to the tower are sagging on one side and taut on the other, possibly indicating structural failure. The staircase is comprised of a mixture of cracked and splintered boards. The hand rail is loose and falling apart and the cat walk is separating from the main structure. Up until 2007 CAL FIRE, which was still using the structure as a lookout at that time, continued to conduct maintenance of the facility, including painting, light carpentry and cleaning. However, at this time the LNF is not doing regular maintenance of the building, which is deemed unsafe for use and would require extensive repair and upgrades, including changes to the facility access to meet standard safety compliance requirements. Because it has been determined eligible for listing on the NRHP, repairs to the building would have to be done in conformance with the Secretary of the Interior’s Standards and Guidelines for Rehabilitation (36 CFR Part 61). 
 Lassen National Forest is currently considering transferring the ownership of the tower site to a private entity who has expressed interest in acquiring the site but who wants the tower removed from the property as a condition of transfer. The eventual goal of that proposal is to convert the location now occupied by the tower to a repeater site. 
 The current conditions at Dyer Mountain Lookout present two separate problems for CAL FIRE to address. Dyer Mountain Lookout is one of the 29 significant historic buildings that CAL FIRE has agreed to preserve and manage over the long term. Prior to 2001, the USFS indicated that it intended to restore and maintain the lookout to preserve its historical values and maintain it as an important functioning public facility. Since CAL FIRE was using the tower to house radio equipment, and on rare occasion provided a firefighter to serve as a lookout, at that time the Department was able to offer limited assistance to the USFS to maintain the structure. 
 Things have changed since then and the USFS has discontinued its previous practice of regular maintenance and repair of the building. Now the lookout has deteriorated to such an unsafe condition that the USFS may pursue demolition rather than restoration. Because CAL FIRE has no control over what happens to the lookout, it has proven to be a poor choice for selection to the list of historic buildings to be preserved. CAL FIRE has decided to de-list Dyer Mountain Lookout immediately upon approval of this Plan update. De-listing the lookout does not necessarily mean that the lookout is doomed to be demolished (although it is recognized that absent maintenance, this is the likely outcome). Instead this action is being taken in recognition of the fact that the USFS, not CAL FIRE, controls the management of the lookout, and consequently, CAL FIRE’s ability to utilize the site and its facilities is limited and is subject to the discretion of the USFS through their approval of the terms of the Special Use Permit.
