Carson National Forest 
                    Rio Arriba County, New Mexico
desc: Located on the El Rito Ranger District of the Carson National Forest in northern New Mexico, Kiowa Lookout was erected 73 years ago in 1923. The 50, steel Aermotor tower is one of only two LL-25 models remaining in the Southwestern Region. The original outside ladder has been replaced with interior stairs. The base cabin was built by the CCC in 1935 and the tower is still in active use.

name: La Mosca Lookout
loc:
Cibola National Forest 
                    Cibola County, New Mexico
desc: Located on a 11,036' mountain top, La Mosca Lookout on the Cibola National Forest is a CL-100 series 14’x14’ metal cab with catwalk with a corrugated metal roof on a 10’ concrete block base. It was built in the 1960s and replaced an L-4 lookout dating to the early 1930s.

name: Mangas Lookout
loc:
Apache National Forest 
                    Catron County, New Mexico
desc: Also listed on the National Register of Historic Places, Mangas Lookout on the Apache National Forest was constructed in 1934. It is a 31.6’ Aermotor MC-24 tower with a 12’x12’ wooden R3 low sill cab without catwalk.

name: McGaffey Lookout
loc:
Cibola National Forest 
                    McKinley County, New Mexico
desc: Two other towers preceded McGaffey Lookout. The first was a wood tower built in the 1920s and a 59’ Aermotor MC-39 tower constructed in 1934. The present 54’ steel tower with a 14’x14’ CL-100 metal cab with catwalk and corrugated roof went into service in 1965.

name: Mogollon Baldy Lookout
loc:
Gila National Forest 
                    Catron County, New Mexico
desc: Located on the Wilderness Ranger District, this 30 feet high Aermotor MI-25 steel tower has a wooden 14'x14' cab. The lookout was constructed in 1948 on the same location which has been utilized for fire detection since at least 1913 when fires were located with a protractor on top of a stump. Adjacent to the lookout is the Observer's Log Cabin constructed in 1923.

name: Monjeau Lookout
loc:
Lincoln National Forest 
                    Lincoln County, New Mexico
desc: The first NHLR listing in New Mexico is one of the most interesting lookouts in the Southwestern Region. Located on the Smokey Bear Ranger District of the Lincoln National Forest, Monjeau Lookout was completed by the CCC in 1940. The 7’x7’ metal cab is built into a 14’ x 14’ native stone tower that houses the living quarters. Still in active use, the lookout is a popular destination with forest visitors. It is also listed on the National Register of Historic Sites.

name: Mount Withington Lookout
loc:
Cibola National Forest 
                    Socorro County, New Mexico
desc: The first lookout at Mt. Withington on the Cibola National Forest was a D-6 cupola built in 1934. It served for 18 years and was replaced with the present station in 1952. It is another example of a special R-3 design of a 14’x14’ cab with slightly sloped gable roof on top of a 10’ concrete block base. A catwalk was added later.

name: Negrito Mountain Lookout
loc:
Gila National Forest 
                    Catron County, New Mexico
desc: Located on the Reserve Ranger District of the Gila National Forest, this Aermotor MC-24, steel tower is 30 feet high with a 12’x12’ wood cab and was erected in 1934. The lookout was extensively remodeled in 1984, with new windows, new steel siding and a new roof. Negrito Mountain Lookout is not currently staffed.

name: Osborne Lookout
loc:
Archuleta Mesa, Jicarilla Reservation 
                    Rio Arriba County, New Mexico
desc: During the late summer of 1959 construction was begun on Osborne Lookout, the fourth on the Jicarilla Reservation. Located on Archuleta Mesa, the unique ground house with cupola was designed by the Bureau of Indian Affairs. The modern structure is both functional and attractive to the site. Completed and staffed in 1960, the new lookout had an important role that year as fires burned over 1,000 acres on and near the reservation.

name: Oso Ridge Lookout
loc:
Cibola National Forest 
                    Cibola County, New Mexico
desc: The first lookout at Oso Ridge was a 25’ steel tower with a 7’x7’ wooden cab and ground house constructed in 1938. While the ground house remains, the lookout was replaced in 1965 with a live-in Cl-100 14’x4’ metal cab with catwalk on a 10’ concrete block base.

name: Picuris Lookout
loc:
Carson National Forest 
                    Taos County, New Mexico
desc: Located high atop Picuris Peak, this ground cab lookout was regularly staffed through 1990. It has been used occasionally since in times of extreme fire danger.

name: Reeds Peak Lookout
loc:
Gila National Forest 
                    Grant County, New Mexico
desc: The 48’ LX-24 Aermotor tower with 7’x7’ metal cab at Reeds Peak Lookout is unique because the outside metal ladder is still intact. Metal stairs were added in 1965. It is reached by a 12 mile trail into the Leopold Wilderness on the Gila National Forest.

name: Ruidoso Lookout
loc:
Lincoln National Forest 
                    Lincoln County, New Mexico
desc: A 30’ Aermotor tower with 14’x14’ wooden cab and steel mesh catwalk, Ruidoso Lookout was erected in 1940 by the U.S. Forest Service. It is also located on the Smokey Bear Ranger District of the Lincoln National Forest and is listed on the National Register of Historic Sites. In the past 56 years the Town of Ruidoso has expanded to nearly surround the tower, which is now staffed by a town employee for the detection of urban/suburban fires.

name: Sacramento Lookout
loc:
Lincoln National Forest 
                    Otero County, New Mexico
desc: Located on the Sacramento Ranger District, this 67 feet high steel tower has a CL100 - 106 series steel cab 14X14 feet square. It was erected in 1968 to replace an Aermotor LX-24 built in 1925 which was destroyed by fire in 1967.

name: Saddle Mountain Lookout
loc:
Gila National Forest 
                    Catron County, New Mexico
desc: The first tower at Saddle Mountain Lookout on the Gila National Forest was an Aermotor MC-24 with a wooden cab. The cab was replaced in 1966 with a metal Cl-100 14’x14’ model with metal catwalk.

name: San Mateo Lookout
loc:
Cibola National Forest 
                    Socorro County, New Mexico
desc: Reached only by a 5 mile trail and now on standby status, San Mateo Lookout is the oldest detection facility remaining on the Magdalena Ranger District of the Cibola National Forest. It is an 59’3" Aermotor LX-25 tower with 7’x7’ metal cab and is one of the last remaining examples in the U.S. of the platform style ladder/stairs.

name: Signal Peak Lookout
loc:
Gila National Forest 
                    Grant County, New Mexico
desc: Signal Peak Lookout is a 30 feet high aermotor MC-24 steel tower erected in 1932. The original 12'x12' steel cab was replaced in 1966 by a steel 14'x14' steel cab of the USDA Forest Service Standard Plan CL-100 to CL-106 series type. all the supporting buildings were erected in the 1960s.

name: St. Peter's Dome Lookout
loc:
Santa Fe National Forest 
                    Los Alamos County, New Mexico
desc: Dome Lookout is a USDA Forest Service Standard Plan CL-100 to CL-106 series type metal 14’x14’ R6 flattop with metal catwalk on a 10’ cinder block base with storage room constructed in 1965 replacing a 1932 L-4 ground house. Dome is currently un-staffed and is being utilized as a communications site due to the Dome fire in 1996, vandalism, and a re-burn by the Las Conchas Fire in 2001. For more details see Barbara Zinn’s  “Fire Lookout History of the Santa Fe National Forest” .

name: Tohatchi Lookout
loc:
Navajo Indian Reservation 
                    McKinley County, New Mexico
desc: There are three active lookouts on the New Mexico portion of the Navajo Indian Reservation. Tohatchi Lookout is located on a nearly 9,000’ high mountaintop. Constructed in 1928, it is the oldest lookout on the Reservation. It is a 62’ Aermotor tower with 7’x7’ metal cab.

name: Tohnitsha Lookout
loc:
Navajo Indian Reservation 
                    San Juan County, New Mexico
desc: Although the Aermotor tower is most common, there were a number of International Derrick manufactured fire towers erected in the southwest in the 1930’s and early 1940’s. One of these is Tohnitsha Lookout on the Navajo Reservation it is 82.9’ high with a 7’x7’ metal cab built in 1936.

name: Washington Pass Lookout
loc:
Navajo Indian Reservation 
                    San Juan County, New Mexico
desc: At 9,179’ in the Chuska Mountains, Washington Pass Lookout is the highest elevation station in the New Mexico section of the Navajo Reservation. The 81’ LS-40 Aermotor tower with 7’x7’ metal cab was built and put into service in 1936.

name: Weed Lookout
loc:
Lincoln National Forest 
                    Otero County, New Mexico
desc: This Aermotor LX-24 lookout is located on the Sacramento Ranger District, Lincoln National Forest, and was erected in 1926. The Weed lookout is the oldest standing lookout on the Lincoln National Forest. The tower is 48 feet high and is topped by a 7X7 foot steel cab.   The site did contain a cabin and shed, which were removed in 1978. The tower originally had wooden steps but were replaced by metal ones in 1966.

name: Wells Lookout
loc:
Jicarilla Reservation 
                    Rio Arriba County, New Mexico
desc: First used as a lookout point in 1930, parts for the Wells Lookout were received in 1931 from International Derrick Co. In June 1932 the 60' steel tower with 7' x 7' cab was erected at a reported cost of $92(!) and put into service. The following year the site was staffed by a "lookout-fireman," meaning the towerman would take initial action on the smokes he reported if they were nearby.

name: Wofford Lookout
loc:
Lincoln National Forest 
                    Otero County, New Mexico
desc: Located on the Sacramento Ranger District, the Aermotor MC-39 steel tower is 80 feet high with a 7X7 foot steel cab. It was erected in 1933 by the CCC.   The site also includes a wood frame cabin (1933)and storage shed (1937). The cabin measures 12X16 feet, and has a simple gable roof and narrow wood slats for siding.   Wofford is listed on the National Register of Historic Places.

name: Bandelier Lookout
loc:
Bandelier National Monument 
                    Los Alamos County, New Mexico
admin: National Park Service - Bandelier National Monument
desc:
Bandelier Lookout was constructed in 1940-41 by the Civilian Conservation Corps for the National Park Service. 
 The structure is a NPS standardized fire lookout, drawing PG-3040, with a wood cab on a stone basement. 
 In 1943 the Atomic Energy Commission (AEC) established Los Alamos National Lab (LANL) next to Bandelier, and in 1948 the Santa Fe National Forest, the AEC and Bandelier made a cooperative agreement for detection and suppression. 
 The lookout was actively used to at least 2016.

name: Brushy Lookout
loc:
Isleta-Acoma Indian Reservation 
                    Cibola County, New Mexico
desc:
Brushy Lookout on Cibollito Peak is an Aermotor 50 foot open steel tower with a 7x7 observation cab atop. 
 A residence cabin is on site as well. Construction date and use status is unknown.

name: Isleta Lookout
loc:
Isleta-Acoma Indian Reservation 
                    Torrance County, New Mexico
desc:
Isleta Lookout is an Aermotor 7x7 observation only cab on a 50 foot open steel tower.  
 A residence cabin is also onsite inside a fenced enclosure. 
 Construction date and use status is unknown.

name: Lookout Mountain Lookout
loc:
Gila National Forest 
                    Sierra County, New Mexico
admin: US Forest Service - Gila National Forest
desc:
Lookout Mountain was constructed in 1965 on the existing Aermotor tower. 
 The original cab was an unusual 12x12 size on an Aermotor MC-24 tower.

name: Manzano Lookout
loc:
Cibola National Forest 
                    Bernalillo County, New Mexico
desc:
Manzano Lookout was constructed for the Department of Defense on the Cibola National Forest. Kirtland Air Force Base is just west of the lookout. 
 The construction date is unknown. The structure is in poor condition and appears to be a 30 foot K-Brace open steel tower with an L-4 cab atop.

name: White Peak Lookout
loc:
New Mexico State Trust Land 
                    Colfax County, New Mexico
desc:
White or White's Peak is located in northeast New Mexico on state trust land. 
 The structure is a 70 foot Aermotor open steel tower and 7x7 observation cab. A ground residence cabin is also onsite. 
 Construction date and use status are unknown.

name: Los Alamos Lookout
loc: Los Alamos County, New Mexico
desc:
Situated at the location of the former Main Gate of the Los Alamos National Laboratory, the Los Alamos Fire Lookout operated on and off for approximately 30 years and was primarily staffed by Los Alamos Fire Department personnel after 1951 (Zinn, pgs. 164-165). This particular tower replaced an earlier structure that was operated jointly by the Atomic Energy Commission and the Forest Service from 1944-1948 (Zinn, pgs. 164-165). 
 SOURCE: Zinn, Barbara, "Fire Lookout History of the Santa Fe National Forest," United States Department of Agriculture/U.S. Forest Service, April 2017.

name: Apache Maid Lookout
loc:
Coconino National Forest 
                    Coconino County, Arizona
desc: Constructed in 1961, Apache Maid Lookout on the Red Rock Ranger District of the Coconino National Forest is a 14'x14' metal CL-100 series cab on a 30' metal tower. Although it is on a 7301' high ridge, it overlooks fire prone lower elevation forest and brush regions.

name: Atascosa Lookout
loc:
Coronado National Forest 
                    Arizona
desc: Built between 1930 and 1933, Atascosa Lookout is a 14’x 14’ groundhouse with an unusual modified hip roof with a 2’ overhang. This historic structure on the Coronado National Forest is not far from the Mexican border. It has gutters to collect rainwater for a cistern, a common-sense solution that was strangely not used often in the West. Atacosa Lookout was destroyed in the Murphy Fire on June 6, 2011.

name: Aztec Peak Lookout
loc:
Tonto National Forest 
                    Arizona
desc: Aztec Peak Lookout was erected in 1956 on the Pleasant Valley Ranger District of the Tonto National Forest. It replaced a wooden D-6 cupola groundhouse built in 1925. It is a steel tower with flat roof steel 14’ x 14’ CL-100 cab. The lookout continues in active service.

name: Baker Butte Lookout
loc:
Coconino National Forest 
                    Coconino County, Arizona
desc: The first fire tower at Baker Butte on the Mogollon Rim District of the Coconino National Forest was a wooden 6'x6' cab on a 20' metal tower with ladder access constructed in 1921. In 1936 the CCC replaced it with the present R-3 12'x12' wooden live in cab without catwalk on a 30' Aermotor MC-24 metal tower.

name: Barfoot Lookout
loc:
Coronado National Forest 
                    Cochise County, Arizona
desc: Constructed by the CCC in 1935, Barfoot Lookout on the Coronado National Forest in Arizona was active for more than 65 years. It was a 14’x 14’ L-4 ground house with a roof-catch cistern once common in the dry Southwestern forests.   This lookout was destroyed in the Horseshoe II fire in June 2011.

name: Bear Mountain Lookout
loc:
Apache-Sitgreaves National Forest 
                    Greenlee County, Arizona
desc: In the back country of the Apache-Sitgreaves National Forest lies 8538' Bear Mountain, the site of a lookout since 1928. The 46' LX-25 Aermotor tower with 7’x7' metal cab was built in 1933 and is in active service.

name: Big Lake Lookout
loc:
Apache-Sitgreaves National Forests 
                    Apache County, Arizona
desc: A 32' Aermotor MC-24 tower with a 12'x12' live-in cab, Big Lake Lookout was constructed by the CCC in 1933 on the Apache-Sitgreaves National Forest. Big Lake Lookout was destroyed in the Wallow Fire in June 2011.

name: Big Springs Lookout
loc:
Kaibab National Forest 
                    Coconino County, Arizona
desc: Big Springs Lookout is located on the north rim of the Grand Canyon on the Kaibab National Forest. This 100 Aermotor tower was constructed in 1934 by contractors from Kanab. A wooden groundhouse was added in 1959. Still in active use, the lookout is also listed on the National Register of Historic Places.

name: Bill Williams Mountain Lookout
loc:
Kaibab National Forest 
                    Coconino County, Arizona
desc: The first lookout on Bill Williams Mountain on the Kaibab National Forest was a high stump with an alidade. It was replaced with a 30' wooden tower in 1924. The present Aermotor MC-39 tower was constructed in 1937 and is in active service. The 7' x 7' metal cab features an unusual raised platform above the roof.

name: Black Pinnacle Lookout
loc:
Navajo Indian Reservation 
                    Apache County, Arizona
desc: Overlooking the north end of Canyon De Chelly National Monument, Black Pinnacle Lookout is a unique wood ground house reached by a series of metal steps atop on a black rock pinnacle (appropriately) with a remarkable 360-degree view. The Navajo Reservation site was constructed in 1936 and remains a key detection station.

name: Blue Lookout
loc:
Apache-Sitgreaves National Forests 
                    Greenlee County, Arizona
desc: Blue Lookout is a sister structure to Big Lake Lookout and was also built in 1933.  It can be reached by trail on the Apache-Sitgreaves National Forest.

name: Buck Mountain Lookout
loc:
Coconino National Forest 
                    Coconino County, Arizona
desc: One of the few towers of its design (CT-2) remaining in the U.S., Buck Mountain Lookout is located on the Long Valley Ranger District of the Coconino National Forest. The 30' wood tower, built in 1939, has an R-3 modified L-4 14' x 14' live-in cab with catwalk. It is also listed on the National Register of Historic Sites.

name: Buckskin Lookout
loc:
White Mountain/Fort Apache Reservation 
                    Navajo County, Arizona
desc: The only International Derrick brand fire tower on the White Mountain Apache Indian Reservation, Buckskin Lookout is also one of the newest, being constructed in 1963. Now in inactive status, the 82' metal tower with 7' x 7' cab will be transferred to the National Historic Lookout Register in 2013 when it is 50 years old.

name: Chediski Lookout
loc:
Fort Apache-White Mountain Indian Reservation 
                    Navajo County, Arizona
desc: Administered by the White Mountain Apache Agency, Chediski Lookout is often mistaken as the tallest tower on the reservation because of the way it juts out from a mountain top. The 121' Aermotor lookout was constructed in 1936 and is in active service. An original log groundhouse has been preserved on the site.

name: Colcord Lookout
loc:
Tonto National Forest 
                    Gila County, Arizona
desc: The original Colcord Lookout was a 50’ Aermotor tower with 7’ x 7’ cab. Three years later, in 1928, a second Aermotor tower, 35’ tall with a 7’ x 7’ cab, was erected and apparently both were operated at the same time. Sometime after 1965 both towers, plus a CCC ground living quarters, were removed and the present 83’ steel tower built. It has a 14’ x 14’ CL-100 series metal flat roof cab with catwalk. The lookout is staffed by the Pleasant Valley Ranger District of the Tonto National Forest.

name: Deer Springs Lookout
loc:
Apache-Sitgreaves National Forest 
                    Navajo County, Arizona
desc: The oldest active lookout in Arizona, Deer Springs, was built in 1923 on the Apache-Sitgreaves National Forest. The Aermotor LL-25 tower with 7’x7' metal cab is one of only two existing in the southwestern U.S. and is on the National Register of Historic Places.

name: Diamond Point Lookout
loc:
Tonto National Forest 
                    Gila County, Arizona
desc: Built on the Tonto National Forest in 1936, Diamond Point Lookout is a Region 3 version of the famous L-4 (and different in many ways). Located at 6157’ on a 30’ Pacific Coast Steel tower with 12’x12’ cab without catwalk, this 1936 lookout replaced a wooden platform tower built in 1924. The active lookout is in the vicinity of the Zane Grey cabin that burned in the Dude fire several years ago.

name: Dry Lake Lookout
loc:
San Carlos Apache Reservation 
                    Graham County, Arizona
desc: Built by the Larson Corporation for the San Carlos Agency in 1984, Dry Lake Lookout is a 80’ steel tower with an 8’x8’ metal cab with a catwalk on three sides. It replaced a 54’ Aermotor tower with 7’x7’ metal cab with had been in service since 1930.

name: Dry Park Lookout
loc:
Kaibab National Forest 
                    Coconino County, Arizona
desc: At 120', Dry Park Lookout is the tallest fire tower on the Kaibab National Forest. Built in 1944, the Aermotor tower replaced an earlier tower constructed in the 1930s. The groundhouse and support buildings were established in 1936 and are listed on the National Register of Historic Places.

name: East Pocket Lookout
loc:
Coconino National Forest 
                    Coconino County, Arizona
desc: Another of the rare CT-2 towers (this one manufactured by Timber Engineering Corp. in 1943), East Pocket Lookout has a 14' x 14' live-in cab with catwalk. Set on an elevation of 7,196' on the Peaks Ranger District of the Coconino, it is an R-3 modified L-4 cab.

name: Elden Lookout
loc:
Coconino National Forest 
                    Coconino County, Arizona
desc: Standing at 9,224' directly above Flagstaff, AZ, Elden Lookout is easily reached by trail from downtown. A 37' Aermotor tower was erected on the site in 1926 and served until damaged by the Radio Fire of 1977 which burned to the crest. The present 54' metal tower with a metal CL 100 live-in cab with catwalk was constructed in 1977. This Peaks Ranger District lookout is in active service.

name: Escudilla Lookout
loc:
Apache-Sitgreaves National Forests 
                    Apache County, Arizona
desc: Escudilla Lookout was built in 1933 on the Apache-Sitgreaves National Forest.  It is a 54' tower with a CL-100 series 14'x14' metal live-in cab with catwalk. Escudilla Lookout was destroyed in the Wallow Fire in June 2011.

name: Fluted Rock Lookout
loc:
Navajo Indian Reservation 
                    Apache County, Arizona
desc: Fluted Rock Lookout overlooks a unique region of the same name within the Navajo Reservation. The 41’ MC-39 Aermotor tower with 7’x7’ metal cab was constructed in the early 1930’s and is in service.

name: Gentry Lookout
loc:
Apache-Sitgreaves National Forests 
                    Navajo County, Arizona
desc: Built in 1965, the 70' Gentry Lookout on the Apache-Sitgreaves Nationa Forest has a 14'x14' CL-100 series metal live-in cab with catwalk.  It replaced a 62' Aermotor tower built in 1927.

name: Grandview Lookout
loc:
Kaibab National Forest 
                    Coconino County, Arizona
desc: Located close to Grand Canyon National Park with an outstanding view of the canyon, it is not hard to determine how Grandview Lookout earned its name. It is one of the original tower sites selected when the early Grand Canyon National Monument was planned in 1909. It had a platform tower before the Forest Service built the 81' Aermotor tower with 7' x 7' metal cab in 1936. A historic lookout residence is also located at the site.

name: Greens Peak Lookout
loc:
Apache-Sitgreaves National Forest 
                    Apache County, Arizona
desc: The 54' metal tower with metal 14’x14' CL 100 live-in cab with catwalk, Greens Peak Lookout, was constructed in 1962 replacing an Aermotor MC24 look-out built in 1933. The Apache-Sitgreaves National Forest site is in active service.

name: Heliograph Lookout
loc:
Coronado National Forest 
                    Graham County, Arizona
desc: Heliograph Lookout is a 100’ Aermotor MC-39 tower with a 7’x7’ steel cab. Still in active service and the tallest tower on the Coronado National Forest, the site also has a well maintained log cabin ground house and related Civilian Conservation Corps structures dating to 1934. It is listed on the National Register of Historic Places.

name: Hilltop Lookout
loc:
San Carlos Apache Reservation 
                    Gila County, Arizona
desc: The Hilltop Lookout on the San Carlos Reservation is an early model L-4 with expanded catwalks constructed by the BIA in 1930. It is part of the San Carlos Agency fire management system.

name: Hopi Lookout
loc:
Grand Canyon National Park 
                    Coconino County, Arizona
desc: The first Hopi Lookout on this site in the Grand Canyon National Park was a tree-top crow's nest in 1909 which was replaced in 1927 with a 40' steel tower with 10'x10' cab.  The lookout was remodeled in 1953 with this 12'x12' cab and the tower lowered to 24'. The site overlooks the Grand Canyon to the north. The lookout is no longer used for fire detection.

name: Horsethief Lookout
loc:
Prescott National Forest 
                    Yavapai County, Arizona
desc: Located in the Bradshaw Range on a mountain in the Prescott National Forest, Horsethief Lookout was constructed in 1934. It is a 40’ Pacific Coast Steel tower with a modified L-4 live-in cab and is active service.

name: Humboldt Mountain Lookout
loc:
Tonto National Forest 
                    Maricopa County, Arizona
desc: Dwarfed by the adjacent air traffic radar dome, Humboldt Mountain Lookout was built by the FAA to Forest Service specifications in 1958. The CL-100 R-6 metal flattop cab with catwalk on a 30 steel tower replaced a 1940 L-4 on a stone foundation. The Tonto National Forest station is in active service.

name: Hutch Mountain Lookout
loc:
Coconino National Forest 
                    Coconino County, Arizona
desc: The original lookout at Hutch Mountain on the Mogollon Rim District of the Coconino National Forest was a wooden tower built in the early 1920s. In 1936 the CCC built the present 31' Aermotor MC-24 tower with a live in 12'x12' wooden R-3 cab without catwalk.

name: Hyde Mountain Lookout
loc:
Prescott National Forest 
                    Yavapai County, Arizona
desc: Hyde Mountain Lookout on the Prescott National Forest is in semi-active status. The L-5 groundhouse was constructed in 1936. It is also listed on the National Register of Historic Places. No longer in service, there is no road access to it, so visitors have to hike a good hour to the tower.

name: Jacob Lake Lookout
loc:
Kaibab National Forest 
                    Coconino County, Arizona
desc: Jacob Lake Lookout, located on the North Kaibab Ranger District, was also built in 1934 by the same contractors from Kanab who constructed Big Springs Tower. It too is a 100’ Aermotor steel tower with a 7’ x 7’ metal cab and is listed on the National Register of Historic Places.

name: Juniper Ridge Lookout
loc:
Apache-Sitgreaves National Forest 
                    Navajo County, Arizona
desc: Overlooking the adjacent Fort Apache Indian Reservation as well as the Apache-Sitgreaves National Forest, Juniper Ridge has a 54' metal tower with a live-in 14’x14' metal CL 100 cab with catwalk built in 1959. With an elevation of 6985' it is in active service.

name: Kanabownitz Lookout
loc:
Grand Canyon National Park 
                    Coconino County, Arizona
desc: Built in 1940, the Kanabownitz Lookout is an 82'6" International Derrick steel tower with a 7'x7' cab overlooking the Grand Canyon.  The lookout is no longer used for fire detection.

name: Kendrick Lookout
loc:
Kaibab National Forest 
                    Coconino County, Arizona
desc: Although the 10’ steel tower with metal 14’x14’ flatroof cab and catwalk was constructed in 1964, the previous L-4 structure on Kendrick Lookout was built in the early 1930s. A log cabin built in 1911 one quarter mile below the peak as sleeping quarters is the second oldest example of a fire detection structure present in the southwest region (Arizona and New Mexico). The current tower is in active service.

name: Lake Mountain Lookout
loc:
Apache-Sitgreaves National Forest 
                    Apache County, Arizona
desc: Built in 1926 atop Lake Mountain, the 48' Aermotor LX-24 lookout and lookout cabin are in active service. The original ladder was replaced in the 1930s with stairs. The lookout is listed on the National Register of Historic Places as is the nearby Los Burros Ranger Station site.

name: Lee Butte Lookout
loc:
Coconino National Forest 
                    Coconino County, Arizona
desc: Located on the Morman Lake Ranger District, Lee Butte is a 46' International Derrick tower with 7' x 7' cab built in 1933. In good condition although inactive, the tower is one of only three of its design in Arizona and is listed, along with its spacious ground house, on the National Register of Historic Sites.

name: Lemmon Rock Lookout
loc:
Coronado National Forest 
                    Pima County, Arizona
desc: The first lookout on Mt. Lemmon within the Coronado National Forest overlooking Tucson was built in 1913. In 1928 a replacement was constructed just south of the summit on Lemmon Rock for a better viewing area.

name: Limestone Lookout
loc:
Fort Apache-White Mountain Indian Reservation 
                    Navajo County, Arizona
desc: Limestone Lookout, also located on the Fort Apache White Mountain Indian Reservation, is the tallest fire tower in Arizona. The 123’ Aermotor tower with 7’x 7’ metal cab was built in 1936. Still active as a lookout, the site is also the base for a helitack fire crew.

name: Maverick Mountain Lookout
loc:
White Mountain/Fort Apache Reservation 
                    Apache County, Arizona
desc: One of three Aermotor MC-39 towers installed in 1934 on the White Mountain Apache Indian Reservation, Maverick Mountain Lookout continues in active service. The 80' steel tower with 7' x 7' cab replaced a similar but shorter (60') tower built on the site in 1925.

name: McFadden Peak Lookout
loc:
Tonto National Forest 
                    Gila County, Arizona
desc: The first lookout on McFadden Peak, located on the Pleasant Valley Ranger District of the Tonto National Forest, was a 20’ steel tower with 7’ x 7’ cab built in 1929. In the 1930s a cabin, stock barn and shed were added. These buildings were removed in 1964 when the present, 10’ concrete blockhouse with a 14’x 14’ CL-100 series flattop metal cab with catwalk, was constructed. The lookout is staffed each year.

name: McKay Lookout
loc:
Fort Apache-White Mountain Indian Reservation 
                    Apache County, Arizona
desc: McKay Peak Lookout is the only Aermotor MC-24 tower with wooden 14’ x 14’ cab on the Fort Apache Reservation. It was built in 1932, replacing a wooden tower, and the original ground house remains on the site. The lookout is still active.

name: Mingus Mountain Lookout
loc:
Prescott National Forest 
                    Yavapai County, Arizona
desc: Constructed in 1935, Mingus Mountain Lookout is a 60’ Pacific Coast Steel tower with a 7’x7’ metal cab located on a wooded mountain. The facility is listed on the National Register of Historic Places. It replaced an earlier 41’ wooden tower.

name: Monte Vista Lookout
loc:
Coronado National Forest 
                    Cochise County, Arizona
desc: The 40’ steel tower with a CL-100 metal 14’x14’ cab at Monte Vista Lookout was built in 1966. It replaced a 30’ Aermotor tower built in 1922 that in turn had replaced a crow’s nest tower dating to 1916. The Coronado National Forest station is in active service and will be initially listed on the National Lookout Register until it reaches 50 years of age in 2016.

name: Moqui Lookout
loc:
Coconino National Forest 
                    Coconino County, Arizona
desc: The tallest tower on the Coconino National Forest is the 83' high Moqui Lookout constructed in 1952. It is a CL-100 series 14'x14' live in cab with catwalk on a metal tower. It replaced an Aermotor fire tower built in 1930.

name: Mormon Lake Lookout
loc:
Coconino National Forest 
                    Coconino County, Arizona
desc: Dating back to 1927, the Mormon Lake Lookout on the Mormon Lake District of the Coconino National Forest is a 48' Aermotor LX-24 tower with a 7'x7' metal cab. It replaced a wooden tower built back in 1915 at a reported cost of only $139.

name: Mount Bigelow Lookout
loc:
Coronado National Forest 
                    Pima County, Arizona
desc: Built in 1958 on the Coronado National Forest, Mount Bigelow Lookout is a 53’ metal tower with an Army design of the CL-100 metal 14’x14’ cab with catwalk. Instead of the corrugated flat roof with overhang, it has a hip roof with no overhang for shade.

name: Mount Ord Lookout
loc:
Tonto National Forest 
                    Gila County, Arizona
desc: The impressive 102’ tall Mt. Ord Lookout has a 14’ x 14’ metal CL-100 cab with catwalk was constructed in 1983. It replaced a 1936 Aermotor MC 39 tower, which has been moved to the Rim Country Museum in Payson AZ.

name: Mount Union Lookout
loc:
Prescott National Forest 
                    Yavapai County, Arizona
desc: Atop a nearly 8,000’ peak stands Mount Union Lookout on the Prescott National Forest. The 30’ Aermotor Mc-24 tower with a modified L-4 cab was built in 1933 and remains in active service.

name: North Rim Lookout
loc:
Grand Canyon National Park 
                    Coconino County, Arizona
desc: This 75' Aermotor tower with a 7'x7' cab was built in 1928 on Bright Angel Point.  It was moved to become North Rim Lookout in 1933. The tower is no longer used for fire detection.

name: Oakridge Lookout
loc:
Navajo Indian Reservation 
                    Apache County, Arizona
desc: One of the International Derrick design towers located on the Navajo Reservation. Oak Ridge Lookout is an 83’ tower with a 7’x7’ metal cab was constructed in 1941 and is in active service.

name: Odart Mountain Lookout
loc:
White Mountain/Fort Apache Reservation 
                    Apache County, Arizona
desc: Constructed in 1934, Odart Mountain Lookout is an Aermotor MC-39 steel tower with a 7' x 7' cab atop an 8,531' mountain. The White Mountain Apache Agency tower itself rises an additional 82'.

name: O'Haco Lookout
loc:
Apache-Sitgreaves National Forests 
                    Coconino County, Arizona
desc: The 100' O'Haco Lookout on the Apache-Sitgreaves National Forest is an Aermotor 1040 tower with a 7'x7' metal cab.  There is a catwalk on one side to accommodate a side door instead of a trap door in the floor.

name: O'Leary Lookout
loc:
Coconino National Forest 
                    Coconino County, Arizona
desc: Overlooking the San Francisco Peaks and the Painted Desert on the Peaks District of the Coconino National Forest, O'Leary Lookout is a 14'x14' CL-100 series live in cab with catwalk on a 32' metal tower. It was constructed in 1959.

name: Piney Hill Lookout
loc:
Navajo Indian Reservation 
                    Apache County, Arizona
desc: One of the early towers on the Navajo reservation, Piney Hill Lookout is still active. The 81’ Aermotor MC-39 tower with 7’x7’ metal cab was constructed in the early 1930’s on an 8102’ mountaintop.

name: Promontory Lookout
loc:
Apache-Sitgreaves National Forest 
                    Coconino County, Arizona
desc: When the original 121' wooden tower was built on Promontory on the Apache-Sitgreaves National Forest in 1913 it was the highest in the U.S. Eleven years later (1924) the current 110' Aermotor with 7’x7' metal cab was erected. The original ladder was replaced with stairs in 1938. In active service, it is listed on the National Register of Historic Places.

name: Ps Knoll Lookout
loc:
Apache-Sitgreaves National Forests 
                    Apache County, Arizona
desc: The CCC constructed the 50' Aermotor MC-39 tower with 7'x7' cab for PS Knoll Lookout in the mid 1930s.  It and a historic cabin are on the Apache-Sitgreaves National Forest.

name: Red Butte Lookout
loc:
Kaibab National Forest 
                    Coconino County, Arizona
desc: Located on a knob jutting into the flat, forested and sagebrush plain south of the Grand Canyon National Park, Red Butte Lookout is a practical structure designed to blend with the arid site. The design done for the Kaibab National Forest is based on the USFS CL 100 plan but with many modifications. The 14' x 14' cab with tinted windows has a permanent roof overhang for shade. There is a metal catwalk and two cistern tanks for water. The lookout is reached by a 1.5 mile trail.

name: Red Hill Lookout
loc:
Kaibab National Forest 
                    Coconino County, Arizona
desc: Red Hill Lookout is on a 7751’ mountaintop on the Kaibab National Forest. In the 1920s a wooden tower was used for detection. It was replaced in 1958 with a metal Cl-100 14’x14’ cab with flat corrugated roof on a 10’ concrete block base. It is often used early in the season when the snowpack does not allow access to other lookouts.

name: Red Mountain Lookout
loc:
Coronado National Forest 
                    Santa Cruz County, Arizona
desc: The newest on the Coronado National Forest, Red Mountain Lookout was constructed in 1973 and overlooks the village of Patagonia. The 10’ concrete foundation supports a wooden R-6 flattop cab with overhang and a catwalk with a wooden railing. There are now several communications towers at the lookout site. In active service, it will be listed on the National Lookout Register until 2023.

name: Reno Lookout
loc:
Apache-Sitgreaves National Forests 
                    Greenlee County, Arizona
desc: The original 48' Aermotor tower with 7'x7' cab for Reno Lookout built on the Apache-Sitgreaves National Forest in 1931 has been replaced with a 54' tower and CL-100 cab with catwalk.

name: Roof Butte Lookout
loc:
Navajo Indian Reservation 
                    Apache County, Arizona
desc: One of the newest lookouts on the Navajo Reservation (1960) and active, Roof Butte Lookout is already surrounded with electronic facilities. The 7’x7’ wooden cab sits in the middle of a 14’x14’ metal platform on a 12’ tower.

name: Rose Peak Lookout
loc:
Apache-Sitgreaves National Forest 
                    Greenlee County, Arizona
desc: The 30' Aermotor MC-24 lookout on Rose Peak built in 1929 to replace several earlier wood platform towers. The original 12’x12' cab was replaced in 1981 with a 14’x14' R-6 wood flat top live-in cab with catwalk. The Apache-Sitgreaves National Forest station is in active service.

name: Round Mountain Lookout
loc:
Kaibab National Forest 
                    Coconino County, Arizona
desc: The 35’ Aermotor MC30 tower with 7’x7’ metal cab on Round Mountain was originally constructed on Saddle Mountain on the Coconino National Forest in 1934. It was moved to its current location on the Kaibab National Forest in 1960 and modified with a side door replacing the customary trap door.

name: Signal Hill Lookout
loc:
Grand Canyon National Park 
                    Coconino County, Arizona
desc: Built in 1929, Signal Hill Lookout is a 35' Aermotor LS-40 tower with a 7'x7'cab.  It overlooks some of the mnost fire prone areas on the noirth rim of Grand Canyon National Park. The tower is no longer used for fire detection.

name: Signal Peak Lookout
loc:
Tonto National Forest 
                    Gila County, Arizona
desc: Signal Peak Lookout is a 59’ MC-39 Aermotor tower with a metal 7’x7’ cab. Built in 1934, it replaced a wooden tower dating to 1920. This active station is located on a 7781’ mountain in the Tonto National Forest.

name: Springer Mountain Lookout
loc:
Apache-Sitgreaves National Forest 
                    Navajo County, Arizona
desc: Constructed by the CCC in 1933, Springer Mountain is a 30' MC-24 tower with 12’x12' cab. In active service, the cab was remodeled in 1967 by the Apache-Sitgreaves National Forest.

name: Spruce Mountain Lookout
loc:
Prescott National Forest 
                    Yavapai County, Arizona
desc: Spruce Mountain Lookout was constructed in 1936 and continues in active service. It is a modified L-4 on a 30’ MC-24 Aermotor tower on a 7693’ high mountain in the Prescott National Forest.

name: Sugarloaf Mountain Lookout
loc:
Chiricahua National Monument 
                    Cochise County, Arizona
desc: Sugarloaf Mountain Lookout was built by the CCC in 1935 on the Chiricahua National Monument, the last stronghold of Cochise. The 14’x14 ground house with stone base and permanent overhang roof is one of two of this NPS design known. The other was Millers Head Lookout in Shenahdoah National Park, VA which was removed in the 1980s. Sugarloaf is linked with Barfoot Lookout (NHLR US#218, AZ#12) for coverage of the Monument as well as adjacent Coronado National Forest.

name: Tower Mountain Lookout
loc:
Prescott National Forest 
                    Yavapai County, Arizona
desc: Visible to travelers on I-17 in the Prescott National Forest, Tower Mountain Lookout sits atop a 7590’ mountaintop. Built 70 years ago (1933) it is a 30’ D-2 style Pacific Coast Steel tower with a modified L-4 cab. It continues in active service.

name: Turkey Butte Lookout
loc:
Coconino National Forest 
                    Coconino County, Arizona
desc: With an outstanding view of the red rocks country near fabled Sedona, Turkey Butte Lookout is a popular destination and viewpoint. The 32' Aermotor MC-24 tower, constructed in 1937, is of the design that was used in New Mexico and Arizona, but rare elsewhere. The wood 14' x 14' cab without catwalk is based on the L-4 design, but appears quite different.

name: Volunteer Lookout
loc:
Kaibab National Forest 
                    Coconino County, Arizona
desc: Located on the Navajo Army Depot, Volunteer Lookout is operated cooperatively by the Army and the Kaibab National Forest and is closed to public access. The 14’x14’ metal CL-100 cab on a 30’ metal tower with catwalk replaced an earlier wooden lookout dating to the 1930s.

name: Webb Peak Lookout
loc:
Coronado National Forest 
                    Graham County, Arizona
desc: Now in inactive status, Webb Peak Lookout was constructed on the Coronado National Forest in 1933 and is listed on the National Register of Historic Places. The 46’ Aermotor MC-40 with 7’x7’ metal cab originally had a platform ladder access with handrails but has been converted and only the last section uses a ladder.

name: West Peak Lookout
loc:
Coronado National Forest 
                    Graham County, Arizona
desc: The West Peak Lookout was built in 1933 by the CCC. Located on Arizona’s Coronado National Forest, the 46’ Aermotor LX-25 tower with 7’x 7’ cab is also listed on the National Register of Historic Places.

name: Woody Mountain Lookout
loc:
Coconino National Forest 
                    Coconino County, Arizona
desc: This 46' steel tower with metal 7' x 7' cab is one of relatively few provided by Pacific Coast Steel. The first lookout on the Woody Mountain Lookout site was a tree stand from 1910 to 1921. It was replaced with a wood tower from 1922-1936 when the current tower was built. It is on the National Register of Historic Sites.

name: Black Rock Lookout
loc:
Arizona Strip District - Bureau of Land Management  
                    Mojave County, Arizona
admin: Department of the Interior - Bureau of Land Management
desc: A unique 2 story BLM lookout design located in Mojave County, Arizona and operated by the Bureau of Land Management, Arizona Strip District Office.

name: Happy Valley Lookout
loc:
Saguaro National Park 
                    Pima County, Arizona
admin: National Park Service - Saguaro National Park
desc:
Happy Valley Lookout is located in the Saguaro Wilderness within the National Park. The structure is a small, rectangular ground cabin with a gable roof. It replaced an earlier and smaller ground cabin. A structure has been on the site since 1904. 
 The current cabin was constructed in 1969, last staffing is unknown.

name: Whitney Pass Lookout
loc:
Arizona Strip District - Bureau of Land Management 
                    Mojave County, Arizona
admin: Department of Interior - Bureau of Land Management
desc:
A very unique limited view aspect lookout cabin facing Arizona from just inside the Nevada border. 
 The primitive site has no water, electricity or propane.  
 Much left to learn about this lookout structure and it's role.

name: Thornton Lookout
loc:
Hualapai Reservation 
                    Coconino County, Arizona
admin: Bureau of Indian Affairs - Hualapai Reservation
desc:
Thornton Lookout was constructed in 1945, an Aermotor 100 foot X-Brace open steel tower with a 7x7 observation only cabin on top. 
 Renovations with new siding and steps were completed in 1998. 
 The lookout continues to be staffed as of 2011.

name: Ella Mountain Lookout
loc:
Ely District - Bureau of Land Management 
                    Lincoln County, Nevada
admin: Bureau of Land Management, Ely District
desc:
There are only three lookouts standing in Nevada, and Ella Mountain is the only remaining staffed structure. One of a handful of lookouts in the U.S. operated by the BLM, it lies in the Clover Mountains south of Caliente NV 80 miles north of Las Vegas near the Utah border. 
 Built in 1962, the 14’x14’ cab with catwalk is a modified R-6 flattop with slightly slanting windows on a 8’ concrete block base.

name: Yellow Peak Lookout
loc:
Sheldon National Antelope Refuge 
                    Washoe County, Nevada
desc: There are only three lookouts remaining in Nevada, and two of them are operated by the Bureau of Land Management (BLM). Yellow Peak Lookout oversees the Sheldon National Wildlife Refuge in the high desert and timber islands of northwestern Nevada. Built in 1981, it is a unique 9' x 9' groundhouse with wooden catwalk on a 2' foundation, and is staffed during periods of high fire danger.

name: Zephyr Point Lookout
loc: Douglas County, Nevada
desc: Zephyr Point, the last U.S. Forest Service lookout in Nevada, is located near the southeast corner of Lake Tahoe. Built in 1932, it is one of only 12 remaining 4AR style cabs, of which six are in California, two each are in Oregon and Arizona, and one each is located in Idaho and Nevada. Inactive for many years, it was last staffed by the Nevada Division of Forestry and has been restored.

name: Belknap Mountain Lookout
loc: Belknap County, New Hampshire
admin: NH Dept. of Resources and Economic Development
desc: Located within a state forest of the same name, the 34' steel tower with the standard and unique New Hampshire wooden cab was constructed in 1915. In a 1979 addition, 10' was added to the Belknap Mountain Lookout tower. Reached by trail from the popular Gunstock Recreation Areas, the lookout has many visitors and reports many fires. In active service.
agency: NH Dept. of Resources and Econ

name: Blue Job Mountain Lookout
loc: Strafford County, New Hampshire
admin: NH Dept. of Resources and Economic Development
desc: First used as a detection site in 1913, Blue Job is a focal point of a small state forest, the 32' steel tower with wood cab was constructed in 1915 and modified in 1930 and again in the 1980s. For many years the lookout served both Maine and New Hampshire under a cooperative agreement. In active service.
agency: NH Dept. of Resources and Econ

name: Cardigan Mountain Lookout
loc: Grafton County, New Hampshire
admin: NH Dept. of Resources and Economic Development
desc: Cardigan State Park and Forest is a well known destination in New Hampshire. The 15' steel tower was fabricated by state crews, not purchased from a supplier, in 1924. It originally had a steel ladder which was later replaced with stairs. In active service.
agency: NH Dept. of Resources and Econ

name: Craney Hill Lookout
loc:
Town of Henniker 
                    Merrimack County, New Hampshire
desc: If ever there was an example of how effective the NATIONAL HISTORIC LOOKOUT REGISTER can be as a catalyst in saving a fire lookout threatened with removal, Craney Hill Fire Tower is it. When word came of a proposal to replace the tower with a commercial electronics tower, the citizens of Henniker, NH went to work, with very happy results. The first lookout on Craney Hill was established in 1912. In 1932 the NH Forestry Commission constructed the current 41’ International Derrick tower with metal 7’ x 7’ cab, later a 10’x 10’ wood cab was placed on top of it, raising the tower ten feet. Regularly staffed until 1981, the lookout is now managed by the Town of Henniker, the Henniker Historical Society and the Craney Hill Fire Tower Association.

name: Federal Hill Lookout
loc: Hillsborough County, New Hampshire
admin: NH Dept. of Resources and Economic Development
desc: The second southern-most active lookout in the state, Federal Hill went into service in 1911 with a 20' treetop platform and used intermittently until 1918. In 1929 the present steel tower with wood cab was built. Damaged in the 1938 hurricane, the tower was repaired and possibly raised. It was raised again during the 1980s and is in service.
agency: NH Dept. of Resources and Econ

name: Great Hill Fire Tower
loc:
Hemenway State Forest 
                    Carroll County, New Hampshire
desc: Constructed by the CCC in 1934 on the Hemenway State Forest, the Great Hill Fire Tower was staffed by NH Forestry until 1974. In 1977 the tower was transferred to the Town of Tamworth with the provision it continue to be available for fire detection when needed.

name: Green Mountain Lookout
loc: Carroll County, New Hampshire
admin: NH Dept. of Resources and Economic Development
desc: Located northwest of Maine’s Ossipee Lookout (NHLR #187, ME#09) Green Mountain lookout was moved from Cedar Mountain, ME in 1922. The original 47' steel tower was shortened to 39' in 1977 with a Maine-style "perched" wooden cab placed on top. Now in part-time service, it is the only such structure in the state.
agency: NH Dept. of Resources and Econ

name: Hyland Hill Lookout
loc: Cheshire County, New Hampshire
admin: NH Dept. of Resources and Economic Development
desc: Located on the Vermont line in southwest New Hampshire, Hyland Hill was placed in service in 1930 and with some interruptions remains in operation. The 53' steel tower is topped with the standard NH wooden cab.
agency: NH Dept. of Resources and Econ

name: Magalloway Lookout
loc: Coos County, New Hampshire
admin: NH Dept. of Resources and Economic Development
desc: Located in the northern tip of the state, Magalloway Lookout went into service in 1910 using funds contributed by the NH Timberland Owners Association (NWOA affiliate). The current 37' steel tower with standard 10’x10' NH wood cab was constructed in 1935. It replaced the second of two wooden towers on the site, the last wood tower in the state. It is in active service.
agency: NH Dept. of Resources and Econ

name: Milan Hill Lookout
loc: Coos County, New Hampshire
admin: NH Dept. of Resources and Economic Development
desc: Used as an aircraft spotting station in World War II and located in a small state park of the same name, the 45' steel tower with standard NH wooden cab was built on Milan Hill in 1932. It is in active service.
agency: NH Dept. of Resources and Econ

name: Mount Kearsarge Lookout
loc: Merrimack County, New Hampshire
admin: NH Dept. of Resources and Economic Development
desc: In 2012 Saco Ranger District personnel completed a restoration on the lookout.  They were led by a Forest Service technician from the Nez Perce National Forest in Idaho with experience in historic preservation of similar design lookouts.   The renovation included an airlift of lumber, tools and equipment; the replacement of the tower legs, cabin girders. fascia boards and cross bracing.    Hikers were educated about the project with a temporary interpretive sign.
agency: NH Dept. of Resources and Econ

name: Mount Prospect Lookout
loc:
Weeks State Park 
                    Coos County, New Hampshire
admin: NH Dept. of Resources and Economic Development
desc: Mount Prospect Lookout is a stone tower that is probably unique in the nation.  Part of the summer estate of U.S. Senator John W. Weeks (author of the Weeks Act which created eastern National Forests), the structure was built as a private observation tower in 1912.  When the estate became a State Park in 1941, the New Hampshire Division of Forests and Lands added a round, enclosed lookout cab which remains in active service.
agency: NH Dept. of Resources and Econ

name: Oak Hill Lookout
loc: Merrimack County, New Hampshire
admin: NH Dept. of Resources and Economic Development
desc: Located not far from the Concord, New Hampshire’s capitol, Oak Hill is an example of the importance of early fire detection in the ever expanding urban/wildland interface. The 55' steel tower was constructed in 1928 it incorporated a new design feature: an observation platform for visitors just below the cab. The tower was raised 10' in 1971 and eventually went into irregular operation. It was returned to full service in 1991, at first with a volunteer lookout, and then as part of the state network.
agency: NH Dept. of Resources and Econ

name: Pack Monadnock Fire Tower
loc:
Miller State Park 
                    Hillsborough County, New Hampshire
admin: NH Dept. of Resources and Economic Development
desc: The newest fire lookout cab in New Hampshire, Pack Monadnock, was constructed in 2004 and placed in service in 2005. It replaces Hyland Hill fire tower which is still maintained. The 41' International Derrick tower with 7'x7' metal cab was constructed in 1939. The small cab was replaced in 1940 with a wooden 10'x10' cab which was burned by a lightning strike in 1960 and repaired.
agency: NH Dept. of Resources and Econ

name: Pawtuckaway Lookout
loc: Rockingham County, New Hampshire
admin: NH Dept. of Resources and Economic Development
desc: Standing on the south knob of the Pawtuckaway Mountain within a state park, this was the first steel lookout tower built in N.H. The station was established in 1913 and the 25' tower erected in 1914. It was modified in 1930 and raised 10' in 1971, with a new cab installed in 1976. It is in active service.
agency: NH Dept. of Resources and Econ

name: Pequawket Fire Tower
loc:
White Mountain National Forest 
                    Carroll County, New Hampshire
desc: A well-known landmark in the Granite State, Pequawket Fire Tower was one of the earliest detection sites in the state, going into service in 1913. The 28' steel tower originally had a 10’x10' standard NH wooden cab which was remodeled in 1953 and 1977. In 2000 a 12’x12' "perched" enlarged wooden cab was constructed and may become a prototype for the state. It is in active service.

name: Pitcher Mountain Lookout
loc: Cheshire County, New Hampshire
admin: NH Dept. of Resources and Economic Development
desc: Pitcher Mountain station was established in 1915 with a wooden tower and open platform. A 25' steel tower with NH standard 10’x10' wooden cab was built in 1925 and destroyed in the Stoddard-Marlow fire of 1941. The state rebuilt it immediately and it is in active service.
agency: NH Dept. of Resources and Econ

name: Red Hill Tower
loc:
Town of Moultonborough 
                    Carroll County, New Hampshire
desc: The Red Hill Tower was constructed by the State of New Hampshire in 1927 as a replacement for the Mt. Israel Lookout. The original 27’ metal tower with 10’x10’ wooden cab was raised to 55’ in 1972 and an observation platform added for visitors. Closed by the state in 1981, the tower is now staffed by the Town of Moultonborough Fire Dept. on land owned by the Lakes Region Conservation Trust, and is now the only active NH tower not owned by the state.

name: Smarts Mountain Lookout
loc:
White Mountain National Forest 
                    Grafton County, New Hampshire
desc: The first fire lookout on Smarts Mountain in New Hampshire was built in 1915. In 1939 the NH Forestry Commission constructed this 41’ steel tower with 7’ x 7’ cab -- which is the last International Derrick tower in the state -- using emergency federal funds following the 1938 hurricane.  It is located on the Appalachian Trail.

name: Stratham Hill Fire Tower
loc:
Town of Stratham 
                    Rockingham County, New Hampshire
desc: The Stratham Hill Fire Tower was constructed in 1931 by the N.H. Department of Forests and Lands on property that had been donated as a community park in 1905. The 53' steel tower, with a public observation platform at the 45' level has a 10'x10' cab with no catwalk. Staffed by the state until 1976, it is now maintained by the Town of Stratham. The original wooden cab was burned in 1997 and replaced with a metal cab.

name: Warner Hill Lookout
loc: Rockingham County, New Hampshire
admin: NH Dept. of Resources and Economic Development
desc: Built with Federal Emergency Funds after the 1938 hurricane, Warner Hill Lookout was commissioned in 1939. The 41' International Derrick steel tower has had several additions. During World War II it was used an an aircraft warning station because of its proximity to the seacoast. It is in active service.
agency: NH Dept. of Resources and Econ

name: Deer Mountain Lookout
loc:
Connecticut Lakes Headwaters Working Forest 
                    Coos County, New Hampshire
admin: New Hampshire Department of Natural and Cultural Resources
desc: The original tower at this site was built by the New Hampshire Timberland Owners Association in 1911. The state took control of the site in 1915 and constructed a new 30-foot wooden tower. The tower was rebuilt in 1922 and later replaced in 1933 by the current steel structure. The tower was closed in 1976 with its cab later removed, but the steel frame remains as of 2022.

name: Bald Mountain Fire Tower
loc: Orleans County, Vermont

name: Burke Mountain Fire Tower
loc:
Town of Burke 
                    Caledonia County, Vermont
admin: Vermont Dept. of Forests, Parks, and Recreation
desc: Established in 1913, Burke Mountain is the second oldest lookout site in Vermont. The current 54’ Aermotor tower with 7’ x 7’ steel cab is the fourth to grace the summit. It replaced a wooden tower with a unique octagonal wooden cab that was blown down in the great hurricane of 1937. Deactivated in the 1970s, the tower was given a facelift in 1990 by the FAA in exchange for hanging a microwave dish. Located in the Darling State Forest, it is open to the public.

name: Elmore Mountain Fire Tower
loc:
Elmore Mountain State Park 
                    Lemoille County, Vermont
admin: Vermont Dept. of Forests, Parks and Recreation
desc: Originally constructed by the Vermont Division of Forestry, and now maintained by the Division of State Parks, Elmore Mountain Fire Tower is a well-recognized local landmark. Following the disastrous New England hurricane in 1938, a federal forestry task force was established to work with the states in rehabilitating the forests of the region. One of their accomplishments was completed the following year when the tower, residence cabin and an underground phone line were established. The lookout remained active until 1974.

name: Monadnock Mountain Fire Tower
loc: Essex County, Vermont
desc: This steel tower was build by the Civilian Conservation Corps between 1938 and 1940. It was only manned for about a decade.

name: Mount Olga Fire Tower
loc:
Molly Stark State Park 
                    Windham County, Vermont
admin: Vermont Dept. of Forests, Parks and Recreation
desc: The original octagonal wooden fire tower on Mt. Olga -- a design possibly unique to the State of Vermont -- was constructed by the Division of Forestry in 1930. Although several towers of this type were built, none remain today. The present steel lookout with 7x7’ metal cab was moved to the site from Bald Mountain in 1949 and was in use until the 1970s. The tower is maintained as a popular hiking destination and view point in Molly Stark State Park.

name: Spruce Mountain Fire Tower
loc:
Plainfield 
                    Washington County, Vermont
admin: Vermont Dept. of Forests, Parks, and Recreation
desc: Three generations of fire lookouts have stood atop Vermont's Spruce Mountain. The first, an open platform with legs integral with the four corners of the ground cabin, was constructed in 1919. It was replaced in 1931 by a taller spruce log tower with a 7'x7' wooden cab. In 1943 the current steel tower with 7'x7' metal cab was moved from Bellevue Hill to Spruce Mountain where it stands today. No longer used for fire detection, the tower is now maintained by the Vermont State Parks Division.

name: Stratton Mountain Lookout
loc:
Green Mountain National Forest 
                    Windham County, Vermont
desc: The first lookout on Stratton Mountain, Vermont dates from 1914 when the Stratton Mountain Club and the Vermont State Forester constructed a 60' steel tower. In 1928 a watchman's cabin was added, and in 1934 the CCC built the present 55' Aermotor tower with 7'x7' metal cab. The state replaced the ground house in 1970, and in 1990 the land and tower were purchased by the USFS for addition to the Green Mountain National Forest and the Appalachian Trail corridor. Green Mountain Club is the Lookout Steward.

name: Okemo Mountain Lookout
loc:
Okemo State Forest 
                    Rutland County, Vermont
admin: Vermont Department of Forest, Parks and Recreation
desc:
In 1921, the State of Vermont acquired two acres of land from the Black River Lumber Company at the summit of Ludlow Mountain in Mount Holly for the purpose of creating a “fire lookout station.” The original tower, built with assistance from the Okemo Mountain Club in 1924, stood 30 feet tall and was constructed of wood. 
 In 1934, the Civilian Conservation Corps began work on a new 60-foot tall steel tower which was completed around 1937. A three-room cabin for the warden was located at the base of the tower. This cabin was completely removed in 1947. In 1943, a new 18'x24' watchman's cabin was constructed 100 feet away from the tower. In 1951, a stone chimney was built for the lookout cabin and this is all that remains of the cabin today. 
 In 2010, a contractor was hired to paint the tower’s stairway, replace 10 steps, install ground wires, install a railing in the tower cab, reinforce the landing floors, and install a chain link fence along the stairs and around the landings. In 2012, the remains of the old tower roof were removed and a new steel plate roof was installed thanks to the generosity of Okemo Mountain Resort.

name: Glastenbury Mountain Fire Tower
loc:
Green Mountain National Forest 
                    Bennington County, Vermont
desc:
This 50-foot steel tower was originally ordered by the Vermont Timberland Owners Association in November 1926. It was dedicated July 4, 1927, along with 5 miles of telephone cable to connect it to the network. 
 Work to improve the access trail, paint the tower, and install a new foundation under the fireman's tower was completed in 1932. A new fire finder map was installed in 1938. 
 The tower was last manned in 1949. It was reconstructed by the Youth Conservation Corps using materials flown in by helicopter in 1976. The first flight of stairs for the tower was removed in 2022 following an inspection, which flagged them as being in poor condition.

name: Beech Mountain Lookout
loc:
Acadia National Park 
                    Hancock County, Maine
desc: Beech Mountain has been the site of a lookout in Maine’s Acadia National Park since 1943. The present prefab steel tower was built between 1960-62 in a project called ‘Operation Beech.” The lookout is now staffed by park rangers only during high fire danger. During the summer park volunteers attend the tower so hikers may climb the structure and visit the cab.

name: Deasey Mountain Lookout
loc: Penobscot County, Maine
desc: One of the very few ground house lookouts in Maine, Deasey Mountain Lookout (also know as Daicey Mountain) was constructed by the Maine Forest Service in 1929 and used for detection until 1969. The 8’x8’ cab is on the Elliotsville Plantation in Penobscot County.

name: Deboullie Mountain Lookout
loc:
Maine Public Reserve Lands 
                    Aroostook County, Maine
desc: Located on Public Reserve Land in the northwoods of Maine is Deboullie Mountain Lookout. Owned by the Maine Forest Service, the 60’ guyed steel tower has an 8’x8’ wooden cab perched somewhat precariously on top. Although aircraft have assumed the detection role in this part of the state, the lookout is maintained for communications and as an emergency detection site.

name: Harris Mountain Lookout
loc: Penobscot County, Maine
desc: Harris Mountain Lookout, a 50 wooden tower with 14 x 14 live-in cab and catwalk was the only tower of its type in the state of Maine. It was built by the U.S. Forest Service and originally stood on the Allegheny National Forest in northwestern Pennsylvania. In 1940 the tower was dismantled and purchased by the Maine Forest Service, which moved it to this location. The tower was removed in 2006.

name: Mitten Mountain Lookout
loc: Washington County, Maine
desc: Mitten Mountain Lookout was built in the late 1940s from a kit that was delivered to the Columbia Falls train station and hauled to the site by truck. Forest warden David Grant worked with Hun Ashe and Arnold Davis to erect the lookout. Its first lookout was Harold Burgess and its second was Ray Pineo. Maine phased out the use of fire towers in the early 1970s.

name: Mount Agamenticus Fire Tower
loc:
Town of York 
                    York County, Maine
desc: Better known as Aggie, Mt. Agamenticus was the site of a 24 fire tower built in 1918. It was replaced by a 47' tower in 1934 which in turn was replaced by the current 65' tower in 1981 with a catwalk added in 1985. Three states can be seen from the structure which remains active and is staffed by the Town of York Fire Department.

name: Mount Hope Fire Tower
loc:
Town of Sanford 
                    York County, Maine
desc: Erected in 1962, the 60’ Mount Hope Fire Tower was one of the last constructed in Maine. The metal Aermotor tower with 7’ x 7’ metal cab replaced a 60’ wooden western tower with live-in cab and catwalk that was located on nearby Ridley Hill. The tower, owned by the Maine Forest Service, is active and is staffed each year by volunteers from the Sanford Township Fire Department.

name: Mount Pisgah Fire Tower
loc:
Town of Winthrop 
                    Kennebec County, Maine
desc: The Maine Forest Service constructed the Mount Pisgah Fire Tower in 1949.  It is a 60’ Aermotor tower with a 7’x7’ cab. It is now owned and maintained by the Town of Winthrop and the Kennebec Land Trust and open to the public.

name: Ossipee Hill Lookout
loc:
Waterboro 
                    York County, Maine
desc: The Ossipee Hill Fire Tower becomes the third lookout in York County to win recognition on the NHLR, joining previous listings Mt. Hope and Mt. Agamenticus. All three are owned and maintained by the Maine Forest Service, and each is staffed by volunteers from the town fire departments. The original tower on Ossipee Hill fell victim to the disastrous Maine forest fires of 1947. The present 30’ treated wood tower with a 13’ x 13’ shingled wood cab was constructed in 1948.

name: Rocky Mountain Lookout
loc:
Maine North Woods (7 Island Land Co.) 
                    Aroostook County, Maine
desc: Rocky Mountain Fire Tower at the northern tip of Maine and Quebec woodlands can be seen to the east, north and west. The original wood tower was built by landowners in 1907. The Maine Forest Service constructed the 54’ steel tower with 8’x 8’ wooden cab in 1921. The tower is guyed and the cab is reached via an open ladder. The summit is reached only by trail and there is a warden residence one mile below. Access is with permit via private timber roads from the Dickey checkpoint.

name: Ross Mountain Fire Tower
loc: Somerset County, Maine
desc: The metal fire towers with seemingly oversized wooden cabs “perched” on top are unique to Maine and have been around a long time. The guyed 60’ tower with 8’x 8’ cab on Ross Mountain was first erected in 1914 at another location and has been moved twice. It came to its present site in the 1940s. No longer in active use, it is maintained by the Maine Forest Service for emergency detection.

name: Squaw Mountain Lookout
loc: Piscataquis County, Maine
desc: Squaw Mountain is the first lookout in Maine and one of the oldest lookout sites in America. The first tower was built in 1905 by the M.G. Shaw Lumber Co. Other lookouts were constructed and in 1909 the state legislature merged all of them into the Maine Forestry District. The present steel tower with wooden cab was built in 1959. The land including Squaw Mountain was purchased by the Maine Dept. of Parks and Recreation in 1975.

name: Azure Mountain Fire Tower
loc: Franklin County, New York
admin: New York Dept. of Environmental Conservation
desc:
There are a number of success stories of restoration of fire towers in the Adirondacks, and Azure Mountain is among them. The first lookout on the site was a wood platform built in 1914. In 1918 New York DEC built the present 35’ Aermotor LS-40 tower with 7’x7’ metal cab at a cost of $300. In 1934 the State added the 535 Azure Mountain tract to the Adirondack Park and continued to staff the lookout until 1978. The 1936 observers cabin was removed in 1995, but in 2001 the fire tower and six others won listing on the National Register of Historic Places. The tower was restored in 2002 by a team from DEC, AmeriCorps, and a group known as Azure Mountain Friends (who published an excellent Fire Tower Interpreter’s Guide).
 

 
From The Observers' Cabin by Bill Starr:  "What I call the `Model 1936' cabin was developed and placed into service that year. Six were built at Azure, De Bar, Makomis, Poke-O-Moonshine, Rock Rift and Stissing mountains. The blue prints call for a stone fireplace on the front wall of the cabin. Yet from very recent photographic research not all these cabins were constructed with the stone fireplace.  Accessibility to material and even to a skilled stone mason was essential. At Azure, De Bar and Poke-O-Moonshine mountains road access to the cabin sites was available, and a stone mason must have been at one of the nearest C.C.C. camps because these three locations all had their 'Model 1936' cabins built with a stone fire place. The only other cabin with a stone fire place was at St. Regis Mountain where this cabin was built in 1939. Two stone chimneys existed on this cabin, the main fireplace in front and a smaller chimney in the rear left corner of the cabin at the pantry, no doubt for a wood burning cook stove."

name: Balsam Lake Mountain Fire Tower
loc:
Balsam Lake Mountain Wild Forest 
                    Ulster County, New York
admin: New York State Dept. of Environmental Conservation
desc: Balsam Lake Mountain is the oldest documented forest fire observatory within New York State. In 1887 the land was owned by the Balsam Lake Club, and fire was a serious concern to large land owners such as the club. They erected a tower made from timbers found on the mountain top and paid a man to staff the tower during dry conditions. This tower was struck by lightning and burned down about 1901. The club built a similar wood tower on the mountain in 1905. When the state began their fire tower system in 1909 operation of the Balsam Lake Mtn. facility was transferred to the state. The tower has been fully restored and is open to the public. It is also registered on the National Register of Historic Places, and the National Historic Lookout Register.

name: Beebe Hill Fire Tower
loc:
Beebe Hill State Forest 
                    Columbia County, New York
desc:
This is the third site that this fire tower has stood upon. In 1928 the Taconic State Park Commission erected the Aermotor LS-40 60' tower on Alander Mtn., just barely within the Commonwealth of Massachusetts, for the sole purpose of detecting fires on park land. In 1930 the area at Alander Mtn. burned, and the land owner asked for the tower to be removed. The tower was dismantled by Park staff and stored at the High Falls facility in the park. The Park re-erected the tower on Washburn Mtn., within the park boundaries, in 1933. Operation of the tower was turned over to Forest Fire Control about 1935 and was actively operated there until 1963. In November of 1963 the tower was dismantled by Forest Rangers and transported by helicopter to the Beebe Hill site and re-erected. The tower was actively operated at Beebe Hill until it was closed in 1987. 
 As of 2025, the tower was recently restored. Upgrades include replacing wooden stairs with metal. 
 Learn more about the Beebe Hill Chapter and work on its restoration at  beebehill.info .

name: Belfry Fire Tower
loc:
Hammond Pond Wild Forest 
                    Essex County, New York
admin: New York State Department of Environmental Conservation
desc: The Belfry Fire Tower overlooks the Champlain Valley and the Green Mountains of Vermont to the east. To the west the high peaks of the Adirondack Park are visible and include Hurricane fire tower. The fire tower was closed in 1988.

name: Berry Hill Tower
loc: Chenango County, New York
admin: New York State Dept. of Environmental Conservation
desc: Berry Hill is the second fire tower in New York erected by the the Civilian Conservation Corps, and is owned by the NY Department of Environmental Conservation. The 59'3" International Derrick tower with 7’X7’ cab was built to overlook the thousands of acres of state reforestation lands planted in the ‘30s in the region just west of the Catskill Mountains.

name: Black Mountain Fire Tower
loc:
Black Mountain Section of the Lake George Wild Forest Adirondack Park 
                    Washington County, New York
admin: New York State Department of Environmental Conservation
desc: The 35-foot steel fire tower on Black Mountain was erected in 1918 for fire spotting purposes. It remained in use until 1988 when it was officially closed. At that time additional reinforcement was made to the fire tower to add a 39' foot extension for state police communications, making the modified tower a total of 80-feet tall. The fire tower is currently closed to the public. There is a modular building at its base, surrounded by fencing.

name: Black Rock Forest Fire Tower
loc:
Black Rock Forest 
                    Orange County, New York
desc: The Black Rock Forest Fire Tower was erected in 1929 as a private lookout on the Stillman Estate which in time became the 3,800 acre Black Rock Forest owned by Harvard University. In 1989 ownership was transferred to the Black Rock Forest Consortium. The tower is an 80' Aermotor LS-42 model with 7'x7' metal cab and has been restored except for the roof.

name: Blue Mountain Fire Tower
loc: Hamilton County, New York
desc: Blue Mountain Fire Tower may be best known and most visited fire tower in the Adirondacks. The site was used as a station in the land survey of 1870 and a wooden tower was built there in 1911. The present 35’ Aermotor LS-40 tower with 7’ x 7’ steel cab was constructed by NYSDEC in 1917 and remained active until 1990. The tower was rehabilitated in 1994 and staffed by volunteers of the Blue Mountain Fire Tower Committee.

name: Cornell Hill Fire Tower at Wilton
loc:
Camp Saratoga 
                    Saratoga County, New York
desc: Previously owned by the Luther Forest Corporation and maintained in partnership with the Town of Wilton, Cornell Hill Fire Tower at Wilton was erected by the NY Conservation Commission in 1924. It is a 60’ Aermotor LS-20 tower with 7’x7 metal cab.   In 2011, the tower was relocated to near Camp Saratoga in the Wilton Wildlife Preserve & Park.

name: Dickinson Hill Fire Tower
loc: Rensselaer County, New York
desc:
Constructed in 1924 by the State of New York and last used for fire detection in the 1980s, Dickinson Hill Fire Tower is a 60' Aermotor LS-40 with 7' x 7' metal cab. During World War II it was used by the Aircraft Warning Service and in the 1970s was the site of communication experiments by the U.S. Navy.
 

 
Additional information courtesy of Bill Starr, NHLR State Registrar:  "A group from the Grafton Lake, N.Y. area has formed to adopt and restore this fire tower. Currently the facility is owned by the State Police who had two-way radio equipment mounted on the tower. This radio equipment has been moved to a new monopole. The group has been working to have the State Police transfer ownership of the land to the adjacent Grafton Lakes State Park, and with this transfer begin restoring the fire tower. With the current ‘Homeland Security’ issues this transfer has been delayed. The tower is registered on the National Historic Lookout Register, and a nomination to the National Register of Historic Places has been submitted for this tower."
 

 
Another Bill Starr story:
 
"As most of you know Randy Kneer 
 
				and I went to visit Dickinson Hill (R4) Observer Helen Ellett 
 
				today at her home in Grafton, NY. Helen turns 95 years old on 
 
				Monday 2-17-09 and she is as sharp and sassy as they come. We 
 
				had a great visit! 
 
				 
 
				"Helen is the ultimate "Tom-Boy." She loves to big game hunt and 
 
				she proudly displays her many Whitetail Deer head mounts, She 
 
				founded the "Grafton Trail Riders" equine club in the late 1940s 
 
				along with an early snowmobiler's club in the early 1960s. She 
 
				married at 18 years of age and she proudly showed me the 5 
 
				generation picture that was taken in December showing Helen, her 
 
				daughter, grandson, great-granddaughter and 
 
				great-great-granddaughter. 
 
				 
 
				"Helen lived about 5 miles away from the fire tower. During the 
 
				week she would ride one of her horses to work at the fire tower. 
 
				On weekends Helen, her daughter and husband would stay in the 
 
				cabin at the fire tower.  
 
				 
 
				"Attached are two very nice pictures of the Observer's cabin at 
 
				Dickinson. In the one picture note Helen's horse in the 
 
				background. Do you recall the concrete block building that was 
 
				attached to the side of the cabin? It turns out that it was a 
 
				garage that District Ranger Charlie Traver had built in 1950 
 
				from the capital construction fund money. He said that he could 
 
				not justify building a horse stable, but she could stable her 
 
				horse in the garage. Note the picture of the garage interior 
 
				with Helen and one of her horses. 
 
				 
 
				"Lou Curth...District 12 never held a Spring meeting bringing 
 
				all of the rangers and observers together. Dickinson Hill never 
 
				had a two-way radio until the present day radio network was 
 
				created in 1965, her last year on the tower. She did however 
 
				talk frequently over the telephone with the observers at Colfax 
 
				and Cornell Hill to triangulate smokes. She did become friendly 
 
				with Observer Jennie Bennett at Colfax. From the last picture 
 
				taken at the Conservation Dept. display at the Schaghticoke Fair 
 
				she was acquainted with Ranger George MacDonald. 
 
				 
 
				"The final question I asked dealt with a rumor I heard at a 
 
				Friends of Dickinson Hill picnic about 5 years ago. I had 
 
				overheard that an Observer was murdered at their fire tower. She 
 
				said that this did indeed happen and she was told about this by 
 
				District Ranger Charlie Traver. She did not recall which fire 
 
				tower it was, but she did say that it happened at one of the 
 
				Adirondack fire towers. It stemmed out of a love triangle
