				between the female Observer, her husband and her lover. One of 
 
				the men went into a jealous rage and killed her in the cabin at 
 
				the fire tower. 
 
				 
 
				"I am guessing that this took place during Helen's first tour on 
 
				Dickinson 1943-1953 being that in 1960 Charlie Traver was 
 
				retired...."

name: Ferncliff Forest Fire Tower
loc:
Ferncliff Forest 
                    Dutchess County, New York
desc: The current overlook is a 1933 International Derrick Fire Tower and is approximately 80 feet high. The overlook offers spectacular views of the Hudson River and Catskill Mountains. The overlook is open everyday all year long and is an easy walk of 15 minutes from the Ferncliff Forest parking lot.   The first overlook was built to aide map makers and was made out of trees from the forest. The Astor Family built a stone overlook in or around 1912. The foundation of that overlook remains on the site. In 1942 the Army Engineers built a wooden tower of 40 feet to protect the President in Hyde Park during the war. That tower was taken out of service in the year 2000. In 2007 an International Derrick fire tower was moved to the Forest. This overlook has over 10,000 visitors per year.

name: Goodnow Mountain Fire Tower
loc: Essex County, New York
desc:
The 60’ Aermotor LS-40 tower with 7’x7’ metal cab on Goodnow Mountain was built by the NY Dept. of Conservation in 1922 and staffed until 1970 when fire towers were gradually phased out. Located near the heart of the Adirondack Forest Preserve, it is reached by a 3 mile trail to a 2,690’ peak on the 5,000 acre Huntington Forest owned by the College of Environmental Science and Forestry at Syracuse University. The College and the Town of Newcomb partnered an exemplary restoration effort in 1995.
 

 
Additional information and photos courtesy of Bill Starr, NHLR Registrar:  "This site is on land owned by the State University of New York, College of Environmental Science and Forestry and is attached to the Huntington Forest in Newcomb. This land was originally logged by the Huntingtons', and an old two stall horse barn, and concrete slab of another building for the logging operations are past on the foot trail to the fire tower. The tower has been restored by SUNY-ESF, and is open to the public. The station is registered on the National Register of Historic Places, and the National Historic Lookout Register."

name: Graham Mountain Fire Tower
loc:
Mount Hope Township 
                    Orange County, New York
desc:
The Graham Mountain Fire Tower was originally erected by the New York State Department of Environmental Conservation on Pocotello Mountain (locally called Sayers Hill) but was dismantled and moved to its present site nearby in 1948. The 60’ Aermotor LS-40 tower with 7x7’ steel cab was a key link in a three state group of towers (Culvers, NJ and Buckhorn, PA). No longer in service, both the tower and the ground house have received some maintenance from the NY/NJ Highlands Group of the Forest Fire Lookout Association.
 

 
History notes from Bob Spear FFLA Historian, fflahistorian@gmail.com: "The access road to the Graham Mountain Fire tower is off "Mountain Road" below Otisville, NY. It usually has a secured gate on it because it also provides access to radio antennas that are also located up there on the Ridge. The neighbor you mentioned nearby has nothing to say about the use of the access road to the tower, it only borders his property- not on it. His main concern in the past were cars parked along his fence line on Mountain road, which is not all that wide and has a deep drainage ditch, grass filled along the side. To get to Graham tower, I always went a bit farther north on Mountain road to the next road on the left which takes you in a winding fashion up toward the top. There was an abandoned house up there at one time where you could park, and from that it was only about a ten minute fairly level walk over to the road that leads to the tower. Note* This also may be private property; but I never encountered an issue with  it.  Graham at one time was a strategic Fire Lookout on the Shawangunk ridge which was always prone to bad fires, there, in the Wurtsboro, NY area and was in a position to work fires in the volatile Cherrytown Road region which is extremely thick with growth. From Graham fire tower it is almost exactly 15 miles South to the High Point Monument, the highest elevation in New Jersey 1800+ feet elevation. When I was active as a Firewarden in both States I often heard the operator at Graham fire tower over the radio, along with Balsam Lake, Mohonk, and Sterling. Sterling fire tower and Graham fire tower are identical "sister towers"  Sterling was built in 1922 and for an accurate date of Graham, refer to Bill Starr's excellent history of NY State fire towers. From Graham fire tower, one looks directly Southwest into Port Jervis on the Delaware River's bend to the South. The thick woods in Sullivan County has always been a rife area for big woods fires, and further out is the Poconos of Pennsylvania, in the very faint distance can be seen Big Pocono Mountain, and to the East, New York City's skyline.  I always had nearly as much a fondness for Graham fire tower as I did my own at Sterling, but property disputes over the area always left it uncertain as to who owned it.  I have only been inside the ground cabin twice in all those years, once when Ranger Dave Mead set up housekeeping there for awhile and another time when I visited with Ranger Greg Tyrrell. My key I had for Sterling tower's gate also use to open the fire cache locker under the cabin, most fire wardens had keys for these things for emergencies. Today, Graham still surveys much of the same vast GREEN of Ulster and Sullivan Counties and the more urbanized areas in Orange County. Fire is STILL very much in evidence here when conditions permit."

name: Hadley Mountain Fire Tower
loc: Saratoga County, New York
desc:
Located west of the popular Lake George tourist area, Hadley Mountain Fire Tower was one of the original ten steel fire towers purchased by the state. The 40’ Aermotor LL-25 structure with 7’ x 7’ metal cab was placed in the middle of a 12,000-acre area that had burned repeatedly during the previous decade.
 

 
From The Aermotor Model LL-25 by Bill Starr, NHLR State Registrar:  "The AerMotor Model # LL-25 was proposed to the State, and ten of these towers were ordered. All were delivered by rail road early in 1916 and nine were immediately erected at Cathead, Fort Noble, Hamilton, Makomis, Moosehead, T - Lake, Tommy, Wakely, and Woodhull Mountains. The last tower was for Ohmer Mountain although the State was unable to secure an agreement with the land owner there, so Hadley Mountain was selected to replace Ohmer. Construction of the tenth tower began late in 1916 on Hadley and was not completed until early in 1917."

name: Hunter Mountain Lookout
loc:
Catskill State Forest Preserve 
                    Greene County, New York
desc: Hunter Mountain has been a landmark in the Catskill Mountains of New York since the region was settled in the late 1700s. This station is one of the first facilities operated by Forest Fire Control. Established in 1909 with a tower made of timbers found at the mountain top the station was established at the 4, 000 foot elevation of the mountain, 40 feet shy of the true summit. In 1917 the present 60' steel Aermotor LS-40 tower was erected next to the wood tower site, and it remained at the 4,000 foot elevation until in 1950 the tower was dismantled and re-erected at the current location on the summit of 4,040 feet. The tower has been fully restored and is open to the public. The facility is also registered on the National Register of Historic Places.

name: Hurricane Mountain Fire Tower
loc:
Adirondack Mountains 
                    Essex County, New York
desc: Hurricane Mountain is a solid rock summit in the Adirondack Mountains with a stunning 360-degree view. Since 1909 it has been the home of a fire tower. The first wooded structure was replaced in 1919 with the present 35' Aermotor LS-40 tower with a metal 7'x7' cab.

name: Jackie Jones Lookout
loc:
Harriman State Park 
                    Rockland County, New York
desc: The last steel fire tower in the Bear Mountain-Harriman State Park, Jackie Jones Lookout was constructed in 1928 by the Palisades Interstate Park Commission, who operated the facility until 1931. From that time the facility was operated by Forest Fire Control until it closed in the 1970s. The 60’ Aermotor LS-40 tower with 7’x7’ metal cab features windows of an unusual design.

name: Kane Mountain Fire Tower
loc: Fulton County, New York
desc: Located in the southwestern corner of the Adirondack Park, Kane Mountain Fire Tower was the only one built in Fulton County. Although established in 1925 the facility did not begin operating until 1926. The 60’ Aermotor LS-40 tower with 7x7’ steel cab was staffed until 1988. The New York Chapter of the Forest Fire Lookout Association has expressed an interest in helping maintain the tower and the groundhouse.

name: Leonard Hill Fire Tower
loc:
Leonard Hill State Forest 
                    Schoharie County, New York
admin: New York State Department of Environmental Conservation
desc: The 80-foot Aeromotor LS40 fire tower on Leonard Hill was originally constructed in 1934 in Gilbert Lake State Par in Oneonta County. It was moved to its current location in 1948 were it was in operation until 1988. The fire tower is currently closed to the public.

name: Loon Lake Mountain Fire Tower
loc: Franklin County, New York
desc: One of the early lookouts in the state, erected in 1917, and reconstructed in 1927 after it was blown down by a hurricane, Loon Lake Mountain Fire Tower is again a popular hiking destination since the NY DEC rebuilt the trail in 2013. The 35’ Aermotor tower is in poor condition and is scheduled for rehabilitation.

name: Lyon Mountain Fire Tower
loc:
Chazy Highlands Wild Forest 
                    Clinton County, New York
admin: New York State Department of Environmental Conservation
desc: With views north into Montreal Canada, east into the Green Mountains in Vermont and south into the high peaks of the Adirondacks, Lyon Mountain played an important role in spotting fires. This 35' Aermotor LS-40 tower was built in 1917. The fire tower was in use until the end of 1988 and was officially closed in 1989.

name: Mount Adams Fire Tower
loc:
Town of Newcomb 
                    Essex County, New York
admin: Open Space Institute of New York
desc:
Located just south of the famed high peaks areas of the Adirondack Forest Preserve, Mount Adams fire tower has become the center of a public debate over the question whether fire lookouts are compatible with wilderness designation. The first tower here was a wooden structure built in 1912 at the request of the Tahawus Club. In 1917 the state erected the present 47’ Aermotor LS-40 tower with 7’x7’ metal cab and staffed it until the mid 1970s. The ground house was constructed in 1922 with improvements made in 1950, Inactive for a number of years, the site had been nominated to the National Register of Historic Places as well.
 

 
Bill Starr, NHLR State Registrar, has furnished additional information:  "The Observer's cabin at Adams is the first style of standard design cabin that the state began building at the fire towers. I call this cabin a Model 1922 for the year it was introduced.  At Adams this cabin is the ONLY surviving Model 1922 in the state. The Friends of Mt Adams began restoration work on the cabin in Sept. of 2007 and the pictures are from that work day..."
agency: Open Space Institute of New Yo

name: Mount Arab Fire Tower
loc: St. Lawrence County, New York
desc: Forest fires swept forests of the Adirondack Mountains repeatedly in the early 1900s, and in 1916 the State of New York began construction of an extensive network of permanent steel fire towers to replace wooden structures that were expensive to maintain. These towers served continuously until 1990 when they were all replaced by air patrol. The Mount Arab Fire Tower, a 35’ Aermotor structure with 7’x 7’ metal cab, was built in 1918, replacing a wooden tower opened in 1911. It is the only tower remaining of the seven that once stood in St. Lawrence County and is a popular hiking destination. The tower and Observer cabin has been fully restored by the “Friends of Mt. Arab” and is open to the public. This facility is registered on the National Register of Historic Places, and the National Historic Lookout Register.

name: Mount Beacon Fire Tower
loc: Dutchess County, New York
desc:
The Mount Beacon Fire Tower was built in 1931 on the site of an earlier wooden tower. It was used by NY State Forest Rangers for 50 years before being decommissioned in 1987. The 60’ Aermotor LS-40 tower with 7’x7’ metal cab overlooks the Hudson River Valley, including the skyscrapers of New York City 55 miles to the south.  Despite the fact that DEC surplused the tower more than a decade ago, there were no buyers, or takers, so the tower remains a DEC tower on City of Beacon land. 

 Additional information courtesy of Bill Starr, NHLR State Registrar:  "This station appears in the 1922 and 1924 Annual Reports to the Legislature as South Beacon Mtn. which was first established with no tower of any kind. During this time when the Observer spotted a fire he had to walk a quarter mile down the foot trail to a tree where the telephone line ended. He then had to climb that tree to dial out on a temporary type telephone. This facility was upgraded to a steel fire tower in 1931. Awaiting restoration group formation. 

 6/22/2013 Re-opening Ceremony 

 The colonials used the 1,400 foot north peak of Mount Beacon during the Revolutionary War to set warning fires to alert General Washington at his headquarters on the western side of the Hudson of any British presence in the valley below. From this activity, the City of Beacon got its name. 

 The Mount Beacon Fire Tower is however located on South Mount Beacon which is just under one mile due southeast and two hundred fifty feet higher than the peak where those early warning fires were built. Constructed on the site of a former wooden fire tower in 1931, it stood for 79 years without any major renovations. The last assigned fire ranger was in 1972. Thereafter, the tower became open to hikers bold enough to ascend the seventy two stairs to the seven foot by seven foot observation room at the top. One learned quickly on such a trip that new steps were badly needed, as were upgraded railings and new steel for most of the cross members. In 2001, "the DEC Division of Lands and Forest Region 3 staff member, George Profous, followed up on informal requests to save the deteriorating tower and sent reports to ascertain project support... ." In 2003 a formal organizational meeting took place with NYSDEC, the NYS Hudson Valley Greenway, the City of Beacon, the Scenic Hudson Land Trust, and the Mt Beacon Incline Railway Restoration Society participating. The Mount Beacon Historic Fire Tower Restoration Committee resulted with John Hupe as its first Committee Chair. A small group of dedicated men and women from the original committee began to seek funding and ways to promote the mission to restore the tower. Their first undertaking was to sell the seventy two replacements steps via a successful public marketing campaign. In 2005 the tower earned special recognition when it was placed on the National Historic Lookout Register. During the next two years much needed funding for the project was gained thanks to former State Senator Steve Saland and the late State Assemblyman Thomas Kirwan. 

 In the fall of 2007, David Rocco joined the MBFTRC organization and became the Project Manager. He brought his enthusiasm and experience from several other historic preservation projects, not the least of which was his five years as a board member for the acclaimed Walkway Over the Hudson. 

 After the replacement steps were installed over the summer of 2008, the next phase was to install new staircase landings and the cabin floor. The two hundred pound steel gratings removed from the historic Poughkeepsie Railroad Bridge, now the Walkway Over the Hudson, were transported up Mt. Beacon, then hand carried across the mountain top to the fire tower by several of the fire tower committee members. Over the course of the next several weekends, all of the landings and the cabin floor were replaced. 

 Then in 2009 the Mt. Beacon Fire Tower again earned notable historic status with its listing on the State and National Registry for Historic Places.  By 2010, engineering inspections were updated and the same dedicated core of committee members worked diligently with the Hudson Valley Four Wheelers Association to get the remaining necessary materials and equipment up to the tower site for the first phase of the cross bracing work. Two years later, Vanna Construction LLC of Saranac Lake, New York, was hired to work alongside all the volunteers to complete the remaining steel cross braces. They also replaced the roof on the cabin. Noteworthy that Dave Vanna, the owner of Vanna LLC, commented that of all the fire tower restoration jobs he had done across the United States, this particular project was the most challenging to reach because of the great difficulty moving vehicles up the mountain and over the large boulders which made the trail to the tower almost impassible for all but the sturdiest and most flexible of four wheel drive vehicles and their skilled drivers. Thanks to the core volunteers, the Hudson Valley Four Wheeler Association, and the New York Army National Guard (1156th Engineering Company and the 204th Engineering Battalion), the cross bracing, cabin walls, raised handrails, and priming and painting of the entire tower were accomplished professionally and passed all inspections. The Beacon Fire Tower was ready for those intrepid hikers adventurous enough to go up to the top to get an even more breathtaking view of the Hudson Highlands, the New York City skyline sixty miles due south and on very clear winter days the New York State Office Towers in Albany ninety miles due north. 

 94 year old Pete Seeger and 82 year old David Amram were two of the first guests of the Fire Tower Committee on the official opening day, June 22, 2013, to arrive at the summit and to climb the tower. These two gentlemen along with the wonderful Hudson Valley Storyteller, Jonathan Kruk, were the featured artists for the re-opening of the tower. Thanks to the twenty-five volunteer four wheel drive vehicle owners, the sixty guests arrived safely up top from the base of Mount Beacon. With the entire Hudson Valley Highlands as the amphitheater, David Rocco stood on one of the granite outcroppings surrounded by the folks who had contributed so selflessly all those years. With great sincerity he thanked each volunteer and contributor for their efforts. Jon Kruk then told a captivating tale of Beacon folks from the Revolutionary Period who came to believe that one man of some questionable means had actually buried treasure up on this mountain. Since it was never found, we are today left with the amazing treasure of this high and special place open for all of us to enjoy for just the price of the challenging hike. David Amram followed with a Lakota Chant accompanied by Jon Kruk on a drum. It was a very special moment: the grand open sky, the simple true structure of the tower, the presence of over sixty dedicated workers and friends----all shared and contributed in silent tribute to the ancient sounds and feelings David and Jon brought to us that magical afternoon. Pete Seeger then asked us all to join him in song as he spoke the words to "Amazing Grace". One thousand six hundred fifty feet above the Hudson River, we responded. 

 The ceremony ended with Pete Seeger thanking all for their dedication to this piece of our history, a piece which just happens to be two miles from his humble house much farther down through the forest. Not often in our lives that we can be present at such a people's special site, to be present when the man who has dedicated his life to living in harmony with our planet once again took such joy in having another audience sing out, when this same man uncharacteristically wonders aloud if we would all consider the creation of another trail from Lake Melzingah deep in the forest below? Will we someday soon act to provide such access for others so they may approach and treasure this unique and hallowed ground? 

 Our Hudson Valley Storyteller Jon Kruk best captures the history and the special meaning this tower and this high ground has for us all--today- when he notes: 

 "Once upon a time, Yankee Doodles kept the fires ready for something revolutionary, a democratically ruled nation. Then, this tower served as a lookout for the destructive danger of forest fires. Now the Fire Tower on South Mount Beacon serves us in a new way. This tower calls us to appreciate this extraordinary landscape formed by the Hudson weaving through a branch of the Appalachians! This Beacon of Beauty calling us to treasure our majestic mysterious Hudson Highlands."

name: Mount Nimham Fire Tower
loc:
Taconic Hills 
                    Putnam County, New York
admin: New York Dept. of Environmental Conservation
desc: Located in the Taconic Hills north of New York City in Putnam County, Mount Ninham Fire Tower was built by the State of New York and the CCC in 1940. The 82'6" International Derrick Model 1937 tower LS-40 with 7' x 7' metal cab is located on state forestland. Although not used for fire detection in many years, it is maintained as a radio repeater site. Vandals burned the observer's cabin in 1994. Restoration of the tower was undertaken by the Town of Kent Conservation Advisory Commission.

name: Overlook Mountain Fire Tower
loc:
Catskill Forest Preserve 
                    Ulster County, New York
admin: New York Dept. of Environmental Conservation
desc: Located in New York’s Catskill Forest Preserve, Overlook Mountain Fire Tower was constructed by the New York Department of Conservation (now DEC) in 1917. The 60’ steel Aermotor LS-40 tower with 7’x 7’ metal cab was in active service for 54 years until it closed in 1971. It has been restored as a joint venture by the Catskill Forest Center (Catskill Forest Assoc., a NWOA affiliate), the Highlands Group of the Forest Fire Lookout Assoc. and the NYS-DEC.

name: Owls Head Fire Tower
loc:
Adirondack Forest Preserve 
                    Hamilton County, New York
desc: The first Owls Head Fire Tower in the Adirondack Forest Preserve was a wooden structure with open platform erected and staffed in 1911 in response to a disastrous series of forest fires. The current 35’ Aermotor LS-40 tower with 7’x7’ metal cab was constructed by the NYS-DEC in 1919 and staffed until 1970. The observers cabin was burned in 1979. In 2003 the DEC and Friends of Owl Head Fire Tower restored the lookout and it is again open for hikers.

name: Perkins Memorial Lookout
loc:
Bear Mountain State Park 
                    Orange County, New York
desc: The impressive 40’ stone lookout tower on Bear Mountain in the New York Highlands was constructed in 1931-34 and dedicated as the Perkins Memorial Tower to honor a Chairman of the Palisades Interstate Park Commission which owns the site and surrounding forest west of the Hudson River near West Point Military Academy. The 20’ x 20’ lookout cab is still used by the Park Commission during periods of high fire danger.

name: Pillsbury Mountain Fire Tower
loc:
Town of Arietta 
                    Hamilton County, New York
desc:
Constructed in 1924, the 60' Aermotor Model LS-40 tower, with a 9' high cab, is typical of the "heavier type" tower with integral shaircase built by the Conservation Commission between 1917 and 1950. The structure consists of a square steel and glass cab with a hip roof enclosing the observation platform atop a riveted and bolted frame of angular steel.
 

 
Additional information courtesy of Bill Starr, NHLR State Registrar:  "This was the fire tower at which I worked in the late 1970s. The station was first established in 1918 by the land owner of the time, the Champlain Reality Company. The facility was equipped with a wood tower made from mountain top timbers, and a log cabin was built to house an observer. The station was operated by the company in conjunction with Forest Fire Control as a secondary station during periods of dry weather. In 1924 operation of the facility was turned over to the state. The company purchased the steel tower, and had it erected, before the station was turned over to Forest Fire Control. Today the tower houses, and supports a solar powered two-way radio repeater, and the cab is closed to the public. Excellent views are still possible from the top landing of the fire tower. This is the only fire tower in which a person can see West Canada Lakes. In 2005 minor restoration work was performed."

name: Poke-o-moonshine Fire Tower
loc: Essex County, New York
desc: The mountain probably got its name from a “bag of corn whiskey” that some traveler found stashed there many years ago.  Another and likely possibility is that the name was derived from the Algonquin name for the hill:  Pohqui moosie. Poke-O-Moonshine Fire Tower was first used as a lookout site in 1912. The 35’ Aermotor LS-40 tower with 7’x7’ metal cab was constructed 81 years ago in 1917. A popular hiking destination in the Adirondack Park, it was deactivated in 1988 and considered for removal. In 1997 the Town of Chesterfield passed a resolution supporting renovation of the tower. The Adirondack Heritage and the Adirondack Mountain Club joined in a Friends of Poke-O-Moonshine tower project.  The above photo was taken by Randy Kneer in August 2007.

name: Red Hill Fire Tower
loc: Ulster County, New York
desc: Located on a State Forest Preserve Tract on the southern edge of the Catskills, Red Hill Fire Tower was constructed by NYS-DEC in 1920 and staffed until 1990. The 60’ Aermotor LS-40 tower with 7x7’ steel cab is equipped with an unusual 1/2” tube alidade.

name: Rock Rift Fire Tower
loc: Delaware County, New York
desc: Rock Rift tower is a 72' 9" International Derrick E-4898 steel tower provided to the State of New York by the US Forest Service and erected by the CCC's in 1934. It is actually located on Tower Mt. Summit elevation is 2382' It remained in service until 1989.

name: Rondaxe Mountain Fire Tower
loc: Herkimer County, New York
desc:
Rondaxe (Bald) Mountain Fire Tower may challenge Blue Mountain as the most-visited fire lookout in the Adirondacks. Located just above the Old Forge tourist area, a wood tower was built in 1912 and the present 35’ Aermotor LS-40 tower with 7x7’ steel cab was built in 1917 and is a very popular destination with hikers. Rondaxe has the distinction of being the last fire tower to be closed by the state in 1990.  The tower was restored in 2005.
 

 
Additional information courtesy of Bill Starr, NHLR State Registrar:  "This facility is not to be confused with the Bald Mtn. near Old Forge, N.Y. Established in 1911 the Bald Mtn. near Old Forge was established in 1912. Two Bald mountains could not exist as fire towers so the name Rondaxe Mtn. was given to the Bald Mtn. near Old Forge, taking the name from the adjacent Rondaxe Lake, a fact that has never rested well with the Old Forge community. Ownership of the Bald Mtn. facility was transferred to the land owner, where it stood, about 1975 since the station was closed and would not re-open. The Diamond Match Co. owner of the land did not want to encourage the public to continue to visit the tower so they had the tower removed. The tower had two of the legs cut and it was pulled over. The tower now rests where it fell nearly 30 years ago.  This tower has been adopted through the “Adopt–A–Natural Resource” program, offered by the NYS-DEC, by the “Friends of Bald Mtn.” and restoration work on the tower is in progress. This tower is listed on the National Register of Historic Places, and the National Historic Lookout Register."

name: Snowy Mountain Fire Tower
loc:
Jessup River Wild Forest Adirondack Park 
                    Hamilton County, New York
admin: New York State Department of Environmental Conservation
desc: A 22-foot steel tower was built on the summit in 1917. In 1933, a 20-foot extension was added to allow a sight line over the trees. The Snowy Mountain fire tower was in operation until 1971. The fire tower was restored in 2001 by a group of DEC staff, Student Conservation Corp, and local citizens with support from the NYS Police helicopter to deliver materials.

name: Spruce Mountain Fire Tower
loc:
Wilcox Lake State Forest 
                    Saratoga County, New York
desc: The Spruce Mountain Fire Tower was renovated in the Fall of 2015 and reopened to the public. The new Spruce Mountain Trail and renovated tower is the result of a successful partnership between the New York State Department of Environmental Conservation (DEC), Saratoga County, and Saratoga PLAN. The new trail is currently managed by the Adirondack Mountain Club. In accordance with the conservation easement agreement for the lands the trail crosses, the trail is closed to public use during the big game hunting season

name: St. Regis Mountain Fire Tower
loc:
Adirondack Forest Preserve 
                    Franklin County, New York
desc: The site of a lookout in the northern Adirondacks since 1909, the present Saint Regis Mountain Fire Tower was constructed in 1918 by the state of New York and staffed for 81 years before being closed at the end of the 1990 fire season. The 35’ Aermotor LS-40 tower with 7’x7’ metal cab is readily visible from the Forest Interpretive Center at Paul Smiths College and is a popular hiking destination.

name: Sterling Fire Tower
loc:
Town of Warwick 
                    Orange County, New York
desc:
Sterling Fire Tower was built by the area fire wardens in fall of 1922 on the Harriman Family's Sterling Park estate.  Constructed using steel hauled to the ridgetop by muletops, the 60’ Aermotor LS-40 tower with 7x7’ steel cab was first used in the spring of 1923. Over the course of its first year, the tower had 137 visitors. More importantly, 104 fires were spotted by Sterling and its companion Jackie Jones Fire Tower.
 

 
In 1968, the tower and cabin were improved. A new access road was also bulldozed. The road was lined with 38 numbered cedar poles carrying a 2-conductor phone line to the tower.
 

 
Sterling Fire Tower was placed on the Federal Register of Historic Places on June 12, 2006 along with the observers cabin.

name: Stillwater Mountain Fire Tower
loc:
Town of Webb, Stillwater Reservoir 
                    Herkimer County, New York
admin: New York State Dept. of Environmental Conservation
desc: The first lookout on this site was a tower made of timbers built in 1912. The current 47' Aermotor model LS-40 tower was erected in 1919 by the New York State Conservation Commission, now the NYS-DEC. The tower stood watch over the watershed of the Stillwater Reservoir of the Beaver River in northern Herkimer County and along a 25 mile stretch of the New York Central Railroad's Adirondack division. The fire tower also provided observation protection over the eastern forest lands owned by the Fisher Forestry and Reality Company.

name: Stissing Fire Tower
loc: Dutchess County, New York
desc:
The Stissing Mountain Fire Tower is an International Derrick Model 1933. It stands 86 feet high as situated and is located n a section of Stissing Mountain in Pine Plains, NY. It opened in 1934 and was in service as a fire observation tower from March 1935 through April 1971. Eventually it became threatened with dismantling. 
 The Friends of Stissing Landmarks (FOSL) was incorporated in 1989 and sought transfer of ownership from New York State. This occurred in May 1989, with subsequent transfer of ownership of one acre beneath it from the Nature Conservancy to FOSL in May 1993. In the same year it was restored for the first time. Subsequent restoration began in 2017 and is expected to be completed in 2018. FOSL maintains the fire tower for public use year round free of charge.

name: Sugar Hill Fire Tower
loc: Schuyler County, New York
admin: New York State Dept. of Environmental Conservation
desc:
This 67'6" International Derrick model 1937 tower was erected in 1941 by CCC, staffed by volunteers until 1951, and then by the State until 1979. Maintained by the NYS-DEC, it is a popular forest recreation area.
 

 
Additional information courtesy of Bill Starr:  "In 1922 the old Bureau of Forest Fire Control began constructing standard design ground cabins at all New York State fire towers. This standard design saw four official modifications reaching the final design in 1941 with a 16 ft X 24 ft rustic style cabin. After all of New York's fire towers were decommissioned in 1990 many of the various ground cabins were lost forever due to vandalism. Most of the surviving grounds cabin found today are in a variety of disrepair, excluding the sites were the facilities have been restored. The model 1941 Observer's cabin at the Sugar Hill fire tower stands out as a cabin in nearly mint condition. Excluding the installations of an electrical service, eve gutters and swapping the bedroom and kitchen around inside the cabin the Sugar Hill cabin retains all of the subtle features not found on most of the ground cabins today. Most notably is the entrance door on the cabin, it has not been kicked in and the door retains the original wrought iron latch and lock-set which was install during it's construction. Also still intact on the entrance door is the small peep window and decorative wrought iron hinge extensions. The original style window shutters still exist along with the wrought iron decorative hinges and holders to keep the shutters open. Many thanks must go out to the staff of the Dept of Environmental Conservation - Region 8 for preserving the Sugar Hill cabin as a treasure of the state's rich forest fire control history. Anyone interested in seeing an Observer's ground cabin in mint condition is urged to visit the Sugar Hill site."

name: Swede Mountain Fire Tower
loc: Warren County, New York
desc: This 47' Aermotor LS-47 tower was built in 1918 because the area was prone to forest fires. The tower was closed in 1968.

name: Tremper Mountain Fire Tower
loc:
Catskill Forest Preserve 
                    Ulster County, New York
admin: New York Dept. of Environmental Conservation
desc: Located in New York’s Catskill Forest Preserve, Tremper Mountain Fire Tower was constructed by the New York Department of Conservation (now DEC) in 1917. The 47’ steel Aermotor LS-40 tower with 7’x 7’ metal cab was in active service for 54 years until it closed in 1971. Like Overlook Mountain, it has also been restored by a joint effort of the Catskill Forest Center, the Highlands Group of FFLA and the NYS-DEC.

name: Utsayantha Mountain Fire Tower
loc: Delaware County, New York
admin: New York State Department of Environmental Conservation
desc: In 1889, a prominent citizen of Stamford, NY purchased 20 acres on the top of Utsayantha Mountain, built an attractive four-story observation house (still there) and deeded the property to the town as a park. In 1934 the NY Dept. of Conservation built a 60’ Aermotor tower that is maintained and open to the public to climb.

name: Wakely Mountain Fire Tower
loc: Hamilton County, New York
desc: Wakely Mountain Fire Tower, at 72 feet, is one of the tallest towers in New York. The Aermotor LL-25 structure has a smaller 6’ x 6’ cab and was one of the first built in the state in 1916. It is of the “windmill” design and originally had a 64-foot outside ladder which was replaced with a safer factory stairway kit in 1930. One of the most remote towers, it offers remarkable views of the Moose River Plains region.     Additional information courtesy of Bill Starr, NHLR State Registrar: "In 2001 Ann Spaziano–Mac Bride and Bill Starr completed field data gathering of this facility so that Indian Lake Town Historian Bill Zullo could nominate the station to the National Register of Historic Places. The Wakely Mtn. station was placed on the National Register in 2003. Awaiting approval to begin restoration work." From The Aermotor Model LL-25 by Bill Starr: "The AerMotor Model # LL-25 was proposed to the State, and ten of these towers were ordered. All were delivered by rail road early in 1916 and nine were immediately erected at Cathead, Fort Noble, Hamilton, Makomis, Moosehead, T-Lake, Tommy, Wakely, and Woodhull Mountains."

name: Vandewhacker Fire Tower
loc:
Vandewhacker Mountain Wild Forest  
                    Essex County, New York
admin: New York State Department of Environmental Conservation
desc:
The 35-foot Aermotor LS 40 tower was placed on the summit of Vandewhacker Mountain in 1918. It was staffed for fire spotting purposes through 1971. 
 The trail to Vandewhacker Fire Tower is 2.5 miles long with an elevation gain of 1686'. For those with low clearance vehicles,  the road to the trailhead is often rough and one may wish to walk the additional 2.6-mile distance along this road.

name: Alma Hill Fire Tower
loc: Allegany County, New York
desc: Located in Allegany County in the Southern Tier of New York, the privately owned Alma Hill Fire Tower is an 80' tall Aermotor LS40 that was erected in 1950. The tower was officially closed in 1971. It was offered through public auction in 1973 and was purchased by the owner of the property where the tower stood. It remains standing today on that private property and is closed to the public.

name: Adirondack History Museum Fire Tower
loc: Essex County, New York
desc: Two Adirondack Fire Towers were removed in the 1980's, West and Kempshall. They were placed in storage and in the 1990's the museum purchased the tower parts and built a single tower as a permanent exhibit at the museum. Visitors must enter the museum to climb the fire tower. Along with other exhibits at the museum, a robust educational program has been developed for local schools where children can visit the fire tower and learn about the history of fire towers around the State.

name: Gomer Hill Fire Tower
loc:
State Forest Preserve 
                    Lewis County, New York
admin: New York State Department of Environmental Conservation
desc: Gomer Hill is a 67'6" International Derrick tower that was placed on the summit in 1940, first staffed in 1941 and then decommissioned in 1989.The site is on public State Lands, but the tower is closed as it contains numerous pieces of radio equipment.

name: Cathedral Rock Fire Tower
loc:
Ranger School Forest at Wanakena 
                    St. Lawrence County, New York
desc: The Former Tooley Pond Fire Tower was dismantled and then re-erected at the site of the New York State Ranger School by students and staff in the late 1990s. The 47-foot Aeromotor LS 40 tower can be visited by following the Latham Trail from the NYS Ranger School to the summit. The tower is sometimes referred to as the Ranger Tower and a nearby boulder contains a plaque that states "Dedicated to all Rangers, Observers, and Wardens who have watched over our forests."

name: Skytop Tower at Mohonk Preserve
loc:
Mohonk Preserve 
                    Ulster County, New York
desc: Located along the Shawangunk Ridge, The Skytop Tower on the Mohonk Preserve is a stone tower built by the Smiley family from 1921 to completion in 1923. It was actively used for spotting fires until 1971. To visit, one must be a guest of the Preserve.

name: Colfax Fire Tower
loc: Washington County, New York
admin: New York State Department of Environmental Conservation
desc: This 80-foot Aermotor LS40 tower was built in 1950 and closed to the public in 1970. Today, the tower houses radio repeater equipment for the New York State Department of Environmental Conservation and is surrounded by fencing.

name: Gore Fire Tower
loc:
Gore Mountain Ski Center 
                    Warren County, New York
admin: New York State Department of Environmental Conservation
desc: The 60-foot Aermotor LS40 tower was built in 1918, replacing an 18-foot wooden tower that had been built in 1909. This original steel tower was blown over in a Hurricane in 1919, but quickly re-erected in 1920. The tower was closed in 1988. It has been repurposed to house a great deal of communication equipment at the summit area of the Gore Mountain Ski Complex. The tower is closed to visitors.

name: Grafton Lakes Nature Explorers Lookout
loc:
Grafton Lakes State Park 
                    Rensselaer County, New York
admin: New York State Office of Parks, Recreation and Historic Preservation
desc: This tower was built in 2017 by Davana LLC utilizing parts of the West Bay Fire Tower from Florida. It is located in the children's playground at the Grafton Lakes State Park and has had some special accommodations to make it suitable for small children. It is hoped that it will encourage families to visit the other fire tower in the park,  Dickinson Hill , during their visit.

name: Buck Fire Tower
loc: Hamilton County, New York
desc: The private land owner, Whitney Park, originally erected the 60-foot tall Aermotor LS-40 steel tower in 1933 to protect its lands. The current private land owner, Cedar Heights Timber LLC, has entered into an agreement with Hamilton County to restore and reopen the tower to the public. Anticipated date for reopening is Summer 2022.

name: Makomis Fire Tower at Speculator
loc:
Speculator Village Park 
                    Essex County, New York
desc: The original Makomis Fire Tower, a 40-foot Aermotor LL25 model was taken down at its original location in Essex County. It was relocated and reassembled in Speculator in 2022.

name: Bramley Mountain Fire Tower
loc:
Bramley Mountain Unit NYC DEP lands 
                    Delaware County, New York
desc:
The structure on Bramley Mountain is an 80-foot Aermotor LS40 tower erected by the Conservation Department in 1950. Bramley Mt. lies 2 1/2 miles south of the Hamlet of Bloomville in Delaware County. There are public trails to the site of the tower. 
 With the advent of aerial detection, this tower was closed at the end of the 1970 season. It was sold for $50 and removed from the mountaintop in 1975 by the Clark family. The family kept the tower in storage in hopes of putting it up on their land. The summit of Bramley mountain is currently owned by NYC DEP. In January of 2020, a Friends of Bramley Mountain group formed and the Clark family donated the tower to the group to be placed back at its original location. Despite several set backs, the tower was returned to the mountaintop in the Fall of 2024, the only tower to be removed and then returned to its original location nearly 50 years later.

name: Cross River Mountain Fire Tower
loc:
Ward Pound Ridge Reservation 
                    Westchester County, New York
admin: Westchester County Parks, Recreation, and Conservation
desc: Original 1926, taken down 1980, restoration in 2026.   The beautiful and historic fire tower was erected in 1926 and was used by the community until the 1970’s. The County Parks operated the tower until the 1930’s when the NYS Conservation Department began its operations. The tower, the only one of its kind in Westchester County, was a critical asset to the community as it served as a monitoring station for forest fires. According to a Westchester County government report from 1975 indicates that about 500 fires were reported from the tower between 1966 and 1968, with tower observers working with aerial support to pinpoint their locations. The tower was decommissioned by the DEC in 1971 and was taken down without county approval around 1982.      The tower stood at the highest point of Cross River Mountain. The tower stood a staggering 960 feet above sea level. It had a spectacular 360 degree view with a visibility of 50-100 miles depending on the weather. From the tower Long Island, New York City, the Hudson River, the Catskill and the Appalachian Mountains can be observed. Over 100,000 people per year visit the reservation, the addition of the restored fire tower would increase tourism in the area as a much sought after destination.

name: Big Flat Fire Tower
loc:
Michael State Forest 
                    Cumberland County, Pennsylvania
desc: Built in 1921, this 60-foot steel Aermotor tower sits on South Mountain overlooking Gettysburg.

name: Big Pocono Lookout
loc:
Big Pocono State Park 
                    Monroe County, Pennsylvania
desc:
Big Pocono Tower is typical of fire tower construction in Pennsylvania between 1914 and 1939. Built in 1921 it is believed to be the oldest tower still in service (there are some older structures standing, but they are inactive). Located in a state park atop Big Pocono Mountain adjacent to Camelback Ski Area, the steel tower with 7’X7’ cab is only 21 ft. tall. An unusual feature at the site is a helicopter fire attack base used during fire season. Owned by the Pennsylvania Bureau of Forestry, the tower is also a focus of attention of the Pocono Forestry Association, which may be the oldest private forest protection association in the U.S. (est. 1901). 
 In 2017, the tower was disassembled as part of Pennsylvania's plan to upgrade its fire tower network. The tower will be replaced with a taller 40-foot tower. A wayside panel with information on the original tower will be installed as part of the upgrade project. The 1921 tower is being relocated to Grey Towers National Historic Site, the home of pioneering forester Gov. Gifford Pinchot, where it will be refurbished and re-erected in 2018.

name: Big Pocono Lookout
loc:
Big Pocono State Park 
                    Monroe County, Pennsylvania
desc: The new Big Pocono Lookout was built in 2017 as part of Pennsylvania's plans to upgrade its fire tower network. This 40-foot tower replaces a 21-foot predecessor, which has been relocated to Grey Towers National Historic Site,  he home of pioneering forester Gov. Gifford Pinchot.

name: Boot Jack Tower
loc:
State Game Lands 44 
                    Elk County, Pennsylvania
desc:
The original Boot Jack Tower was a 100-foot Aermotor built in 1939. 
 As part of Pennsylvania's late-2010s fire tower upgrades, the original tower was replaced in 2018 with a new 100-foot steel structure. The original tower was removed but its stone observer's cabin remains on-site.

name: Brooks Run Fire Tower
loc: Cameron County, Pennsylvania
desc: Located in a remote corner of the Pennsylvania Wilds, this 80-foot Aermotor tower was relocated to this site in 1941. It was previously located at Grove Mountain, also in Cameron County.

name: Buckhorn Ridge Lookout
loc:
Delaware State Forest 
                    Pike County, Pennsylvania
desc: Buckhorn Ridge tower is one of the few remaining Blaw-Knox (as compared to the more common Aermotor brand) towers in Pennsylvania, and the only one in District 19. Located within the Delaware State Forest. The 60’ tower with 7’ x 7’ metal cab serves as a cooperative fire detection point with the New Jersey Forest Fire Service. In active service, it overlooks the Gifford Pinchot estate (U.S. Forest Service) and the Upper Delaware National Scenic and Recreation River.

name: Cherry Springs Fire Tower
loc:
Susquehannock State Forest 
                    Potter County, Pennsylvania
desc: Located along PA 44 in remote Potter County, Cherry Springs Fire Tower overlooks the headwaters of East Fork First Fork Sinnemahoning Creek and Pine Creek. A fire tower has graced this site since 1917.

name: Clarks Knob Fire Tower
loc: Franklin County, Pennsylvania
admin: Pennsylvania Department of Conservation and Natural Resources
desc: This tower was built in 1945 by AT&T to replace a former state fire tower that had been on the same location. AT&T uses the large cab on the top of the tower for communication equipment. The cab from the previous tower was relocated to a lower level and used by PA DCNR staff for fire monitoring as needed.

name: Coffin Rock Fire Lookout
loc: Clinton County, Pennsylvania
desc: The newest lookout in Pennsylvania, Coffin Rock was constructed by the Pennsylvania Bureau of Forestry in 1987. It replaced a 1921 60' Aermotor destroyed by a tornado in 1985. It is a 93' Aermotor with an uncommon full catwalk around the 7'x7' cab.

name: Cole Hill Lookout
loc: Warren County, Pennsylvania
desc:
This Aermotor LS-40 tower with 7'x7' cab was originally constructed by the Pennsylvania Bureau of Forestry in 1925 as a 60' tower and located on land approximately 1/2 mile from the present location. It was relocated to its present location and raised to 80 feet in 1932 after a dispute with the landowners of the original site. 
 The tower is now privately owned, and the lower steps have been removed.

name: Eagle Field Tower
loc: Centre County, Pennsylvania
desc: Eagle Field Tower stands in Centre County on top of Bald Eagle Ridge eight miles west of State College, Pennsylvania. The 90 Aermotor steel tower with 7x7 cab and rooftop catwalk was built by the PA Dept. of Forests and Waters in the 1930s near Reynoldsburg and known as Elliot Tower.

name: Fire Tower #9
loc:
Cook Forest State Park 
                    Clarion County, Pennsylvania
admin: Pennsylvania Department of Conservation and Natural Resources
desc: This 87.5-foot steel tower was originally built as a tourist scenic viewing attraction in 1928. It was manned as a paid forest observer position from 1946-1966. Volunteers manned it from 1967 until a tornado took out its phone and electric lines in 1977. It currently functions as it was originally designed, for the public to take a scenic view of the area. Heavily visited during the summer season, often seeing 200-400 visitors every two hours. Although the tower is open to visitation year round, the cab is open only during interpretive programming.

name: Grandview Lookout
loc:
Ricketts Glen State Park 
                    Luzerne County, Pennsylvania
desc: This 100-foot steel tower was built in 1942. It is not open to the public but is staffed during fire season. Three states and 11 counties are visible from the lookout during clear weather.

name: Greenwood Fire Tower
loc: Huntingdon County, Pennsylvania
desc: This 60' Aermotor tower was built in 1921.

name: Hopewell Tower
loc:
William Penn Forest 
                    Berks County, Pennsylvania
desc: This 80' steel McClintic-Marshall tower with 7'x7' cab was built in 1935 by the CCC/French Creek Recreation project.

name: Keffers Fire Tower
loc: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania
desc: Keffers Fire Tower, located in Schuykill County, Pennsylanvia, is a good example of the innovation that is frequently seen in forest fire detection networks. The round wooden cab was built on top of a metal tower that originally supported a domed military radar. When the radar network was discontinued, the mountaintop tower and the concrete block base station became surplus. The Pennsylvania Bureau of Forestry acquired the site and constructed the round cab on the tower.

name: Knobs Fire Tower
loc:
Moshannon State Forest 
                    Clearfield County, Pennsylvania
desc: Knobs Fire Tower was built in 1921 to oversee the northern unit of the Moshannon State Forest by the Pennsylvania Bureau of Forestry which still maintains it. The 60’ steel tower with metal 7’ x 7’ cab has an adjacent cabin and also has a residence cabin built in 1933. The tower was refurbished in 2004 by the Bureau of Forestry with new steps and interior. It is one of three of the original towers that are still standing in Dist. 9 and is active during fire season.

name: Mauch Chunk Fire Tower
loc:
Weiser State Forest 
                    Carbon County, Pennsylvania
desc:
This Aermotor steel fire tower was built by CCC crews in 1936. 
 One of the lookouts to work at this site was Righter Reabold, who staffed this tower for 17 years.

name: Mount Dunlap Fire Tower
loc: Franklin County, Pennsylvania
desc: This 80-foot Aermotor MC-39 lookout tower was built in 1936 by CCC workers based at Old Forge. The tower is currently used for communications equipment and is closed off by a fence.

name: Pohopoco Fire Tower
loc:
Delaware State Forest 
                    Monroe County, Pennsylvania
desc: Located in the heart of the historic Pocono Mountains, Pohopoco Fire Tower is an 80’ lnternational-Stacey tower with 7’x 7’ cab.  It was constructed by the Pennsylvania Bureau of Forestry in 1935 within the Delaware State Forest.

name: Pondfield Fire Tower
loc:
Forbes State Forest 
                    Fayette County, Pennsylvania
desc: The Pondfield Fire Tower was constructed in 1935 by the Marshal McClintock Company and erected by the Civilian Conservation Corps. A watchman's ground cabin sits near the tower. The watchman jobs were seasonal and paid poorly. The jobs were usually held by farmers, housewives, etc. The Tower was staffed until the 1970s and is used today for educational purposes. The tower and ground cabin have fallen into disrepair and need major repairs.

name: Pump Station Fire Tower
loc: Lycoming County, Pennsylvania
desc: This 60' steel Aermotor tower was built in 1919 at a cost of $939, replacing a wood and tree tower built in 1914. The cabin was replaced in 1935.

name: Rattlesnake Fire Tower
loc:
Moshannon State Forest 
                    Centre County, Pennsylvania
desc:
One can easily imagine how Rattlesnake Fire Tower got its name. The original tower was built in 1933 on a rocky ridge in Pennsylvania’s Moshannon State Forest. This 80-foot steel tower with 7’x7’ metal cab is strategically located and remains in active service. 
 As part of Pennsylvania's late-2010s fire tower upgrades, the original tower was replaced with a new 80-foot steel structure. The original tower was removed but its stone observer's cabin remains on-site.

name: Rockton Fire Tower
loc: Clearfield County, Pennsylvania
desc:
A 95-foot Aermotor tower was originally built at this site in 1975. It is located atop Rockton Mountain, northwest of Clearfield. 
 As part of Pennsylvania's late-2010s fire tower upgrades, the original tower was replaced with a new 80-foot steel structure.

name: Sand Mountain Fire Tower
loc: Union County, Pennsylvania
desc: The original tower here was a 60' Aermotor built in 1917. It was replaced in 1950 by a 80' Aermotor tower moved in from Eastville (a.k.a. Hartley), also in Union County.

name: Silver Creek Fire Tower
loc:
Broad Mountain, Blythe Township 
                    Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania
desc: Silver Creek Fire Tower was erected in the spring of 1926 on property now owned by the Blythe Township, just south of Weiser State Forest.  In World War II is was used as an Aircraft Warning Service station.  The 60’ Aermotor tower with metal 7’x7’ cab was damaged in a storm in the mid 1940’s and rebuilt.  The new cab has an updated window design.

name: Snow Shoe Fire Tower
loc: Centre County, Pennsylvania
desc: The current Snow Shoe tower was built circa 2018 as part of Pennsylvania's project to modernize its fire tower fleet. It replaced a 60-foot Aermotor tower that was built in 1921.

name: Snowy Mountain Lookout
loc:
Michaux State Forest 
                    Franklin County, Pennsylvania
admin: Pennsylvania Department of Conservation and Natural Resources
desc: Located eight miles north of the Maryland, Snowy Mountain Lookout is in the Michaux State Forest not far from the historic Mont Alto Forest Ranger School. An 80-foot Aermotor tower with 7' x 7' metal cab was constructed in 1930. It made the news on October 29, 1973 when vandals felled the tower, cutting two of the four legs using only hacksaws. The criminals were eventually caught and charged with replacing the tower in 1975 at a cost of $45,800. The new 80-foot Aermotor LS-40K tower with a catwalk on one side is located on the Appalachian Trail and is used during peak fire periods.

name: Stony Mountain Moon Lookout
loc: Dauphin County, Pennsylvania
desc:
Built in 1922 by the Philadelphia & Reading Coal & Iron Company, the Stony Mountain Lookout is a 100-foot steel tower offering views of Harrisburg, Duncannon, and the Susquehanna River. The tower features a wrap-around catwalk, which is unusual for Pennsylvania. 
 The tower is colloquially known as "The Moon Tower" for its unobstructed panoramic views of the sky. Despite a 4-hour hike required to access the site, the area is commonly used as a hangout spot and for camping.

name: Tamarack Fire Lookout
loc: Clinton County, Pennsylvania
desc:
In service since 1919, the Tamarack Fire Lookout is still staffed by the Pennsylvania Bureau of Forestry in fire season. It was a 65' Aermotor tower with a 7'x7' cab. 
 Circa 2020, the original tower was replaced with a modern steel structure.

name: Tionesta Fire Tower
loc: Forest County, Pennsylvania
desc: This 80-foot Aermotor LS-40 tower has been protected the northwestern corner of Forest County since 1928.

name: Wheeler Fire Tower
loc:
Allegheny National Forest 
                    Warren County, Pennsylvania
desc:
The Wheeler Fire Tower on the Allegheny National Forest is an unusual Blaw-Knox tower with 7’x7’ metal cab. Built in 1923, the tower has sloping legs until the last four sections which are vertical. 
 The tower is located in the Hearts Content Recreation Area, an area designated as a National Natural Landmark, that was one of the first tracts acquired for Allegheny National Forest upon its founding in 1923.

name: William Penn Memorial Fire Tower
loc:
City of Reading 
                    Berks County, Pennsylvania
desc: Built in 1939 by the City of Reading as a tourist attraction and fire observation post and staffed by the Pennsylvania Bureau of Forestry untill 1988, William Penn Memorial Fire Tower is one of the most impressive lookouts in the U.S. This 120' stone tower with round copper dome cab replaced a wooden tower dating to 1889 which had burned in 1923. The City of Reading and Pagoda-Skyline, Inc. have restored the tower.

name: Little Flat Fire Tower
loc:
Rothrock State Forest 
                    Centre County, Pennsylvania
desc: This steel Blaw-Knox tower was built in 1922 to replace an earlier 1915 wood tower. On the northeast corner of the tower site is a small 3-room cabin with a natural stone veneer, believed to have been used by tower watchmen.

name: Marienville Fire Tower
loc:
Cornplanter State Forest 
                    Forest County, Pennsylvania
desc:
Two 1920s newspaper articles mention this tower: 
 October 13, 1921: "Fire Warden Rowland who is in charge of the forests in this end of the state, is completing the erection of the first fire tower to be erected in this section. The tower which is of steel is being erected near Marienville on a commanding height from which thousands of acres of woodland can be scanned by the warden at work in the tower with his glasses. The tower is a huge affair and stands 60 feet in height and is built of steel. In the foundations for the tower there were used eight tons of concrete and the foundation is solid. Eight tons of steel also enter into the construction of the fire tower which is fashioned to withstand mountain winds. The towers are the same type as are used in the western forests where men are kept constantly on watch to prevent destructive fires." (McKean Democrat)  October 31, 1924: "Recently the Marienville towerman had the interesting experience of watching two bears as they prowled about in the brush within a quarter of a mile of the tower. The animals were in sight for half an hour the towerman stated." (The Kane Republican)

name: Albert Mountain Lookout
loc:
Nantahala National Forest 
                    Macon County, North Carolina
desc: Albert Mountain Lookout is a popular way station on the Appalachian Trail a few miles north of the Georgia state line within the Nantahala National Forest. The 14x14’ live-in cab with catwalk on a 40’ steel tower was built by the U.S. Forest Service in 1951. It replaced a wooden tower located nearby on Standing Indian Mountain. The lookout, which overlooks the well-known Coweeta Watershed research area, is maintained and used on an emergency basis to supplement air patrols.

name: Barnett Knob Fire Tower
loc:
Cherokee Indian Reservation 
                    Swain County, North Carolina
desc: Located in the middle of the Qualla Boundary of the Cherokee Indian Reservation adjacent to the Great Smokey Mountains National Park, Barnett Knob Lookout Tower is the last active lookout on the Reservation. Constructed in 1932, the 80' metal tower with 7'x7' metal cab has been a favorite tourist attraction for those driving on the nearby Blue Ridge Parkway.

name: Bearwallow Mountain Lookout
loc: Henderson County, North Carolina
desc: The North Carolina Forest Service constructed Bearwallow Mountain Lookout in 1934. The 47’ Aermotor tower with 7’x7’ metal cab stands on the Eastern Continental Divide and is a popular hiking destination with views of Hickory Nut Gorge. Restoration of the lookout is planned for 2011-2012.

name: Buck Mountain Fire Tower
loc:
Uwharrie National Forest 
                    Montgomery County, North Carolina
desc:
The Buck Mountain tower rises from its 830-foot namesake in the community of Uwharrie. This metal structure dates to 1936 and was likely built by the Civilian Conservation Corps. The base of its 7-foot-by-7-foot cab is 94 feet from the ground. 
 Years ago, Jessie Sanders sometimes logged 14-hour shifts, seven days per week, in the Buck Mountain tower. (He and his fellow spotters also liked the bonus pay that came with fighting fires on the ground.) The tower used to be staffed consistently during dry weather, but now, with limited resources, Sanders or another ranger is dispatched to monitor our forests only during extreme conditions. It’s primarily used for locating fires after the USFS receives a smoke report. Sanders notes they receive more calls these days because so many people have cell phones. This mobile technology has replaced the tower’s old radio system, but its Osborne Fire Finder – a simple device developed almost a century ago – is still in operation. 
 A recently completed USFS study determined the Buck Mountain tower is eligible for the National Register of Historic Places. Many fire towers have been removed, so the ones that remain have a special significance. The Buck Mountain tower helps rangers protect our forests, but it also stands as a reminder of how our nation’s history has been shaped by fire.

name: Camp Creek Bald Lookout
loc:
Pisgah National Forest 
                    Madison County, North Carolina
desc: Camp Creek Bald Lookout, located in the Pisgah National Forest on the NC/TN state line was built in 1928 with a 14’x14’ cab on a 21’ steel tower. In the 1960’s one of two prototypes round cabs was installed. No longer active, the lookout has been partially restored by the U.S. Forest Service and a local radio club.

name: Chambers Mountain Lookout
loc: Haywood County, North Carolina
desc: One of the last active lookouts in western North Carolina, Chambers Mountain Lookout was constructed by the N.C. Forest Service in 1936. It is a 45’ Aermotor tower with a 7’x7’ metal cab.

name: Cowee Bald Lookout
loc:
Nantahala National Forest 
                    Jackson County, North Carolina
desc: Also located within the Nantahala National Forest is Cowee Bald Lookout, whose view includes much of the southern flank of the Great Smoky Mountains. Built in 1936, the 40’ steel tower with 14x14’ live-in cab with catwalk, was rebuilt in 1980. Although not staffed on a regular basis since the 1960s, the lookout is used jointly by the NC Forest Service and the U.S. Forest Service on an emergency basis.

name: Duckett Top Lookout
loc: Madison County, North Carolina
admin: North Carolina Division of Forest Resources
desc: One of a very few two-story lookouts left in North Carolina, Duckett Top was built in 1936 by the CCC for the US Forest Service. In 1966 it was transferred to the NC Forest Service, which continues to staff it. The 14’x 14’ wooden cab with catwalk is atop a 12’ rock foundation located on a “bald mountain” northwest of Asheville.

name: Fryingpan Mountain Lookout
loc:
Pisgah National Forest 
                    Transylvania County, North Carolina
desc: Overlooking the Cradle of Forestry in America on the Pisgah National Forest, Fryingpan Mountain Lookout was established in 1941. At 70’, the steel tower with a 12’x12’ metal live-in cab is the tallest lookout west of Asheville. Now used as a radio relay point, it is easily accessible from the Blue Ridge Parkway.

name: Green Knob Lookout
loc:
Pisgah National Forest 
                    Yancey County, North Carolina
desc: A classic “dunce cap” R-8 steep pyramid roof design once common in the southern National Forests, Green Knob is one of the few remaining. It is located in the Pisgah National Forest along the Blue Ridge Parkway, not far from Mt. Mitchell, the highest point in eastern America. The 32’ steel tower is topped with a 14’x 14’ wooden cab and catwalk built by the CCC and USFS in 1932,and restored in 1996. It is staffed occasionally by volunteers.

name: Hassell Lookout
loc: Martin County, North Carolina
desc: Located near the Roanoke River in eastern North Carolina, this state-owned tower was built in 1936.

name: Hibriten Mountain Lookout
loc: Caldwell County, North Carolina
desc: Built in 1927, the Hibriten Mountain Lookout is today part of a cluster of towers that graces the skyline of Lenoir, North Carolina.

name: Joanna Bald Lookout
loc:
Nantahala National Forest 
                    Graham County, North Carolina
desc: Built in 1952, the 31’ metal tower with 14’x14’ wooded live-in cab with catwalk on Joanna Bald on the Nantahala National Forest was a replacement for a wooden lookout house with cupola built in the early 1930s. Staffed by the U.S. Forest Service, and then the N.C. Forest Service until 2002, it is now maintained for emergency use.

name: Little Snowball Lookout
loc: Buncombe County, North Carolina
desc: The most historically complete restoration in western North Carolina, Little Snowball Lookout has been reconstructed at the Big Ivy Historical Society Center near Bernardsville. Constructed in 1934, the 14’x14’ wooden live-in cab with Catwalk on a 21’ steel tower overlooked a fire-prone section of the Great Craggy Mountains within the Pisgah National Forest. Reached only by trail, it was dismantled and hand carried out by volunteers in the 1980s.

name: Moores Knob Lookout
loc:
Hanging Rock State Park 
                    Stokes County, North Carolina
admin: NC Department of Environment and Natural Resources
desc: Erected in Hanging Rock State Park in 1938, the original Moores Knob Lookout was a steel tower with a 7’x7’ metal cab. In 1951 it was replaced with a two story stone structure, which was heavily damaged by Hurricane Hazel in 1954. Restored as a viewpoint with the cab removed, it is maintained as a state park hiking destination.

name: Mount Noble Lookout
loc:
Cherokee Indian Reservation 
                    Swain County, North Carolina
desc: One of two fire towers remaining on the Cherokee Indian Reservation, Mt. Noble Lookout was built by the Bureau of Indian Affairs in 1957, replacing a wooden tower dating from the 1930s. Unused for many years, the 60’ Aermotor tower with 7’x7’ metal cab, the BIA and the NC Div. of the Forest Fire Lookout Association are working together on a restoration plan.

name: Mount Sterling Tower
loc:
Great Smoky Mountains National Park 
                    Haywood County, North Carolina
desc:
Located on one of the highest points in the Great Smoky Mountains National Park, the Mount Sterling Fire Tower offers a commanding view. The 60’ steel Aermotor tower with 7’x7’ metal cab was constructed by the CCC in 1933. 
 The site is a popular backcountry hikers camp. Each year from February 15 to May 15, and then again from October 15 to December 15, the tower was manned by lookouts who lived on the premises on two-week tours. When he wasn't at his station, the watchman stayed in a cabin that once stood just north of the tower. 
 Today the National Park Service uses the tower as a radio repeater. The trap door is still open, and if you don't mind a shaky old structure, the views are breathtaking.

name: Panther Top Lookout
loc:
Nantahala National Forest 
                    Cherokee County, North Carolina
desc: Located on the Nantahala National Forest in the southwestern tip of North Carolina, Panther Top Lookout was constructed in 1940 on a knob known by locals as “PainterTop.” The 30’ Marshall-McClintock tower with a R-8 wooden 14’x 14’ cab with catwalk is still used in periods of high fire danger and is a popular visitor destination.

name: Rendezvous Mountain Lookout
loc:
Rendezvous Mountain Educational State Forest 
                    Wilkes County, North Carolina
admin: NC Department of Environment and Natural Resources
desc: Famed in Revolutionary War history, Rendezvous Mountain Lookout is the centerpiece of the state forest of the same name. Constructed by the North Carolina Forest Service in 1936, the 50’ Aermotor tower with 7’x7’ cab is now restricted for electronics use.

name: Rich Mountain Lookout
loc:
Pisgah National Forest 
                    Madison County, North Carolina
desc: Located on the NC/TN state line on the Pisgah National Forest, Rich Mountain Lookout is just off the Appalachian Trail. The 14’x14’ live-in cab with catwalk is on a 30’ metal tower.

name: Shuckstack Tower
loc:
Great Smoky Mountains National Park 
                    Swain County, North Carolina
desc: Long a landmark on the Appalachian Trail, the Shuckstack Fire Tower was constructed by the PWA and the NPS in 1934. It is a 60’ steel Aermotor tower with a 7’x7’ metal cab. Reached by three trails, it is a popular hiker destination.

name: Walker Top Lookout
loc:
Private Tract 
                    Burke County, North Carolina
desc:
Walker Top Lookout is a 100’ Aermotor tower with 7’x7’ cab built by the NC Forest Service near Carthage in 1951. In 1990 it was moved to its present site. 
 The tower is located on a private tract inside South Mountains State Park.

name: Warren County Lookout
loc: Warren County, North Carolina
desc: Built in 1932, the Warren County Fire Tower was the first State Division of Forestry lookout in North Carolina to be staffed by a female observer -- Mrs. Bessie Haithcock. Her husband, Earlie, helped construct the tower on land that was part of his farm and staffed it until his passing. Located at the Bessie Haithcock Forestry Center, the 100, Aermotor tower was in active use through 1990. The interior has been restored and is maintained as a historic exhibit.

name: Wauchecha Bald Fire Tower
loc:
Nantahala National Forest 
                    Graham County, North Carolina
desc:
Wauchecha Bald Fire Tower is an Aermotor live-in-cab tower of a style purchased primarily by the U.S. Forest Service. It is approximately 35 feet tall with a 13’x13’ cab and catwalk. It has all-metal construction, with storm shutters, and a pyramid hip roof with standing-seam metal roofing. The bottom steps have been removed, and all glass is broken or missing. Shutters have been torn off, but are mostly stacked inside the cab. 
 The tower was built by the CCC between 1933-1942. The Appalachian Trail used to pass beside it before being rerouted west of the tower.   According to a local historian and retired watchman, The Wachacha Bald (note difference in spelling) is said to have been named for a Cherokee man by the name of Jack Wachacha who lived in a small cabin on the level flat before the steep climb to the tower. Wachacha is said to mean grasshopper in the Cherokee language. People spoke of seeing him there in 1913. He had a garden fenced in with a rail fence head high to keep free ranging livestock out. Wachacha Bald had a much larger open grassy area in those days and people would herd their sheep there in the summer, according to local history.

name: Wayah Bald Tower
loc:
Nantahala National Forest 
                    Macon County, North Carolina
desc: The 53’ stone Wayah Bald Lookout on the Nantahala National Forest was constructed by the CCC in 1937. Faulty mortar ended its use as a fire lookout in only 8 years. In 1947 the cab was removed, and the stone tower restored as a popular observation site on the Appalachian Trail.

name: Wesser Bald Lookout
loc:
Nantahala National Forest 
                    Macon County, North Carolina
desc: A popular landmark on the Appalachian Trail in the Nantahala National Forest, Wesser Bald Lookout was a 14’x14’ live-in cab with catwalk on a 30’ metal tower built in 1936. Burned by vandals in 1979, and the Forest Service replaced the cab with a viewing platform in 1993.

name: Yellow Mountain Lookout
loc:
Nantahala National Forest 
                    Macon County, North Carolina
desc: Yellow Mountain Lookout is a 14'x14' wooden cab with a steep pyramid roof atop an 8' stone base. Once a common sight in the southern Appalachians, this design has all but disappeared. Unused for 20 years, the structure has been restored by volunteers and the staff of the Highland Ranger District of the Nantahala National Forest.

name: Wilmar Fire Tower
loc: Craven County, North Carolina
desc: This tower appears to be 50-75 feet tall and in good condition as of 2020. The tower may have been sold in a 2018 state auction.

name: Currituck Fire Tower
loc: Currituck County, North Carolina
desc: This 100-foot Aermotor LS-40 was built sometime in the 1940s or 1950s and actively used until the 1980s. The tower structure is still standing as of 2022, but its cab has been removed. The tower is now privately owned.

name: Aycock Fire Tower
loc: Wayne County, North Carolina
desc: Previously owned by the NCFS, now out of service. Lower stairs have been removed.

name: Dudley Lookout Tower
loc: Wayne County, North Carolina
desc:
No longer in operation. Lower stairs have been removed to prevent access for safety.  
  Older correspondence with the NC Forest Service shows that they sold the tower at auction (along with several others) to a Christopher Faust on 4/12/2018.  
 Here is a more recent video of the tower.

name: Alton Fire Tower
loc: Halifax County, Virginia
desc: Alton Fire Tower is located in the Cluster Springs quad in Halifax County, VA. It is a 80 foot Aermotor tower.

name: Ark Fire Tower
loc: Gloucester County, Virginia
desc: As of 2019, this tower was still standing but disused as a fire tower. The structure is host to two radio antennas.

name: Bald Knob Lookout
loc:
Warm Springs Mountain Preserve 
                    Bath County, Virginia
desc: Built in 1934 by the CCC for the Virginia Department of Forestry on a state-owned easement from the Hot Springs Company, this 35’ steel Aermotor 7'x7' tower was purchased on a cooperative basis, the State and the Bath County Protective Association each providing 50% of the funds. The property was later purchased by the U.S. Forest Service. It is currently part of The Nature Conservancy's Warm Springs Mountain Preserve.

name: Bearwallow Lookout
loc: Tazewell County, Virginia
desc: This 60' Aermotor tower was built in 1933 on the Tazewell-Buchanan county line. It was one of many towers along the ridges above what is now the Coal Heritage Trail in southwestern Virginia. Access to the tower is limited.

name: Bedford Fire Tower
loc: Bedford County, Virginia
desc:
Bedford Fire Tower is an 80-foot Aermotor steel tower located in Bedford County, Virginia. It serves as a prominent landmark for many miles for travelers on US Route 460 between Roanoke and Bedford.
 

 
Originally owned by the Virginia Department of Forestry, Bedford tower is now privately owned.

name: Birdnest Lookout
loc: Northampton County, Virginia

name: Blackstone Fire Tower
loc: Nottoway County, Virginia
desc: The Blackstone aka Nottoway Fire Tower is an 125 feet high steel tower. It has a wooden cab. Still in good condition, it is privately owned and no longer in use as a fire lookout.

name: Blakey Ridge Fire Tower
loc: Madison County, Virginia
desc:
Built by the Virginia Department of Forestry in the late 1930s, Blakey Ridge Fire Tower was active for only 20 years. The 80’ Aermotor tower with 7’x7’ metal cab was later owned by the Rappahannock Electric Cooperative as a radio site. 
 The tower was removed in 2018 due to liability concerns.

name: Bull Mountain Lookout
loc: Patrick County, Virginia
desc: The Bull Mountain Forest Fire Lookout Tower in Patrick County was originally a wooden structure built in 1943 for the Virginia Forest Service (VDF). It was replaced by the current 60’ Aermotor tower with 7’ x 7’ metal cab in 1949, and a one-room ground residence cabin was added in 1950. In 1989 the site -- now an emergency lookout -- was dedicated to Virginia Governor Gerald L. Baliles, who grew up near the tower and visited it many times in his youth.

name: Butt Mountain Lookout
loc: Giles County, Virginia
desc: Butt Mountain Lookout is a steel tower with wooden steps. The tower is currently in poor condition, with the cab floor rotted out and the bottom flights of stairs removed.

name: Carters Mountain Fire Tower
loc: Albemarle County, Virginia
desc: This privately owned 100-foot steel tower was built in 1933. Prior to its removal in March 2023, it was fenced in with communications equipment on the tower and in the cab. The cab was approximately 8-foot square.

name: Chancellor Lookout Ii
loc: Spotsylvania County, Virginia
desc:
This 80-foot Aermotor tower was built in February 1928. It was the second tower named Chancellor to be built in Spotsylvania County. The property it is on is a beautiful wooded lot that was originally intended to be small neighborhoods but the funds for such never came to allow that to happen. The tower was open to the public for visits in the 1920s and 1930s. It was manned until the late 1960s. The most special feature of this tower is the inscription in the concrete at the bottom of the stairs up the tower: "Prevent Forest Fires." It appears to be the only tower so inscribed. 
 The tower was removed circa 2019.

name: Cove Mountain Lookout
loc:
Cove Mountain 
                    Wythe County, Virginia
desc:
Cove Mountain is an 83 feet tall steel tower located in Wythe County, VA. It has a 14x14 cab. It is near Max Meadows, in the Miller's Creek area.
 

 
Tower is not in use.  Access to the tower is by permission of the landowner only.

name: Crafton Gate Lookout Tower
loc: Charlotte County, Virginia
desc: The Crafton Gate Lookout Tower is a 120-foot steel tower built in the 1930's, originally as a lookout for the thriving lumber industry in Charlotte County, as was the Phenix Fire Tower. It was used in unison with the VA Dept of Forestry. It is still owned by them today.

name: Cumberland Fire Tower
loc: Cumberland County, Virginia
admin: Virginia Department of Conservation and Recreation
desc: Built in 1941, Cumberland Tower sits behind Cumberland Court House. The steel tower replaced a wooden tower that was built in 1938. The original wooden tower was 66 ft tall with an 8x8 cabin.

name: Dewitt Lookout
loc: Dinwiddie County, Virginia
desc: Like its sister tower, Crafton Gate, this 110' Aermotor tower was built with the dual-purpose of being a fire lookout as well as being used to oversee the forest for local lumberyards. Later, it was manned on an as needed basis because of its proximity to Fort Pickett.
