name: Duncan Knob Lookout
loc: Bath County, Virginia
desc: Built in the late 1930s, this 60' Aermotor tower is the second of two towers in Bath County. At 3819 feet, Duncan Knob tower is short but special because it features a wrap-around catwalk.

name: Elliot Knob Lookout
loc:
George Washington National Forest 
                    Augusta County, Virginia
desc: Elliott Knob Lookout is in the George Washington National Forest some 150 miles west of Washington D.C. It is a metal 14’x14’ live-in cab with catwalk atop a 30 tower built in 1948 to replace an earlier tower built in the 1920s. Once one of many, it is now one of only three lookouts of its type remaining in Virginia and can be reached by road or trail.

name: Groundhog Mountain Tower
loc:
Blue Ridge Parkway 
                    Patrick County, Virginia
desc: Built in the 1930's as a fire lookout, on the Blue Ridge Parkway, Groundhog Mountain is not the usual "look" of fire tower in Virginia. Located in Patrick County, it is a 20 feet high tower, built to look like an old tobacco barn.

name: Hayters Knob Lookout
loc:
The Channels Natural Area Preserve 
                    Washington County, Virginia
desc:
The Department of Forestry, after being founded in 1914, started building steel towers in the 1930s.  The tower was constructed in 1939 by the Civilian Conservation Corps men.  The tower construction materials were carried to the construction site on mules and the men's backs.  The tower was in use from 1939 until the spring of 1970.  The tower commands a view of over 60 miles on a clear winter day and fewer than six feet when the fog settles over the mountain.
 

 
The lookout tower is located in The Channels Natural Area Preserve which was created in 2008 by the Commonwealth of Virginia to protect a unique sandstone formation located approximately 100 feet east. A common access route is just over a three mile hike from a parking lot on VA Route 80 at Hayters Gap on a dirt private road (easement obtained for hikers only), then forest roads.

name: Hazel Mountain Fire Tower
loc: Russell County, Virgnia
desc: Completed on August 31, 1939 by the Virginia Department of Forestry, this 90' Aermotor tower sits on the Dickenson/Russell County line. It is atop the Clinch Mountain range.

name: High Knob Lookout
loc:
George Washington National Forest 
                    Rockingham County, Virginia
desc: High Knob Lookout is one of but three fire towers remaining on the George Washington National Forest where there once were 24.     Located at an elevation of 4,107 feet, on the state line between Virginia’s Rockingham County and West Virginia’s Pendleton County, the High Knob Fire Lookout Tower is one of the most outstanding viewing spots in the George Washington National Forest. The 20’ stone tower has a wooden 14’x14’ cab with a catwalk. It is the only stone lookout in Virginia and is a memorial to the veterans and CCC personnel who built it. The tower was restored in 2003.    Construction on High Knob Lookout Tower, started in 1939 by World War I veterans, was under the supervision of John Moffett of Stuarts Draft, Virginia. The tower was completed in 1940 by men working out of North River Camp #2 of the Civilian Conservation Corps. Milford C. Howard of Bridgewater, Virginia, was the Forest Supervisor at that time.

name: High Knob Lookout
loc:
High Knob Recreation Area 
                    Wise County, Virginia
desc:
High Knob Lookout on the Clinch Ranger District of the Jefferson National Forest is the second lookout of this name to be listed on the NHLR in Virginia. The other High Knob (US#76, VA#01) is located on the George Washington National Forest. The original lookout was constructed by Company 2348 of the Civilian Conservation Corps of Norton, VA in 1938-39. It was a 14’ x 14’ hip roof live-in wooden ground house.
 

 
In 1978-79, the Job Corps’ Flatwoods Conservation Center -- also operated by the U.S. Forest Service -- built a three-story, eight-sided structure. A small visitor center was on the second floor and the lookout occupied the top floor. This lookout was destroyed by arson early on October 31, 2007. The current tower opened as a replacement in 2014.

name: High Knob-leemaster Lookout
loc: Buchanan County, Virginia
desc: Like its sister tower, Bearwallow Tower, High Knob Leemaster sits atop the Coal Heritage Trail in southwestern Virginia. This 110' Aermotor tower was built in the early 1930s.

name: Leigh Mountain Fire Tower
loc: Prince Edward County, Virginia
desc: This 80-foot steel Aermotor has a 7'x7' cab. It is still owned by the Virginia Department of Forestry but has been decommissioned and is in poor condition. The land where the tower is located has been for sale for many years. A new owner could move the tower and restore it.

name: Louisa Fire Tower
loc: Louisa County, Virginia
desc: Fire towers located adjacent to county forestry units were once common sights throughout the South, but the Louisa Fire Tower is the only example in Virginia. Built in 1944 by the CCC for the Virginia Forest Service -- now the VA Department of Forestry -- the 100’ Aermotor tower with 7’ x 7’ steel cab is maintained for emergency use.

name: Matthews State Forest Lookout
loc: Grayson County, Virginia
desc: Built originally in Tazewell County, as Morris Knob tower, this tower now stands at the forestry office of Matthews State Forest. It is part of a trail of trees ans serves as a museum, so to speak, of forestry history in rural southwestern Virginia.

name: Mendota Fire Tower
loc: Washington County, Virginia
desc: Mendota Fire Tower sits atop Clinch Mountain, in Washington County, VA. It is a 100-foot  steel tower. No longer manned, it is mainly a hot spot for birdwatching as well as a hiking destination for many. Its sister tower, Hayters Knob, is down the Clinch Mountain ridge from it.

name: Partlow Lookout
loc:
Lake Anna 
                    Spotsylvania County, Virginia
desc: This 110' Aermotor tower with a 7'x7' cab was built in 1961 by 13 locals. The hardest part was the aluminum roof. The tower had been brought from Prince William State Forest where it had been since World War II. This tower was manned by Virginia's first female watchperson, Grace Newton.

name: Pleasant Shade Fire Tower
loc: Brunswick County, Virginia
desc: Located near Pleasant Shade in Brunswick County, Virginia, Pleasant Shade Fire Tower was first erected in 1933. This tower is constructed of galvanized steel and has a 7’x7’ cab. Manufactured by Aermotor Co., the tower is 100' tall. The tower is still operational during periods of high fire danger to support aerial detection.

name: Prince George Forest Lookout
loc: Prince George County, Virginia
desc: Fire towers in eastern Virginia were tall enough to see out over the flat landscape. The Prince George Forest Lookout is no exception. This 120’ Aermotor tower with 7’x7’ metal cab was constructed in l937 by the CCC for the Va. Dept of Forestry. Now inactive and one of the tallest remaining in the state, it is owned by Prince George County and maintained cooperatively by the Virginia Chapter of the FFLA.

name: Red Oak Mountain Lookout
loc: Rappahannock County, Virginia
desc: Built in the 1930s, Red Oak Mountain Lookout is the only cupola-style lookout in Virginia. Each day during the fire season, the fire lookout walked from the vicinity of Laurel Mills to the top of Red Oak Knob to watch for wildfires.

name: Sounding Knob Fire Tower
loc: Highland County, Virginia
desc:
Located atop Jack Mountain east of Monterey, 80-foot Sounding Knob Tower was built in 1935 for the Virginia Department of Forestry by CCC workers. The tower was staffed until the 1960s. After years of abandonment, the tower was removed in 2002. It was bought by by local businessman Steve Good of Highland Welding, who salvaged and stored the components. 
 In 2016, the tower was purchased by Hammill "Skip" Jones. Working with Highland Welding and the Virginia Department of Forestry, the tower's components received a comprehensive overhaul including re-galvanization and new wooden stair treads. It was reinstalled at Sounding Knob in 2017 with a public dedication ceremony on July 8, 2017. 
 The tower is privately owned by Skip Jones. Access to the tower is gated, but Jones plans to periodically allow the public free access. As of November 2020, the tower and cab are being  left open indefinitely  for the public to visit during daylight hours.

name: Tobacco Row Lookout
loc: Amherst County, Virginia
desc: This steel tower atop Tobacco Row Mountain is now surrounded by a microwave communications structure owned by American Tower Corporation.

name: Woodstock Lookout Tower
loc:
George Washington National Forest 
                    Shenandoah County, Virginia
desc: The Woodstock Tower is a steel observation tower that was built in 1935 by the CCC. It was funded by the Woodstock Chamber of Commerce. It was jointly used for fire spotting & recreational purposes. It has been repaired over the years by the USFS.

name: Meadows Fire Tower
loc: Henrico County, Virginia
desc: This tower is about 110-feet high and is located just off US 60.

name: Deer Head Lookout
loc:
Virginia Department of Forestry 
                    Shenandoah County, Virginia
desc: This International Derrick tower is between 40-60 feet tall. It has graced the hills outside Conicville since 1930.

name: James City Fire Tower
loc: James City County, Virginia
desc: This 100-foot tall Aermotor LS-40 Tower that was built in 1933. As it sits today, a majority of the boards are missing, but the cab seems to have a majority of its glass panels still in there, as well as the stand for where the Osborne fire finder would have been, but the fire finder itself is no longer present there.

name: King William County Fire Tower
loc: King William County, Virginia
desc:
This 80-foot Aermotor tower was built in 1935. 
 From a 2014 historic survey by King William County: “The fire tower is a tall tapering metal truss structure with a square plane metal frame lookout cab at the top. The lookout cab is clad with metal sheeting and features multiple- light metal fixed windows across each elevation. The lookout cab has a pyramidal roof covered in seamed metal and is accessed by an open metal staircase located within the metal truss structure. The King William Fire Warden position was created in 1933 and the first fire tower was constructed shortly after.”

name: Surry Fire Tower
loc: Surry County, Virginia
desc: This Aermotor fire tower along VA 31 is in poor condition. The first flight of steps appear to have been removed but the rest remains intact.

name: Smith Mountain Fire Tower
loc: Bedford County, Virginia
desc: The tower is an Aermotor MC-39 measuring fifty nine feet and four inches tall from the ground to the floor of the cab. The exact construction date of the tower is unknown. Currently the tower has been repurposed with the bottom two flights of stairs being removed, and radio equipment has been mounted, adding about 15-20 feet to the total height of the tower.

name: Miskimon Fire Tower
loc: Northumberland County, Virginia
desc:
The Miskimon Fire Tower in Miskimon, Virginia, was built between April and June 1938. It is 100 feet high with a 10 by 10 cab at the top. A cell phone tower has been built next to it. 
 The Miskimon Tower has landings/platforms (some currently in disrepair) at each ten foot level. It has guardrails that extend all the way up to the cab. The platforms at each landing are wooden. The roof, like the lower portion of the cab, is made of galvanized steel. The cab has two windows on each side. A trap door permitted ingress to and egress from the cab for the spotter. There was a lock on the stair-side of the trap door and a lock inside the cab. In 1938, the Virginia Conservation Commission and the Virginia Forest Service hired local workers for the construction. Land at the desired elevation was purchased from Samuel Haynie. The counties of Northumberland and Lancaster paid $25.00 each toward the cost of $1800. The unassembled Tower was sent from the manufacturer, Aermotor of Chicago, Illinois. 
 The Miskimon Tower was used by spotters or lookouts from March/April until fall of each year. Lookouts generally worked a 10 to 4 P.M. shift. From the time of its completion and well into the 1980s or slightly beyond, the Miskimon Tower was vital to these farming and lumbering counties for fire detection and for fire suppression

name: Bald Knob Fire Tower
loc:
Cass Scenic Railroad State Park 
                    Pocahontas County, West Virginia
desc: Few -- if any -- mountaintop lookouts in the U.S. are reached by steam railroad, but Bald Knob Tower in West Virginia’s Cass Scenic Railroad State Park is one of them. The 47’ tower with l’ x 7’ metal cab was built in the early 1930s on land then owned by the Mower Lumber Co. and was staffed until 1977. It is now maintained as a park view point.

name: Barton Knob Fire Tower
loc:
Monongahela National Forest 
                    Randolph County, West Virginia
desc:
From high on Cheat Mountain, Barton Knob provides expansive views of the Shavers Fork and Tygart Valley River headwaters. It was built by the State of West Virginia circa 1926 and features a 7'-by-7' steel cab. 
 The tower later came under control of Monongahela National Forest. The tower remains standing, although its lower sections of stairs have been removed and its cab is missing its roof.

name: Bell Knob Fire Tower
loc:
Monongahela National Forest 
                    Grant County, West Virginia
desc:
Located high atop the Allegheny Front near Dolly Sods, Bell Knob Fire Tower was built with a wooden cab atop 30' steel legs. It was originally built along Rohrbaugh Plains Trail in 1931 and relocated to this site in 1943. 
 Portions of the cab collapsed prior to October 2015, although the cab platform, steel legs, and stairs remain.

name: Bickle Knob Fire Tower
loc:
Monongahela National Forest 
                    Randolph County, West Virginia
desc: The cab of Bickle Knob tower has been replaced with an open viewing deck providing expansive views of the Shavers Fork watershed and Otter Creek Wilderness. It is a popular stop for visitors to Monongahela National Forest.

name: Big Ridge Fire Tower
loc:
Lost River State Park 
                    Hardy County, West Virginia
admin: West Virginia Division of Natural Resources
desc: The WV Division of Forestry erected the Big Ridge Fire Tower in the 1935 on the Lost River State Park in 1935. It is an Aermotor 7x7' on a 80' tower.

name: Caddell Mountain Lookout
loc: Preston County, West Virginia
desc: This 80-foot steel tower was originally located at Carlin Hill in Wetzel County. During the summer of 1946, it was dismantled and relocated to Caddell Mountain, where it was re-erected that fall.

name: Hanging Rock Lookout
loc:
Jefferson National Forest 
                    Monroe County, West Virginia
desc: The Hanging Rock Fire Tower has an unusual history. It was built in 1934 by the West Virginia Division of Forestry atop a sloping “hanging rock” outcrop. In 1956 the state rebuilt the lookout with plans supplied by the U.S. Forest Service and it became one of only two lookouts in the state system with a live-in cab. The site was staffed until 1972 and was discontinued in 1981. In 1983 the land was acquired by the Jefferson National Forest. The Forest Service and a volunteer group of hawk watchers completely restored the tower in 1995. Vandals burned the structure in 1996, but once again community spirit rallied and the tower was reconstructed in 1999.

name: Huff Knob Fire Tower
loc: Raleigh County, West Virginia
desc: Located on Flat Top Mountain, the Huff Knob Fire Tower is now sits amid a large antenna farm. It was the last regularly staffed fire tower in West Virginia, with  staffing ending in 1990 .

name: Ivy Knob Fire Tower
loc: Raleigh County, West Virginia
desc: Located on Guyandotte (Bolt) Mountain, Ivy Knob Fire Tower overlooks the headwaters of the Coal and Guyandotte rivers. The tower was built in 1924 by Emory "Pop" Wriston to replace an earlier 1916 tower at this site which was the first fire tower in West Virginia.

name: Keeney Knob Fire Tower
loc: Summers County, West Virginia
desc: This 88-foot steel tower was built in 1937 by the Civilian Conservation Corps on one of the highest points in southern West Virginia.

name: Lambert Knob Fire Tower
loc:
Lambert Knob 
                    Wyoming County, West Virginia
desc: The 86' tower was built by the Civilian Conservation Corps. It was operated by the West Virginia Division of Forestry until it was closed in 1991.

name: Mann Mountain Fire Tower
loc: Fayette County, West Virginia
admin: West Virginia Division of Natural Resources
desc: Located on state land in the hill country of southern West Virginia, Mann Mountain Tower is the first lookout registered in the state. It was built in 1935 by the CCC. An unusual feature is a stone ground house surrounded by a stone wall. The structure is a 45’ Blaw-Knox tower with a 7’X7’ cab.

name: Mingo Mountain Fire Tower
loc: Logan County, West Virginia
desc: Built in 1926, Mingo Mountain Fire Tower sits atop the summit of Horsepen Mountain, which serves as the Mingo-Logan county line in southern West Virginia. The summit has several communications towers in addition to the fire tower. The tower was staffed until the end of the WV fire tower system in 1990.

name: Nathaniel Mountain Fire Tower
loc:
Nathaniel Mountain Wildlife Management Area 
                    Hampshire County, West Virginia
desc: This tower was built prior to 1941.

name: Olson Tower
loc:
Monongahela National Forest 
                    Tucker County, West Virginia
desc:
Built in 1963, Olson Tower replaces one of West Virginia's first observation towers,  Backbone . It provides views of the Parsons area including the Blackwater River, Dry Fork, Black Fork, and Cheat River watersheds. 
 The tower was dedicated on September 29, 1963, in honor of Ernst B. "Pete" Olson, a fire control assistant for the Cheat Ranger District who was killed in a 1961 car accident near Parsons.

name: Panther Fire Tower
loc:
Panther State Forest 
                    McDowell County, West Virginia
desc: The 41’ Panther Tower was built in 1940 by the West Virginia Division of Forestry to oversee the Panther State Forest. It is one of a handful of distinctive Blau-Knox towers remaining. The windows in the 7’x 7’ metal cab swing open in a four pane block.

name: Pilot Knob Fire Tower
loc: Mercer County, West Virginia
desc: This tower stands along the Mercer/Wyoming county line.

name: Point Mountain Fire Tower
loc: Webster County, West Virginia
desc: A 60 Aermotor LS-40 tower with 7’ x 7’ cab on Point Mountain was built by the West Virginia Conservation Commission in 1925. An additional 40’ section was added in 1965, bringing it to 100 feet. In 1952 a concrete block observer’s cabin was added near the base. With a viewing area of 500 square miles, it is no longer regularly staffed but is maintained for emergencies.

name: Red Oak Knob Fire Tower
loc:
Monongahela National Forest 
                    Webster County, West Virginia
desc:
Located on Cranberry Ridge east of Cowen, Red Oak Knob Fire Tower overlooks the Williams River and Cranberry River watersheds in Monongahela National Forest. The 80-foot steel tower was erected in 1964 to replace an earlier 30-foot wooden tower built by the CCC in 1934. The present tower features a 14'x14' CL100-series all metal cab with wrap-around catwalk. 
 As of 2023, Monongahela National Forest has been working with AmeriCorps on  restoring the tower to be reopened as an overnight rental . Roof, floor, and window repairs have been completed on the tower. A lightning protection system and lighting have been installed and modern pit toilets have been constructed on the site. A RV pad and hookup are planned to allow for a 2025 opening.

name: Snowshoe Fire Tower
loc: Pocahontas County, West Virginia
desc: The  former Rich Mountain Fire Tower  now stands at the privately owned Snowshoe Mountain ski resort. It was relocated to its current place in 1999 and restored to original condition in 2000.

name: Tams Mountain Tower
loc: Raleigh County, West Virginia
desc: The first road and trail to Tams Mountain Tower was built in 1933 under a federal law designed to provide “forest work” during the Great Depression. The 80’ Aermotor tower with 7’ x 7’ cab was built by the CCC the following year, along with a log cabin observer quarters. Located on Beaver Coal Company lands, the WV Division of Forestry tower is now used only in emergencies.

name: Thorny Mountain Fire Tower
loc:
Seneca State Forest 
                    Pocahontas County, West Virginia
admin: West Virginia Division of Natural Resources
desc:
Originally built in the 1920s by the CCC on the eastern side of Seneca State Forest, Thorny Mountain Fire Tower was reconstructed to its present location in 1935 to provide better coverage of the Greenbrier River valley. The 53’ steel tower with 12x12 live-in wooden cab and catwalk is one-of-a-kind in West Virginia.
 

 
In 2015, the West Virginia Division of Natural Resources completed a renovation of the tower and began permitting overnight rentals.

name: Tick Ridge Fire Tower
loc:
Cabwaylingo State Forest 
                    Wayne County, West Virginia
desc: Built in a remote site in Cabwaylingo State Forest, Tick Ridge Fire Tower stands uphill from a picnic area. The 80' steel tower was built in 1937. It is fenced off and the lowest flight of stairs have been removed.

name: Whittaker Station Fire Tower
loc:
Cass Scenic Railroad State Park 
                    Pocahontas County, West Virginia
admin: West Virginia Division of Natural Resources
desc: The former Gauley Mountain Fire Tower was relocated to the Whittaker Station area of Cass Scenic Railroad State Park in October 2009 to join a collection of exhibits on West Virginia forestry. The Blaw-Knox tower is accessible by train from Cass.

name: Olga No. 2 Fire Tower
loc:
Private Land 
                    McDowell County, West Virginia
desc: This was one of three towers built by the Olga Coal Company.

name: Sugar Grove Fire Tower
loc: Greenbrier County, West Virginia
admin: Private owner (formerly West Virginia Division of Forestry)
desc: This Greenbrier County fire tower was built by the West Virginia Division of Forestry but was sold to the land owner.

name: Ben's Knob Fire Tower
loc:
Privately Owned Land 
                    Hampshire County, West Virginia
desc:
Ben's Knob Fire Tower is an Aermotor LS-40 7x7 all steel cab and  60 foot tower  constructed circa 1952-53. 
 Last staffing by the West Virginia Division of Forestry is unknown. By 2017, it had been disposed from the Division's inventory and is located on private land. 
 A residence cabin may survive on the property as well.

name: Sleepy Creek Fire Tower
loc:
Sleepy Creek Wildlife Management Area 
                    Morgan County, West Virginia
desc:
It was an 80 foot Aermotor LS-40. The tower was completed in 1950.    
  Sleepy Creek fire tower was sold for scrap and removed many years ago.

name: Altamont Lookout
loc: Grundy County, Tennessee
desc: Altamont Lookout in Grundy County is a Carnegie steel tower built in the 1940s. It is located at a Tennessee Div. of Forestry Work Center and available for emergency use.

name: Model Fire Tower
loc:
Land Between The Lakes NRA 
                    Stewart County, Tennessee
desc: Located on the Land Between the Lakes NRA, this 80' Aermotor LS-40 tower with a 7'x7' metal cab and wooden steps is also known as Model Tower. The tower was constructed for the Tennessee Division of Forestry (TDF) around 1954. The land that it was built on was leased to TDF in 1954 from the Heath and Molloy families. The tower is still utilized today for fire detection.

name: Dunlap Lookout Tower
loc: Sequatchie County, Tennessee
desc:
This is a traditional Aermotor tower with a 7'x7' cab. At its base is an old house which may have been the watchman's home. In 2017, the tower was open for visitors but may not be any longer. 
 May otherwise be known as Bennett or Signal Mountain.

name: Black Creek Tower
loc: Scott County, Tennessee
desc: Also known locally as the Grassy Knob tower, Black Creek was built by the State of Tennessee in 1951. The tower is still serviceable when the need to use it arises.

name: Catoosa Fire Tower
loc:
Catoosa Wildlife Area 
                    Morgan County, Tennessee
desc: This 80-foot fire tower is located atop Pilot Knob in the Catoosa Wildlife Area.

name: Lebanon Fire Tower
loc:
Cedars of Lebanon State Park 
                    Wilson County, Tennessee
admin: Tennessee Department of Environment and Conservation
desc: Located in Middle Tennessee's Wilson County, Lebanon Fire Tower is a central feature of Cedars of Lebanon State Park.

name: Chimney Top Fire Tower
loc: Hawkins County, Tenneessee

name: Cookeville Fire Tower
loc: Putnam County, Tennessee
desc: This 80-foot steel tower was built between 1944 and 1953. It currently houses a radio repeated for the Tennessee Division of Forestry.

name: Cove Creek Tower
loc: Campbell County, Tennessee
desc: Located in the heart of Cove Creek Wildlife Management Area, Cove Creek Fire Tower is a 100’ Aermotor with 7’x7’ cab. If affords remarkable views, including Norris Lake, and is in need of restoration.

name: Cove Mountain Tower
loc:
Great Smoky Mountains National Park 
                    Sevier County, Tennessee
desc: The Cove Mountain Fire Tower in the Great Smoky Mountains National Park was constructed by the CCC in 1935. It is a 60’ steel Aermotor tower with 7’x7’ metal cab. It is now used as an air quality monitoring site.

name: English Mountain Fire Tower
loc: Cocke County, Tennessee

name: Fall Creek Falls Lookout Tower
loc:
Falls Creek Falls State Park 
                    Bledsoe County, Tennessee
desc: Originally constructed in 1865 for the dedication of the Chickamauga Battlefield, Fall Creek Falls Lookout Tower was moved in 1943 to present site for use as a fire tower.

name: Flat Woods Lookout
loc: Wayne County, Tennessee
desc: The Flat Woods Fire Tower is located in Wayne County, west of Columbia and just State Route 13. It is a 100’ structure with diagonal stairs and still used by the Tennessee Division of Forestry as a radio repeater site.

name: Garden Mountain Fire Tower
loc:
Bays Mountain Park 
                    Hawkins County, Tennessee
desc: Built in 1937 by the Civilian Conservation Corps, this was one of over 90 fire towers constructed in Tennessee. This 100-foot tower offers a commanding view of Kingsport.

name: Halls Top Fire Tower
loc:
Cherokee National Forest 
                    Cocke County, Tennessee
desc: This tower was built by the U.S. Forest Service in 1936. It is accessible via the 9.9-mile Stone Mountain Trail.

name: Hiwassee Knobs Fire Tower
loc: Monroe County, Tenneessee

name: Hohenwald Lookout
loc: Lewis County, Tennessee

name: Holston High Knob Lookout
loc:
Cherokee National Forest 
                    Carter County, Tennessee
desc: The lookout atop Holston High Knob on the Cherokee National Forest in Tennessee near the Virginia state line is a remarkable tower for its location. Located on the southern high knob of Holston Ridge, it offers an extraordinary view from ground level, but has a 100’ steel tower with 12’x 12’ cab with catwalk. Originally located in the flat piney woods of Mississippi, it was moved to Tennessee in 1943, replacing a wooden 60’ tower that had been built nine years earlier and accidentally burned. The lookout was staffed until 1991 and is now used on an emergency basis.

name: Kettlefoot Lookout Tower
loc: Johnson County, Tennessee
desc: Kettlefoot Lookout Tower is planned to become part of a new multiple-use recreation area being developed by the State of Tennessee. The tower is named for a large bear that caught his foot in a kettle.

name: Liberty Lookout Tower
loc:
Town of Cleveland 
                    Bradley County, Tennessee
desc: When John Williams decided to build a fire tower on his property, he purchased two surplus Aermotor towers from the Tennessee Division of Forestry and combined them into one 80' tower called Liberty Lookout.  The former towers were Sparta and Sale Creek.

name: Beardstown Lookout Tower
loc: Perry County, Tennessee
desc:
Constructed around 1950, this tower was in use through the early 1970s. It is a steel Aermotor tower, approximately 73 feet tall. 
 The site is also occupied by two modern communications towers.

name: Maynardville Fire Tower
loc: Union County, Tennessee
desc: This 100-foot tower on Hinds Ridge overlooks Maynardville and Norris Lake.

name: Meadow Creek Lookout
loc:
Cherokee National Forest 
                    Cocke County, Tennessee
desc: The current block tower is the fifth to stand on the site. One of the earlier towers, standing in 1926, was just a platform mounted between three chestnut trees.

name: Montlake Mountain Lookout
loc: Hamilton County, Tennessee
desc:
At one time, Montlake was one of 28 fire towers in the Chattanooga District. They were all in sight of each other, watching jointly over thousands of acres of land. It is a traditional Aermotor style tower, 80' tall, with 7'x7' cab and wooden steps. The lookout is in good condition, and was safe to climb in 2019. The tower is located next to the forestry office, which allows guests to climb the tower. 
 The tower was manned for 17 years by forestry technician Jim Brown, and into 2014 by Frank Westwood.

name: Mooresburg Lookout
loc: Hawkins County, Tennessee
desc: This tower was built in 1937 and originally known as the Flat Gap tower.  Its name was later changed to Mooresburg.

name: Mount Cammerer Lookout
loc:
Great Smoky Mountains National Park 
                    Cocke County, Tennessee
desc: Mount Cammerer Lookout located on the northeastern end of the Great Smoky Mountains National Park in Tennessee is an impressive two-story octagonal stone structure built in 1937-1939 from materials on the site by the CCC. Located near the Appalachian Trail, it is a popular if strenuous destination for hikers. In spite of stunning views over the Tennessee and North Carolina mountains, the site was not used for detection very long and was abandoned in the 1960s. The lookout has been restored by the Friends of Great Smoky Mountains National Park, the Panther Press and the National Park Service.

name: Pinnacle Fire Tower
loc:
Buffalo Mountain 
                    Washington County, Tennessee
desc: Pinnacle Lookout has been landmark above Unicoi, Tennessee for 75 years.   The Cherokee National Forest station is a 14’x14’ live in wooden tower with catwalk on a 40’ steel tower.   Last staffed in the 1980s, it has been restored by the Friends of Pinnacle Tower including a grant from the FFLA. See link below for photo of restored tower.

name: Prentice Cooper Fire Tower
loc: Marion County, Tennessee
desc: This tower was built in the 1930s to protect the newly formed Prentice Cooper State Forest.

name: Sewanee Fire Tower
loc: Franklin County, Tennessee
desc: This 60ft International Derrick fire tower was built by the Civilian Conservation Corps in 1933.

name: Smyrna Lookout Tower
loc: Rhea County, Tennessee
desc: This 65-foot Aermotor tower was built in the late 1950s and features a 7'x7' cab. While the cab is locked, signage allows visitors to climb the tower at their own risk. The tower offers a beautiful view of surrounding farmland, to the valley near Crossville, and across the mountains of the Grandview area. The tower is actively used as of 2019.

name: Sneedville Lookout Tower
loc: Hancock County, Tennessee

name: Springdale Lookout
loc: Claiborne County, Tennessee

name: Summer City Fire Tower
loc: Bledsoe County, Tennessee
desc: This steel tower is believed to be an Aermotor design. It features a 7'x7' cab and is located beside a small Tennessee Division of Forestry office. The cab is locked, but signage on the tower states that visitors may climb the tower.

name: Summertown Lookout Tower
loc: Lewis County, Tennessee

name: Towerview Fire Tower
loc:
Towerview Farm 
                    Houston County, Tennessee
admin: Joel Clark and Jason Clark, Towerview Farm, owners
desc: Towerview Fire Tower, a 70’ Aermotor tower with 7’x7’ metal cab was built by the CCC in 1935-36 for the Tennessee Division of Forestry at Stoney Point in Dickson County. A 14’x 24’ chestnut log cabin was constructed as the towerman’s residence. In 1997 the tower was purchased by Joel & Jason Clark and moved intact by truck 12 miles to their Towerview Farm, along with the chestnut cabin. The Clarks also acquired a forestry fire truck which remains active as the Towerview Farm Independent Volunteer Fire Service.
agency: Joel Clark and Jason Clark, To

name: Little War Gap Fire Tower
loc: Hawkins County, Tennessee
admin: Private Owners (Portia Gibson and Carolyn G. Courtney)
desc: War Fire Tower sits on a rocky outcrop high above Little War Gap. Offering a very dramatic view, the tower and its accompanying watchman's cabin are in poor repair as of 2019.

name: Windswept Lookout
loc:
Windswept Farm 
                    Morgan County, Tennessee
desc: Located on Windswept Farm in Morgan County, TN, this 60’ Aermotor steel tower with 7’ x 7’ cab originally stood on Walden Mountain near Harriman, 15 miles to the south. The Tennessee Forestry Division sold the tower in 1994. The new private owners completed their reconstruction and restoration of the tower in 1998.

name: Wolfpen Mountain Lookout
loc: Sequatchie County, Tennessee
desc:
Wolfpen Mountain was the first fire tower in Tennessee. Also known as Cagle Tower, it was a unique 60’ structure with 8’x8’ cab with catwalk. Each of the five landings ran from corner to corner. 
 In the 1930s the tower was replaced by the 80’ Aermotor that stands today and is lightly maintained.

name: Worthington Knob Fire Tower
loc: Bledsoe County, Tennessee
desc: Worthington Knob Fire Tower, also known as the Luminary Tower, stands tall overlooking the Sequatchie Valley. It is 50 feet tall and believed to be an Aermotor tower. The tower was constructed in 1961-1962.

name: Wright Mountain Lookout
loc: Fentress County, Tennessee
desc: The first lookout on Wright Mountain was a wooden tower built in 1942 by the Tennessee Div. of Forestry. The agency replaced it in 1960 with an 80' Aermotor tower with a 7'x7' cab. It is now privately owned and restored.

name: Laconia Fire Tower
loc: Fayette County, Tennessee
desc: This is an 80ft Aermotor on private property.  The site includes a small out building.

name: Hornsby Fire Tower
loc: Hardeman County, Tennessee
desc: This tower is located on an active TN Division of Forestry work center.  It contains a 90ft Aermotor Tower.

name: Big Hill Pond Lookout Tower
loc:
Big Hill Pond State Park 
                    McNairy County, Tennessee
desc: Located in Big Hill Pond State Park, this tower is a 70ft Aermotor Observation tower.

name: Ramer Fire Tower
loc: McNairy County, Tennessee
desc: An Aermotor style tower that appears to be on private property.

name: Hardin Creek Fire Tower
loc: Wayne County, Tennessee
desc: This is an 80ft Aermotor tower with a diagonal internal staircase.   The site also contains the original Forester's cabin.  This cabin is of a similar design of the cabin located at the Towerview Fire Tower.

name: Dyersburg Lookout Tower
loc: Dyer County, Tennessee
desc: This is an Aermotor style tower with no obvious access points.

name: Ripley Lookout Tower
loc: Lauderdale County, Tennessee
desc: This is an 80ft Aermotor tower with a parallel internal staircase.  The manufacture date of this tower was sometime after 1964 since the name badge references Broken Arrow, Oklahoma.  The site is a active TN Forestry location.

name: Open Lake Lookout Tower
loc: Lauderdale County, Tennessee
desc: This is an 80ft Aermotor tower with a parallel internal staircase.  The manufacture date of this tower was sometime after 1964 since the name badge references Broken Arrow, Oklahoma.  The tower is in a very rough condition.

name: Natchez Trace Fire Tower
loc: Henderson County, TN
desc:
This International Derrick Model 1933 tower is located in the Natchez Trace State Park.  It was constructed by the CCC in 1937.  The tower is 70ft tall. 
 Site Visit - 1/28/23

name: Maple Lake Fire Tower
loc:
Natchez Trace State Forest 
                    Carroll County, TN
desc:
This is an Aermotor tower that measured 90ft tall.  The Aermotor name badge has been removed, but the outlined shape indicates it's from the Broken Arrow, OK era.  This dates the tower being installed sometime after 1964. 
   
 Site Visit - 1/28/23

name: Camden Fire Tower
loc: Benton County, TN
desc:
This is a 80ft Aermotor LS-40 tower.  The original Chicago Aermotor badge is missing but the outline can be seen.  The tower is located at an active TN Forestry site.  
 Site visit - 1/28/23

name: Paris Fire Tower
loc: Henry County, TN
desc:
This is a 80ft Aermotor LS-40 tower.  The tower is located at an active TN Forestry site.  
 Site visit - 1/28/23

name: Puryear Fire Tower
loc: Henry County, TN
desc:
This is a 80ft Aermotor LS-40 tower.  The tower is still owned by the state but it's surrounded by private property. 
 Site visit - 1/28/23

name: Leach Fire Tower
loc: Carroll County, TN
desc:
This is a 80ft Aermotor LS-40 tower.  The original Chicago Aermotor badge is missing but the outline can be seen.  The tower is located at an active TN Forestry site.  
 Site visit - 1/29/23

name: Jack's Creek Lookout Tower
loc: Chester County, Tennessee
desc:
This site is no longer owned by the TN Forestry Department.  It still contains the tower, a housing trailer, quonset hut, and a small office.

name: Franklin State Forest Lookout Tower
loc:
Franklin State Forest 
                    Marion County, Tennessee
desc:
This tower is a 80ft Aermotor LS-40. 
 Franklin State Forest - Size: 8,836 acres/3,576 ha. The land was acquired in 1936 from the Cross Creek Coal Company and was highly degraded. Tennessee Department of Agriculture, Forestry Division assumed management of the area in 1940. The larger northern section of the forest was obtained in a land swap with The University of The South in 2008. Additional acreage was later obtained in the southwest portion of the forest through purchase from the Sherwood Mining Company. The Forest is on the Cumberland Plateau and located in south-central Tennessee, in Marion and Franklin Counties. The forest is 35-40 miles west of Chattanooga. About 99% of the land is forested and about 90% of the land is in hardwood forest types both young and mature. About 10% of the Forest is pine. The area has a history of timber abuse by diameter-limit cuts and uncontrolled wildfires. Silvicultural prescriptions are geared towards timber stand improvement, management of wildlife habitat and age class structure and diversity. It is home to a diverse number of wildlife species. The forest has been traditionally used for hunting, hiking, horse riding, off-road and ATV riding, and in designated areas camping.  
  Site Visit - 11/24/23

name: Burns Lookout Tower
loc:
Montgomery Bell State Park 
                    Dickson County, Tennessee
desc:
This steel International Derrick MC-39 tower was built in the early 1950s. It is approximately 80 feet tall with steel stair treads. It was erected by the Tennessee Division of Forestry for fire detection in Dickinson County and surrounding areas. 
 The tower is situated within the 5,000-acre Montgomery Bell State Park. The park contains a 1,086-acre natural area with two tracts of high-quality oak/hickory forest.

name: Green Top Fire Lookout
loc: Sevier County, Tennessee
admin: TN Department of Agriculture - Division of Forestry
desc: The tower is a 47ft tall Aermotor, model LS-40.

name: Mt. Roosevelt Fire Tower
loc:
MT Roosevelt State Forest - MT Roosevelt Wildlife Management Area 
                    Roane County, Tennessee
admin: State of Tennessee / (Several Agencies deny ownership)
desc:
Five landing International Derrick and Equipment Company tower. Abandoned mid 1980s. Large star placed on tower in late 1990s by Rockwood Electric. Illuminated in November and December. Locals have named the tower Star. The MT Roosevelt Scenic Overlook has thousands of visitors a year. Six states are visible from the cab of Star. Star has one of the most spectacular views in the East. Star is structurally sound. The steps have rotted out. Numerous people dangerously climb the tower yearly. The Overlook is not maintained by the State and is basically an attractive nuisance. Rockwood is blamed for the litter and being unkempt. Rockwood arranges cleanup a couple times a year, even though it is not in the Rockwood. A volunteer group in Rockwood has asked Tennessee for Star and has a plan to restore and allow visitors to safely climb. The rotten steps will be replaced with slip resistant galvanized steps and goat wire infill panes will be installed under the railings and around the landings. A series of cameras will be installed and remote-controlled gates will be installed. Ownership would be transferred to Rockwood. The site originally had a Rangers house. Reconstructing the removed Ranger house has been discussed to use as a museum.   
  Located at the Mt Roosevelt Scenic Lookout - 1.4 miles on paved road off US 70 Rockwood Tennessee. MT Roosevelt is the highest point in Roane County. US 70 is being rebranded as the Walton Road Scenic Byway, and this will be a prominent stop.

name: Black Mountain Fire Tower
loc:
Chattahoochee National Forest 
                    Union County, Georgia
desc: Located on the Chattahoochee National Forest and one of the few remaining towers in Georgia with a 13’x13’ live-in cab with catwalk, Black Mountain Lookout is a 33’ metal tower with a CL-100 series metal cab. It was constructed in 1949.

name: Brawley Mountain Lookout Tower
loc:
Chattahoochee National Forest 
                    Fannin County, Georgia
desc:
Brawley Mountain Lookout Tower is a 50' steel tower with a 13'x13' CL-100 series metal live-in cab with catwalk and flat roof. This lookout is one of the only fire towers that remain standing along the Benton MacKaye Trail in Georgia. 
 The first flight of steps has been removed to prevent access, and the cab is falling into disrepair; but the tower is still strikingly majestic, guarding it's mountain peak. The tower is in use for various antennae for Fannin County EMS, and TVA.

name: Brogdon Hill Lookout
loc: Gordon County, Georgia
desc: This lookout is believed to have been built in the 1940s. It protects Calhoun and the surrounding area.

name: Chenocetah Mountain Tower
loc:
Chattahoochee National Forest 
                    Habersham County, Georgia
desc: A classic design built by the Works Progress Administration (WPA) in 1936 for the Chattahoochee National Forest, Chenocetah Mountain Lookout, is a 40’ high stone tower with a 14’ x 14’ wood cab covered by a 15’ high peaked slate roof which curves out slightly at the eaves. After World War II it was dedicated to three forest workers who died during the war. In active service until 1975, it was unused until 1989 when the Georgia Forestry Commission took over staffing during fire season. The tower has been adopted by neighbors living in residential areas near the mountain who have formed the “Chenocetah Conservation Corps” to provide grounds maintenance. It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1983.

name: Crown Mountain Fire Tower
loc:
Lumpkin County forestry office 
                    Lumpkin County, Georgia
desc:
This 60-foot Aermotor tower stands beside a Georgia Forestry Commission office in Dahlonega, Georgia. It is no longer in active use but continues to be maintained by the office. The tower is signed as state property, but the office staff will escort visitors up the tower. 
 The tower predates the office and the workshop on site, having been erected sometime in the late 1950s or early 1960s.

name: Decatur County Fire Tower
loc: Decatur County, Georgia
desc: One of the last generation of Aermotor towers, Decatur County Fire Tower was erected by the Georgia Forestry Commission in 1953. Located at a ranger station, the 100’ tower with 7’x7’ metal cab was staffed until the 1990s and is now used for communications.

name: Early County Fire Tower
loc:
Town of Blakely 
                    Early County, Georgia
desc: The 100’ Aermotor Early County Fire Tower with a 7’x7’ metal cab was constructed by the Georgia Forestry Commission in 1952 and staffed until 1987. It is now a community landmark and used as a radio facility.

name: Fairwood Fire Tower
loc: Walton County, Georgia
desc: Fairwood Fire Tower was originally erected in 1952 as the Ila Tower in Madison County for the Georgia Forestry Commission. The 80’ Aermotor LS-40 steel tower with 7’ x 7’ metal cab was assembled by a crew of oil well derrick builders from Texas. In 1973 the tower was moved to Walton county and an exterior catwalk added. It is privately owned and located on the Fairwoods Stewardship and Educational Forest belonging to Don and Edith Shedd. It is the first fire tower in Georgia to be listed on the NHLR.

name: Fargo Fire Tower
loc: Clinch County, Georgia
desc: Built in 1928 by the Speir Pine Lumber Company to protect pinelands west of the famous Okefenokee Swamp, Fargo Fire Tower was later transferred to the Georgia Forestry Commission and remains in active service. Located at a state ranger station, the 100' International Stacey steel tower has a metal 7' x 7' cab. It is also considered a local tourist attraction. A large electric star mounted on the side of the cab is lighted annually at Easter, and the fire tower site is used for sunrise services.

name: Girard Lookout Tower
loc: Burke County, Georgia
desc: Built around the late 1930s or early 1940s, this 80' Aermotor LS-40 type steel tower with 7'x7' cab has the bottom steps removed to prevent entry.  The site sppears to be abandoned.

name: Glassy Mountain Fire Tower
loc:
Chattahoochee National Forest 
                    Rabun County, Georgia
desc: Glassy Mountain Lookout, built in 1941, is a 55’ metal tower with a 13’x13’ CL-100 series metal live-in cab with catwalk, located in the Chattachoochee National Forest in north Georgia. In the 1960’s an additional ground residence and garage were added.

name: Grassy Mountain Fire Tower
loc:
Chattahoochee National Forest 
                    Murray County, Georgia
desc: Grassy Mountain Lookout, not to be confused with Glassy Mountain Lookout, also located on the Chattahoochee National Forest in north Georgia, was built in 1938. It is a slightly larger 14’x14’ CL-100 series metal live-in cab with catwalk on a 50’ metal tower.

name: High Point Lookout

Chattahoochee National Forest 
                    Chattooga County, Georgia

name: Lafayette Lookout

desc: This tower was constructed to watch a nearby section of Pigeon Mountain and the town of Lafayette. While the tower was still standing without its cab, it was auctioned off on February 12, 2019, with plans for removal.

name: Mathis Fire Tower
loc:
Oconee National Forest 
                    Putman County, Georgia
desc: The tallest federal fire tower remaining in Georgia, Mathis Lookout was built by the USFS in 1942 on the Oconee National Forest. The 110’ Aermotor tower with 7’x7’ metal cab is 110’ tall.

name: McDuffie Lookout
loc: McDuffie County, Georgia
desc: This lookout appears to be an 82-foot Aermotor LS-40 galvanized tower with a 7'x7'x10' steel cab. Two radio antennas are visible, suggesting it may be used as a repeater station. It is located next to an active Georgia Forestry Commission office.

name: McGaughey Lookout Tower
loc: Whitfield County, Georgia
desc:
This early fire tower is located in extreme northern Georgia, less than five miles from the Tennessee state line. 
 According to the Georgia Forestry Commission, this tower was originally staffed by Mrs. Crow, whose family owned the land where the tower is located. Sometime after her death, and the end of the Georgia Forestry Commission's lease of the land, the tower was scheduled for removal. Because of sentimental ties and proximity to the family home, Mrs. Crow's son purchased the tower from the state around 2009. As of 2019, the tower is now owned by his widow. 
 This tower and its site are not open to the public.

name: Miller County Fire Tower
loc:
Town of Colquitt 
                    Miller County, Georgia
desc: The Miller County Fire Tower was constructed by the Georgia Forestry Commission in 1956 in the southwest corner of the state. The 99’ International Stacy tower with metal 7’x7’ cab is unusual in that it has a catwalk. Staffed until the late 1980s, it is maintained for emergency detection and radio communications for the forestry station on the site.

name: Newton Firetower
loc: Mitchell County, Georgia
desc: Built between 1935 and 1940, this 80' Aermotor LS-40 galvanized steel tower with 7'x7' cab is one of 20 or 30 firetowers in Georgia that are still occasionally manned, with a part time operational forestry station at its base.

name: Oakland Fire Tower
loc:
Oconee National Forest 
                    Greene County, Georgia

name: Oaky Woods Fire Tower
loc:
Oaky Woods Wildlife Management Area 
                    Houston County, Georgia
desc: Originally known as the Kathleen Fire Tower, this 110-foot tower was built circa 1950 to provide fire protection to the vast woodlands in central Georgia around the Oaky Woods and Ocmulgee Wildlife Management Areas. The tower sits on land purchased by the Georgia Department of Natural Resources in 2010, at which time the tower was renamed as the Oaky Woods Fire Tower The tower has been unmanned since the 1980s but houses radio equipment for local government.

name: Old Fort Fire Tower

Fort Mountain State Park 
                    Murray County, Georgia

Built by the CCC in 1938, this 50' stone tower originally had a top made of wood and glass, which was was burned by vandals in the early 1970s. The original top was rebuilt as part of a restoration around 2018. 
 The tower is famous for its "heart stone" crafted into the tower by the crew foreman as a tribute to his fiancee.

name: Piney Mountain Lookout
loc: Fannin County, Georgia

name: Rabun Bald Fire Tower

name: Thomas Lookout Tower

The tower is in fair to good condition and likely manned on an as-needed basis. It currently houses radio repeater eqipment.

name: Lowndes County Fire Tower

 As of 2020, the tower remains in active use due to restricted airspace around nearby Moody Air Force Base.

name: Bibb Lookout Tower
loc: Bibb County, Alabama
desc: One of the newer lookouts in Alabama, Bibbs Fire Tower was built in 1949. It is a 100' MC-39 Aermotor tower with 7'x7' cab.

name: Black Pond Lookout Tower
loc:
Bankhead National Forest

name: Blacksher Lookout Tower

name: Blalock Lookout Tower
loc: Marion County, Alabama

Cab has some windows missing. Did not have permission to climb it so could not check it out. Almost no vandalism since site is now private property.

name: Boar Tush Lookout
loc: Winston County, Alabama
