name: Bridge Creek Lookout Tower
loc: Lawrence County, Alabama
desc: The 100' Bridge Creek Lookout Tower was the only steel fire tower in Lawrence. It is an Aermotor MC-39 erected by the Alabama Forestry Commission in 1949.

name: Brooks Tower
loc: Conecuh County, Alabama
desc: The original Brooks Fire Tower was a 100' wooden tower. In 1962 the Alabama Forestry Commission replaced it with this 100; Aermotor MC-39 tower with 7'x7' cab.

name: Bunker Fire Lookout Tower
loc:
Cheaha State Park 
                    Cleburne County, Alabama
admin: Alabama Department of Conservation and Natural Resources
desc: Located on the highest point in Alabama in Cheaha State Park, Bunker Fire Tower was constructed by the CCC in 1934-35 atop the park lodge using a design provided by the National Park Service. It has a 10’x10’ cab on top of a 40’ native stone shaft.

name: Butler Mountain Tower
loc: Choctaw County, Alabama
desc: Still in use on high fire days, Butler Mountain Lookout Tower is a 100'Aermotor MC-39 with a 7'x7' metal cab. It was constructed in 1948.

name: Cahaba Lookout Tower
loc:
Talladega National Forest 
                    Perry County, Alabama
desc: Located on the Talladega National Forest, Cahaba Lookout is a 100' MC-39 Aermotor tower with a 7'x7' cab. It was built by the U.S. Forest Service in 1935.

name: Cain's Ridge Lookout
loc: Fayette County, Alabama
desc: This is a 100-feet steel tower. While it is missing some windows and boards from the steps, it is in overall good shape.

name: Carpenter Lookout Tower
loc: Baldwin County, Alabama
desc:
One of its last fire tower projects, Carpenter Lookout was started by the CCC and completed by the Alabama Foresry Commission in 1942. It was a 120' International Derrick tower with a 7'x7' cab. 
 The tower was removed by early 2018.

name: Carrollton Fire Tower
loc: Pickens County, Alabama
desc: When completed in 1948, Carrollton Fire Tower became the third lookout in Pickens County. It is a 100' Aermotor MC-39 with 7'x7' cab.

name: Cedar Grove Lookout
loc: Mobile County, Alabama
desc: This tower is owned by the Alabama Forestry Commission.

name: Central Lookout Tower
loc:
Bankhead National Forest 
                    Lawrence County, Alabama
desc:
This is a 100ft tower.  I believe it was fabricated by the International Derrick Company but haven't been able to confirm this detail.  I can say with certainty that it is not an Aermotor tower.  
  According to the Bankhead USFS website , "The 1930 map shows the addition of a fire tower at Kinlock Knob and another east of Cheatham Road, the Central Tower."  
 Site Visit - 11-26-22

name: Chimney Peak Fire Lookout Tower
loc:
Choccolocco Mountain 
                    Calhoun County, Alabama
desc: Situated on Choccolocco Mountain, Chimney Peak Tower was built by the CCC in the 1930s for the Alabama Forestry Commission. It is a 100’ International Derrick tower with metal 7’x7’cab located near the Jacksonville State University Planetarium.

name: Crooked Oak Lookout Tower
loc: Colbert County, Alabama
desc:
Located in Colbert County, Crooked Oak Lookout Tower is another example of the last group of towers erected to complete fire detection statewide. Built in 1971, this 100' Aermotor model MC-39 continued in service through the early 1980s. 
 Update- this tower is no longer standing - 11-27-21 http://www.firetower.org/lookouts/us/al/crooked-oak-lookout-tower/

name: Daniel's Gap Tower
loc: Cherokee County, Alabama
desc: Located in Cherokee County, the Daniel's Gap Fire Tower was completed by AFC in 1960. It is a 100' Aermotor MC-39 with 7'x7' cab.

name: Desoto Falls Tower
loc:
DeSoto State Park 
                    DeKalb County, Alabama
desc: Managed by the Alabama Division of State Parks, the DeSoto Falls Tower was beautifully situated on Lookout Mountain near the 104' DeSoto Falls. The 100' Aermotor MC-39 steel tower with 7'x7' cab was relocated by the AFC and reconstructed on this site in 1952. It was removed around 2010.

name: Evergreen Lookout Tower
loc:
Evergreen 
                    Autauga County, Alabama
desc: Construction of Evergreen Lookout, a 100' Aermotor MC-39 tower with 7'x7' cab, was completed by the Alabama Forestry Commission in 1949.

name: Fabius Lookout Tower
loc: Jackson County, Alabama
desc:
One of the few 120' Internatioinal Derrick fire towers erected by the Alabama Forestry 

 
Commission, Fabius Lookout is also one of the most recent, having been built in the mid 1950s.  

 
It has a 7'x7' metal cab.

name: Fatama Lookout Tower
loc: Wilcox County, Alabama
desc: This 100-foot steel tower was built by workers from the Vrendeburgh CCC camp in October and November 1941.

name: Flagg Mountain Lookout
loc:
Weogufka State Forest 
                    Coosa County, Alabama
desc:
The honor of listing #250, one quarter of the way to the goal of 1,000 registrations, goes to Flagg Mountain Lookout Tower on the Weogufka State Forest in Coosa County, Alabama. Built by the CCC in 1935, the 50’ stone tower is a unique structure. The walls are 2 to 3’ thick. Large timbers were laid in the rock in a criss-cross pattern and have been replaced with inlaid stone. The 12’x 12’ cab lookout was staffed by the Alabama Forestry Commission until 1989. 
 In the late 2010s, the Alabama Hiking Trail Society and Friends of Flagg volunteer group have rowked to reopen the 240-acre site that includes Flagg Mountain Lookout. As of 2019, several CCC-era cabins have been renovating and are available for overnight rentals. Work is planned on restoring lookout to its former glory.

name: Grandview Lookout
loc: Cullman County, Alabama
desc: This 100-foot steel tower is missing its lower section of stairs. It previously was used to house communications equipment but is no longer.

name: Green Mountain Lookout Tower
loc:
Green Mountain Nature Preserve 
                    Madison County, Alabama
desc:
This tower is 80ft tall with diagonal staircase.  It was originally located on the Redstone Arsenal.  
 Site Visit - 11/27/21

name: Grove Hill Lookout Tower
loc: Clarke County, Alabama
desc: This steel lookout tower is located at the Clarke County office of the Alabama Forestry Commission.

name: Horn Mountain Fire Lookout Tower
loc:
Talladega National Forest 
                    Talladega County, Alabama
desc: When the CCC constructed the Skyway Motor Way along the crest of the Talladega National Forest in the 1930s, they also constructed Horn Mountain Fire Tower on one of the highest points. It is a 100’ International Derrick Tower with 7’x7’cab.

name: Horseblock Lookout Tower
loc:
Talladega National Forest 
                    Cleburne County, Alabama
desc:
100ft Aermotor Tower with a diagonal staircase  
 
 Found on Ron Kemnow's website. 
  July 19, 1976:     "The son of a federal judge was killed Sunday, authorities said, by the premature explosion of a small homemade bomb he was carrying up the twisting stairs of a fire tower.         Cleburne County Sheriff's Investigator Joe Jacks identified him as Robert Watson, 20, son of L. Chandler Watson, a federal referee in bankruptcy.         Three other men who were watching as Watson climbed the tower atop Horse Block Mountain escaped harm.  They told investigators Watson was trying to set a timing device when the bomb exploded.         Jacks said the bomb was not large enough to have destroyed the tower.  He said the men may have been planning just to make a loud noise.         Fragments from the bomb pierced Watson's body and the force from the blast slammed him against the stairway railing.         The type of explosive was not determined immediately but Jacks said it was not dynamite.         Watson was almost to the top of the tower when the bomb went off.         The tower received some structural damage."     (The Decatur Daily)

name: Joe B. Shirley Fire Tower
loc:
Monte Sano State Park 
                    Madison County, Alabama
admin: State of Alabama, Monte Sano State Park
desc: The 100' Joe B. Shirley Fire Tower is an Aermotor model with 7'x7' metal cab constructed in 1968 by the Alabama Forestry Commission. It replaced an earlier wooden tower dating to the 1940s. Located in Monte Sano State Park, the lookout was used in the 1950s by NASA to track and record telemetry from Sputnik 1 and Explorer 1 satellites.

name: Jordan Lookout Tower
loc: Washington County, Alabama
desc: There was a concentration of fire towers in Washington County, AL. One of them is the Jordan Lookout Tower built in 1935 by the CCC. It is an 100' Aermotor MC-29 structure with a 7'x7' cab.

name: Joyce Hill Tower
loc: Perry County, Alabama
desc: On a high point in Perry County stands the 100' Joyce Hill Fire Tower. It is an Aermotor MC-39 with 7'x7' cab.

name: Kennedy Hill Fire Tower
loc: Barbour County, Alabama
desc:
In 1940, the Barbour County Board of Revenue requested the AFC to establish better fire tower coverage. In response, the AFC built this 100' Aermotor MC-39 steel tower with 7'x7' cab in 1941. By 1944, four fire towers were operating the county, completing the planned system. 
 The tower was sold by the state in a surplus auction around early 2020.

name: Kentuck Lookout Tower
loc:
Talladega National Forest 
                    Talladega County, Alabama
desc:
100ft Aermotor with a diagonal staircase. 
 Site Visit - 5/1/22

name: Longleaf Lookout Tower
loc:
Georgiana 
                    Butler County, Alabama
desc: When the 100' International Derrick model Huxford fire tower with 7'x7' cab (1939) was declared surplus by AFC in 2006, Jerry Watson purchased, moved and carefully restored the structure as his own Longleaf Lookout Tower. It now stands in Butler as a historic complement to his own longleaf pine forest known as Georgiana.

name: Lookout Hill Fire Tower
loc: Monroe County, Alabama
desc: Built by a junior African-American Company 4435 at CCC camp P-76 in 1939, Lookout Hill Fire Tower is a 100' MC-39 tower with 7'x7' cab.

name: Luverne Lookout Tower
loc: Crenshaw County, Alabama
desc:
Once the only remaining fire tower in Crenshaw County, Luverne Lookout was a 100' MC-39 Aermotor with a 7'x7' cab built in 1948 by the Forestry Commission. 
 The tower was removed prior to April 2019.

name: Mashmayer Lookout Tower
loc:
Pineview 
                    Escambia County, Alabama
desc: The honor of the 50th lookout listed on the NHLR in Alabama goes to the Mashmayer Lookout Tower. It is a 120' metal tower with 7'x7' cab built in 1938.

name: McCain Tower
loc: Clay County, Alabama

name: McGowin Lookout Tower
loc:
Chapman 
                    Butler County, Alabama
desc: The tall 120' McGowin Lookout was built by the CCC and known as McKenzie Lookout. It was moved in 1966 by the Alabama Forestry Commission to its present location.

name: Moreland Lookout Tower
loc:
Bankhead National Forest 
                    Winston County, Alabama
desc: This 100-foot steel Aermotor tower was built by CCC workers in 1933. The tower is currently surrounded by trees and shrubbery. The bottom set of stairs have been removed and all windows are missing from the cab. The site is popular vulture roost. This tower is a MC-39

name: Morgan Springs Lookout Tower
loc: Perry County, Alabama
desc: This tower was designed by the State of Alabama as AL 141.

name: Mount Willing Lookout Tower
loc:
Mount Willing 
                    Lowndes County, Alabama
desc: The Mount Willing Lookout Tower in Lowndes County dates to 1936. The 100' Aermotor MC-39 steel tower with 7'x7' cab was built by CCC Company 4434, which was also a junior African-American unit.

name: Mountain Mills Lookout Tower
loc: Colbert County, Alabama
desc: The last fire tower to be completed by the CCC in Alabama, Mountain Mills Lookout Tower was built in 1942. It is a 100' International Derrick tower with 7'x7' cab.

name: Oak Grove Tower
loc: Cleburne County, Alabama
desc: Oak Grove Fire Tower is the only AFC lookout ever constructed in Cleburne County to complement the four nearby USFS lookouts on the Talladega National Forest. Built in 1949 it is a 100' Aermotor MC-39 with 7'x7' cab. Views into the State of Georgia are possible from the cab of this tower.

name: Open Pond Lookout
loc:
Conecuh National Forest 
                    Covington County, Alabama
desc:
The presence of history is evident at the Open Pond Lookout Tower located on the Conecuh National Forest just north of the Florida-Alabama state line. Built in 1938-39 by Company 3474 of the CCC, the 100’ structure was manufactured by Jones & Laughlin Steel. This tower, and the Parker Springs Lookout -- also on the Conecuh -- are the only two towers in the state with 12’ x 12’ wooden cabs and catwalks. The other 13 towers still remaining on the national forests in Alabama all have 7’ x 7’ steel cabs. 
 Fire wardens from the tower have included S.T. Brogden, Glover Colvin, L.T. Sanders, and Martha Odom. The tower has been unstaffed since about 1975.

name: Orvin Lookout Tower
loc: Mobile County, Alabama
desc:
This 100' Aermotor MC-39 steel tower with 7'x7' cab was constructed in 1933 by CCC Camp S-52, one of the first chartered in the state. The builders were Company 1485, a junior African-American unit that also built four other fire towers. 
 This tower was removed in the late 2010s.

name: Parker Springs Lookout
loc:
Conecuh National Forest 
                    Escambia County, Alabama
desc: Located in the Conecuh National Forest on the Florida state line, Parker Springs Lookout is an unusual live-in 12’x’12’ hip roof cab with catwalk mounted on a 100’ Aermotor tower. Unique to the southern National Forests, there are only four left, two of them in Alabama. One of them is  Open Pond Lookout  nearby.

name: Peach Lookout Tower
loc:
Clanton 
                    Chilton County, Alabama
desc: Built by the Alabama Forestry Commission within a peach orchard in 1949, Peach Lookout is 100' Aermotor MC-39 tower with 7'x7' cab.

name: Perry Lakes Birding Tower
loc:
Perry Lakes Park 
                    Perry County, Alabama
desc: The Perry Lakes Tower was originally called the Rumley Lookout in Sumter County, erected by the CCC in late 1930s. In 2005 students from Judson College and the Auburn University Rural Studio, with help from AFC and Perry County, moved and restored the lookout to the its current home at Perry Lakes Park. The tower was reconstructed without the 7'x7' cab for the open-sky canopy effect for bird-watching. The 100' Aermotor MC-39 is now billed as the "tallest bird viewing tower in the United States."

name: Perry Mountain Lookout Tower
loc:
Talladega National Forest 
                    Chilton County, Alabama
desc: Perry Mountain Lookout on the Talladega National Forest is a 100' Aermotor tower with 7'x7' cab built by the Forest Service in 1937.

name: Pine Mountain Lookout
loc: Tuscaloosa County, Alabama
desc: This 100-foot steel tower is currently being used to house communications equipment. Its cab is rusting, with a missing floor and windows.

name: Pinnacle Lookout Tower
loc: Shelby County, Alabama
desc: Construction of this 100' International Derrick & Equipment Company steel tower with 7'x7' cab in Shelby County was begun in the late 1930s by the CCC and finished by the Alabama Forestry Commission in 1942.

name: Pioneer Tower
loc: Pickens County, Alabama
desc: The first Pioneer-Grove Fire Tower was destroyed by a tornado in 1947. The 100' Aermotor MC-39 with 7'x7' cab replaced it in 1966.

name: Pleasant Hill Fire Lookout Tower
loc:
Tuskegee National Forest 
                    Macon County, Alabama
desc: Built by the USDA Resettlement Administration Land Use Project in1937, later to become theTuskegee National Forest, Pleasant Hill Fire Tower is 100’ tall with a metal 7’x7’ cab.

name: Pondville Tower
loc:
Talladega National Forest 
                    Bibb County, Alabama
desc: The Pondville Lookout Tower on today's Talladega National Forest was constructed in 1937 to protect 82,000 acres of land newly acquired by the Resettlement Administration.

name: Potash Lookout Tower
loc: Randolph County, Alabama
desc: Known locally as "Tin Shop Tower," Potash Lookout Tower was constructed by the Alabama Forestry Commission in 1949. It is a 100' Aermotor with 7'x7' metal cab.

name: Redland Fire Lookout Tower
loc: Elmore County, Alabama
desc: The 100’ Redland Fire Lookout Tower was constructed by the Alabama Forestry Commission in 1948. Now in use as a radio relay station, the Aermotor tower is in Elmore County.

name: River Falls Fire Tower
loc: Covington County, Alabama
desc: This tower, believed to be a 100-foot Aermotor, is abandoned and in poor condition as of 2020.

name: Sand Mountain Lookout
loc: Blount County, Alabama
desc: This 100-foot steel tower formerly belonged to the Alabama Forestry Commission. Now part of Palisades Park, it has been restored.

name: Sanders Hill Fire Tower
loc: Pike County, Alabama
desc: One of the last lookouts built in the state, Saunders Hill was constructed in 1957 by a private contractor for the Alabama Forestry Commission. It is a 100' MC-39 Aermotor with a 7'x7' cab.

name: Sandhill Lookout
loc: Clarke County, Alabama
desc: This 100-foot steel tower is located in Clarke County.

name: Scott Mountain Tower
loc: Choctaw County, Alabama
desc: A tall, 120' Aermotor MC-39 model, Scott Mountain Lookout Tower was completed in 1949. It is still used on very high fire danger days.

name: Searles Lookout
loc: Tuscaloosa County, Alabama
desc:
This 100-foot steel tower is in poor shape and is no longer in use. As of April 2016, the owner of the property where it is located wants for it to be removed. 
 The tower was removed by October 2016.

name: Sepulga Tower
loc: Conecuh County, Alabama
desc: Little is known about this tower, which is located near the Bowles community. It is approximately 120 feet tall.

name: Simerly Fire Tower
loc: Baldwin County, Alabama
desc: The Simerly Fire Tower is a roadside landmark for travelers to the Alabama beaches. Built after 1942, the 100' Aermotor MC-39 tower replaced a 91' creosote lookout tower.

name: Smith Mountain Fire Lookout Tower
loc: Tallapoosa County, Alabama
desc: Situated on the highest point on the shoreline of Lake Martin, Smith Mountain Fire Lookout Tower is an 82’ Aermotor structure with a 7’x7’ cab and ranger station nearby. It was constructed by the WPA in 1938, and is now under restoration. See article link below.

name: Smith-westervelt Lookout
loc: Tuscaloosa County, Alabama
desc: This 100-foot steel tower was built in circa 1940 to replace a previous wooden tower which burned. The tower was dedicated to Herbert E. Westervelt, founder of Gulf States Paper (now the Westervelt Company), in July 1940.

name: Tedd Joy Lookout
loc: Jefferson County, Alabama
desc: This 100-foot steel tower is missing its bottom section of stairs. It is in overall poor shape.   There is a stone marker on site dedicating it to F.M. "Tedd" Joy (1878-1943), a conservationist, developer, and official of TCI (US Steel).

name: Thomasville Lookout
loc: Clarke County, Alabama
desc: Little is known about this Clarke County tower. It is located behind a gate that is posted with no trespassing signs.

name: Town Hill Fire Hill Lookout
loc:
Alabama Forestry Commission 
                    Marion County, Alabama
desc:
This lookout stands tall next to the busy I-22 interstate.  It has an internal diagonal staircase.  
 Site visit - 5/3/2015

name: Underwood Lookout Tower
loc:
East Brewton 
                    Escambia County, Alabama
desc: There is no other lookout cab like Underwood Lookout Tower in the 900+ listings on the NHLR. Constructed in 1938, the Alabama Forestry Commission builders stopped at 60' where the sloped legs measured 14'x14' at the top, instead of 90' where a 7'x7' cab would be mounted. Two 7' wide sections of a metal cab were joined on each of the four sides creating a unique 14'x14' cab. The picture tells the story.

name: Union Grove Lookout Tower
loc:
Jemison 
                    Chilton County, Alabama
desc: The Union Grove Lookout was built by the Alabama Forestry Commission inn 1948.  It is a 100' MC-39 Aermotor with 7'x7' cab.

name: Union Hill Lookout Tower
loc: Morgan County, Alabama
desc:
One of the newest in the state, Union Hill Lookout Tower was erected in 1964 and is one of a limited number of 80' towers used in Alabama. It is an Aermotor MC-39 steel tower with 7'x7' cab. 
 The tower and surrounding buildings were sold to a private owner in 2019. Access is now only by permission of the landowner.

name: Wallace Fire Tower
loc: Escambia County, Alabama
desc: This was Alabama Tower #62.

name: Wharton Tower
loc:
Birmingham 
                    Jefferson County, Alabama
admin: City of Birmingham and Birmingham Board of Education
desc: Also known as East Lake Tower, Wharton Lookout Tower is the only lookout in Alabama with a rooftop observation platform. This was an option forAermotor 7'x7' cabs, and is found in some mid-Atlantic states, but very unusual in the south. It is on this tower because the FM once had an aircraft beacon on the roof. Located in the City of Birmingham's Ruffner Mountain Nature Preserve, this is a 100' MC-39 Aermotor built by the CCC in 1941.

name: Wildfork Lookout Tower
loc: Monroe County, Alabama
desc: Another of the few remaining 120' towers, Wildfork Lookout is an International Derrick model with sun visors on the cab. It started by the CCC and completed by AFC in 1941.

name: Wininger Lookout Tower
loc:
Cumberland Mountain 
                    Jackson County, Alabama
desc:
Also built in the 1950s Wininger Lookout is also a 120' International Derrick structure 

 
identical to its neighbor Fabius Lookout.

name: Womack Hill Fire Tower
loc: Choctaw County, Alabama
desc: The Womack Hill Lookout Tower is a 100' Aermotor MC-39 with a 7'x7' cab. It was constructed in 1951.

name: Payne Lookout Tower
loc:
Talladega National Forest 
                    Hale County, Alabama
desc:
This tower is located off an unmarked Forest Service Road, inaccessible by vehicle. The tower can be accessed by a three quarter mile hike. As of August 2025, the tower is in great condition, no vandalism seen, stairs are mostly intact. A fence lined with razor wire around the stair case has evidently played a role at maintaining this tower's condition. 
 The tower has mostly been forgotten, Forest Service volunteers at the Payne Lake Recreation area did not know if the tower was still standing.

name: Jimmy K. Lanier Fire Lookout Tower
loc:
Overlook Park 
                    Tallapoosa County, Alabama
desc: This 110' tower used to reside in Vicksville, just outside of Sedley, VA. It stood at the intersection of Ivor and Unity Road in Southampton County since the 1930's, until the owners of the property and tower (Michael and Christina Upton) donated it to CRATA, and in 2021, the association began the process of taking it apart and relocating it to Alabama. Thanks to CRATA, volunteers from Tallapoosa and Elmore counties, It was fully restored, with new steel and wooden steps and flooring being installed into the tower along with new fencing along the steps and landings. In November 2025 the freshly restored tower was opened to the public, and is now easily accessible by car on the southern end of Lake Martin.   This project was made possible by:   Mike and Christina Upton   F. Allen and Louise K. Turner Foundation   Alabama Power   Steve Fuller, Chris McConnell, Clint Weldon, Red Hill and Union Volunteer Fire Departments   Salvatore Granada, PE,SE   Steve Martin Engineering   Butch Nabors   Wayne Bylsma   Sitemix   Contour Engineering   Paul Wright   Eddie Voss   Charles Chambers   Vulcan Materials   M&M Trucking   Russell Materials   Tallapoosa County   Dixie Electric   Jimmy Jehle   Mitchell Griffith   Diversified Steel   Chris George   Wendell Hornsby   John Howell   Jerry Bynum   Arnold Lumber Co.   Russel Do-It Center   Ethan Colley   Tallapoosa Publishing   Lake Martin Resource Association   Lake Martin Tourism Association

name: Appleton/bramlett Tower
loc: Allendale County, South Carolina
desc: This 80' Aermotor LS-40 steel tower with 7'x7' cab was originally built near the crossroads of Appleton, SC in the late 1930s.  The tower was  purchased in the late 1990s from the SC Forestry Commission by Mickey Scott and moved about 3 miles to its new home and reconstructed.  It is within view of Edisto/Butterfield tower (US941, SC10) owned by Dr. Mike Finch.

name: Atkins Fire Tower
loc: Lee County, South Carolina
desc: Built near 1936, this 110-foot galvanized Aermotor LS-40 tower features a 7'-by-7' steel cab. The tower appears to be in its original location. The site is abandoned and featured a tower keeper's house until about 2010. The tower overlooks an agricultural area in the Pee Dee District of Lee County.

name: Bamberg Lookout Tower
loc: Bamberg County, South Carolina
desc: This 100-foot tower was built circa 1936 and appears to be a Bethlehem Steel tower. It features a 7'x7'x10' steel cab. Still located in its original location, it looks to be in fair to good condition. The keeper's house is located nearby, along with an original SC Forestry Commission sign, and the tower still appears to host SCFC radio repeater equipment. The tower and ground residence are now privately owned.

name: Barnwell Lookout Tower
loc: Barnwell County, South Carolina
desc: This 80-foot steel tower with a 10'x7'x7' steel cab appears to be an Aermotor LS-40 and was built about 1935. Still standing in its original location, this tower appears to be in fair condition. While fire observation use of all South Carolina towers was ended in 1993, this tower is still in use to host a radio repeater. The lowerst staircase has been removed to prevent unauthorized access.

name: Bennettsville Tower
loc: Sumter County, South Carolina
desc: Built in 1938, this 100' Aermotor LS-40 steel tower with 7'x7' steel cab was originally located near the town of Bennettsville in Marlboro County, SC. The tower was purchased from the SC Forestry Commission by Billy McIntosh in the late 1990s and moved to Sumter County, reconditioned, and re-erected on Mr McIntosh's property.  He refers to it as the Mine Hill tower.

name: Bonneau Tower
loc: Sumter County, South Carolina
desc: Built in 1938, this 100' Aermotor LS-40 steel tower with 7'x7' steel cab was originally located near the town of Bonneau, SC in Berkeley County.  The tower was purchased from the SC Forestry Commission by Billy McIntosh in the late 1990s and moved to Sumter County, reconditioned, and re-erected on Mr McIntosh's property. The tower affords a nice view of the Wateree River basin to the West.

name: Bull Island Lookout
loc:
Cape Romain National Wildlife Refuge 
                    Charleston County, South Carolina
desc: This 110' Aermotor steel tower with 7'x7' glass-enclosed cab, constructed by the Bureau of Biological Survey circa 1932-1934, is the tallest in the state. Bull Island is an undeveloped barrier island within the Cape Romain National Wildlife Refuge. Since the early settlements, Bulls Island has been the scene of much historical activity. Bulls Bay and the creeks behind Bulls Island were reputed hideouts for pirates plundering ships along the coast. During the Revolutionary War, British warships used the island to replenish supplies. For 240 years, 36 parties claimed ownership of Bulls Island. In 1925, New York banker and broker Gayer Dominick purchased the island. An avid outdoorsman, Dominick built a large vacation home and developed the island into a hunting preserve. In 1936, Dominick conveyed the island to the U.S. Government and Bulls Island became part of the Cape Romain NWR.

name: Cassatt Tower
loc: Sumter County, South Carolina
desc: Built in 1936, this Aermotor LS-40 steel tower with 7'x7' steel cab, formerly 100', reconstructed to 40' on the original concrete footings, was originally located near the town of Cassatt in Kershaw County, SC.  The tower was purchased from the SC Forestry Commission by Billy McIntosh in the late 1990s and moved to Sumter County, reconditioned, and re-erected on Mr. McIntosh's property.  It is used as a hunting and wildlife observation spot.

name: Eastover Tower
loc: Richland County, South Carolina
desc: Built around 1936, this 120' Aermotor LS-40 steel tower with 7'x7' steel cab was named Eastover Tower by the SC Forestry Commission. The tower was purchased in 1995 by Dr. Ken Huggins and moved to family property.  Dr. Huggins sold the tower to Ray Littlejohn in 2007, but it has yet to be moved.

name: Edisto/butterfield Tower
loc:
Butterfield Plantation 
                    Allendale County, South Carolina
desc: Constructed circa 1933 by the CCC, this Bethlehem Steel tower is 110 feet tall with a 7'x7' steel cab and centered pivot-out type windows, was first referred to as the "Edisto Tower" by the SC Forestry Commission (SCFC). It was originally located at about 12 miles ESE of Bamburg, SC. The tower was purchased from SCFC and moved to private property in October 2005.

name: Gaston Firetower
loc: Lexington County, South Carolina
desc: Built around 1936, this 100' Aermotor LS-40 tower with 7'x7' cab is one of three still owned by the SC Forestry Commission in Lexington county. A nearby keeper's house is currently used part time as a law enforcement substation for the Lexington County Sheriff's Department.

name: Honey Hill Lookout
loc:
Francis Marion National Forest 
                    Charleston County, South Carolina
desc: Honey Hill Lookout, constructed in the 1930s, is the oldest remaining tower in one location on the Francis Marion National Forest and was one of several lookout stations used in the comprehensive fixed-point fire detection of the earlier years of the Forest Service. The LS-40 100’ Aermotor tower with 7’ x 7’ metal cab and hip roof was used by the U.S. Forest Service until 1989. The South Carolina Forestry Commission staffed it until October 1993. Located within a Francis Marion National Forest Picnic area, it is maintained on standby status.

name: Horsehead Lookout
loc:
Cape Romain National Wildlife Refuge 
                    Charleston County, South Carolina
desc: Built in the 1930s, this 60' steel tower located on the Atlantic Intracoastal Waterway is now abandoned. After years of rust, two of its legs collapsed on about June 14, 2014.

name: Issaqueena Tower
loc:
Clemson Experimental Forest 
                    Pickens County, South Carolina
desc: The Issaqueena Fire Tower and extensive ground facilities were considered a local attraction as an example of modern rural living for the 1930s, including the first electricity in the area. The 100’ Aermotor tower with 7’x7’ metal cab was built in 1938 by the CCC and WPA. It is located on the Clemson Experimental Forest.

name: Leeds Tower
loc:
Sumter National Forest 
                    Chester County, South Carolina
desc: Built around 1936, this 100' Aermotor LS-40 tower with 7'x7' metal cab with a low hip roof was used by the Forest Service until 1989.

name: Leesville Fire Tower
loc: Lexington County, South Carolina
admin: believed to be South Carolina Forestry Commission
desc: This is one of the original ~140 fire towers built by the South Carolina Forestry Commission between the mid-1930s and the abandonment of the system in 1993. This tower is one of two still standing in its original location in Lexington County.   The lookout is a Bethlehem Steel tower with a 7'-by-7' steel cab on top of an 80-foot galvanized steel tower. It is in poor condition. There is a small shed at the base that appears to house radio equipment and several antennas are mounted on the tower.

name: Liberty Hill Lookout
loc:
Sumter National Forest 
                    Edgefield County, South Carolina
desc: This 100' LS-40 Aermotor tower with 7'x7' galvanized sheet metal cab with hip roof was constructed in the 1940s on the Sumter National Forest and used by the Forest Service until 1989. The Liberty Hill tower was one of several lookout stations used in the comprehensive fixed-point fire detection of the earlier years of the Forest Service. The buildings around the Liberty Hill lookout tower were used as the fire dispatching office for the Edgefield and Long Cane districts as well as a fire equipment cache and staging area during extreme fire days.

name: Long Creek Tower
loc:
Sumter National Forest 
                    Oconee County, South Carolina
desc: Built around 1935, this 54' Bethany tower (similar to the Aermotor style tower) with 7'x7' metal cab with a low hip roof, also known as Round Mountain Lookout, is still used by the Forest Service on emergency Extreme High Fire Danger days.

name: Long Mountain Tower
loc:
Sumter National Forest 
                    Oconee County, South Carolina
desc: Built around 1935, this 54' Aermotor LS-40 tower with 7'x7' metal cab with a low hip roof has  an atypical window configuration. It was used by the Forest Service until the 1980s.

name: McClellanville Lookout Tower
loc: Charleston County, South Carolina
desc: Located on the Intercoastal Waterway just inland from the Atlantic Ocean, the McClellanville Fire Tower was erected by the U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service in 1940 and staffed by the South Carolina Forestry Commission until recent years. In 1989 the 100’ Aermotor tower with 7’ x 7’ cab withstood a direct hit from Hurricane Hugo which devastated the surrounding forests. The tower is now owned by the Town of McClellanville which is setting up a non-profit organization to restore and maintain it as an interpretive site and museum. It has the distinction of being the first lookout in South Carolina to be placed on the National Historic Lookout Register.

name: Moore Farms Botanical Garden Lookout
loc: Florence County, South Carolina
desc: This tower was originally built in 1934 at Olanta, about 6 miles northwest of Lake City. It was purchased from the South Carolina Forestry Commission and moved to the Moore Farms Botanical Garden property in 2004. It is the only fire tower in the United States known to have permanent flower plants along the staircases and at each landing.

name: Parsons Mountain Lookout
loc:
Sumter National Forest 
                    Abbeville County, South Carolina
desc: This 73' LS-40 Aermotor tower with 7'x7' galvanized sheet metal cab with hip roof was constructed in November 1935 and used by the Forest Service actively until 1989. The Parsons Mountain Lookout is the oldest remaining tower standing on the Sumter National Forest and was the third tower built within the Long Cane Division. It is one of several lookout stations used in the comprehensive fixed-point fire detection of the earlier years of the Forest Service.

name: Stringer Ridge Lookout
loc: Anderson County, South Carolina
desc: This 120-foot tower, possibly a Bethlehem Steel model, is located in a rural area near Clemson University. The tower has been abandoned since 1993 and is missing its floor as well as some windows.

name: Timmonsville Tower
loc: Sumter County, South Carolina
desc: Built in 1936, this Aermotor LS-40 steel tower with 7'x7' steel cab, formerly 100', reconstructed to 40' on the original concrete footings, was originally located near the town of Timmonsville in Florence County, SC.  The tower was purchased from the SC Forestry Commission by Billy McIntosh in the late 1990s and moved to Sumter County, reconditioned, and re-erected on Mr. McIntosh's property.  It is used as a hunting and wildlife observation spot.

name: Tip Top Tower
loc:
Sumter National Forest 
                    Laurens County, South Carolina
desc: Built around 1936, this 100' Aermotor LS-40 tower with 7'x7' metal cab with a low hip roof was used by the Forest Service until the 1980s.

name: Ulmer Lookout Tower
loc: Allendale County, South Carolina
desc: This 100-foot tower was built circa 1935. It features a 7'x7'x10' steel cab and appears to be a Bethlehem Steel model. Still located in its original location, the tower currently appears to be in poor condition.

name: Varnville Lookout Tower
loc: Hampton County, South Carolina
desc: This 100-foot steel tower features a 10'x7'x7' steel cab and was built circa 1936. It appears to be a Bethlehem Steel model. Currently in poor condition, it is currently used to house radio repeaters. The tower has a different style of alidade than seen in most other South Carolina towers.

name: Way Lookout
loc: Orangeburg County, South Carolina
desc: This lookout protected Orangeburg County. It was previously staffed by a lookout named Mildred Zeigler.

name: Weddell Tower
loc:
Sesquicentennial State Park 
                    Richland County, South Carolina
admin: SC Dept. of Parks, Recreation and Tourism
desc: This 90'  Aermotor LS-40 steel tower, 7'X7' cab, sits atop a prehistoric sand dune in Sesquicentenial State Park, which was built  in 1936 by the CCC to commemorate the 150th anniversary of the founding of Columbia, SC in 1786.  The SC Forestry Commission operated the tower until 1993, then later turned ownership over to the SC Dept. of Parks, Recreation and Tourism.

name: Whitmire Tower
loc:
Sumter National Forest 
                    Union County, South Carolina
desc: Built around 1935, this 100' Aermotor LS-40 tower with 7'x7' metal cab with a low hip roof was used by the Forest Service as a lookout and dispatching center until the 1980s.

name: Winyah Bay Lookout
loc: Georgetown County, South Carolina
desc: Built by the South Carolina Forestry Commission in 1937, this 100' Aermotor tower is located along US 17 south of Georgetown, South Carolina. It is presently inactive.

name: Witherbee Lookout
loc:
Frances Marion National Forest 
                    Berkeley County, South Carolina
desc: One of the few remaining examples of South Carolina’s once extensive fire lookout network, Witherbee Lookout was originally erected on the Bethera tower site with a ground house in the 1930s. It is the oldest remaining tower on the Witherbee Ranger District and was one of several lookout stations used in the comprehensive fixed-point fire detection of the earlier years of the Forest Service. In 1952 the tower was moved to the Witherbee Ranger Station on the Francis Marion National Forest. The 100’ LS-40 Aermotor steel tower with 7’ x 7’ metal cab retains the original design and materials and was used by the Forest Service actively until 1989.

name: Woodlawn Lookout
loc:
Sumter National Forest 
                    McCormick County, South Carolina
desc: This 100' LS-40 Aermotor tower with 7'x7' galvanized sheet metal cab with hip roof was constructed in May 1936 and was used by the Forest Service actively until the 1980s. The Woodlawn Lookout, also known as the Clarks Hill Lookout, was the fourth tower to be built in the Long Cane Division by the Bradley CCC camp. The Woodlawn tower was one of several primary lookout stations used in the comprehensive fixed-point fire detection of the earlier years of the Forest Service.

name: Little Mountain Fire Tower
loc: Anderson County, South Carolina
desc: This 75-foot Bethlehem Steel fire tower was built circa 1938 by the South Carolina Forestry Commission. It was sold to a private owner in 1990 after the abandonment of South Carolina's fire tower system. As of 2017, the tower is being renovated by its new owner.

name: Lesslie Fire Tower

name: Clear Springs Lookout Tower
loc:
Bienville National Forest 
                    Smith County, Mississippi
desc:
This tower is a 100ft Aermotor MC-39  
  On the Bienville National Forest eight fire towers were built from 1934 to 1940. Three towers were erected on the old Bienville Ranger District (Forkville, Shockaloo/Moore, and Sun Fire Towers) and five on the former Strong River Ranger District (Clear Springs, Heater, Polkville, Montrose, and Spinola Fire Towers). The Shockaloo Tower was dismantled in 1940 and rebuilt further south in Scott County and renamed as the Moore Fire Tower. This move helped to place it in a more central location to serve as the central dispatcher’s headquarters. The last of the fire towers to be erected was Clear Springs Tower sometime between 1937 and 1939. After World War II, the Heater Fire Tower was renamed the Coursey Fire Tower in honor of one its former lookouts who was killed during the war. Today only two towers remain standing: Moore and Clear Springs Fire Towers.

The    state park    surrounds 150-acre Shadow Lake at the western edge of    Bienville National Forest , between    Jackson    and    Meridian . It is managed by the    Mississippi Department of Wildlife, Fisheries and Parks . The park was one of the original Mississippi state parks built by the    Civilian Conservation Corps    in the 1930s. The CCC began work August 1935; the park opened in April 1940. 
 Site Visit - 7/1/23

name: Gum Springs Lookout Tower
loc:
Kisatchie National Forest 
                    Winn Parish, Louisiana
desc: This 80' Aermotor tower model LS40 with steel frame and 7'x7' cab was built during 1935-1936 by the U.S. Forest Service and CCC Troop F-6.  It is adjacent to the CCC-built Gum Springs Recreation Area, which was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in December 2011. The tower is not included in the NRHP boundary. Adjacent to the tower is the original firemen's dwelling, constructed in phases from 1935-1958.  The dwelling is a wood-frame, pier and beam, three-bay, one-story, side-gabled cabin, and is the last remaining building of the CCC period on National Forest property within the state of Louisiana.  The firemen's dwelling has been moved about 280' from its original location.

name: Kisatchie Lookout

The tower was used as part of the Forest Service fire suppression system until 1982 when the task was taken over by State overflights.

name: Merryville Fire Tower

Unusually high (110’) for a metal 13’x13’ cab with catwalk, this model was rare in the southeast where 7’x7’ cabs are the norm. Built in the late 1940’s and staffed until 1981, the tower is to be moved and restored on a hill at the site of the nearby CCC camp where the tower it replaced once stood.

name: Mount Pleasant Lookout

                    Rapides Parish, Louisiana
desc: In the flat piney forests of central Louisiana where 100' trees stretch for miles in all directions, it takes a tall tower to see out over the top and the LA Dept. of Agriculture and Forestry has one in Woodworth Fire Tower. Located on the Alexander State Forest, Woodworth has been the site of a tower for years, but the current 175' Aermotor with 7x7 cab was not constructed until 1951. To withstand the hurricane winds that sometimes rake the area, the structure is set on four huge concrete foundations measuring 10’ x 10’ by 15’ deep.

name: Almond Lookout Tower
loc: Independence County, Arkansas
desc:
This is an Aermotor MC-39 standing 100ft tall.  The first flight of stairs were removed.   
   
 site visit - 1/22/22

name: Bee Mountain Lookout
loc:
Ouachita National Forest 
                    Polk County, Arkansas
desc: Bee Mountain Lookout is nearly identical to Tall Peak (US No. 183) and was also built by the CCC in 1938. The single-story stone base (with room) supports a live-in 12’ x 12’ wooden cab with catwalk of a style that was unique to the Southern Region of the U.S. Forest Service (although at least one similar lookout -- High Knob -- was built in Virginia in what was then the Eastern Region). Extensively vandalized, the site is also on the National Register of Historic Places.

name: Boat Mountain Lookout Tower
loc: Newton County, Arkansas
desc:
100ft Aermotor with a diagonal staircase 
 6 Landings/7 Flights 
 Site Visit - 3/20/22  
 
 Information from Ron Kemnow's  site  
  March 2, 1936:   "Fifty of our boys under the supervision of Foreman Reid and Hale of Camp Harrison and Foreman Holt of Camp Jasper are rapidly bringing the construction of the Boat Mountain road to a close.  The road will be about three miles long and will in the next few days be open for traffic.       A fire tower is being constructed on the top of the mountain.  This road and tower will do much good in the suppression of forest fires.  In addition, it should be a source of interest to sightseers, as many beautiful scenes are to be found there."   (Harrison Daily Times - from the CCC newspaper 'The Dirt Dauber')

name: Bud Hill Lookout Tower
loc: Calhoun County, Arkansas
desc:
This tower stands 100ft tall with a diagonal internal staircase. 
 Site visit - 1/24/21

name: Buffalo Lookout Tower
loc: Searcy County, Arkansas
desc:
This tower is a 100ft Aermotor LS-40. 
 Site Visit - 3/20/22

name: Buffalo Tower
loc:
Ozark-St. Francis National Forest 
                    Newton County, Arkansas
desc: Constructed by the U.S. Forest Service in the mid-1930s, Buffalo Lookout Tower remained active until 1987. The 100’ Aermotor tower with 7’x7’ metal cab is located on the Bayou/Buffalo Ranger District of the Ozark National Forest.

name: Cominto Lookout Tower
loc: Drew County, Arkansas
desc:
This privately owned tower is a 100ft Aermotor MC-39.   
 Site Visit - 1/24/21

name: Compton Lookout
loc: Newton County, Arkansas
desc: This 85' Aermotor tower with 7'x7' metal cab was built in 1945 by the Arkansas Forestry Commission. When surplused, Ed Porter bought the tower, ground house and land. The ground house has been restored and is available as a lookout rental site – rare in the Eastern U.S.

name: Crossroads Fire Tower
loc:
City of Hamburg 
                    Ashley County, Arkansas
desc: Crossroads Fire Tower was constructed in 1935 by the Arkansas Forestry Commission. It was a 100' Aermotor tower with 7'x7' metal cab. In ca. 1940 the cab was raised when an additional 20' vertical section was added, making it one of the highest towers in the state. Decommissioned in 1985, it is now owned by the City of Hamburg.

name: Forum Lookout Tower
loc:
McIlroy State Game Mangement Area 
                    Madison County, Arkansas
desc:
50ft Aermotor with a diagonal staircase 
 6 Landings and 7 Flights 
 This is not the original location of the tower.  I was moved to the current location in the late 1960's/early 1970's. 
 Fun Fact! This tower can be seen in HBO's True Detective Season 3 
  QUOTE (The Madison County Journal / Huntsville, AR on May 30, 1940) – “It is pointed out that the forest fire lookout tower located six miles south of Huntsville has been completed all except the telephone installation. The   second tower in Madison County   is now nearing completion, this one being located on Swain mountain about one mile from Madison-Carroll county line near highway 23.”  
  Site Visit - 4/24/22

name: Gravel Ridge Lookout Tower
loc: Bradley County, Arkansas
desc:
This 100ft Aermotor MC-39 is located at an active Arkansas Forestry site.  The lower level stairs have been removed. 
 Site visit - 1/22/22

name: Hardy Lookout Tower
loc: Sharp County, Arkansas
desc:
100ft Aermotor with a parallel staircase 
 Site Visit - 4/10/22

name: Horn Lookout Tower
loc:
St. Francis National Forest 
                    Lee County, Arkansas
desc: Horn Mountain was one of two lookout towers constructed on the St. Francis National Forest in eastern Arkansas near the Mississippi River. The 110’ steel tower with 7’ x 7’ metal cab was built by the Resettlement Administration in 1936. The land was transferred to the Farm Security Administration in 1937 and to the Bureau of Agricultural Economics in 1938. The Soil Conservation Service administered the site from 1938 until 1954 when it was transferred to the U.S. Forest Service.

name: Ico Lookout Tower
loc: Grant County, Arkansas
desc:
This is an Aermotor tower possibly on private property.  
 I added pictures of the surrounding businesses. I enjoyed seeing how a tower design was incorporated into the logos. 
   
 Site visit 1/22/22

name: Iron Mountain Tower
loc: Stone County, Arkansas
desc:
This tower sits outside of Mountain View Arkansas.  The tower is no longer maintained.  On my last visit I remember the horseflies were so bad we couldn't get out of the truck! 
 Site Visit - September 2020

name: Iron Springs Lookout Tower
loc: Nevada County, Arkansas
desc: This tower is located in Nevada County, Arkansas. As of 2024, it is missing its roof.

name: Key Hill Lookout Tower
loc: Dallas County, Arkansas
desc:
This tower is a 100ft Aermotor MC-39. 
 Site Visit - 1/24/21

name: New London Lookout Tower
loc: Union County, Arkansas
desc:
This tower is still standing but appears to be on private land.  All access roads were locked. 
 Site visit - 12/24/21

name: Nick Springs Lookout Tower
loc: Union County, Arkansas
desc:
This tower is a 100ft Aermotor MC-39. 
 Site Visit - 1/24/21

name: Pinetree Lookout Tower
loc:
U of A - Pine Tree Research Station  
                    St. Francis Country, Arkansas
desc:
100ft Aermotor with a diagonal staircase 
 The Arkansas  Division of Agriculture obtained the property in 1960 from the U.S. Forest Service  
  Site visit - 9/20/20

name: Poison Springs Fire Tower
loc:
Poison Springs State Forest 
                    Ouachita County, Arkansas
desc: Constructed by the CCC in 1938, the Poison Springs Fire Tower served Poison Springs State Forest and surrounding counties until 1985. The 100, steel Aermotor tower with 7’ x 7’ cab is now used by the Arkansas Forestry Commission as a radio relay site.

name: Push Mountain Firetower
loc:
Ozark-St. Francis National Forest 
                    Baxter County, Arkansas
desc: The 60’Aermotor LX-25 Push Mountain Fire Tower was erected on the Ozark National Forest in 1929. An unusual feature is that the steps between landings are actually ladders, a transition between the earlier exterior vertical ladder design and the later interior stairs.

name: Rich Mountain Fire Tower
loc:
Ouachita National Forest 
                    Polk County, Arkansas
desc: Located on the Talimena Scenic Highway on the Ouachita National Forest, Rich Mountain Fire Tower is at the highest point on the road and is a popular picnic spot.  The 42’ steel tower with a 14’x14’ Cl-100 metal cab was constructed in 1952 and used for fire detection until 1975.  It replaced an unusual 6’x6’ wooden cab perched atop a 20’ log tower with a Spartan groundhouse living quarters.

name: Round Mountain Lookout Tower
loc: Cleburne County, Arkansas
desc:
This Aermotor tower is privately owned.  It appears to be a LS-40 model. 
 Site Visit - 7/8/16

name: Sugarloaf Fire Tower
loc:
Ozark National Forest 
                    Stone County, Arkansas
desc: The Sugarloaf Fire Tower historic district was accepted on the National Register of Historic Places in October, 1995. The mountaintop, located on the Ozark National Forest, is the site of a remarkable group of stone structures constructed by the CCC in 1937 as living accommodations for the 100’ steel lookout tower with 7’x7’ cab.

name: Tall Peak Fire Tower
loc:
Ouachita National Forest 
                    Polk County, Arkansas
desc: Once there were 43 lookouts on the Ouachita National Forest in Arkansas, and today only six remain. Tall Peak Lookout is one of them. The 12’x12’ live-in wooden cab with catwalk atop a one-story stone base was constructed in 1938 by the CCC. Although inactive as a lookout for many years and extensively vandalized, the site is on the National Register of Historic Places.

name: Velvet Ridge Lookout Tower
loc: White County, Arkansas
desc:
The Arkansas tower still stands on a small patch of land owner by the Arkansas Forestry Commission.  The parcel was once much larger and contained housing for the area forester. The tower has a diagonal interior staircase and metal treads.  The cab no longer has a floor. 
 Site visit - 9/29/20

name: Wolf Mountain Lookout
loc: Miller County, Arkansas
desc: This tower is located in Miller County, Arkansas.

name: Chandler Lookout
loc: Henderson County, Texas
desc: This 100-foot tower was built in 1970 as part of a program to expand Texas' fire tower network. Macon Carver was one of the first lookouts employed at this tower, working at the site by September 1970.

name: Love's Lookout
loc:
Jacksonville 
                    Cherokee County, Texas
desc: The first listing in the State of Texas, Love’s Lookout is one of the few fire towers remaining of a network in the East Texas pineywoods that once numbered more than 100. The 125’ Aermotor tower with 7’x 7’ metal cab was built by the Texas Forest Service in 1935 and remained active until 1970. It is now owned by the City of Jacksonville, TX.

name: Pine Mills Fire Tower
loc: Wood County, Texas
desc: This is believed to be a 7'x7' Aermotor cab on a 70-foot tower. It currently houses a Texas A&M Fire Service radio repeater.

name: Spring Fire Tower
loc:
Cypress Creek Park 
                    Harris County, Texas
desc:
This is a refurbished Aermotor MC-39 originally manufacutred in Chicago in the 1930s and installed in western Montana for the U.S. Forest Service. It was in service for 60 years and then decommissioned in 1995. It was then refurbished by Davanna LLC at Bloomingdale, NY and refitted with metal stairs, platform, and cabin. 
 The tower was reconstructed in January 2023 at its new location in Spring, Texas.

name: Woodville Fire Tower
loc: Tyler County, Texas
desc: Only 20 of the 142 fire towers that once covered East Texas remain in place. Woodville Fire Tower was built by the Civilian Conservation Corps in the 1930s at the Woodville District Office of the Texas Forest Service. The 70' steel tower with 7' x 7' metal cab was provided by the Emsco Oil Derrick Co. and is accessed by an external vertical ladder. No longer in active service, it houses a radio repeater and is host to a lighted Rudolf the Rednosed Reindeer each holiday season, assigned to the post by Santa Claus to report if the children in Woodville have been naughty or nice.

name: Beaver Fire Tower
loc:
Cookson Hills Wildlife Management Area 
                    Cherokee County, Oklahoma
desc: Located in the Cookson Hills Wildlife Management Area in Northeast Oklahoma, Beaver Fire Tower is a 100’ Aermotor tower with metal 7’ x 7’ cab. Constructed in 1950, it remained in active service until 1997. A unique roofed hollow stump (large enough to hold four people) serves as a visitor registration site.

name: Carnasaw Lookout
loc: McCurtain County, Oklahoma
desc: The first state fire tower in Oklahoma, Carnasaw Lookout was built in 1926. The original wood tower was replaced with a 100’ wood tower in 1937. That tower blew down in 1974 and was replaced with a 100’ Aermotor tower with a 7’ x 7’ metal cab. By the time the builders reached the 75’ level, it became apparent that a measuring error at the footings would make it impossible to continue higher. A deck was placed at that level, with the cab in the middle, explaining the unusual configuration. It is still in active service.

name: Carter Mountain Lookout
loc: McCurtain County, Oklahoma
desc: Carter Mountain Lookout was the second in Oklahoma. Also located in the southeastern corner of the state, the original wooden tower was built in 1927 and replaced with a 100’ Aermotor tower with 7’ x 7’ cab in 1936. It remains in service.

name: Jadie Tower
loc:
Ouachita National Forest 
                    McCurtain County, Oklahoma
admin: Oklahoma Forestry Services and Tiak Ranger District
desc: Built in the 1930s by the U.S. Forest Service, Jadie Tower is a 100' Aermotor tower with a 7'x7' cab.  Over the years it has been staffed by either the Ouachita National Forest or the Oklahoma State Forestry Division.

name: Bear Mountain Lookout
loc: McCurtain County, Oklahoma
admin: Oklahoma Department of Agriculture, Food, and Forestry
desc: This 80' steel Aermotor tower was built in the 1930s by the Civilian Conservation Corps.

name: Blue Buck Fire Tower
loc:
Mark Twain National Forest 
                    Douglas County, Missouri
desc: The Blue Buck Fire Tower was built by the CCC in 1935 on the Mark Twain National Forest. No longer used, but a well known landmark, the 110' steel tower with 7'x7' cab is in need of restoration.

name: Camdenton Lookout
loc:
Camdenton Conservation Service Center 
                    Camden County, Missouri
desc:
Camdenton Lookout, a 60' steel tower, was built in 1942 on a 40-acre site acquired the previous year by the Missouri Conservation Commission. The cab was overhauled in Fiscal Year 1970. 
 A watchman's dwelling was constructed in 1946. It received new wiring, sheetrock, insulation, cabinets, and a water filter in Fiscal Year 1966. A new roof, ceramic tile in the bath, storm windows, and new gutters were added in Fiscal Year 1970. A new heating system, duct work, well pump, and porch repairs were completed between 1972 and 1974.

name: Coot Mountain Lookout Tower
loc:
Rocky Creek Conservation Area 
                    Shannon County, Missouri
desc:
The Coot Mountain Lookout Tower is a (currently) Missouri Department of Conservation-owned tower, built in 1940 by the CCC. The tower features a cabin and garage for lodging tower staff, these appear to be younger than the tower and built in the MDC modern style used throughout Missouri. 
 The tower steps as of July 2024 are in an older but functional state. From the top, the tower has views of the hills surrounding Eminence to the west, and the Current River water channel between two hills to the east.

name: Deer Run Lookout
loc:
Current River Conservation Area 
                    Reynolds County, Missouri
desc: Believed to be the first permanent lookout in Missouri, Deer Run was located in the former Deer Run State Park. It is an 85-foot steel tower and features a 7'-by-7' cab.

name: Doniphan Lookout
loc: Ripley County, Missouri
desc: This 100-foot Aermotor LS40 tower was built in 1958-1959. As of 2023, the tower is not open to the public but is in good shape, with portions of the wood treads recently having been replaced. The tower is not actively used for fire detection except for during peak fire season.

name: Garwood Lookout
loc: Reynolds County, Missouri
desc:
The Garwood Lookout was erected in 1950 on a small site (approx. 40 acres) owned by the Missouri Department of Conservation. Revisions were made to the tower in 1969-70. The tower is a metal structure that is 100 feet in height. Overall, it was in pretty good shape as of March 13, 2025. The tower can be climbed, though signage says it must done "at your own risk" and "no more than five people on the tower at one time." 
 As of 2025, the cab in inaccessible. The area is also under video camera surveillance.

name: Indian Trail Lookout
loc:
Indian Trail Conservation Area 
                    Dent County, Missouri
desc: Built in 1927 as the second lookout in Missouri, this 85-foot steel tower features a 7'-by-7' cab. It is still actively used for fire detection.

name: Mountain View Fire Tower
loc: Howell County, Missouri
desc: Located not far from the Arkansas state line, Mountain View Fire Tower was built by the Missouri Department of Conservation in 1949. It is a 100' Aermotor with a 7'x7' cab.

name: Perry Fire Tower
loc: Perry County, Missouri
desc:
This 100-foot steel Aermotor tower is of the LS40 type. It was built by the Missouri Department of Conservation for the detection and prevention of forest fires in the Southeast Missouri region. 
 The tower was part of the Perryville Fire Protection District which included several other tower sites throughout SE Missouri. Tower usage was discontinued in the 1980s but Missouri Department of Conservation continued maintenance of 5-acre tower site, and established a separate communications tower at the site. In 2022-23 ownership of the tower site was deeded to Perry County for historical purposes. Tower and site planning are in development, and presently tower is in caretaker status and is prohibited from climbing until plans for restoration are complete.

name: Pilot Knob Lookout
loc:
Mark Twain National Forest 
                    Phelps County, Missouri
desc:
Mark Twain National Forest was established by President Roosevelt by proclamation on September 11, 1939. The metal lookout tower was erected in 1953-54 and the cab was refinished in 1969-70. 
 In August 2023, a visit to the tower showed the tower and cab remain standing, though they are in poor shape (especially the cab). The base of the lookout tower has a chain link fence around it with barbed wire on top. 
 There was at least one other Pilot Knob Lookout in Missouri in Stone County.

name: Rocky Mount Fire Tower
loc:
Runge Conservation Nature Center 
                    Cole County, Missouri
desc: This tower was built at Rocky Mountain in the summer of 1949. It was equipped with an Osborne Fire Finder, and was staffed by towerman P.A. Hess from 1956 to 1987.

name: Taum Sauk Lookout
loc: Iron County, Missouri
desc: Taum Sauk Lookout Tower was constructed by the Missouri Department of Conservation in 1949. The 72’ steel tower with wooden cab--the first to be listed on the register in the state--is located on the highest point in the Missouri Ozarks (1,772’) within a state park. The name is derived from a Piankashaw Indian Chief: Sauk-ton-qua.

name: Thomasville Fire Tower
loc: Shannon County, Missouri
desc: Still staffed in periods of high fire danger, Thomasville Fire Tower was built by the Missouri Department of Conservation in 1957. It is a 100' Aermotor tower with a 7'x7' cab.

name: Twin Knobs Fire Tower
loc:
Mark Twain National Forest 
                    Douglas County, Missouri
desc: This tower is located in Mark Twain National Forest. It is currently locked behind a tall chain link fence.

name: Fremont Fire Lookout
loc:
Mark Twain National Forest, Eleven Point Ranger District 
                    Shannon County, Missouri
desc: Likely constructed by the Bartlett CCC Camp 3752 in 1939. Associated structures were also built. Towerman residence and garage (standard plans) as well as an associated recreation site with pavilion as the tower site was located along the newly constructed US Hwy 60. Unsure of date of removal of residence and pavilion. Tower was staffed (intermittently) until 2019. The retirement of a longtime employee left lookout vacant. Lookout has been utilized for prescribed fire monitoring since 2016, has been outfitted by the Missouri Department of Conservation with antenna to track a recently reintroduced species of bird to the Pine savannah restoration area. Solar panels were added sometime after 2010 provide power to a wildfire monitoring system that was largely unsuccessful. Addition of these components provided an avenue for water to enter the structure causing water damage that will result in the replacement of some interior lower wall sections. Lookout is still functional with lookout stand and fire finder in place. Restoration activities are being planned pending approvals. Stairway landings will likely be replaced with metal grating during the 2027-28 fiscal years.

name: Briar Fire Lookout
loc:
Mark Twain National Forest, Eleven Point Ranger District 
                    Ripley County, Missouri
desc: Constructed by Bardley CCC Camp 3751 in 1938 along with towerman dwelling (plan B34-01) and two garages (plan B-16). Site was used as area work center and housing until the mid 1970's. unsure of date of removal of housing and garage. Lookout was staffed frequently by employees until 2005. After that time lookout was used for afternoon checks and locating reported smokes. Lookout was used infrequently after vandalism destroyed the Osborne fire finder between 2005 and 2010. Lookout was in disrepair until 2016 when efforts of a few district employees and AmeriCorps crews initiated restoration activities. During this time, grounds were again maintained, many steps replaced, and broken windows replaced. Lookout was used primarily used for monitoring prescribed fire smoke monitoring during this time. Lookout fire finder stand was damaged beyond repair by vandalism in 2021. Lookout stand was rebuilt and interior lower walls and floor repainted. Missouri department of Conservation was contacted to procure another fire finder. The fire finder from the recently removed Fort Leonard Wood Lookout was gifted to the Forest, restored and placed in the lookout in 2024. Restoration activities are ongoing including the addition of a radio repeater on the structure, restoration of electric power, planned replacement of all stairway landings with grated metal, and planned replacement of lookout ceiling as well as historic interior features. Lookout does not have dedicated staff but is still utilized for prescribed fire monitoring as well as occasional visits from fire staff during fire season.

name: Flatrock Fire Tower
loc:
Flatrock State Wildlife Area 
                    Texas County, Missouri
desc: This tower is a 100ft  Aermotor LS-40.  Online resources indicate that the land for the tower was obtained in 1942, and the tower was erected in 1943. There are only light amounts of graffiti across the tower, and it is in decent condition, however some wood planks are wobbly. It is only climbable to the top, just beneath the cabin. There is no functioning catwalk, only a locked hatch door that leads into the cab. Condition of the cab is unknown.

name: Fairview Fire Tower
loc:
Mark Twain National Forest 
                    Pulaski County, Missouri
desc: Resources regarding the Fairview tower are extremely limited, however it allegedly was erected in 1937, as a steel tower (Possibly a Aermotor MC-39, 1934). It is located in a small clearing off the road of highway 17 and is surrounded by fencing and barbed wire. There is a small sign posted that informs you of the towers original purpose for preventing forest fires, in addition to an explanation for its closure (vandalism) and informs you that the site is under active surveillance. Cab is relatively small, and the tower is in good shape! Most windows are intact and stairs seem to have been recently replaced.

name: Roby Fire Tower
loc:
Mark Twain National Forest 
                    Texas County, Missouri
desc: Roby tower is allegedly the first fire tower in Missouri, with the steel tower erected in 1934. Located just outside of Roby, (Nicknamed for its proximity to the area) it is located in northeastern Texas County Missouri in Plato.

name: Marcoot Lookout Station
loc:
Mark Twain National Forest 
                    Reynolds County, Missouri
desc:
November 22, 1934:     "The foundation for the Marcoot tower is being dug at present time and the tower will be completed in about a week after the foundation is poured.  Assistant Leader Bierman and his detail under the supervision of Construction Foreman Jones will build this tower which is three miles from Marcoot, Mo.   The new tower will be slightly different than the present towers at Buick and Czar, in that a stairway will be used instead of the ladder, to reach the cab.  The tower will be ninety-nine feet, nine inches height, to the floor of the cab"     (The Salem Post and The Democrat-Bulletin)  
 The tower is a model MC-39.

name: Big River Lookout
loc:
Big River State Forest 
                    Henderson County, Illinois
desc: The Illinois Department of Conservation once had a network of 10 fire towers across the state, and the U.S. Forest Service had an additional 7 in the Shawnee National Forest. All of the federal towers are gone and only two state towers remain. Big River Lookout is located on the eastern bluffs along the Mississippi River within the Big River State Forest. The 60’ steel tower with 7’x7’ cab was constructed in 1941.

name: Trigg Tower
loc:
Shawnee National Forest 
                    Johnson County, Illinois
desc:
Trigg Lookout Tower is the last remaining tower of sixteen built in the Shawnee National Forest from 1934 to 1939. A 40 foot wooden fire tower was constructed in 1934 by the Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC) enrollees of Camp Simpson. In 1938, the original tower was replaced by the present metal tower built by CCC enrollees from Camp Eddyville. It originally stood 100 feet tall. Fifty feet of its frame was removed in  1973 because of safety hazards. 
 The CCC built both towers and provided the first tower men to stand watch for fires. Tower men needed a keen eye to spot distant clouds of smoke. By quickly locating the fire, tower men helped ground crews reach the fire early. Ferdinand A. Silcox, Chief of the Forest Service in 1936 stated, "Perhaps the most important contribution the CCC made during its existence has been protecting the forests from fire." By 1967, airplanes replaced lookout towers as the principle method of spotting the fire, and the other fifteen towers have been abandoned and torn down. 
 623rd Company F-4, one of the original companies of the CCC, was organized at Fort Sheridan in May 1933. The company moved several times before it came to Camp Eddyville in southern Illinois. Camp Eddyville stood on the edge of Hayes Canyon. The 623rd Company was divided in half in August 1935. Half of the enrollees were sent to Simpson, Illinois where they formed the 2676th Company, F - 12, CCC Camp Simpson.

name: Union Lookout
loc:
Trail of Tears State Forest 
                    Union County, Illinois
desc: The Union Lookout, also known as Trail of Tears Lookout, is located in southern Illinois in Trail of Tears State Forest. It was constructed between 1936 and 1938 by the CCC. The 80’ steel tower with 7’x7’ cab is one of the few points from which visitors may view the Shawnee Hill Country. The unusual name relates to the forced move of 10,000 Cherokee Indians from North Carolina to Oklahoma in 1839. Because of floating ice in the Mississippi River the expedition camped near the site in January before crossing.

name: Buzzville Lookout
loc:
Chautauqua National Wildlife Refuge 
                    Mason County, Illinois
desc: In 1936, President Franklin Roosevelt established Chautauqua Refuge by executive order. The refuge consists of  4,388 acres  of Illinois River bottomland.

name: Hartwell Fire Tower
loc:
Pike State Forest 
                    Pike County, Indiana
desc: Located in Pike State Forest, this tower overlooks the Patoka River valley.

name: Henryville Fire Tower
loc:
Clark State Forest 
                    Clark County, Indiana
desc: Built around 1930, the Henryville Fire Tower is one of the landmark attractions in southern Indiana's Clark State Forest.

name: Hickory Ridge Lookout Tower
loc:
Hoosier National Forest 
                    Monroe County, Indiana
desc:
Hickory Ridge Lookout is located on the edge of the Charles C. Deam Wilderness on the Hoosier National Forest in Indiana. It is a 110-foot steel tower with 7- by 7-ft. cab built by the CCC in 1936 and is the last remaining fire tower, out of an original number of eight, remaining on National Forest land in Indiana. The tower was restored in 1989. 
 Indiana Public Media featured the tower in a November 2013 segment of The Weekly Special  available here.

name: Lilly Lookout
loc: Brown County, Indiana
admin: Indiana University Research and Teaching Preserve
desc: Built in the 1930s by the CCC, this 75' tower with 7'x7' steel cab and wooden steps is located on property that was donated to Indiana University by the Lilly Family, relatives of Eli Lilly who started Lilly Pharmaceutical, in 1942. Access to the tower is by permission only.

name: Lincoln State Park Fire Tower
loc:
Lincoln State Park 
                    Spencer County, Indiana
desc: This 120-foot Aermotor tower was built by CCC crews in 1935. As of 2025, it is open to the public.

name: McCormick's Creek Fire Tower
loc:
McCormick's Creek State Park 
                    Owen County, Indiana
desc: This 86’ steel tower with 7’x7’ metal cab was constructed in 1935 by CCC Company #589. The McCormick’s Creek Fire Tower was active until 1967 and is now a popular state park viewing site.

name: O'Bannon Woods Fire Tower
loc:
O'Bannon Woods State Park 
                    Harrison/Crawford County, Indiana
desc: The first fire tower on this site on the Harrison Crawford State Forest was constructed by the CCC in 1937. It was damaged by fire and replaced with the 88’ steel tower with 7’x7’ metal cab in 1941. When the land was transferred to the O’Bannon Woods State Park, the tower became known as the O'Bannon Woods Fire Tower.

name: Ouabache Fire Tower
loc:
Ouabache State Park 
                    Wells County, Indiana
desc: Ouabache (pronounced O-bah-chee) Fire Tower was constructed in 1935 (per onsite signage) by the Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC). The tower in located in the northeast part of the state of Indiana south of Fort Wayne near the city of Bluffton in Ouabache State Park. Some references may use the name Wells County Fire Tower as this state park was originally the Wells County State Forest. It was refurbished in 2019 using funds raised by the Friends of Ouabache State Park.

name: Skyline Drive Lookout
loc:
Jackson-Washington State Forest 
                    Jackson County, Indiana
desc: Skyline Drive Lookout Tower is located on the Jackson-Washington State Forest in Indiana. The 80-ft steel tower, with 7'x7' cab, was built by the CCC between 1931 and 1935. Although not used for fire detection since the 1970s, the tower is maintained by the Indiana Department of Natural Resources as a popular public viewing site of the countryside.

name: Weed Patch Hill Lookout
loc:
Brown County State Park 
                    Brown County, Indiana
desc:
The 90-100 foot tall Weed Patch Hill Fire Lookout Tower was constructed in the 1927 (or 1930s based on signage at site) atop the tallest point in Southern Indiana and third-highest named summit in the state. Originally built as a fire lookout, today it is used as both a communications tower and an observation tower for the public visiting the state park. The tower is a popular attraction as it is easy to access and located along the main road through the state park. 
 Additional information from the website, indianafiretowers.com.  Weed Patch was originally built in 1927. The 1926 Department of Conservation annual report says: “Weed Patch Hill… It is the intention to erect an 80-foot steel tower on the hill, which is the second highest point in the state.” The 1927 Department of Conservation annual report mentions that the Division of Engineering: “Supervised construction of fire tower at Brown County game reserve.” The 1928 Department of Conservation report says: “An eighty-foot steel tower for the purpose of detecting forest fires was erected in 1927.” The first Hohenberger photo below is attributed to 1927. 
 The wooden sign currently standing at Weed Patch tower says that it was built in the 1930s. 
 Brown County State Park opened in 1929. Around that time, part of the current park was originally the Brown County Game Preserve. 
  Note – January 2026: The   Friends of Brown County State Park   have announced a fundraising initiative for restoring the Weed Patch tower.

name: Willow Valley Fire Tower
loc:
Martin State Forest 
                    Martin County, Indiana
desc: Built by the CCC camp at Martin State Forest in 1932, the 100’ Willow Valley Fire Tower was once part of a network that overlooked the forested hills of southern Indiana. Removed from active service in 1976, it is still maintained as an emergency lookout and is mainly used as a viewpoint by the public. There in an observation deck two-thirds of the way up.

name: Winamac Fire Tower
loc: Pulaski County, Indiana
desc: Constructed by the Works Progress Administration in 1937 within Indiana's Tippecanoe River State Park, Winamac Fire Tower is a 90' Aermotor with a 7'x7' cab. Reached by a quarter-mile trail, it is open for visitors to climb.

name: Mason Ridge Fire Tower
loc:
Morgan-Monroe State Forest 
                    Morgan County, Indiana
desc:
According to Dean Alger's book Indiana's Historic Fire Towers 
          The Mason Ridge Fire Tower was erected in the forest in 1930 and rebuilt later by the Young Hoosiers Conservation Corp (YHCC) in 2009 and 2010. Prior to this renovation the fire tower had been condemned. The YUCC is a state funded program providing young men and women. from low income families, with employment on state projects, at state-owned properties. It took YHCC crews approximately 10 months of total work, over two seasons, to complete this work. During this time, the YHCC removed two of the tower's three sections. The upper cabin, and a 50-foot-tall central section of the tower were taken off and placed on the ground for restoration. The lower section of the tower was restored in-place. After the three sections were individually rebuilt, the tower was re-erected. Completed work included replacing the wooden steps on the stairways, and safety fencing along the stairways and landings; installing a new white oak ceiling and floor in the cabin; and refabricating and replacing the cabin windows. While the fire tower was being manufactured, the shipping location, in this case a nearby farm, was stenciled on the steel tower to help prevent it from being lost during transportation. This stencil was found during the tower restoration work.

name: Ferdinand Fire Tower
loc:
Ferdinand State Forest 
                    Dubois County, Indiana
desc:
According to Dean Alger's book Indiana's Historic Fire Towers 
 This state forest currently covers over 7,700 acres and it is well known as an exceptional deer hunting locale. Multiple roads, service buildings, and other land improvements were completed in the state forest by the CCC, Company 1513, Camp F-76 during the Great Depression. Workers at the CCC Camp also erected the Ferdinand Fire Tower in 1935 and this fire tower was restored during the summer of 2009. The fire tower worked in unison with other towers, including the Lincoln City Fire Tower in Spencer County, to determine the exact locations of forest fires. Local firefighters responded to reported fires. The Ferdinand Fire Tower was last used in the late 1950s or early 1960s for fire detection purposes.   
 According to the Forest Fire Lookout Association, Indiana Chapter, there was another fire tower in the Ferdinand State Forest. This tower was in place for only a couple of years. It was located less than a mile southeast of the present tower, and there was a small dwelling for the tower lookout at the site. It is not known for sure, but the Ferdinand Fire Tower might have been moved to its current site from the location of the first tower.

name: Cincinnati Fire Tower
loc:
Private Property 
                    Greene County, Indiana
desc: According to Dean Alger's book, Indiana's Historic Fire Towers.  The Cincinnati Fire Tower was erected prior to 1940 on property leased by the State of Indiana. Over 85 years later, this tower is now in complete disrepair. The tower's cabin is still on top of the structure, even though the cabin's roof and floor are missing. Wooden steps on the tower's stairways are rotten. Further, the wood planks on the tower's various landings are rotten as well. Climbing the tower is definitely unsafe, and even visiting the tower is illegal without landowner permission.

name: Nsa Crane Lookout
loc:
Naval Weapons Station Crane 
                    Martin County, Indiana
desc: According to  Indianafiretowers.com.   In the 1930s, this area in Martin County was being called the White River Land Utilization Project as a project between the USDA Soil Conversation Service and the Indiana Department of Conservation. This area in Martin County becomes a naval ammunition facility as WW2 begins.

name: Nsa Crane Lookout
loc:
Naval Weapons Station Crane 
                    Lawrence County, Indiana
