desc: According to  Indianafiretowers.com.   In the 1930s, this area in Martin County was being called the White River Land Utilization Project as a project between the USDA Soil Conversation Service and the Indiana Department of Conservation. This area in Martin County becomes a naval ammunition facility as WW2 begins.

name: Nsa Crane Lookout
loc:
Naval Weapons Station Crane 
                    Martin County, Indiana
desc:
According to  Indianafiretowers.com.   In the 1930s, this area in Martin County was being called the White River Land Utilization Project as a project between the USDA Soil Conversation Service and the Indiana Department of Conservation. This area in Martin County becomes a naval ammunition facility as WW2 begins. 
 The southern Crane tower is the only one that seems to have a name (or two.) Indian Springs and Trinity Springs are both town names near the southern tower. I think both of these names have been applied to this southern tower. There is an NGS mark named INDIAN SPRINGS LOOKOUT TOWER ( JA1932 ) referring to the southern-most of the Crane towers. I think this is fairly solid evidence that the southern tower was primarily named Indian Springs. 
 The name “Trinity Springs” is mentioned in the text on a USDA flyer about Hickory Ridge Lookout Tower:    “The CCC camp, located in Kurtz, not only built the lookout tower at Hickory Ridge and Dutch Ridge, but also one at Trinity Springs.”  
 I have not see any names associated with the other three towers.

name: Nsa Crane Lookout
loc:
Naval Weapons Station Crane 
                    Martin County, Indiana
desc:
According to  Indianafiretowers.com.   In the 1930s, this area in Martin County was being called the White River Land Utilization Project as a project between the USDA Soil Conversation Service and the Indiana Department of Conservation. This area in Martin County becomes a naval ammunition facility as WW2 begins. 
 The OSBORN RM 3 JA1940 mark, which is not at any of the four known tower sites, has a 1946 station description that says it is “ABOUT 1 MILE NORTHWEST OF A PROMINENT WATER TOWER THAT IS BUILT OVER AND AROUND AN OLD FOREST SERVICE LOOKOUT TOWER”. It’s easy to find Water Tank 4 (mark JA1930) at that location, and that’s where there is a water tank that also has a lookout tower.

name: Salem Fire Tower
loc:
Private Property 
                    Washington County, Indiana
desc:
According to Dean Alger's book, Indiana's Historic Fire Towers. 
 1954 the Indiana Division of Forestry moved the Borden Fire Tower, located in Clark County, Indiana, to its current location in Washington County, Indiana. After being moved the fire tower was renamed the Salem Fire Tower, and it helped the state protect more than 150,000 acres of timber from forest fires. This steel fire tower has four legs, it is 80 feet tall, and it has been painted silver (see Figure 17). Today the tower is on private property, not in a state park or forest; however, the Jackson-Washington State Forest is nearby. 
  Ron Kenmow  August 11, 1954: "The Indiana Department of Conservation announces that personnel of the Division of Forestry has moved the 80-foot Borden Fire Tower, in Clark county, to a more favorable location about 8 miles north of Salem in Washington county. In its new location the tower will connect the Skyline Tower in Jackson State Forest and the fire tower in Clark County State Forest, giving added protection to more than 150,000 acres." (Jackson County Banner)

name: Ofs Cool Springs Fire Tower
loc:
Privately Owned 
                    Pike County, Indiana
desc:
According to Dean Alger's book, Indiana's Historic Fire Towers - The Spears Fire Tower was located in Hoosier National Forest in Crawford County, Indiana, about 13.0 miles south-southeast of the town of French Lick and 5.4 miles northwest of the town of English. The Indiana DOF erected the tower in or around 1936 and later transferred ownership to the U.S. Forest Service. Sometime around 1987, the Forest Service sold the Spears Fire Tower so they could erect a newer and taller tower at the site. 
 The fire tower buyer dismantled the structure, moved it from the original site, and placed it in storage. Later on, a private individual bought the Spears Fire Tower to fulfill his dream of restoring and rebuilding this tower in Indiana. The new owner unfortunately passed away before he was able to re-erect this notable fire tower in his home state. His son, however, worked with OFS Brands, an Indiana furniture manufacturer, to completely restore and re-erect the tower at OFS Brands' Cool Springs Campus in Velpen, Indiana. The Cool Springs Campus is utilized by OFS Brands for company retreats, and to showcase for dients the company's sustainability and craftsmanship. The property covers 1,000 acres and contains an extensive forest, tree nursery, lake, educational center, horse barn, and marina. The fire tower at the campus, now called the Cool Springs Fire Tower, has decorative lights on it. Invited guests can climb the tower, and if inclined to do so there is another structure they can zipline down. 
 Visits to the campus and this fire tower are by invitation only.

name: Armintrout Fire Tower
loc:
Ohio State Fairgrounds 
                    Franklin County, Ohio
desc: Originally located in Pike County, Ohio, this tower was rehabilitated and moved to the ODNR Natural Resources Park at the Ohio State Fairgrounds in 2016.

name: Ash Cave Fire Tower
loc:
Hocking Hills State Forest 
                    Hocking County, Ohio
desc: Located on the Hocking Hills State Forest, Ash Cave Fire Tower was constructed in 1934. The 80’ Aermotor tower with 7’x7’ metal cab has recently been restored and repainted by the fire tower restoration project of the Ohio Division of Forestry with the cooperation of the Ohio Division of the Forest Fire Lookout Association.

name: Atkinson Ridge Fire Tower
loc:
Zaleski State Forest 
                    Vinton County, Ohio
desc: Another Ohio restoration is the Atkinson Ridge Fire Tower on the Zaleski State Forest. Built in 1929 this 60’ Aermotor tower with a 7’x7’ metal cab was recently restored by the fire tower restoration project of the Ohio Division of Forestry with the cooperation of the Ohio Division of the Forest Fire Lookout Association.

name: Beaver Creek Fire Tower
loc:
Beaver Creek State Forest 
                    Columbiana County, Ohio

name: Blue Rock Fire Tower
loc:
Blue Rock State Forest 
                    Muskingum County, Ohio
desc: The honor of Number 700 of the NHLR goes to Blue Rock Fire Tower on the Blue Rock State Forest. Constructed in 1937, the Aermotor tower with a 7’x7’ metal cab is the last 100’ fire tower remaining in Ohio.

name: Brush Ridge Lookout
loc:
Tar Hollow State Forest 
                    Ross County, Ohio
desc: Located in the Tar Hollow State Forest, Brush Ridge Lookout was constructed in 1933. It is a 73' McClintock-Marshall metal tower with a 7'x7' metal cab. It has been restored by the Fire Tower Restoration Project of the Ohio Division of Forestry.

name: Copperhead Fire Tower
loc:
Shawnee State Forest 
                    Scioto County, Ohio
desc: The first forest lookout tower in Ohio, this tower was constructed in 1924.

name: Green Ridge Fire Tower
loc:
Pike State Forest 
                    Pike County, Ohio

name: Keystone Fire Tower
loc:
Scioto Grove Metro Park 
                    Franklin County, Ohio
admin: Columbus and Franklin County Metro Parks
desc:
This is 45-foot high steel tower was originally located in  southeastern Jackson County, Ohio . 
 In 2023, the tower was  restored and relocated  to the Scioto Grove Metro Park in Franklin County. It is now open to the public during daylight hours.

name: Lone Pine Fire Tower
loc:
Wayne National Forest 
                    Lawrence County, Ohio

name: Mohican Lookout
loc:
Mohican-Memorial State Forest 
                    Ashland County, Ohio
desc: This 125-foot high tower is located in Mohican-Memorial State Forest.

name: Scioto Trail Fire Tower
loc:
Franklin Township 
                    Ross County, Ohio
desc: Built in 1925, Scioto Trail Fire Tower overlooks a portion of the Scioto Trail State Forest. It is a 60’ Aermotor tower with a 7’x7’ metal cab.

name: Senecaville Fire Tower
loc: Noble County, Ohio
desc: This tower is privately owned and hosts radio equipment for the Muskingum Watershed Conservancy District.

name: Shawnee Lookout Tower
loc:
Wayne National Forest 
                    Hocking County, Ohio
desc: Shawnee Lookout is the last fire tower standing on the Wayne National Forest in Ohio. The 110-foot galvanized steel tower, with a 7- by 7- ft. cab, was constructed by the CCC in 1936. Shawnee Tower is the first to be listed in Ohio and the third nationwide.

name: Snake Ridge Lookout Tower
loc:
Wayne National Forest 
                    Athens County, Ohio
desc: The CCC built the 100' Snake Ridge Lookout on the Wayne National Forest in the 1930s. In 1964 the top 20' and the 7'x7' cab was moved to Hocking College. In 2007 the Forest Service reacquired the tower and restored the full 100' at the new Forest Headquarters for historic display.

name: Sugar Grove Lookout Tower
loc: Fairfield County, Ohio
desc: This is a 110-foot high steel tower.  As of 2014, there is an active effort to relocate and restore the tower.

name: Tappan Fire Tower
loc: Tuscarawas County, Ohio

name: Woods Ridge Fire Tower
loc: Scioto County, Ohio

name: Buck Hill Lookout
loc:
Pictured Rocks National Lakeshore 
                    Alger County, Michigan
desc: This 100-foot tower overlooks the Beaver Basin area. While the floor of the cabin has failed, the steel is in good shape. The tower currently hosts a repeater for the Michigan State Police radio network.   David O. Evans worked at this fire tower during the mid-1950s.

name: Demond Hill Fire Tower
loc:
Hiawatha National Forest 
                    Chippewa County, Michigan
desc:
Built about 1925, Demond Hill Fire Tower sits atop the highest hill near the lumbering town of Raco, Michigan. 
 During the Great Depression, the tower worked in conjunction with the Civilian Conservation Corps camp in Raco to handle fire suppression. By 1942, when Raco was the only camp left in the district, its fire protection area covered 151,140 acres.

name: Feldtmann Lookout
loc:
Isle Royale National Park 
                    Keweenaw County, Michigan
desc: Feldtmann Lookout is a 40-foot tower and features a CL-100 cab with catwalk.

name: Gibbs City Fire Tower
loc:
Ottawa National Forest 
                    Iron County, Michigan
desc: Company 3611 (James Lake) of the Civilian Conservation Corps erected Gibbs Fire Tower in 1939-40. The 100’ Aermotor tower with 7’x 7’ metal cab remained active until 1970 when it was replaced by air detection. This is the only remaining fire tower on the Iron River district of Michigan’s Ottawa National Forest.

name: Tepee Lookout Tower
loc:
Ottawa National Forest 
                    Iron County, Michigan
desc: Erected by the men of the CCC Paint Lake Camp in 1933, Tepee Lookout Tower is one of the last of a network that covered the Ottawa National Forest in northern Michigan. The 100' Aermotor steel tower with 7' x 7' metal cab was accessed with an outside ladder. It was staffed until the late 1960s. The groundhouse and CCC garage are gone.

name: Bergland Lookout Tower
loc:
Ottawa National Forest 
                    Ontonagon County, Michigan
desc: This tower is believed to have been built in the 1950s, around the time the town of White Pine and its company homes were established.

name: Udell Lookout Tower
loc:
Manistee National Forest 
                    Manistee County, Michigan
desc: Constructed by the CCC in 1940, this tower is the last remaining tower in the Manistee National Forest.

name: Bagley Lookout
loc: Oconto County, Wisconson
desc: This 100-foot Wisconsin standard tower features an external protected ladder. It was built in October 1939.

name: Beaver Lookout
loc: Marinette County, Wisconsin
desc: This 73-foot International Stacy tower features an inside corner ladder. It was built in November of 1933 and staffed intermittently during spring fire season until 2015 when Wisconsin decommissioned its lookout network.

name: Bruce Mound Lookout
loc: Clark County, Wisconsin
desc:
This 70-foot tower is referred to in historical records as a “Baker Latest Rebuilt (1932)” type tower. It appears very similar to the Wisconsin standard tower and features an external cage protected ladder. It was built in 1932. 
 The tower's original cab burned during the 1950s and was rebuilt the following year.

name: Brule Lookout
loc: Douglas County, Wisconsin
desc: This 80-foot Wisconsin standard tower features an external protected ladder and was built in 1932.

name: Buckeye Lookout
loc: Florence County, Wisconsin
desc: This 80-foot International Stacy tower features a corner leg ladder. It was built in November 1933.  It was staffed regularly during spring fire season until 2015 when Wisconsin decommissioned its lookout network.

name: Camp Douglas Lookout
loc:
Volk Field Air National Guard Base 
                    Juneau County, Wisconsin
desc:
The 68-foot Camp Douglas Tower was a Wisconsin standard stairway style featuring internal dogleg stairs, rather than the much more common cage-protected external ladder variant.  Both styles were developed by the Wisconsin Conservation Commission in the early 30’s.  While the external ladder type is abundant across Wisconsin, the stair style such as Camp Douglas is quite uncommon with relatively few ever being constructed.  The Camp Douglas Lookout was built in 1932 and was staffed intermittently during spring fire season until 2015 when Wisconsin decommissioned its lookout network. 
 This tower was removed in 2023.

name: Cedarville Lookout
loc: Marinette County, Wisconsin
desc: This 80-foot International Stacy tower features an internal corner leg ladder. It was built in November 1933.

name: Chetek Lookout
loc: Barron County, Wisconsin
desc: This 100-foot Aermotor tower features an inside corner ladder and was built at its current location in 1951. This style tower appears consistent with towers built much earlier in the 1930s, so it’s possible this tower was relocated from a different site in 1951.

name: Clevedon Lookout
loc: Douglas County, Wisconsin
desc: The Clevedon tower features an inside corner leg ladder. Year of construction and height is unknown, but it appears to be a 100-foot Aermotor tower.

name: Connors Lake Lookout
loc: Sawyer County, Wisconsin
desc: This 100-foot Aermotor tower features a US Forest Service-style stairway. It was built in 1934.

name: Cranberry Rock Lookout
loc: Juneau County, Wisconsin
desc: This 100-foot USFS style tower features an inside corner ladder and was manufactured by Bethlehem Steel. It was built in 1932.

name: Dairyland Lookout
loc: Douglas County, Wisconsin
desc: This 100-foot USFS style tower features an inside corner ladder and was manufactured by Bethlehem Steel. It was built in August 1937 for the Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources. The tower and property was sold in a state land parcel sale and is now under private ownership.

name: Danbury Lookout
loc: Burnett County, Wisconsin
desc: This 84-foot Wisconsin standard tower features an external protected ladder. It was built in November 1932.

name: Dunbar Lookout
loc: Marinette County, Wisconsin
desc: This 100-foot Wisconsin standard tower features an external protected ladder. It was built in October 1939.

name: Dyracuse Lookout
loc:
Dyracuse Off-Road Park 
                    Adams County, Wisconsin
desc: This 80-foot Wisconsin standard tower features an external protected ladder. It was built in 1939. Dyracuse Lookout was historically named Dorro Couche after nearby Dorro Couche Lake.

name: Fifield Lookout
loc:
Chequamegon-Nicolet National Forest 
                    Price County, Wisconsin
desc: The Wisconsin Conservation Commission (now the DNR) constructed Fifield Fire Tower in 1932, one year prior to the establishment of the Chequamegon-Nicolet National Forest. The 100’ Aermotor tower with a 7’x7’ metal cab has a vertical ladder access. Restored by the U.S. Forest Service, it was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 2007.

name: Five Mile Lookout
loc: Washburn County, Wisconsin
desc: This 84-foot Wisconsin standard tower features an external protected ladder. It was built in August 1932.

name: Flannagan Lookout
loc: Douglas County, Wisconsin
desc: This 84-foot Wisconsin standard tower features an external protected ladder. It was built in August 1939.

name: Friendship Lookout
loc: Adams County, Wisconsin
desc: Friendship, also historically called Skyline, is a 100-foot Wisconsin standard tower featuring an external protected ladder. It was built in December 1939. Friendship tower was staffed intermittently during spring fire season until 2015 when Wisconsin decommissioned its lookout network.

name: Glidden Lookout
loc: Ashland County, Wisconsin
desc: This 80-foot Wisconsin standard tower features an external protected ladder. It was built in 1932.

name: Goodman Lookout
loc: Marinette County, Wisconsin
desc: This 110-foot Wisconsin stsandard protected ladder-type tower was built in October 1939.

name: Gordon Lookout
loc: Douglas County, Wisconsin
desc:
Gordon tower is a 100-foot Aermotor, likely an MC-39 model. Originally built in August 1935 in the SWSE, Section 36, T.44N.-R.12W. at an elevation of 736' it was moved to its current location at an unknown date. Gordon features a US Forest Service-style stairway and at some point its stair treads and landings were upgraded to expanded steel rather than wood. Gordon tower was staffed intermittently during spring fire season until 2015 when Wisconsin decommissioned its lookout network. 
 Douglas County has been working with a Friends of the Bird Sanctuary organization to preserve the tower since it was deactivated by the state.

name: Hayward Lookout
loc: Sawyer County, Wisconsin
desc: This 100-foot Aermotor tower features a US Forest Service-style stairway. Year of construction is unknown. A tower survey dated 1940 indicates a wooden stairway style tower was in place at that time.

name: Hodag Lookout
loc: Oneida County, Wisconsin
admin: Private Owner (formerly Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources)
desc: Hodag Tower has stood sentinel over nearby Rhinelander since its construction in 1949. It’s named after the mythical creature that terrorized logging camps in Wisconsin’s Northwoods during the lumbering heyday of the early 1900’s and which has become a namesake of the Rhinelander community. The tower is a standard design created by the Wisconsin Conservation Commission (now DNR) in the 30’s referred to as the Wisconsin Standard Ladder Protected. It features an external, cage-protected ladder. At 120 feet, Hodag is one of the tallest lookouts in the State and in its early years also served as a base station in the State’s early radio network. The lookout was staffed intermittently during spring fire season until 2015 when Wisconsin decommissioned its lookout network. It is now under private ownership.

name: Indian Lake Lookout
loc: Oneida County, Wisconsin
desc: This 100-foot Aermotor tower features a US Forest Service-style stairway. It was built in 1936.

name: Iron River Lookout
loc:
Chequamegon-Nicolet National Forest  
                    Bayfield County, Wisconsin
desc: The Iron River Tower serves as evidence of the cooperative effort by the Forest Service and the Wisconsin Conservation Commission to conserve and protect the State’s forest resources in the early 30’s. Built in February of 1934 by the Conservation Commission on National Forest system lands, the State operated the lookout for 81 years until 2015 when the DNR decommissioned its lookout network. The 79’ 6” tall tower was manufactured by the International Stacey company and features an internal corner leg ladder.

name: Jack Pine Lookout
loc: Oneida County, Wisconsin
desc: This 74-foot International Stacey tower was built in 1933. It features an internal leg ladder.

name: Kinepoway Lookout
loc:
Private Property - Menominee Indian Reservation 
                    Menominee County, Wisconsin
admin: Formerly Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources, now Menominee Tribal Enterprises
desc: Coast and Geodetic Survey notes indicate the Kinepoway Lookout Tower was in place by 1934, although the exact date of construction is unknown.  The Wisconsin Conservation Commission built the lookout and it was staffed intermittently during spring fire season until 2015 when the Wisconsin DNR decommissioned its lookout network.  Fire protection on the reservation is done cooperatively by both the DNR and Tribe, and although the lookout is still standing, it’s unknown if the Menominee Tribe staffs the tower for fire detection.

name: Knapp Mound Lookout
loc: Jackson County, Wisconsin
desc: Lookout towers have been atop Knapp Mound dating back to at least 1932. At that time a 72-foot tall “Baker Improved Strengthened” type tower featuring an external unprotected ladder was in place. The current tower, a 68-foot Wisconsin standard model with external cage protected ladder was built at an unknown later date. Due to years of vandalism the cab of Knapp Mound was replaced in 2008 and the tower was in service and staffed intermittently during spring fire season until 2015 when Wisconsin decommissioned its lookout network.

name: Kolpack Lookout
loc: Shawano County, Wisconsin
desc: This 100-foot Wisconsin standard tower features an external protected ladder. It was built in June 1932.

name: Lake Tomahawk Lookout
loc: Oneida County, Wisconsin
desc: This 100-foot Wisconsin standard tower features an external protected ladder and was built in September, 1939. The Lake Tomahawk Lookout was never retrofitted with the cable fall-arrest system found on other DNR ladder towers and clearly hasn’t seen active service in decades. From the ground a large hole in the roof is visible along with one missing floorboard in the cab. Alternating segments of the tower frame and cab are painted orange, likely to identify it as an aerial hazard due to its close proximity (1/2 mile) to a private airfield. Historical records indicate this tower was originally called Tomahawk Lake Lookout.

name: Little Switzerland Lookout
loc: Washington County, Wisconsin
desc: This 93-foot tower stands atop of the Little Switzerland Ski Hill. It is most likely an Aermotor LS-40 tower and has an internal stairway. The tower was built by the Wisconsin Conservation Corps and it was moved to thislocation in 1935.

name: Lookout Mountain Lookout
loc:
Lincoln County Forest 
                    Lincoln County, Wisconsin
desc: This 84-foot Wisconsin standard tower features stairs rather than the much more common cage-protected external ladder typically found on this type of tower. Also unique is that all landings and stair treads are solid 1/4” thick galvanized plate steel instead of wood or metal grating commonly found on stair type towers. Identical to the tower frame members, the underside of the landings and stairs are labeled “84’ For Woodruff No. 1” indicating they are clearly original to the tower. It was built in 1932.

name: Marengo Lookout
loc:
Chequamegon-Nicolet National Forest 
                    Ashland County, Wisconsin
desc:
No less than three lookout towers have stood atop this point within the ancient Penokee Mountain range of Northern Wisconsin. The first, a 100-foot Wisconsin Standard model with external cage-protected ladder, was built in 1939 and destroyed in September of 1941 during a fall windstorm. Photographs of the wreckage show a twisted mass, with the heavy steel legs of the tower broken off from the footings. 
 The mountain presumably stood vacant until approximately 1949 by which time photographs show a replacement had been erected. Geodetic Survey notes indicate the second Marengo tower was a 65-foot tall steel structure with an enclosed cab. This tower served until the late 1980s when according to a local resident, the surrounding vegetation simply grew up too tall rendering the 65-footer inadequate. In 1987, the third and present structure was erected, a 100-foot stair-type tower, likely an Aermotor MC-39. The DNR very commonly moved and rebuilt towers but by the 1980s was replacing towers on an extremely limited basis. It’s likely that the current Marengo Tower was deemed surplus elsewhere in the state, disassembled and rebuilt to replace the previous shorter structure. Located on National Forest System lands, the tower has always been owned and operated by the state and saw active service until 2015 when Wisconsin decommissioned its lookout network.

name: Matson Lookout
loc: Marathon County, Wisconsin
desc: This 94-foot tower features an inside corner ladder and appears to be an Aermotor. Built in 1951 and historically named “N” Tower, it was renamed Matson in 2005 to honor John Kenneth Matson (Ken). Ken worked 45 years as a DNR fire lookout with the majority spent in N/Matson Tower. He climbed until he was 81 years old. Matson Tower was staffed intermittently during spring fire season through 2009 and continued to be used as a radio tower for Marathon County until approximately 2012.

name: Meteor Lookout
loc: Sawyer County, Wisconsin
desc: This 100-foot Aermotor tower features a US Forest Service-style stairway. It was built in 1934.

name: Middle Inlet Lookout
loc: Marinette County, Wisconsin
desc: This 100-foot Wisconsin standard tower features an external protected ladder. It was built in October 1939.

name: Monahan Lookout
loc: Vilas County, Wisconsin
desc:
Constructed in 1934, this structure is a 100' Model MC-39 Aermotor steel tower with 7'x7' cab and an inside stairway. The land on which the tower stands was purchased in 1932 for back taxes by Edmund and Matilda Drager. In 1934, scouts were roaming the courntryside to find suitable sites for the construction of lookout towers, preferably on state-owned land. The scouts happened on the site, a small, but high, wooded knob and construction began shortly thereafter. Meanwhile, as construction got underway, Mr. Drager searched for the noise and commotion of construction. Mr. Drager, himself conservation-oriented, found the activity to be on his land. He happily granted an easement to the government to build the tower. 
 This tower was removed by August 2023.

name: Mosinee Lookout
loc: Marathon County, Wisconsin
desc: This 100-foot tower features an inside corner ladder. Mosinee Tower sits along Ranger Street within the City of Mosinee, adjacent to a former Wisconsin DNR Ranger Station. Built in 1951, Mosinee tower was staffed intermittently during spring fire season until 2015 when Wisconsin decommissioned its lookout network.

name: Mountain Lookout Tower
loc:
Nicolet National Forest 
                    Oconto County,Wisconsin
desc: Mountain Lookout Tower was once part of an extensive lookout network on the Nicolet National Forest in Wisconsin. Today the 100-ft steel Aermotor tower, with a 7'x7' cab, is the only remaining lookout on the Forest.

name: Necedah Lookout
loc: Juneau County, Wisconsin
desc: This 80-foot Wisconsin standard tower features an external protected ladder and was built at its current location in 1951. A statewide tower survey dated September, 1940 indicates that Necedah tower was originally an 84-foot steel ladder tower built in 1939 in the NENE Section 24, T18N.-R3E. It’s unknown if the original structure was moved and rebuilt in its current location or if a new tower was built in 1951. Necedah tower was staffed intermittently during spring fire season until 2015 when Wisconsin decommissioned its lookout network.

name: Oak Ridge Lookout
loc: Jackson County, Wisconsin
desc: Located on a ridge near Millston, this lookout was constructed in the late 1930s.  Oak Ridge is a 100-foot tall tower manufactured by the Aermotor Company featuring an internal corner leg ladder.  Oak Ridge tower was staffed intermittently during spring fire season until 2015 when Wisconsin decommissioned its lookout network. One previous observer at this site was Russell Young.

name: Ogema Lookout
loc:
Timms Hill County Park 
                    Price County, Wisconsin
desc: This 80-foot Wisconsin standard tower features an external protected ladder and was built in 1932. It sits atop Timms Hill, Wisconsin’s highest natural point. Adjacent to the lookout is a wooden observation tower open to the public.

name: Park Falls Lookout
loc: Price County, Wisconsin
desc: The Park Falls tower features a US Forest Service-style stairway. Year of construction and height is unknown, but it appears to be a standard 100-foot Aermotor tower.

name: Pattison Lookout
loc: Douglas County, Wisconsin
desc: This 100-foot tower features a US Forest Service-style stairway and was manufactured by the McClintock-Marshall Steel Company, a subsidiary of Bethlehem Steel. It was built in 1934.

name: Paust Lookout
loc:
Governor Thompson State Park 
                    Marinette County, Wisconsin
desc: In 1934 the CCC built the 100' Aermotor tower for the State of Wisconsin at Pembine. It served until the 1980s. Declared surplus, the State sold the tower to Dale Paust in 1990. He moved and rebuilt it at Paust's Woods Lake Resort. The State purchased the resort for a state park in 2000.

name: Phelps Military Hill Veterans Lookout Tower
loc: Vilas County, Wisconsin
desc: This tower is an Aermotor MC-39 Series tower standing 120 feet tall including a 10-foot tall cabin creating a total height of 132 feet to the peak of the roof. It has 153 steps.   The tower was constructed in 1936, one of 38 Depression-era towers built throughout the Chequamegon Nicolet National Forst. In the early 20th Century, wildfire was rampant throughtout northern Wisconsin as a consequence of unwise havesting methods. Use of the tower ended in 1960.   In 1978, the U.S. Forest Service was approached by Lowell Buell who asked to purchase the Military Hill Fire Lookout Tower. Following purchase it was his his stated desire to donate the tower to the Town of Phelps. On April 11, 1978, Mr. Buell completed this donation.

name: Quarry Lookout
loc: Marathon County, Wisconsin
desc: This 100-foot International Stacy tower features an inside corner ladder. Exact construction date is unknown however it was likely after 1940 as the tower was not included in a statewide tower survey dated September 1940.

name: Rock Falls Lookout
loc: Lincoln County, Wisconsin
desc: This 100-foot Aermotor tower features a US Forest Service-style stairway. It was built in 1934.

name: Saddle Mound Lookout
loc: Jackson County, Wisconsin
desc: A tower has been located at this site since at least 1931.

name: South Bluff Lookout
loc:
Wood County Forest 
                    Wood County, Wisconsin
desc: This tower was built in 1933 by the Wisconsin Department of Conservation to replace an earlier tower built at a lower, more accessible, site nearby.

name: Squirrel Hill Lookout
loc:
Minocqua Winter Park 
                    Oneida County, Wisconsin
desc: This 84-foot Wisconsin standard tower features an external protected ladder. It was built in September 1939.

name: Thunder Mountain Tower
loc: Marinette County, Wisconsin
desc: This tower sits in the privately owned Thunder Mountain Ranch.

name: Twin Mound Lookout
loc: Clark County, Wisconsin
desc: This 82-foot Wisconsin standard tower features an external cage protected ladder and was built in the early 1930s.  National Geodetic Survey notes from 1934 indicate a fire tower was in place at this site by that time.  Twin Mound tower was staffed intermittently during spring fire season until 2015 when Wisconsin decommissioned its lookout network.

name: Villas Lookout
loc: Langlade County, Wisconsin
desc: This 100-foot Aermotor tower features an inside corner ladder. It was built in October 1936.

name: Wolf River Lookout
loc: Forest County, Wisconsin
desc: This 79-foot International Stacy tower features an inside corner ladder. It was staffed intermittently during spring fire season until 2015 when Wisconsin decommissioned its lookout network.

name: Worcester Lookout
loc: Price County, Wisconsin
desc: This 100-foot tower features an inside corner ladder. Exact construction date is unknown however it was likely after 1940 as the tower was not included in a statewide tower survey dated September 1940.

name: Zenith Lookout
loc: Lincoln County, Wisconsin
desc: This 100-foot Wisconsin standard tower features an external protected ladder. It was built in December 1939.

name: Wisconsin Dells Lookout
loc: Columbia County, Wisconsin
desc:
According to a Wisconsin Conservation Commission Bulletin dated 1958, there has been a lookout structure at this location since 1934: "Approved construction of a $6,140 steel lookout tower at Wisconsin Dells to replace a 24-year-old wooden tower." (Wisconsin Conservation Bulletin, Vol. 23, 1958) 
 The Wisconsin Dells Lookout was staffed intermittently during spring fire season until 2015 when Wisconsin decommissioned its lookout network. The tower is now surrounded by private land and only accessed by a DNR easement.

name: Norway Ridge Lookout
loc: Monroe County, Wisconsin
desc:
This tower was built in 1932. Its cab was replaced in 2008 after damage had taken its toll on the previous cab. 
 The tower was staffed intermittently during spring fire season until 2015 when Wisconsin decommissioned its lookout network. As of early 2022, this tower was for sale by the state.

name: Jump River Fire Tower
loc:
Chequamegon-Nicolet National Forest 
                    Taylor County, Wisconsin
desc:
The Jump River Company of the CCC had a camp one half mile east by southeast of here. The tower was built during their occupancy. 
 Also remaining is a small outhouse about 30 feet from the base.

name: Aiton Heights Fire Tower
loc:
Itasca State Park 
                    Clearwater County, Minnesota
desc: The Aiton Heights fire tower has a colorful history. Originally erected by the MN Division of Forestry in the 1920s, it was moved to Itasca State Park in 1937 and assigned dual roles: visitor education and fire detection. The CCC ground house was occupied until 1957, and then later moved to serve a boat launching site. The 80’ Aermotor tower with 7’x7’ metal cab continues in service with David Quam (MN FFLA Director) as the park interpreter.

name: Ash River Lookout
loc:
Kabetogama State Forest 
                    Saint Louis County, Minnesota
desc:
This 81-foot Pittsburgh-Des Moines windmill-style tower is one of the only examples of its type in the United States. An octagonal cab is attached to the top of the tower where a windmill would otherwise be mounted. 
 There is a second set of concrete anchors on the site from a previous tower that was built in 1924 and removed in 1935.

name: Badoura Lookout Tower
loc:
Badoura State Forest 
                    Hubbard County, Minnesota
desc: Built by the CCC and the Minnesota Division of Forestry in 1934 to oversee an area of high fire danger, Badoura Lookout Tower was staffed until 1979 when it was replaced by air detection. The 100’ Aermotor tower with a 7’x7’ metal cab is still used as a radio antenna and emergency lookout by personnel from the nearby Badoura Forest Nursery.

name: Bemidji Fire Tower
loc: Hubbard County, Minnesota
admin: Northern Lights Council No. 429, Boy Scouts of America
desc: Built in 1935 by the Minnesota DNR, the Bemidji Fire Tower served as a lookout for 60 years. Decommissioned and transferred to MN DOT for an antenna site, the 100’ Aermotor tower with 7’x7’ metal cab became surplus again in 2006. In 2007 the Boy Scouts moved it to BSC Camp Wilderness where it was restored and reconstructed as an 80’ tower next to the mess hall.

name: Ben Draper Lookout
loc: Cass County, Minnesota
desc: The Ben Draper Lookout Tower is a 110’ Aermotor structure with 7’ x 7’ metal cab built by the CCC and the Minnesota Division of Forestry in 1937. It is located on the Land ‘o Lakes State Forest on a tract donated by Ben Draper, an early settler in the area. Still used on an emergency basis, the historic site will be interpreted with an information kiosk.

name: Sandy Lake Fire Tower
loc:
Savanna State Forest 
                    Aitkin County, Minnesota
desc: Big Sandy Lake Fire Tower is a 94’ tower with 7x7’ cab constructed in 1933 by the Minnesota Division of Forestry. The lookout is one of the few manufactured by the Pittsburg-Des Moines Co. Still active and very popular as a tourist attraction, the lookout was restored in 1992.

name: Birchdale Lookout
loc: Koochiching County, Minnesota
desc: Erected in 1928 by the state forest service it is an 81 foot tall ladder tower. A cabin and warehouse were originally near the tower. A county garage is located there now.

name: Black Bay Lookout Tower
loc: Koochiching County, Minnesota
desc: The Black Bay Lookout Tower was built by the CCC in 1939. It is a 100 foot stairway tower. MnDOT proposed a site improvement that would open the tower to the public in 2008, but nothing has happened.

name: Bois Forte Lookout
loc:
Nett Lake Indian Reservation  
                    Koochiching County, Minnesota
desc:
One of three lookout towers in the Nett Lake Indian Reservation. 
 It is a stairway tower. Survey notes describe the tower as 125 ft in overall height. Inscriptions on one of the tower footings is dated Sept. 6, 1934. 
 The wood steps and landing boards have been recently replaced and are in good condition.

name: Boulder Hill Fire Tower
loc:
Grand Rapids 
                    Itasca County, Minnesota
desc: Built in 1934 by the CCC on the Chippewa National Forest, along with a towerman’s cabin and garage, Boulder Hill Tower remained in active service until the late 1960s. In 1976 the 100’ steel tower with 7’ x 7’ metal cab was moved to the Forest History Center in Grand Rapids, MN, but not open to the public. Restored to its original condition in 1997, the tower is now staffed by interpreters and open seven days a week from Memorial Day through October 15. It is one of the most climbed towers in the U.S.

name: Elba Fire Tower
loc:
Whitewater State Park 
                    Winona County, Minnesota
desc: Elba Tower was constructed by the CCC in 1936 and is the farthest south of Minnesota's fire towers. No longer manned by the State Division of Forestry, the lookout is located on Division of Wildlife land immediately adjacent to Whitewater State Park. The 110-foot tower, with a 7- by 7-ft. cab, was transferred to the Division of State Parks for restoration and use as an interpretive site.

name: Elephant Lake Lookout
loc: St. Louis County, Minnesota
desc: This ladder-style tower is 80 feet tall. This tower previously stood at Ash River from 1924-1935, and was later re-erected by the CCC in 1940 at Elephant Lake. This means it is likely the oldest remaining tower in Minnesota.   This tower currently houses communications equipment.

name: Gheen Lookout
loc: St. Louis County, Minnesota
desc:
Gheen Hill is a 100-foot stairway tower built by the CCC in 1934. An earlier wood tower was built on the site in 1921. 
 There is communications equipment on the tower as of 2020. Multiple other communications towers are on the same hill.

name: Heritage Lookout
loc:
Nett Lake Indian Reservation  
                    Koochiching County, Minnesota
desc: This stairway tower is one of three towers in the Nett Lake Indian Reservation. Nett Lake is visible from this tower. Gheen Hill, where another lookout stands is visible from this tower 14.2 miles to the SE with the help of binoculars.

name: Jasper Peak Fire Tower
loc: Saint Louis County, Minnesota
desc:
Jacob Peak Fire Tower was is a 60-foot steel internal stairway tower constructed in 1934. It is not the first tower at this site. 
 Minnesota state forester William T. Cox said of a previous tower at this site in 1920: "The equipment for the Jasper Peak Lookout at Tower was completed and gave excellent service this season. This is perhaps the most valuable observation post in the state. It gives a view over a large scope of country and has saved many times its cost by making possible quick action on fires."

name: Kabetogama Lookout
loc: St. Louis County, Minnesota
desc: Kabetogama is an 80 foot stairway tower. Also called Arbutus, it was made by the McClintic Marshall Corp of Bethleham PA. It was erected by the CCC in September 1934 at a cost of $168.30. There was a four post timber tower located here that was torn down in 1934.

name: Loman Fire Tower
loc: Koochiching County, Minnesota
desc: Loman is privately owned. The tower, residence and garage were all a state forestry office at one time. Loman was built in 1927 and is an 80 foot ladder tower.

name: Marshall Lookout Tower
loc: Koochiching County, Minnesota
desc: This tower is described in survey reports as 136 feet in height, making it possibly the tallest tower in Minnesota. The tower is sometimes also called the Bob Marshall Tower after the famous forester and conservationist. As of 2019, the wooden steps on the tower have been recently replaced.

name: Minnesota State Fair Lookout
loc:
Minnesota State Fair 
                    Ramsey County, Minnesota

name: Nimrod Fire Tower
loc: Wadena County, Minnesota
desc: Nimrod Fire Tower was constructed by the Minnesota Division of Forestry in 1928. The 94’ Aermotor tower with an unusual 6’8” octagonal crow’s nest cab reached by a vertical ladder is the first of this unique style to be listed on the REGISTER. A landmark for canoers on the Crow Wing River, the lookout observes a fire-prone jack pine forest.

name: Pequot Fire Tower
loc:
Paul M. Thiede Fire Tower Park 
                    Crow Wing County, Minnesota
desc: Minnesota’s second listing, Pequot Lookout Tower, was built by the CCC and MN-DNR Division of Forestry crews in 1934. At 100’ with a 7x7 cab, it is still valued as a detection site in the popular wooded lakes region of central Minnesota.   The tower is now the centerpiece of Paul M. Thiede Fire Tower Park, named after a former Crow Wing County commissioner who spearheaded preservation of the tower.

name: Vermillion Dam Lookout
loc: St. Louis County, Minnesota
desc: Vermillion Dam is an 80 ft tall stairway lookout built in 1934 by the CCC.

name: Yellow River Fire Tower
loc:
Yellow River State Forest 
                    Allamakee County, Iowa
desc: Another first-time listing in the Register is the Yellow River Fire Tower in Iowa which is also the only fire lookout in the state. The 100’ Aermotor tower with 7’ x 7’ metal cab was acquired from the U.S. Forest Service in the 1950s and rebuilt in 1962 on the Yellow River State Forest by the Iowa Department of Natural Resources.  PDF

name: Rugby Tower
loc:
Prairie Village Museum 
                    Pierce County, North Dakota
desc: This 110-feet steel tower was originally one of four located at the J. Clark Salyer National Wildlife Refuge in North Dakota. In 1992, it was relocated to the Prairie Village Museum in Rugby, North Dakota at a cost of $12,000 following a successful fundraising campaign by locals.

name: Turtle Mountain Tower
loc: Rolette County, North Dakota
desc: Turtle Mountain Tower is the only fire lookout in North Dakota. The 100-foot steel tower was originally erected in the J. Clark Salyer National Wildlife Refuge, but it became surplus to needs of the U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service. Transferred to the North Dakota Forest Service in 1957, the tower was reconstructed in the Turtle Mountains to be used for fire detection. It is now primarily used as a radio relay station.

name: Battle Mountain Lookout
loc:
Battle Mountain – Friendshuh Game Production Area 
                    Fall River County, South Dakota
desc:
Battle Mountain Lookout is a 22 foot open steel tower with a small observation only cab atop. 
 The structure was built in 1965. The area is managed by the state fish and game department.

name: Bear Mountain Lookout
loc:
Black Hills National Forest 
                    Pennington County, South Dakota
desc: Bear Mountain Lookout is an all-steel tower with and L-4 cab. It is located at the third highest point in the Black Hills at 7166 feet. It is easily accessible with a gravel road leading all the way to the summit.

name: Black Elk Peak Lookout
loc:
Black Hills National Forest 
                    Pennington County, South Dakota
desc:
Black Elk Peak Lookout, formerly known as Harney Peak Lookout, is the highest point in the Black Hills (and the highest point that far east of the Rocky Mountains). The rock structure is unique in that it was designed by an architect especially for the site. 
 It was constructed by the CCC over a three-year period and was completed in 1938. Now located within a Wilderness Area, Black Elk Peak is visited by nearly 40,000 people each year. 
 The lookout was last used for fire detection in 1967, the structure and its history are being maintained by the Custer Ranger District of the Black Hills National Forest. 
 Formerly known as Harney Peak, the site was  renamed Black Elk Peak  by the U.S. Board on Geographic Names in 2016.

name: Custer Peak Lookout
loc:
Black Hills National Forest 
                    Lawrence County, South Dakota
desc: The first fire lookout atop Custer Peak on the Nemo Ranger District of the Black Hills National Forest was built of wood in 1911.  It had shutters but no glass, and it sat atop a platform without railings.  By 1935 it had been replaced with a cupola building.  The current structure is two stories high and was built of native stone in 1941.  The cab is 14- by 14-ft. with a catwalk.  The architect of the lookout was W. Ellis Groben who designed the building specifically to match its surroundings and environment.

name: Elk Mountain Lookout
loc:
Black Hills National Forest 
                    Custer County, South Dakota
desc: Located on the Wyoming-South Dakota state line, on the Black Hills National Forest, Elk Mountain Lookout remains active and reports an average of eight to twelve fires a year. The 67.5' steel tower, with 7'x7' cab, along with a 32'x22' log cabin living quarters, was constructed by the CCC in 1941.  The log cabin burned down during the Elk Mountain Fire in the late 90s.

name: Mount Coolidge Lookout
loc:
Custer State Park 
                    Custer County, South Dakota
admin: South Dakota Game, Fish, and Parks
desc: This unique stone lookout was built in 1939 by CCC workers.
agency: South Dakota Game, Fish, and P

name: Rankin Ridge Lookout
loc:
Wind Cave National Park 
                    Custer County, South Dakota
desc: Rankin Ridge Lookout is an International Derrick CL100 design.  It has a 14'x14' cab with a  surrounding catwalk.  Built in 1956 to replace the earlier Crows Nest Tower on Elk Mountain, this tower sits at the high point of Wind Cave National Park.

name: Seth Bullock Lookout
loc:
Black Hills National Forest 
                    Pennington County, South Dakota
admin: US Forest Service - Black Hills National Forest
desc:
The current CL-100 13x13 cab and 55 foot open steel tower were constructed in 1975. 
 This lookout replaced an earlier 30 foot open wood tower and L-4 cab built in 1939.

name: Summit Ridge Lookout
loc:
Black Hills National Forest 
                    Pennington County, South Dakota
desc:
A sister tower to Elk Mountain, and located nine miles due north, Summit Ridge Lookout was built in 1942, also by the CCC. The 67.5' steel tower, with 7'x7' cab also has a log cabin living quarters. Last staffed in 1972, it is now used for emergency detection only. The Elk Mountain Ranger District has restored the facility. 
 The tower has a somewhat unusual roof style that is different than what was shown on its construction plans.

name: Terry Peak Lookout
loc:
Black Hills National Forest 
                    Lawrence County, South Dakota
desc: Terry Peak was the first fire tower in the Black Hills to receive electricity, so in its earlier day was one of the most important lookouts in the area. The lookout was out of service by 1973 as a fire lookout location but the U.S. Forest Service converted the location into a viewing area for tourists. The cab has been removed but the base remains. Terry Peak being one of the more popular lookouts in the Black Hills of course received a record number of visitors. In the beginning the lookout room was put on stilts and a special room for visitors was built between it and the lookout's bachelor quarters on the first floor. The location is still popular with those visiting the Black Hills area.

name: Scott Mountain Lookout Tower
loc:
Nebraska National Forest 
                    Thomas County, Nebraska
desc:
The first tower was constructed in 1916. The present tower constructed in 1944 is the third, and it remains active today. 
 The tower's cab was destroyed in a 2022 forest fire.

name: Crescent Lake North Lookout Tower
loc:
Crescent Lake National Wildlife Refuge 
                    Garden County, Nebraska
desc:
1935:    A 60-foot steel tower was erected.  
  According to the USFWS  website  - The fire tower is one of two such structures built on the Refuge in the early 1940's by the Civilian Conservation Corps. Although the towers are no longer used for fire observation, they are serving wildlife.

name: Crescent Lake South Lookout Tower
loc:
Crescent Lake National Wildlife Refuge 
                    Garden County, Nebraska
desc:
January 31, 1937:     "At the Garden county refuge, work was started by the WPA in 1936, and 25,208 'man hours' was devoted by relief laborers in improving it.  They built a 100 foot steel lookout tower; service building and seed storage cellar."   (Nebraska State Journal) 
 According to the USFWS  website  - The fire tower is one of two such structures built on the Refuge in the early 1940's by the Civilian Conservation Corps. Although the towers are no longer used for fire observation, they are serving wildlife.

name: Valentine Nwr Lookout
loc:
Valentine National Wildlife Refuge 
                    Cherry County, Nebraska
desc: 1935:   A Type MC-39 Aermotor steel tower, 100 feet high, was erected by the CCC.

name: Valentine Nwr Lookout
loc:
Valentine National Wildlife Refuge 
                    Cherry County, Nebraska
desc:
A Type MC-39 Aermotor steel tower, 100 feet high was erected by the CCC.  
  Valentine Migratory Waterfowl Refuge was established in 1935 by an Executive Order of President Franklin Roosevelt.  Some 70,000 acres of land in the Sand Hills of Cherry County, Nebraska were purchased by the Bureau of Biological Survey “as a breeding ground for migratory birds and other wildlife.”  The Nebraska Game Preserve and Fish Commission worked cooperatively with the Bureau of Biological Survey to bring the project to fruition. (The bureau morphed into the US Fish & Wildlife Service in 1940).  
 By October 1935, Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC) workers had set up camp and started work under the direction of the Biological Survey. It was thought that they could keep CCC workers busy until 1940.  A system of canals and diversion works were planned to connect the lakes so that the Bureau could control the water level in each lake. (see historic plaque, below)  
 In August 1936, 150 men from the Works Progress Administration (WPA) were also present in the refuge, building ninety miles of fence near Hackberry Lake.  The fence would keep cattle out of the reserve and have the added benefit of delineating the area in which hunting was prohibited.    Source

name: Bald Knob Tower
loc:
Land Between the Lakes National Recreation Area 
                    Trigg County, Kentucky
desc: The Bald Knob Fire Tower was built in 1937 by the CCC as the  Wildland #2 Tower . It was originally located on a hard-to-access part of the Kentucky Woodlands National Wildlife Refuge and managed by the state forestry division. The 80' Aermotor tower with 7'x7' metal cab is now owned by the U.S. Forest Service on the Land Between The Lakes National Recreation Area,

name: Bernheim Lookout
loc:
Bernheim Arboretum and Research Forest 
                    Bullitt County, Kentucky
desc: Located on the Bernheim Arboretum & Research Forest in Bullitt County, KY, Bernheim Lookout, an 48’ Aermotor tower with 7’x7’ metal cab was constructed in 1929 by the Kentucky Division of Forestry. It was regularly staffed until 1980, and used to monitor a wildfire in 1986. Restoration and maintenance is now handled by the Bernheim Foundation with volunteers from the local community.

name: Big Knob Lookout
loc: Pulaski County, Kentucky
desc: This tower was built in the 1930s and is believed to have been previously operated by the Kentucky Division of Forestry. As of 2018, the tower is abandoned but still in generally good condition, with some broken glass and minor rust. It is located adjacent to modern communications towers owned by the American Tower Corporation.

name: Black Mountain Lookout
loc: Harlan County, Kentucky
desc: Located just inside the Virginia state line, Black Mountain Lookout sits atop the highest point in Kentucky. The cab and lowest flight of stairs have been removed, but the rest of this tower still stands.

name: Chunklick Lookout
loc: Harlan County, Kentucky
desc: As of August 2014, this tower is still standing but is in poor shape. It is heavily rusted, with most of the wooden stairs and cab floor gone.

name: Rennox Lookout
loc: Metcalfe County, Kentucky
desc: This lookout sits at the intersection of Metcalfe, Adair, and Cumberland Counties atop Dividing Ridge.

name: Hematite Fire Tower
loc:
Land Between The Lakes NRA 
                    Lyon County, Kentucky
desc:
Located on the Land Between the Lakes NRA, this 80' Aermotor LS-40 tower with a 7'x7' cab and wooden steps is also known as Curry Hollow or Wildland Tower #1. 
 The tower was built by the CCC in the 1930s in what was known as the Kentucky Woodlands Wildlife Refuge.

name: Hickory Flats Fire Tower
loc: Rowan County, Kentucky
desc: Only the fourth fire tower to be registered in the Blue Grass State, and the first project of the new Kentucky Chapter of the Forest Fire Lookout Association, Hickory Flats Fire Tower, was built by the U.S. Forest Service on the Cumberland National Forest (later renamed Daniel Boone NF). The 80’ steel Aermotor tower with 7’x7’ metal cab is the late model design with steel mesh steps and landings with full protective railings. When it went out of active service, the National Forest land was exchanged and the tower nearly forgotten. The site is now being transferred to the Hwy 377 Rural Fire District who will maintain the site with the Kentucky FFLA.

name: Gilboa Lookout
loc: Marion County, Kentucky
desc: This tower is missing portions of its cab. No history is known.

name: Pine Mountain Lookout
loc: Letcher County, Kentucky
desc: This is an Aermotor LS-60 tower.

name: Pinnacle Knob Fire Tower
loc:
Cumberland Falls State Resort Park 
                    Whitley County, Kentucky
desc: Pinnacle Knob Lookout, a USFS R-8 model 14’x14’ live-in cab on a 40’ steel tower, is the last of its kind in Kentucky. Built by the CCC in 1937 on the Cumberland Falls State Park, it overlooks a part of the Daniel Boone National Forest. Restored in 2008, it is a state park historic site.

name: Putney Lookout Tower
loc: Harlan County, Kentucky
desc: This lookout sits atop Pine Mountain in Harlan County, Kentucky.

name: Camp Robinson Lookout Tower
loc:
Robinson Forest, Univ. of Kentucky 
                    Breathitt County, Kentucky
admin: Department of Forestry, University of Kentucky
desc: The woodlands of Kentucky were once covered by a network of more than 100 state towers, now there is one that remains in active service. The 100’ Aermotor Robinson Tower was built by the CCC in 1934 replacing two wooden towers and the Tip Rock observation site within the 15,000-acre Robinson Forest. It is staffed by the Department of Forestry at the University of Kentucky which owns the forest.

name: Stearns Fire Tower
loc:
Daniel Boone National Forest 
                    McCreary County, Kentucky
desc:
The CCC constructed the Stearns Fire Tower in 1934 on the Cumberland National Forest (since renamed the Daniel Boone National Forest). The 110' Aermotor tower with 7'x7' metal cab was later owned and maintained by Nolan Johnson. 
 As of 2024, this tower has been demolished. A home now stands on the site.

name: Tater Knob Tower
loc:
Daniel Boone National Forest 
                    Bath County, Kentucky
desc: Constructed by the Forest Service in 1934, Tater Knob Tower is the last remaining federal tower on the Daniel Boone National Forest.   The U.S. Forest Service, Daniel Boone National Forest, has reported on its website: "The historic Tater Knob Fire Tower in Bath County, Ky. is closed to the public after an arson fire destroyed the structure on December 3, 2008. The fire burned all of the supporting wood frame of the lookout cab underneath its metal exterior. The tower is no longer safe for visitors. Forest Service officials are uncertain at this time if the structure will be rebuilt."

name: Argillite Lookout Tower
loc: Greenup County, Kentucky
desc:
This tower is owned by David Baldridge. His mother previously worked here as a lookout from 1966 to 1969. 
 David reports that, as of 2025, he recently made reports to the tower including replacing its flooring.

name: Bell Lookout Tower
loc:
Daniel Boone National Forest 
                    Clay County, Kentucky
admin: Forest Service, Daniel Boone National Forest (presumed)
desc:
The tower is in rough condition. A fenced building is located near the lookout tower that houses a radio antenna. This building is marked as the Bell Tower Comm site on the USDA's Forest Service Interactive Forest Visitor Map.  
  Unknown year built -  present on the 1954 USGS Beverly, KY Quadrangle (field checked in 1954).  
  QUOTE (The Commonwealth / Somerset, KY on October 15, 1941) – “The name of the Icy Cliff lookout tower of the Forest Service in Clay County was changed Sunday, October 5, to the John William Bell Tower and dedicated to the memory of the former Pulaskian who at the time of his death was district state forester.”

name: Church Creek Forestry Tower
loc: Dorchester County, Maryland
desc:
The 100’ Church Creek Forestry Tower is a 120’ Aermotor tower with 7’x7’ metal cab with a rooftop catwalk. It was constructed by the Maryland Forest Service in 1932. Located at the Church Creek Forestry station, it is used in emergencies. 
  As of 2024, the state had completed work to reduce the tower to 40-feet in height and renovate it as part of an educational display. While the tower has been renovated, it is not open for climbing.

name: Dan's Rock Lookout
loc:
Dan's Rock Overlook Park 
                    Allegany County, Maryland
desc: This is an Aermotor tower, about 70 feet, with a 7'-by-7' cab. Its steps have been removed and the floor and roof of the cab are missing.

name: Elder Hill Forestry Tower
loc: Garrett County, Maryland
desc:
This 110-feet steel tower was built in the late 1930s on a site acquired by the State of Maryland in January 1934. As of 2007, the tower hosted communications equipment for the Maryland Forest Service and Garrett County EMS. 
 While the tower site is owned by the state, the access road is privately owned. Legal access to the tower site is not possible, but the tower is visible from Maryland Route 42.

name: Green Hill Fire Tower
loc: Somerset County, Maryland
desc: This 120-foot steel tower was built by the Civilian Conservation Corps in 1935. As of 2017, the Maryland Department of Natural Resources plans to remove the tower.

name: High Rock Tower
loc: Garrett County, Maryland
desc: The High Rock Lookout on the Savage River State Forest in Maryland is 90’ steel tower with 7’x7’ metal cab. Constructed in 1934 it has been recently repainted and is used as a communications and emergency detection site.     To volunteer and schedule staffing times, contact: highrocklookout@hotmail.com.

name: Nassawango Forestry Tower
loc: Worcester County, Maryland
desc: Although it is not been active in many years, the Nassawango Forestry Tower is maintained by the Maryland Forest Service as a communications site and for emergency fire detection. The cab was removed and the stairs replaced in 1996.

name: Powellville Fire Tower
loc: Wicomico County, Maryland
desc: At 140 feet, this steel tower is the tallest in Maryland was built using US Navy funds during World War II for both fire detection and as an aircraft and watercraft warning service site. As of 2017, Maryland DNR plans to remove the tower.

name: Quantico Lookout
loc:
Chesapeake Fire Museum 
                    Wicomico County, Maryland
desc: Maryland once had 35 fire towers but only 12 remain standing today. One of the tallest was Quantico Lookout. The 140' Aermotor steel tower with 7' x 7' metal cab -- with a "widow's walk" on the roof -- was constructed near Hebron in Wicomico County in 1941 by the Maryland Forest Service. Financed by the federal government, it was used both for fire detection and as an Aircraft Warning Service (AWS) site in World War II. Last staffed in the 1970s, the fire tower was moved in 1999 to the nearby Chesapeake Fire Museum where the top 60' has been reconstructed and restored.

name: Thayerville Fire Tower
loc:
Deep Creek Lake State Park 
                    Garrett County, Maryland
admin: Maryland Department of Natural Resources - Forest Service
desc:
One of the first lookouts constructed in Maryland (1921), Thayerville Fire Tower is located on Deep Creek Lake State Park. The current 100’ steel Aermotor tower with a 7’x7’ metal cab was built in 1938. Last used for fire detection in 1993, it has been restored. A plaque honoring forest wardens and fire towers was installed October 15, 2006. 
 Thayerville Fire Tower is open on a weekly basis during the summer. Contact  Deep Creek Lake State Park  for details.

name: Welcome Forestry Tower
loc:
Welcome Forestry Tower 
                    Charles County, Maryland
desc: This tower was erected by CCC crews from the Doncaster Camp in 1934. It is 120 feet high and has various State Police and DNR antennas mounted to its surface.

name: Smyrna Fire Tower
loc: New Castle County, Delaware
desc: Smyrna Fire Tower is last of the very tall (130 ft.) towers that once dotted the mid-Atlantic states. Located along divided highway US 13 adjacent to a State Visitor Center, the tower was built by the Delaware Forest Service in 1941.  The tower was sold and moved in Aug 2004.

name: Viola Fire Tower
loc: Kent County, Delaware
desc: Also located in Delaware is the Viola Fire Tower built in 1935. Originally designed as a 100 ft. structure, modifications resulted in a total height of 123 ft. As in all Delaware towers, the roof the the cab was also utilized for observation (the hurricane deck), with access through a trap door in the ceiling.  The tower was removed between 2004 and 2006.

name: Apple Pie Hill Station Fire Tower
loc:
Tabernacle Twp. 
                    Burlington County, New Jersey
desc: Originally there was a cupola lookout on Apple Pie Hill overlooking the NJ Pinelands Reserve, built about 1912.  In 1950 the present 60’ Aermotor tower with 7’x7’ metal cab was moved from Big Hill where it first stood in 1938.  Like most NJ towers, it is painted red and white.

name: Bass River Fire Tower
loc:
Bass River State Forest 
                    Burlington County, New Jersey
desc: Bass River Fire Tower is located on the Bass River State Forest just off the Garden State Parkway in southern New Jersey. It was constructed by the CCC in 1937, reportedly in just 11 days. The 80 steel tower with 7’ x 7’ metal cab is a McClintock-Marshall style but has an Aermotor Co. nameplate. It is in active service.

name: Batsto Manor House Lookout
loc:
Batsto Village State Historic Site 
                    Burlington County, New Jersey
admin: New Jersey Division of Parks and Forestry
desc: When it comes to fancy living quarters, New Jersey’s Batsto Manor House Lookout takes the prize. When the NJ Forest Fire Service was locating lookout sites in the flammable pine barrens, the imposing mansion of the iron master at the old Batsto Iron Works caught their eye. Actually, the widow’s walk on top of the manor house had been used to look for fires during dry spells for many years and may be one of the oldest detection sites in the nation. The 9’x9' enclosed wooden cab was constructed in 1919 and used for fire detection until 1924 when the Batsto Fire Tower was constructed nearby.
agency: New Jersey Division of Parks a

name: Batsto Station Fire Tower
loc:
Wharton State Forest 
                    Burlington County, New Jersey
desc: The first lookout in this area was a rooftop observation floor on the Batsto iron makers mansion which may have been used for fire detection as early at the 1840’s.  In 1919 a 10’x10’ wooden cab was added at the lookout went into regular service (NHLR US#79, NJ# 3).  It was soon recognized that more height was needed, and the 60’ Basto Station Fire Tower went into service in 1924.  It was later raised again to a full 100’ feet and is in active service.

name: Bearfort Fire Tower
loc:
Newark Watershed (Pequannock Watershed) 
                    Passaic County, New Jersey
desc: The original lookout on Bearfort Mountain -- circa 1880 -- was a wooden platform or tree lookout. An iron frame tower was built in 1909 by the Newark, NJ Watershed Department, and replaced with a 50’ wooden tower which burned in 1932. A tree platform was used until the current 68’ steel tower was built in 1934. It is a McClintock-Marshall design and may have been supplied by Aermotor under contract. Bearfort remains an active lookout with over a century of service.

name: Belleplain Fire Tower
loc:
Belleplain State Forest 
                    Cape May County, New Jersey
desc: Constructed on the Belleplain State Forest in 1921 as a 60’ tower, Belleplain Fire Tower was soon overtaken by surrounding trees. In the 1930s, an additional 40’ section was added. The 100’ Aermotor steel tower with 7’ x 7’ metal cab is in active service.

name: Blue Anchor Station Fire Tower
loc: Camden County, New Jersey
desc: The original fire tower at Blue Anchor Station was a LS-47 Aermotor.  In 1932 it was moved to the Stokes State Forest as the Culver tower.  The current McKlintock Marshall 86’ steel tower with 7’x7’ metal cab was constructed by the CCC in 1932.

name: Budd Lake Fire Tower
loc: Morris County, New Jersey
desc:
Originally known in 1905 as the “95 Mile Tree Lookout” because of its location at Mile 95 of the old state turnpike on the west shore of New Jersey’s largest fresh water lake, Budd Lake has served as a lookout point for 92 years. 
 The current 60-foot steel Aermotor tower with 7’ x 7’ metal cab was constructed in 1924. It is the only lookout in the state equipped with an Osborne fire finder and is active. The tower was repainted in April 2023.

name: Catfish Fire Tower
loc:
Delaware Water Gap National Recreation Area 
                    Warren County, New Jersey
desc:
Located on the Appalachian Trail in the Delaware Water Gap National Recreation Area, Catfish Fire Tower was constructed in 1922, replacing a wooden tower. In 1993 the 7’ x 7’ cab was rebuilt on this 60’ Aermotor LS-40 tower. 
 The tower was repainted in May 2022, with other repairs planned, in recognition of its 100th anniversary.

name: Cedar Bridge Fire Tower
loc: Ocean County, New Jersey
desc: The original Cedar Bridge Fire Tower was built seven miles south of the present location in 1924. It was moved three more times, coming to the present site on County Route 539 in 1983. The 100’ International Derrick steel tower with 7’x7’ metal cab has an unusual wooden gable roof. This is due to the fact that the tower fell over years ago and the original roof was heavily damaged. The NJ Forest Fire Service replaced the roof themselves, with a more traditional peaked roof (we thank John Bensch for this additional information). The tower is still in active service.

name: Culvers Lookout
loc:
Stokes State Forest 
                    Sussex County, New Jersey
desc: Culvers Lookout was originally established in 1908 and the site was first known as Normanook Fire Tower.  In 1918, a steel tower was constructed and was staffed by a state observer.  The present Aermotor 47' tower, with a 7'x7' cab, was erected in 1933. The lookout is located in the Appalachian Trail corridor in Stokes State Forest.

name: Dias Creek Station Fire Tower
loc: Cape May County, New Jersey
desc: The southernmost tower in NJ is Dias Creek Station located on Cape May.  At 15’ above sea level it is the lowest elevation lookout in the state.  The 60’ Aermotor with 7’x7’ metal cab was built in 1944 and raised to 100’ in 1970.  It has recently been put back into service due to the need for prompt fire detection in this rapidly developing area.

name: Green Pond Mountain Lookout
loc:
Picatinny Arsenal 
                    Morris County, New Jersey
desc: The only fire tower in New Jersey to have a catwalk, Green Pond Mountain Lookout was built in 1942 as a sentry and fire detection site overlooking the fuse and explosive assembly area by the U.S. Army in the Picatinny Arsenal. With reduced military activity in recent years, the site has not been used and plans were underway to remove the cab and refurbish the steel tower as an antenna site. Restoration of the tower is complete, and the New Jersey Chapter of the Forest Fire Lookout Association has accepted the task of rebuilding the cab. A forest fire in April, 1994 was stopped with a backfire at the tower and it is anticipated that the structure will again be staffed during periods of high fire danger.

name: Greystone Station Fire Tower
loc:
Union Hill 
                    Morris County, New Jersey
desc: Greystone Station fire tower was built by the NJ Forest Fire Service in 1937. The top 47’ and 7’x7’ metal cab was moved from the Edison fire tower (1920s), with an extended base provided by the Aermotor Co. increasing the height of the rebuilt tower to 92’ It is the tallest fire tower in northern New Jersey and is in active service.

name: Jamesburg Station Fire Tower
loc:
Thompson Park 
                    Middlesex County, New Jersey
desc: Originally erected as the Old Bridge fire tower in 1942 under the wartime security program, this LS-42 60’ Aermotor tower may even have an as yet unconfirmed earlier life dating to 1924. In 1963 it was moved to its present location as the NJFFS Jamesburg Station fire tower and is in active service. In is one of four Aermotor cabs known to have an unusual small windowpane design.

name: Lakehurst Hangar Forest Fire Lookout
loc: Ocean County, New Jersey
desc: The Lakehurst Forest Fire Observatory is certainly historic, but is not one the public is likely to visit because it is a military classified area. A memo dated May 31, 1922 refers to a contract to have a phone installed at the fire lookout station on the Aerodrome at Lakehurst Naval Air Station. The observer would have witnessed the explosion of the Zeppelin Von Hindenburg in 1937. The lookout operated until after World War II when military security restrictions led to construction of other lookouts in the region. The 7’x7’ standard metal cab on a 6’ tower atop the roof of the 95’ hangar remains in place.

name: Lakewood Station Fire Tower
loc: Ocean County, New Jersey
desc: The Lakewood Station fire tower was built in 1944 by five employees of Jersey Central Power & Light Co. for the sum of $360! The construction of the 80’ Aermotor tower with 7’x7’ metal cab was to be done “after normal working hours” in two weeks. In 1974 this NJFFS tower was moved 300’ because of a property dispute and remains active. During World War II the tower was used to listen to German U-boat communications in the Atlantic Ocean 12 miles to the east.

name: Lebanon Station Fire Tower
loc:
Brendan Byrne State Forest 
                    Burlington County, New Jersey
desc: At 54 years, Lebanon Station fire tower is one of New Jersey’s oldest. The NJFFS 80’ Aermotor tower with 7’x7’ metal cab replaced the old Four Mile tower overlooking the fire-prone “pinelands.” In recent years a CCC era pine plantation grew to 80’ tall, restricting the view. A timely timber harvest restored the vista and supplied lumber for a variety of state projects.

name: McKeetown Fire Tower
loc: Atlantic County, New Jersey
desc: Located just west of Atlantic City, NJ, McKeetown Fire Tower was first a wooden and iron braced tower built by the coast resort water department in 1917. The state built this 80’ Aermotor tower with 7’x7’ metal cab in 1924. In 1946 a 20’ addition was clamped to the top, raising the tower to its current 100’.

name: Medford Station Fire Tower
loc:
Piper's Corner 
                    Burlington County, New Jersey
desc: Plans for the Medford Station Fire Tower were set in 1940, but construction was not accomplished until 1948 after World War II. The 100’ Aermotor tower with 7’x7’ metal cab is in active service.

name: Millville Station Fire Tower
loc: Cumberland County, New Jersey
desc: The Millville Station Fire Tower was built in 1922 replacing an earlier structure of local design.  The 60’ Aermotor tower with 7’x7’ metal cab was later raised to 100’.  Renovated under the “extended use” program, it is in active service.

name: Milton Station Fire Tower
loc:
Morris County Park 
                    Morris County, New Jersey
desc: Back in 1937 the CCC constructed the Milton Station Fire Tower under the Woodlands Protective Expansion Project.  The 80’ International Derrick tower with 7’x7’ metal cab is on Morris County park property.  A key facility, every other “A” Division NJ Forest Fire Service tower can be seen.  It has been rehabbed and a new stainless steel roof added.

name: Mizpah Station Fire Tower
loc: Atlantic County, New Jersey
desc: Originally constructed in 1924 near the old Mizpah Hotel, Mizpah Station Fire Tower was moved in 1959 one mile up the road to its present site. The original 60’ Aermotor tower with 7’x7’ metal cab was raised to 100’ at this time. Recently restored, it is the key tower of the southern region of the Pinelands.

name: Old Sentinel Tower
loc: Essex County, New Jersey
desc:
This 100-foot Blaw-Knox tower may have been built as early as 1904. It is the only one of its type remaining in New Jersey and perhaps the entire United States. It features an inside stairway and still retains a section of its original vertical rung ladder on the upper section. Its standard 6'x6' cab still contained a dial telephone in 1998 but had no fire finder.
 

 
The tower is on private watershed land and is not open to the public. This immense structure is all but hidden in the mature forest growth in this otherwise heavily industrialized and residential area. It cannot be seen until driving up under the tree canopy to within a hundred feet of the base. The old observer house now a private residence still is nearby. At one time the Watershed had it's own 1926 Chevrolet brush-truck and employee fire crew housed nearby. Foresterd Roper studied European Forestry techniques abroad and managed the watershed as an early form of sustainable forestry.
 

 
Old Sentinel Tower was never used in conjunction with the State Network.

name: Ramapo Lookout
loc:
Ramapo Mountain State Forest 
                    Passaic County, New Jersey
desc: Ramapo Lookout was previously known as the Wind-beam Lookout (1920) and has been moved twice in its history.  It has occupied its present location since 1983.  The LS-40 Aermotor, with 7'x7' cab, is located on the Ramapo Mountain State Forest just south of the New York state line.

name: Mohawk Mountain Lookout
loc:
Mohawk State Forest 
                    Litchfield County, Connecticut
desc: Mohawk Mountain was the last fire tower operated in the State of Connecticut being phased out by aircraft detection in 1988. The 7’x 7’ metal cab is unique in that it is mounted on top of a much larger microwave transmission tower. The original fire tower, sans cab, is located nearby and open to the public as an observation site.

name: Orenaug Park Fire Tower
loc:
Orenaug Park 
                    Naugatuck Valley Planning Region, Connecticut
desc: The Orenaug Park Fire Tower was built in 1911, and stands at 80 ft tall from base to roof. It was built to watch for fires in the Pomperaug Valley. The tower has not been restored, but was repainted in 2018.

name: Buck Hill Fire Tower
loc:
Town of Burrillville 
                    Providence County, Rhode Island
desc: A 65' steel tower with a unique 8'x8' cab, Buck Hill Fire Tower is the only lookout in Rhode Island with a catwalk. During World War II this tower was able to listen in on German radio broadcasts and relay their movements to Allied forces landing on Normandy beaches during the D-day invasion. This tower is one of only two still standing for fire detection within the Blackstone Valley of Rhode island.

name: Chopmist Fire Tower
loc: Providence County, Rhode Island
admin: Rhode Island Department of Environmental Management
desc: The current tower is the third one on this site. The original wooden tower was located on the southeastern corner of the lot and was replaced by a steel tower in 1946 in approximately the same location as the current tower.

name: Escoheag Hill Fire Tower
loc: Kent County, Rhode Island
admin: Rhode Island Department of Environmental Management
desc: The Escoheag Hill fire tower is an 80ft modified Aermotor tower that was first built in 1934 on an unnamed knoll in the George Washington State Forest in Burrillville. In 1937 the tower was moved and in 1938 it was reconstructed at its present location. Sometime after 2009 the non-standard wooden cab was burned by vandals. The fire destroyed most of the upper landings of the tower and damaged the upper stairs. Burn spots can be seen on the remaining wood, and charred boards litter the ground around the lookout. Presently it is not maintained, and has not been an active lookout since around 1990.

name: Mowry Fire Tower
loc:
Woonsocket Hill, Town of North Smithfield 
                    Providence County, Rhode Island
desc: Now the only lookout in northeastern Rhode Island, Mowry Fire Tower is a 65' steel tower with a Massachusetts style 10'x10' wooden cab.

name: Nooseneck Hill Fire Tower
loc:
Town of West Greenwich 
                    Kent County, Rhode Island
desc: The Nooseneck Hill Fire Tower is a 60' International Derrick tower with a 7'x7' metal cab. It was originally constructed in 1933 in the Wickaboxet State Forest.  In 1950 it was moved to the West Greenwich Fire Station.

name: Pine Hill Lookout Tower
loc: Washington County, Rhode Island
admin: Rhode Island Department of Environmental Management
desc: The original wooden tower at this site was built in 1917. It was replaced with the current 65-foot steel tower in 1946.

name: Shannock Hill Fire Tower
loc: Washington County, Rhode Island
admin: Rhode Island Department of Environmental Management
desc:
This 80-foot tower was built in 1986. It replaced a tower that had previously been on the site since 1926. 
 The cab burned in a fire on July 7, 2022. Replacement plan is unknown.

name: Tunk Hill Fire Tower
loc:
Providence City Watershed 
                    Providence County, Rhode Island
desc: Tunk Hill Fire Tower is the first listing in Rhode Island and is the first lookout to be registered that is owned by a municipality, the City of Providence.
